a08_0124454.text: Apollo 8, we'd like to dump your tape again, if you are not using it. And the reason we want to do this is we have some that we didn't completely get dumped before the burn. We would like to get that and get the rest of the burn data. There's no hurry on it. We can do it whenever it is convenient for you.

a08_0124454.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0124454.text: Okay. Thank you. Say, we're curious what you did about your Mae West? [Long pause.]

a08_0124454.speaker: Anders
a08_0124454.text: We thought we might bleed the CO 2 out into the vacuum connector here in our next water dump. We forgot it the last time. [Pause.] Did you copy?

a08_0124454.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0124454.text: Rog. Doesn't seem like there is any problem with going ahead and dumping it in the cockpit if you like. [Long pause.]

a08_0124454.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0124454.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We asked it again, and it looks like no problems at all with going ahead and bleeding it down in the cockpit. And then if you need it again on entry or after entry, why, we can blow it up with oral tube.

a08_0124500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0124500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 12 hours, 45 minutes into the flight. At the present time, Apollo 8 is just beyond 60,000 miles from the Earth - 60,536 nautical miles [112,112 km] and the spacecraft velocity is continuing to decrease gradually. At the present time, the speed is about 7,500 feet per second [2,300 m/s]. During the past 30 minutes, we recorded about five minutes of conversation with the spacecraft. We'll play that back for you now.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Apollo 8, Houston. [No answer.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Apollo 8, Houston. [No answer.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Apollo 8, Houston. [No answer.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Read you loud and clear. How us?

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Okay. Loud and clear now. Didn't get you there for a while.

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: We were reading you all along, Houston.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Rog. Did you attempt to transmit, or were you just not getting through?

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: Roger. We attempted to transmit, and it sounded like you had a stuck mike there for a little while.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Okay. That shouldn't make any difference to us on this duplex mode. [Pause.] Okay. What I was calling for, Apollo 8 - we've got a maneuver PAD that is TLI plus 25. I would like to read up to you when you're ready for it. [Long pause.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: Go ahead, Houston. TLI plus 25.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Okay. TLI plus 25, and this will be an SPS/G&N. 63087; minus 1.62, plus 1.29; 027:56:29.64; minus 0016.3, plus 0000.1, plus 5275.9; 177, 137, 001; November Alpha, plus 0020.1; 5275.9, 6:23, 5254.3; 14, 234.7, 33.7; 023, up 19.5, left 1.7; plus 11.45, minus 165.00; 1278.0, 35890, 074:38:16; north stars: 068, 097, 356; no ullage. For the fast return P37 Delta-V, 7900 to the Indian Ocean. High-speed procedures are not required. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Lovell
a08_0130211.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Maneuver PAD as follows. How do you read? Over.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Loud and clear.

a08_0130211.speaker: Lovell
a08_0130211.text: Roger. TLI plus 25; SPS/G&N; 63087; minus 1.62, plus 1.29; 027:56:29.64; minus 0016.3, plus 0000.1, plus 5275.9; 177, 137, 001; not applicable, plus 0020.1; 5275.9, 6:23, 5254.3; 14, 234.7, 33.7; 023, up 19.5, left 1.7; plus 11.45, minus 165.00; 1278.0, 35890, 074:38:16; north set; 068, 097, 356; no ullage, P37 fast return of 7 - 700 and 7900 Delta-V, Indian Ocean. High speed not required.

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: That's correct, Apollo 8. And we'll have a couple of more things for you before too long. We're working an a flyby PAD at this time. And we're going to be talking some more to you about the problems of looking at stars in the sextant and the telescope. And what we'd like to do as soon as the Black Team comes on the MOCR, while we have two teams here, we'd like to get a rehash from you on exactly what you see and what you don't see under what conditions, and see if we can define it so that everyone here understands what you've been telling us. And if you have any comments concerning the timelin

a08_0130211.speaker: Borman
a08_0130211.text: Roger. We have one request. CDR would like to get clearance to take a Seconal. [Pause.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Okay, Apollo. That's a Go. [Pause.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: Roger.

a08_0130211.speaker: Lovell
a08_0130211.text: And, Houston, this is 8. We might go over our future Nav sighting schedule if it's going to be revised at all. [Pause.]

a08_0130211.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0130211.text: Okay, Apollo 8. There are no planned revisions.

a08_0130211.speaker: Anders
a08_0130211.text: Roger.

a08_0131600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0131600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 13 hours, 16 minutes into the flight. We're in communication now with the spacecraft and we have some accumulated tapes of previous conversations during the past 30 minutes and we'll play back the tape first and then pick up with whatever conversation's going on when we finish.

a08_0132002.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0132002.text: Okay. [I] have your flyby PAD now so I can give that to you whenever you're ready for it. [Pause.]

a08_0132002.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0132002.text: Okay, Apollo 8. Here we go on a flyby maneuver PAD. This will be an SPS/G&N; 63087; minus 1.62, plus 1.29; 060:59:48.04; plus 0096.2, plus 0056.8, minus 0207.7; 000, 000, 000; November Alpha, plus 0020.2; 0235.9, 0:22, 0228.2; 03, 039.9, 31.4; 013, up 04.8, right 3.7; plus 14.18, minus 165.00; 1290.4, 36160, 146:29:11; north stars; 323, 090, 056; no ullage. Remarks: number one, this requires realignment to preferred REFSMMAT . Two, this will raise the perilune to 550 nautical miles. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0132002.speaker: Anders
a08_0132002.text: Flyby; SPS/G&N; 63087; minus 1.62, plus 1.29; 060:59:48.04; plus 0096.2, plus 0056.8, minus 0207.7; 000, 000, 000; N/A. Are you with me so far?

a08_0132002.speaker: Anders
a08_0132002.text: Plus 0020.2; 0235.9, 0:22, 0228.2; 03, 039.9, 31.4; 013, up 04.8, right 3.7; plus 14.18, minus 165.00; 1290.4, 36160, 146:29:11; north; 323, 090, 056; no ullage. Realign for preferred REFSMMAT , and perigee is 50.

a08_0132713.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0132713.text: Okay. We've completed the dump and the tape recorder is yours, and we listened to the call data voice playback, and you've been given a Go for your first test in creative writing.

a08_0132713.speaker: Anders
a08_0132713.text: Roger. Are we in low bit rate now?

a08_0132713.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0132713.text: That's negative. You're in high bit, and you understand that it's your tape recorder?

a08_0132713.speaker: Anders
a08_0132713.text: Rog. Are you going to stay in high bit [rate] all along, or are you going to be back to low [bit rate] here soon, [pause.] not that it matters much to us, really.

a08_0132713.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0132713.text: Okay. We plan to stay in high bit rate. We're going to ask you if it made any difference, and you read our minds. That's pretty good for 63K [i.e. 63,000 nautical miles].

a08_0132713.speaker: Anders
a08_0132713.text: Rog. That's an altitude record for mind reading.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Roger. Onboard calculations indicate that at 13 hours and 30 minutes GET, we are now 64,200 [nautical] miles above the Earth. [Pause.] That's using Aldrin's slide rule.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: We've got 63,855 [118,259 km]. [Long pause.]

a08_0133059.speaker: Anders
a08_0133059.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. We're going to try to keep the conversation down here for a while so the CDR can go to sleep.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay. We would like to get some comments from you before you sign off concerning the telescope and sextant; and a verification that you have done something with the CO 2 in your Mae West and comment on the window status.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Roger. Is it a requirement that we do something with the CO 2 at this time? Over.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: No. That's negative.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Roger. We have maintained the same condition. We have left it as it was, and will take care of it later.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Let me at this time go over the comments about the navigation as I see it so far.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Go.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: In the beginning, the operation with the S-IVB precluded immediate starting up of our sightings as we had scheduled since we had another evasive maneuver. The dumping of [propellant from] the S-IVB caused a tremendous amount of - of pseudo-stars in the area which made an optics calibration practically impossible. The method which we had worked out did not seem to work too well. The method which I finally used was to go into P23 , go to Sirius, which was our brightest star, get the shaft and trunnion, and then fly the spacecraft up to Sirius to use that for the optics cal, which we did at a lat

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay. Fine; thank you very much.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: We are going to do - Houston - future maneuvers for P23 in a lower - in a slower mode of auto maneuver. Essentially, we're going to load the DAP with 11101 to save fuel.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Roger. That will be a 11101 DAP load.

a08_0133059.speaker: Lovell
a08_0133059.text: Rog. We are going to try to save fuel that way.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Good show. [Pause.]

a08_0133059.speaker: Anders
a08_0133059.text: With respect to the windows, Houston, the windows 1 and 5 have moderate haze on them. Satisfactory for visual observation, but possibly not for photography. Windows 2 and 4 are clear. Window 3 is almost opaque. Over.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay. Thank you.

a08_0133059.speaker: Anders
a08_0133059.text: And how's battery B looking to you? [Long pause.]

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Apollo 8, Houston. It looks like it may take another 6 hours on this battery B charge. It turns out that the charge rate is less than what we're getting on the ground curves, but it is still above the Apollo 7 curves, and it looks like it is going along now in good shape. And I would like to have verification that the timeline leading up to the midcourse correction was satisfactory from your point of view.

a08_0133059.speaker: Anders
a08_0133059.text: Roger. Seemed quite satisfactory.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay. Thank you. And we'll stay off the loop until you give us a call.

a08_0133059.speaker: Anders
a08_0133059.text: Roger. You don't bother us, but our replies make a lot of noise.

a08_0133059.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0133059.text: Okay.

a08_0134400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0134400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. During that rather lengthy series of conversations with the spacecraft, we heard Commander Frank Borman request permission from the ground to take a Seconal tablet. That is a short acting sleeping pill. Frank was scheduled to begin his sleep period at about 11 hours GET or about 12 hours - or rather of about 2 hours, 45 minutes ago. We also, during that pass, heard a number of sequences of numbers passed up to the spacecraft. This is part of the block data updates that are routinely sent up at specified periods in the Flight Plan, so that the crew always has onboard dat

a08_0134400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0134400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 14 hours, 14 minutes, 28 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Here in Mission Control Center we've just had a change of shift briefing. The Black Team is now aboard. The Black Team with Flight Director Glynn Lunney now relieving Milton Windler and his Maroon crew. At the present time Mr. Lunney is going around the room talking to his flight controllers who have been briefed for the past 40 plus minutes by the earlier team, talking over the situation which is very nominal at the present time. We've had no conversation with the crew whatsoever since the last

a08_0134400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0134400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 14 hours, 36 minutes, 07 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. We're continuing in our quiet mode with the crew. There has been no conversation since our last report - no conversation. Things are settled and quietly paced in the Mission Control Center at the present time. Glynn Lunney discussing various aspects of the mission that have - has preceded this shift with his various flight controllers. One thing that has been truly remarkable has been the communications thus far in the mission. Our prime acquisition site at the present is a wing site at Honeysuckle

a08_0144300.speaker: Anders
a08_0144300.text: Houston. Apollo 8. How do you read? [Pause.]

a08_0144300.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144300.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're very weak. You got the proper Omni? [Long pause.]

a08_0144300.speaker: Anders
a08_0144300.text: Houston. Apollo. How do you read?

a08_0144300.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144300.text: Loud and clear, Bill. Go ahead.

a08_0144300.speaker: Anders
a08_0144300.text: Okay. I'm just wondering how your tracking's doing. [Pause.]

a08_0144300.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144300.text: Okay. We're still tracking you. We don't have any firm solutions, yet.

a08_0144300.speaker: Anders
a08_0144300.text: Okay. Things [are] looking nominal up here. How about down there?

a08_0144300.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144300.text: Okay. The systems basically look good, Bill. We're going to be coming up on a cryo fan cycle period in another few minutes, and you can go ahead and do that when you get ready.

a08_0144300.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144300.text: And I guess we picked up some suspicions about the fuel cell 2 radiator out tab. How does that compare on board?

a08_0144756.speaker: Anders
a08_0144756.text: Roger. We're showing Rad[iator] Out Temp on fuel cell 2 to be about 90 degrees, and on 1 and 3 to be slightly lower - maybe 75, 80 degrees. About an hour ago, plotted out fuel cells performance; it looks like 1 and 2 are lower performance than 3. Over.

a08_0144756.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144756.text: Rog. We're showing the same numbers on your outlet temperatures and it appears to us that that's a sensor failure. We've been watching the thing and we'll keep you advised of anything we see.

a08_0144756.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144756.text: And on the performance, you're right - they are not quite the same, 1 and 2 are a little bit lower but all these are sitting within the ballpark.

a08_0144756.speaker: Anders
a08_0144756.text: Roger. Fuel cell 1 has shown slightly a proportionately higher H 2 flow than O 2 flow all day long.

a08_0144756.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144756.text: Rog. We'll take some cal[ibration] curves on those. [Long pause.]

a08_0144756.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144756.text: Okay. These things look reasonable to us and we'll keep looking at them. Our readout shows about 0.43 as opposed to your 0.48 on the oxygen, and we'll keep an eye on the cal curves and just sort of watch it for you.

a08_0144756.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0144756.text: If you'd like to set up some kind of a comm check or specified time like every 30 minutes or so on these quiet periods, that would be okay with us. Might help to let us know that we're still in business.

a08_0144756.speaker: Anders
a08_0144756.text: Alright. Just give me a call every now and then.

a08_0150330.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0150330.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Sometime when it's convenient, get your biomed switch over to the right, and you don't need to answer; just pass it up to you.

a08_0160027.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0160027.text: Apollo 8, Houston. How about a comm check, and did you get that fuel cell purge - correction, the cryo fans, On?

a08_0160027.speaker: Anders
a08_0160027.text: Roger. We had the cryo fans, On, each for about 3 or 4 minutes.

a08_0160027.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0160027.text: Okay. Real good. We weren't real sure that's what we were watching, and you're coming through loud and clear.

a08_0160100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0160100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 16 hours, 1 minute, 4 seconds into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time, 73,818.6 nautical miles [136,711.8 km] in altitude; our current velocity reading, 6,659.5 feet per second [2,029.8 m/s]. Bill Anders and Jim Lovell should be finishing up on an eat period very shortly here, while spacecraft Commander Frank Borman, still in his sleep period, has about 2 hours to go. About 30 minutes from this time, where the Apollo 8 crew is scheduled for a guidance and navigation platform alignment, that coming at approximately 16 hours, 30 minutes in

a08_0161406.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0161406.text: Okay, Jim. Got an update here to the Flight Plan. You've got the 16:55 star visibility check, and what we've got on that, [it] looks like Navi is still our star, and the numbers associated with that are roll, 102.6; pitch, 328.9; yaw, 346.3. That gives you a shaft and trunnion of zero. And if you think you can - if you think you can do something with this, why, we'd like to go ahead and give it a try and see if we can either verify it or maybe we'll both learn something if we verify it if you can't do it with Navi.

a08_0161952.speaker: Lovell
a08_0161952.text: Roger. We'll maneuver at this present time and try to pick up that attitude and get Navi, although I think it's a waste of time, but we will give it a try.

a08_0162000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_0162000-pao.text: Roger. We'll maneuver at this present time and try to pick up that attitude and get Navi, although I think it's a waste of time, but we will give it a try.

a08_0162000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0162000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 16 hours, 20 minutes, 25 seconds now into the flight of Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft, at this time, 75,034.9 nautical miles [138,964.4 km] in altitude. Velocity reading on our display is 6,588.7 feet per second [2,008.2 m/s]. We've had a brief contact with Jim Lovell aboard the Apollo 8 spacecraft. This we'll pass along to you now.

a08_0162000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0162000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 16 hours, 22 minutes. That concluded our conversation with Jim Lovell and the Apollo 8 spacecraft. From the ground, by the way, that was Ken Mattingly, our Capsule Communicator. They have just exchanged head sets only moments ago. The discussion dealt with the star visibility sightings that are due to take place in Ground Elapsed Time of 16 hours, 55 minutes. Some 30 minutes from this time. So at 16 hours, 23 minutes, 8 seconds into the flight of Apollo 8, continuing on its precise course, very nominal, very good; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0163810.speaker: Lovell
a08_0163810.text: Roger. We're at that attitude right now. I'm looking through the scanning telescope. I can barely see any stars at all, and every time that the thruster will fire, you know, just completely blanks out my vision.

a08_0163810.speaker: Lovell
a08_0163810.text: Now the attitude is good, Houston, as far as not having glare in the optics, and it might be a certain amount of dark adaptation is required here. [Pause.]

a08_0164800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0164800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 16 hours, 48 minutes, 32 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time: 76,800 nautical miles [142,200 km] in altitude; our velocity now down to 6,489.6 feet per second [1,978.0 m/s]. We've had a brief conversation with the Apollo 8 spa - crew, and we'll play that for you now.

a08_0164800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0164800-pao.text: That was Command Module Pilot Jim Lovell who had - was describing results of his star visibility exercise. At 16 hours, 50 minutes into the flight, still looking good; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0170857.speaker: Comm Tech (Goddard)
a08_0170857.text: Houston, Goddard Voice. Negative Quindar keys.

a08_0171333.speaker: Carr
a08_0171333.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. I've got a new PTC attitude for you when you finish P23 . Give you a better look at the Earth. Over.

a08_0171333.speaker: Comm Tech (Honeysuckle)
a08_0171333.text: Houston Comm Tech, Honeysung - Honeysuckle. Negative Quindar keying.

a08_0171333.speaker: Carr
a08_0171333.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_0171333.speaker: Lovell
a08_0171333.text: Roger. We're taking our time going to this new P23 attitude; going to Navi is quite a ways away from the attitude we need for P23. I have a correction to make on 20 - on Navi, after getting dark adapted; you can pick out Cassiopeia and you can pick out Navi itself. It's difficult to see what stars are around. We still have quite a bit of particles that are floating with the spacecraft, especially when we move the optics and shaft. It seems to throw off a lot of particles.

a08_0171333.speaker: Carr
a08_0171333.text: Roger. We copy that. What's your spacecraft lighting situation inside now?

a08_0171333.speaker: Lovell
a08_0171333.text: We have the center window - the round window covered, and we have - the other windows are open.

a08_0171900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0171900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 17 hours, 19 minutes, 58 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 now at an altitude of 78,339.1 nautical miles [145,083.7 km]. 78,339.1 nautical miles away from the Earth. Its velocity at this time, 6,383 feet per second [1,946 m/s]. We've had a conversation with Jim Lovell aboard the spacecraft and we'll play that now. Jerry Carr as you heard passed along new Passive Thermal Control attitudes. Passive Thermal Control, this the barbecue mode, slow roll that the spacecraft undergoes to give even Sun distribution to the skin of the spacecraft. Also, you h

a08_0172415.speaker: Carr
a08_0172415.text: Apollo 8, Houston. While you're maneuvering for your P23, we have an update for Delta-H for you if you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a08_0172415.speaker: Lovell
a08_0172415.text: Roger, Houston. You say you have a Delta-H update for us? Just what do you mean?

a08_0172415.speaker: Carr
a08_0172415.text: This is as a result of your P23 calibration; the update follows: Verb 24, Noun 01, Enter 1354, Enter, all balls, Enter, 21450, Enter; comments: continue to mark on the horizon definition that you've used previously. Your marks are looking very good.

a08_0172415.speaker: Lovell
a08_0172415.text: Roger. Delta-H update as follows: Verb 24, Noun 01, Enter, 1354, Enter, all zeros, Enter, 21450, Enter. Understand those are two octal numbers.

a08_0172415.speaker: Lovell
a08_0172415.text: Roger. When do we get the maneuvers here? I'll go out of [P]23, and I'll put these in; then I'll continue.

a08_0172415.speaker: Carr
a08_0172415.text: Apollo 8, Houston. There's no requirement for you to leave P23; you can enter those right now if you want to.

a08_0173600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0173600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 17 hours, 36 minutes, 45 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft now at an altitude of 79,761 nautical miles [147,717 km]; velocity at the present time, 6,329 feet per second [1,929 m/s]. We've just had another conversation with Jim Lovell and we'll pass that along now.

a08_0173600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0173600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. That concluded the conversation. We did observe on our displays that Jim Lovell did punch in his Delta-Horizon update and at last report was proceeding with his program 23 cislunar navigation. Incidentally our current weight of the spacecraft in flight now reads 63,045 pounds [28,597 kg]. At 17 hours, 39 minutes, 50 seconds into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: Houston, are we in low bit rate now?

a08_0174925.speaker: Carr
a08_0174925.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're in high bit rate.

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: Roger. We'd like to record you this P23 stuff.

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: How about commanding low bit rate, Record, Forward.

a08_0174925.speaker: Carr
a08_0174925.text: Roger. Low bit rate, Record, Forward. [Long pause.]

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: Alright, Houston. Have you sent those commands yet?

a08_0174925.speaker: Carr
a08_0174925.text: Apollo 8, Houston. They have been sent.

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: Alright, Roger. Thank you. I'm on the other side, too lazy to go over and get it.

a08_0174925.speaker: Carr
a08_0174925.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'd like to go back to high bit rate in order to get this P23 data recorded. Over. [Long pause.]

a08_0174925.speaker: Anders
a08_0174925.text: Our checklist says low bit rate, Houston. If you want high, you can have it.

a08_0174925.speaker: Carr
a08_0174925.text: Roger. We're going high bit rate.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: How's that, sports fans? All balls.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: As soon as you've got an audience, you do great.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_0175325-onboard.text: How many markings for this set is that?

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: There's three stars and three marks per set.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: That's three for that second - that's the same star, second set, third set of marks. And then you've got...

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Do I have six marks, total?

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: You got six marks, total. You need three more on this same star, right?

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Yeah, okay. There's the third one, there.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: It only went down 17. Wait a minute.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Okay, what is it, 22, star - what's the code after it?

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Which way are you going to be going? Far horizon?

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Yeah, it'll be at the same horizon.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Yeah, 03. It won't be a far move, though. 21 plus 22, Enter; proceed; that should be a zero.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Let's... No, why don't you Proceed? Let's see where it's going to take it.

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Okay, we're - Pitch 123, yaw 305 - Oh, we're getting right under it [probably means the gimbal-lock region].

a08_0175325-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0175325-onboard.text: Okay, CMC and Auto [settings required before an automaneuver].

a08_0180300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0180300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 18 hours, 3 minutes, 5 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 at the present time, 81,340 nautical miles [150,642 km] in altitude. Current velocity reading via our displays, 6,247.4 feet per second [1,904.2 m/s]. We've had a brief conversation with Jim Lovell which we'll play now.

a08_0180300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0180300-pao.text: We have a correction - that gentlemen onboard the spacecraft was not Jim Lovell. That was in fact Bill Anders, the Lunar Module Pilot. We're at the time in the Flight Plan now when Frank Borman should be awakened shortly. However, this will probably turn out to be a crew option. At the present time, Jim Lovell is still performing certain aspects of his cislunar navigation program. That's program 23. So at 18 hours, 5 minutes, 2 seconds into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0180915.speaker: Carr
a08_0180915.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Do you want us to turn off your DSE for you? It's probably about half full. We're getting good high bit rate down.

a08_0180915.speaker: Borman
a08_0180915.text: Do you want to get the rest of this data?

a08_0180915.speaker: Carr
a08_0180915.text: We're getting good high bit rate down.

a08_0180915.speaker: Carr
a08_0180915.text: Okay. And, also, we're - your state vector is now based on about 5 hours of tracking . We have you on a pericynthion of 69.7 miles with a free return. Your entry flight path angle looks like about minus 14. You will need only a few feet per second to get you back on a nominal entry angle. [Long pause.]

a08_0180915.speaker: Carr
a08_0180915.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Did you get the words on the state vector? [Long pause.]

a08_0180915.speaker: Borman
a08_0180915.text: Houston, did you read? Apollo 8. We got a lot of noise.

a08_0180915.speaker: Borman
a08_0180915.text: Roger; we lost you when you started talking about the....

a08_0180915.speaker: Carr
a08_0180915.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston reading you fairly weak. I'll repeat the state vector information. Your state vector is now based on 5 hours of - more than 5 hours of tracking. We show you on a pericynthion of 69.7 [nautical] miles with a free return with an entry path flight angle of minus 14 degrees. Will only need a few feet per second at the lunar distance to get you back on a nominal entry angle. Over.

a08_0182215.speaker: Carr
a08_0182215.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Go. Reading you weak, but clear.

a08_0182215.speaker: Borman
a08_0182215.text: Roger. Our sighting schedule is complete, and I'm maneuvering to PTC attitude.

a08_0182500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0182500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 18 hours, 25 minutes, 45 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. We've had additional conversations with the Apollo 8 crew, and we'll pass those along now.

a08_0182500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0182500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. We've had no definite indication yet from the crew as to change of shift on their sleep/wake cycle. However we suspect that at this point in time Command Module Pilot Jim Lovell and Lunar Module Pilot Bill Anders are just about ready for their sleep period. They were awakened at the Cape this morning at 2:36 Eastern Standard Time. It's been a long day. It's been a day that so far has carried them to an altitude of 82,867 nautical miles [153,469 km]. Our velocity reading at this time; 6,169.7 feet per second [1,880.5 m/s]. At 18 hours, 29 minutes, 5 seconds into the flig

a08_0184203.speaker: Borman
a08_0184203.text: Roger. I'm at the PTC maneuver now. I'd like a systems status from you; how do the batteries looks and how the fuel cells look and et cetera . Over.

a08_0184203.speaker: Carr
a08_0184203.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We figure battery B will be charged in about 2 to 3 hours. All your systems look Go; your RCS usage so far is about 60 pounds [27 kg], six-zero pounds over nominal. Over.

a08_0184203.speaker: Anders
a08_0184203.text: Roger. How about fuel cell 2; is that looking all right now?

a08_0184203.speaker: Carr
a08_0184203.text: Roger. Fuel cells are all looking good.

a08_0184203.speaker: Anders
a08_0184203.text: Okay. We're going to have two of us hit the hay now and one man minding the store so you might have everybody keep an extra sharp eye on [garble].

a08_0184203.speaker: Carr
a08_0184203.text: Roger, Bill. You think you'll going to be able to sleep okay?

a08_0184203.speaker: Anders
a08_0184203.text: Yeah. I think we kinda warmed up to a good sleep here by now.

a08_0184203.speaker: Lovell
a08_0184203.text: Onboard navigation indicates a pericynthion altitude of 38.4 [nautical] miles [71.1 km].

a08_0184203.speaker: Lovell
a08_0184203.text: That's affirmative. It's on the DSKY right now, if you're reading it out.

a08_0184737.speaker: Carr
a08_0184737.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Be advised your downlink now is getting very noisy.

a08_0184952.speaker: Carr
a08_0184952.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston with some comments on navigation.

a08_0184952.speaker: Carr
a08_0184952.text: Good morning, Frank. Apollo 8, this is Houston. We're wondering about your GDC backup align; we'd like your opinion on the possibility of doing this align using Sirius and Rigel rather than Navi, as it's in the north set at this time. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0184952.speaker: Lovell
a08_0184952.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. We concur. Sirius and Rigel would be two stars that would be much better than Navi and Polaris. However, I did Cassiopeia after I became [dark-]adapted, but I'm afraid that the time required to do that type of alignment would be extensive if we ever had to go to that alignment.

a08_0184952.speaker: Carr
a08_0184952.text: Roger, Jim. We understand. We'll go ahead and work in that direction, and we'll quit bothering you. Good night.

a08_0184952.speaker: Carr
a08_0184952.text: Apollo 8, Houston. At 19 [hours] GET, we're due for another cycle through on the cryo fans. Over.

a08_0184952.speaker: Carr
a08_0184952.text: Roger. Give us a call when you're complete.

a08_0185300-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0185300-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. At 19 [hours] GET, we're due for another cycle through on the cryo fans. Over.

a08_0185300-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0185300-pao.text: Roger. Give us a call when you're complete.

a08_0185300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0185300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 18 hours, 53 minutes now into the flight. During the past several minutes we've had conversations with the Apollo 8 crew. They have just shifted their sleep wake cycle. And we'll pass on those conversations at this time.

a08_0185300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0185300-pao.text: This is Apollo - This is Apollo Control; we've just played out the conversation and it turned out this was one of those rare occasions, at least this time of the morning, over a brief span of time where conversation took place with all three crew members. No doubt Jim Lovell and Bill Anders are in the early phases of their sleep period. At the present time, Apollo 8; 84,593.7 nautical miles [156,667.2 km] in altitude. Our velocity reading 60 - ah correction 6,084, that's 6,484 feet per second [first number is correct, 1,854 m/s] and decelerating. At 18 hours, 58 minutes, 30 seconds into the fl

a08_0190233.speaker: Borman
a08_0190233.text: Why don't you give me a call when it is time to quit charging the battery, will you? I can't watch it very well over there.

a08_0190233.speaker: Borman
a08_0190233.text: And I'm starting with the fans now.

a08_0191123.speaker: Borman
a08_0191123.text: Okay, Houston. We cycled through the fans, 2 minutes each, and we'll stand by for the call for battery charges.

a08_0191123.speaker: Carr
a08_0191123.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The battery charge will be complete around 21 hours.

a08_0191123.speaker: Borman
a08_0191123.text: Okay. Just give me a call.

a08_0191600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0191600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 19 hours, 16 minutes, 50 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 at the present time, 85,685 nautical miles [158,688 km] above the Earth. Current velocity reading; 6,030 feet per second [1,838 m/s]. We have a short strip of conversation with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman which we'll play for you now.

a08_0191600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0191600-pao.text: That's it! We expect - spacecraft Commander Borman is presently having breakfast. We should be hearing from him again before too awfully long with a report - a crew status report. At 19 hours, 18 minutes, 34 seconds into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0193038.speaker: Carr
a08_0193038.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Go ahead. [No answer.]

a08_0193038.speaker: Borman
a08_0193038.text: Roger, Houston. Crew status report here. We're behind on water - behind on water and food, and we don't seem to have too much of an appetite. We're trying to stay up with the water, but the food is - not that there's anything wrong with the food, but we're just not very hungry.

a08_0193038.speaker: Borman
a08_0193038.text: The CDR got 5 hours of fitful sleep and rest, and the other two people are trying to sleep now.

a08_0193700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0193700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 19 hours, 41 minutes, 40 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. We now read an altitude on Apollo 8 of 87,109.9 nautical miles [161,327.2 km]. Our current velocity on spacecraft Apollo 8; 5,962.8 feet per second [1,817.5 m/s]. Spacecraft Commander Frank Borman has delivered a short status report - crew status report to capsule communicator Jerry Carr and we'll pass that along now.

a08_0193700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0193700-pao.text: That's the end of the conversation. Commander Borman indicated he received or took advantage of about 5 hours of sleep and his fellow crew members are trying to sleep now. And you can readily appreciate an absence of appetite since these are the first three gentlemen to have been 87,201 nautical miles [161,495 km] above the Earth. At 19 hours, 43 minutes, 30 seconds; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0193700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0193700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 20 hours, 10 minutes, 18 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 now 88,735.6 nautical miles [164,338] in altitude. Its current velocity, 5,886.8 feet per second [1,794.3 m/s]. We had no conversation with Apollo 8 since our last announcement but this is understandable. To quickly recap our status. Commander - spacecraft Commander Frank Borman is currently awake. The other two crew members, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders, are in their sleep period. There are no scheduled events for the Flight Plan with the ground at least for a period of time. And at 20 hour

a08_0193700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0193700-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 20 hours, 41 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft now 90,465 nautical miles [167,541 km] in altitude. Our current velocity, 5,807.8 feet per second [1,770.2 m/s]. We've had no conversation since our last announcement with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman. We've had no requirement for a conversation so we have not bothered him. At 20 hours, 41 minutes, 45 seconds into the flight, all systems continue to look Go. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0205746.speaker: Carr
a08_0205746.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston at 21 hours. We'd like you to terminate the battery B charge and start battery A charge and then begin an O 2 purge. Over.

a08_0205746.speaker: Borman
a08_0205746.text: Roger. Understand; terminate battery B, start battery A, and an O 2 purge.

a08_0210047.speaker: Borman
a08_0210047.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We're now charging battery A, and say again about the purge. [Pause.]

a08_0210047.speaker: Carr
a08_0210047.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Roger. Copy your battery charge setup; now begin a fuel cell O 2 purge. Over.

a08_0210100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0210100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 21 hours, 1 minute now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 now at 91,576 nautical miles [169,598 km] in altitude; now a velocity of 5,758.1 feet per second [1,755.1 m/s]. We've had a brief contact with the crew or with Commander Frank Borman I should say, and passed on some procedural information- let's pick up that conversation.

a08_0210100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0210100-pao.text: That was a conversation between capsule communicator Jerry Carr and spacecraft Commander Frank Borman. Otherwise very quiet here in Mission Control Center at 21 hours, 2 minutes, 48 seconds into this, the Apollo 8 mission. This is Apollo Control, Houston."

a08_0210100-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0210100-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Roger. Copy your battery charge setup; now begin a fuel cell O 2 purge. Over.

a08_0210909.speaker: Borman
a08_0210909.text: Houston, the fuel cells are all purged. [Pause.]

a08_0210909.speaker: Borman
a08_0210909.text: How's the tracking coming, Jerry? [Long pause.]

a08_0210909.speaker: Carr
a08_0210909.text: It's looking good, Frank. We just took in another batch of data, and we're processing it. It looks initially like we won't even need a midcourse number 2. As soon as we process this data, we will have some confirmation for you. It should take anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes to finish the job.

a08_0211345.speaker: Carr
a08_0211345.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We're showing your pericynthion 64 nautical miles. Your next mid-course at 28 [hours] will be less than 1 foot per second. We'll have a firm confirmation on this in about 2 hours.

a08_0211900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0211900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 21 hours, 19 minutes, 39 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at the present time, 92,600 nautical miles [171,500 km] in altitude. Our velocity display shows 5,712.9 feet per second. Speed of 57.9 - 5,712.9 feet per second [1,741.3 m/s]. CapCom Jerry Carr has described to spacecraft Commander Frank Borman what his trajectory - what the Apollo 8 trajectory looks like. We'll pass along that conversation.

a08_0211900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0211900-pao.text: As you heard, the present track appears quite good. The point of closest approach to the Moon predicted [to be] 64 nautical miles [118.5 km]. And this consideration of the midcourse correction, the midcourse correction, if one were made for MCC-2, at least at this point in time appears to be one of less than a foot per second. Therefore, it appears unlikely that we'll do a second midcourse, but the Flight Dynamics Officer here in Mission Control will continue to look over the data for a couple more hours before we make such a decision. At 21 hours, 22 minutes, 18 seconds into the flight, Apoll

a08_0211900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0211900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 21 hours, 51 minutes, 44 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 now showing a velocity of 5,637.5 feet per second [1,718.3 m/s]. Its current altitude; 94,351 nautical miles [174,738 km]. Members of the Green Team of flight controllers are now being briefed in the Mission Operations Control Room by their Black Team counterparts. We're due for a change of shift here shortly. There will be no change of shift news briefing with the Black Team. We repeat, there will be no change of shift news briefing with the Black Team. And during this - the past 30 minut

a08_0224124.speaker: Borman
a08_0224124.text: Houston. How do you read, Apollo 8?

a08_0224124.speaker: Collins
a08_0224124.text: Reading you loud and clear, Frank. Good morning. How are you doing?

a08_0224124.speaker: Borman
a08_0224124.text: Hi Michael. We just broke lock for a minute, and I wondered why.

a08_0224124.speaker: Collins
a08_0224124.text: Roger. Your break lock is due to the fact we switched our antennas over from Honeysuckle to Madrid. Over.

a08_0225000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0225000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 22 hours, 50 minutes, 48 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time 97,513 nautical miles [180,594 km] in altitude. Its present velocity reads 5,504.2 feet per second [1,677.7 m/s]. We have, a short while ago, broke our communications silence with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman. He called down and asked a question [about a communications break], let's play that for you.

a08_0225000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0225000-pao.text: That crisp and chipper voice from the ground was Mike Collins who has taken over the Capsule Communicator's role here in Mission Control Center. Meanwhile at 22 hours, 52 minutes, 28 seconds into the flight, Apollo 8, we're looking good and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0225000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0225000-pao.text: Apollo Control here at 23 hours, 10 minutes into the flight. And on behalf of the Green Team, good morning. We've had a shift change in the Control Center. And our Capsule Communicator Mike Collins is about to engage Frank Borman in a conversation in which he will cover, among other things, the fact that based on the track of the last 12 hours, we see only a need for another midcourse of on the order of 0.7 feet per second, which is too small, within our ground rules, to bother with. And that is the position we will take. Don't really expect the crew would have a different view. All the other

a08_0231148.speaker: Collins
a08_0231148.text: Roger, Frank. We'd like to bring you up to date on your trajectory. This midcourse coming up at 28 hours GET turns out to be very small, 0.7 feet per second, and we would like not to do it. Our data is looking extremely good and extrapolating it forward, it shows that the midcourse number 4 at LOI minus 8 hours would be about 4 feet per second. In the meantime, the free return trajectory is looking very good with a water splash point off the coast of Africa. So it looks like you're right down the old center line, and we propose not to do the next midcourse. Over.

a08_0231148.speaker: Collins
a08_0231148.text: Okay. And in regard to your timeline here, we suggest that you let Bill and Jim sleep for an extra period of time and don't wake them up until 26:30 GET, and that would cause deletion of P52 and P23 at 26 hours GET. Over.

a08_0231148.speaker: Borman
a08_0231148.text: Roger. Understand. Delete the P52 and P23.

a08_0231148.speaker: Collins
a08_0231148.text: Affirmative. Delete those at 26 hours, wake the other two guys up at 26:30 at which time they can eat, and then chlorinate the water supply after they have eaten.

a08_0231148.speaker: Collins
a08_0231148.text: This would put us back on our nominal Flight Plan at 28 hours GET. Over.

a08_0231700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0231700-pao.text: Apollo Control here. That apparently wraps up the conversation for this opening shift period this morning. We're - one other item of interest. We're rapidly nearing the 100,000-[nautical] mile point presently. 98,891 [183,146 km]. And we'll certainly note the passage of the 100,000-mile mark - the big yellow line extending on our Earth/Moon map. System [sic] is now roughly half way to its target, a small little white dot off in the far right, which is out at the 210,000-mile mark for our mapping purposes. And all in all, that's our status at 23 hours, 17 minutes into the flight.

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: Roger, we're switching antennas again at 23:40 GET. You can expect a momentary break lock, and also we'd like to bring you up to date on the Passive Thermal Control. We expect to keep the same PTC [Passive Thermal Control] attitude until 28 hours GET. Over.

a08_0233839.speaker: Borman
a08_0233839.text: Fine; thank you. How is the thermal control working?

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: Working good, Frank. I can give you some details if you want them.

a08_0233839.speaker: Borman
a08_0233839.text: I am all ears, Houston. Go ahead with the details.

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: Okay. Stand by one until we switch our antennas, Frank. We'll be right with you.

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: On your PTC, [the temperatures of] quads A, C, and D seem to be just about identical. Quad B is running slightly cooler, but only very slightly so. The temperature read-outs in all respects are normal, so apparently the PTC is working well from a thermal viewpoint. And as far as the fuel consumption goes, it's minimal, just about like we expected. Have you got any comments about PTC? How does it seem to you?

a08_0233839.speaker: Borman
a08_0233839.text: Seems fine. Seems to be working all right, just like you said. I was just wondering how the readouts on the SPS were, too. [Long pause.]

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The SPS temperature is normal. If anything, it's slightly warmer than we expected, so you're in real good shape in that respect.

a08_0233839.speaker: Collins
a08_0233839.text: Frank, the PU valve temperature is running about 72 degrees [Fahrenheit, 22°C], which is better control than we got here in this room.

a08_0234721.speaker: Collins
a08_0234721.text: Roger. It is time to do a cryo fan cycle, Frank, on all four fans; a short burst from each of them as you did before.

a08_0234721.speaker: Borman
a08_0234721.text: Understand. 2 minutes each on all cryo fans.

a08_0234800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0234800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 23 hours, 48 minutes into the flight. Mike Collins has been chatting with Frank Borman about this and that for the past few minutes. Here's how that conversation is going.

a08_0234800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0234800-pao.text: Apparently Borman - Lovell and Anders are sleeping quite soundly. We could almost detect that Frank Borman is keeping his voice in a low measured tone to avoid rousing them. We have suggested that their sleep period be extended as much as an hour - hour and a half. They were up nearly 24 hours, in fact, probably every bit of 24 hours due to the fact that they were roused about 2:30 yesterday morning Cape time and they went to sleep, oh, about 6 hours ago. It sort of made for a long day and apparently had no trouble sacking out. We have passed the 100,000 [nautical] mile mark. We are now 100,73

a08_0235512.speaker: Borman
a08_0235512.text: Cryo fans, Off, and cycled, Houston. [Pause.]

a08_0235512.speaker: Borman
a08_0235512.text: I said the cryo fans are Off, and completed the cycle.

a08_0242418.speaker: Collins
a08_0242418.text: Rog. Just a comm check, Frank. Do you read me alright?

a08_0243700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0243700-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston; 24 hours, 37 minutes into the flight. We've had one establishing call since we last talked to you 20 minutes ago and it was nothing more than an establishing call. We're 103,000 [nautical] miles [191,000 km] from Earth at this point. And let's cycle through some of our consumables and other items this morning and we'll just look at them on our monitor and tell you what we see. The first chart we come to - and this is - this is data, this is live data coming to us via Madrid. The biomedical harness is, well, a moment ago it was on Frank Borman but apparently

a08_0244255.speaker: Borman
a08_0244255.text: How've you been reading our tape dumps?

a08_0244255.speaker: Collins
a08_0244255.text: Stand by one, Frank. We noticed that you've got your PTC attitude tweaked up a bit, and I'll check on your tape dump. [Long pause.]

a08_0244255.speaker: Collins
a08_0244255.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The quality of the tape dumps has been very good. We have about 15 minutes to dump, which we'll do the next time we get High Gain. Over.

a08_0244255.speaker: Borman
a08_0244255.text: Okay. We'll send you something down here shortly.

a08_0244715.speaker: Collins
a08_0244715.text: Frank, on this tape recorder, we have the tape motion stopped right now. If you would like to record some, we'll give you a - the tape in motion so that you may do so. Is that what you would like? Over.

a08_0244715.speaker: Borman
a08_0244715.text: Roger. Houston, why don't you just give us salvo so we can control the switches here.

a08_0244715.speaker: Collins
a08_0244715.text: You should have it now. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Are you capable of taking a high-bit FM dump for voice on the Omnis?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: That's negative, Bill. Not quite, on the Omnis.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Okay. We'll catch you next time around then.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Thank you.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Morning, Mike. How are things going down there?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Hi, Jim. Things are going real fine. How're you going up there? Did you get a good night's sleep?

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Oh, you know. The first night in space all the time; it's a little slow.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: The old man woke you up earlier than he needed to.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Well, we just couldn't sleep any longer.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Rog. Understand. [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The next time you're locked up on the High Gain, give us a call, and we're configuring for a dump. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. We would like an evaluation of the voice comments. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Understand. So far, it's been very good. We will evaluate this one as soon as we can. [Long pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: How are the systems looking down there, Houston?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Go ahead.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. I've been in the sack. How do the systems look?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Everything's looking real good, Bill.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Okay. How much longer do you expect on charging battery A? [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Stand by, Bill. We will get you an exact number on it.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Just a rough estimate. And also, have you seen any more hints of that sensor problem on fuel cell 2? [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Stand by one. I'll get the latest scoop on it for you, Bill. [Long pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Bill, there's nothing new on fuel cell number 2. We don't think there's anything at all wrong with the fuel cell. It's some sort of a sensor problem, but we don't have any new information on it.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Okay. They all look pretty good from here, Mike.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Rog. Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: I've got some updates for you whenever you are ready to copy.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Stand by.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: What kind?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Well, I've got a TLI plus 35-hour update, and then I have an update to Jim's checklist. [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Let's have the TLI plus 30 before we get the checklist update.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: They never give up on the checklist, do they?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. This - when you get your maneuver PAD book out, the last maneuver PAD we gave you for the flyby PAD still remains valid. We'd just like to remark that the entry angle, the Gamma, is slightly steeper than we consider ideal, but it's within our - sort of the noise level of our ability to predict at this time. So that flyby maneuver PAD remains valid. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Roger, Houston.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. Now on that page with the flyby maneuver, under your north set of stars, I have some new numbers for you because we've changed those stars from Navi and Polaris. As you recall, we changed to Sirius and Rigel, so - And that also, by the way, is the checklist update which I'll give you later - but on that maneuver PAD, I have got three new angles for you using Sirius and Rigel when you're ready to copy those. [Long pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, Houston. How do you read? Over. [No answer.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over. [Long pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Houston. Apollo 8. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger, Apollo 8. Houston. You're loud and clear now. We had a lot of background noise there for a few minutes. How're you reading me?

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. I'm reading you okay, Mike, and I read you the last time you asked me that, so I guess maybe I wasn't getting through to you.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. Well, did you copy on this flyby maneuver PAD? We've got three new angles. Are you ready to copy those?

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: I'm ready to copy the flyby angles.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. Roll, 137; pitch, 310; yaw, 340. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Roll, 137; pitch, 310; yaw, 340.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: That's affirmative, and I have the TLI plus 35-hour PAD when you are ready for it.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Ready for the TLI plus 35.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. TLI plus 35 hours: SPS/G&N; 63023; minus 1.62, plus 1.29. Are you with me so far?

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Loud and clear.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Loud and clear.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Good. 12, 138.3, 32.7; 023, up 17.2, left 2.2; plus 12.93, minus 165.00; 1290.5, 36180, 074:11:16. Comments: on your stars, Sirius and Rigel; roll, 010; pitch, 294; yaw, 320; no ullage. Other: one, fast return P37, Delta-V equals 7821, for mid-Pacific landing for MTL; two, high speed procedures not required. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Alright. Are you ready for the readback?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: All set.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Yeah, I'm with you, Bill. That last one should be 001.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Y, 001; N/A, plus 0020.2; 4642.0, 5:47, 4621.1; 12, 138.3, 32.7; 023, up 17.2, left 2.2; plus 12.93, minus 165.00; plus 1290.5, plus 36180, 074:11:16. Sirius, Rigel; 010, 294, 320; no ullage, fast return P37, 7821 mid-PAC; high speed not required. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: That's about the size of it. You're getting pretty good at this thing, Bill, for a rookie.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Not bad. I just learned to read about a year ago.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Hey, I've got a Flight Plan update for Jim. It's on page G, George, 82 Able of his checklist. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Roger. I've got it open. Go ahead, Mike.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. It's simply changing these north set of stars around. For Navi substitute Sirius, which is number 15, and for Rigel - correction - for Polaris substitute Rigel, number 12.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Substituting Rigel for Polaris and Sirius for Navi. How about shaft and trunnion; remain the same?

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Your shaft and trunnion [angle]s remain the same. Sirius remains on the 50° line just like Navi used to be. Rigel is down 1.3° from your horizontal, from your M-line. Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Understand.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. And let me know when it gets to be breakfast time. I've got a newspaper to read up to you and a few other things.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: We're ready.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. I've got a [Paul] Haney special here for you. The Interstellar Times latest edition says the flight to the Moon is occupying prime space on both paper and television; It's THE news story. The headlines of the Post says "Moon, here they come." We understand that Bill Anders will be in private conversation or communication today with an old man who wears a red suit and lives at the North Pole. A suspect in the Miami kidnapping was captured late yesterday, and the 11 GI's that have been detained 5 months in Cambodia were released yesterday and will make it home in time for Christmas.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Roger. With reference to the first, we saw him earlier this morning, and he was heading your way.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. We'll pass the word along. David Eisenhower and Julie Nixon were married yesterday in New York. He was described as "nervous".

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Right.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: The Browns took Dallas apart yesterday 31 to 20. We're sort of curious, who do you like today, Baltimore or Minnesota? Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Baltimore.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: How many points are you giving?

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: [Laughter] He's not making many points at home with that comment.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Rog. Understand. Oh, I've got another - another score for you when you're ready to copy. Are you ready to copy?

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Stand by. [Long pause.] Go ahead.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Roger. Navy 14, Army 21. Would you like for me to repeat that? Over.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: You are very garbled; Houston; I'm unable to read. Will call you back in another year.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Okay. We also notice the University of Houston lost their first home basketball game in 3½ years last night. Illinois edged them out 97 to 84. And some really big news: the State Department announced only a few minutes ago that the Pueblo crew will be released at 9 pm tonight.

a08_0245352.speaker: Lovell
a08_0245352.text: Sounds good. Outboard calculations indicate that Apollo 8, at 25 hours, is 104,000 [nautical] miles from home.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Yeah. Our plot board shows a similar number.

a08_0245352.speaker: Borman
a08_0245352.text: Mighty nice view from here.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: We're showing about 104,800 [nautical] miles [194,100 km], and we're guessing another 8 to 10 hours on your battery charge.

a08_0245352.speaker: Anders
a08_0245352.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Frank, say again about the view. You were blocked, I think.

a08_0245352.speaker: Borman
a08_0245352.text: It's a mighty nice view we have down there today. A little bit more than a half-Earth. Looks like Africa and the Red Sea is visible; we're not quite sure as there is quite a bit of cloud cover; but even through the hazy windows, it's mighty nice.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: How are your windows? Do you have a couple left that are real clear?

a08_0245352.speaker: Borman
a08_0245352.text: The rendezvous windows are good. The others are all about the same as they were when we last reported. One and five have a slight haze and a little fog on the inside.

a08_0245352.speaker: Collins
a08_0245352.text: Rog. Understand.

a08_0245900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0245900-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston at 24 hours and 59 minutes into the mission. Within the last few minutes, we've heard from Jim Lovell and Bill Anders. Jim Lovell sounds the sleepiest of the group and over a 104,000 miles of intervening space, here's the conversation as it has progressed.

a08_0251600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0251600-pao.text: And at 25 hours, 16 minutes into the flight - whoops, here goes some more. We'll cut back.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_0251655.speaker: Lovell
a08_0251655.text: [Garble.]

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Roger. Just as a matter of curiosity for Bill, we can say a few words about the heaters for the cryo tanks, and also for the fans. We've noticed that the heaters are doing their thing normally, cycling on and off; and as time goes by, the - this cycle rate increases, indicating a little bit of stratification in the tanks. And then when we've been turning the fans on every 4 hours for a couple of minutes, this stirs things up and the heaters then cycle on and off again more slowly for a while, until again a little bit of stratification occurs, and the cycling becomes slightly more rapid. This i

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: Rog. I haven't really been following it that close. One thing I have noticed is when you turn the fans on you get a glitch in the quantity, which might correspond to a glitch in AC. Maybe the next time we'll look at the AC volts and see what happens. [Pause.]

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Our experts say that's not the reason for the glitch. They say the stratification fakes out the capacitance sensor there for a second.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: I knew they would have some big deal answer for me.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: First gotcha today.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: I'll buy that. Rog.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Any other information you want us to send up to you?

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: No, we're going to zap you with the High Gain here shortly.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. How do you read on the High Gain?

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Reading you loud and clear, Bill. How me?

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: I'm reading you loud and clear. I'll go ahead and dump this. You might want to listen to it in real time to evaluate the voice.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Okay. We'll do that as soon as we can.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: Give me a call when you're ready.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Do you want to dump it by your command, or would you like us to command the dump, On? Over.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: Oh, you can go ahead and command whenever you're ready.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Okay. We are starting now; thank you.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: I've already rewound.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Roger.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: Rog. I've already rewound. [Long pause.]

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: There's only about 5 minutes worth on the tape, Houston.

a08_0251655.speaker: Collins
a08_0251655.text: Rog. Understand, Bill. [Pause.] You promised me you'd wait 3 days before you started doing this, Bill.

a08_0251655.speaker: Anders
a08_0251655.text: It's been a long trip.

a08_0251800-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0251800-pao.text: Our experts say that's not the reason for the glitch. They say the stratification fakes out the capacitance sensor there for a second.

a08_0251800-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_0251800-pao.text: I knew they would have some big deal answer for me.

a08_0252648.speaker: Collins
a08_0252648.text: Roger, Bill. We've got your dump, and the voice quality is very good. We're going to take about 20 minutes or so to get it back to Houston to play it.

a08_0252648.speaker: Anders
a08_0252648.text: Roger. [Pause.] Where are you taking it through, Houston?

a08_0252648.speaker: Collins
a08_0252648.text: It comes through Madrid and then Ascension, Bill.

a08_0254056.speaker: Collins
a08_0254056.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_0254056.speaker: Anders
a08_0254056.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0254056.speaker: Collins
a08_0254056.text: Roger, Bill. We're reading you loud and clear now. We had an antenna problem down here. We had an unexpected switch of antennas, which probably caused your High Gain to quit.

a08_0254056.speaker: Collins
a08_0254056.text: Roger, Jim. When we lost our antenna down here, we interrupted your tape dump, so we are in the process of doing some rewinding and continuing the dump, in case Bill is wondering what's going on with the tape recorder.

a08_0254100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0254100-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control Houston at 25 hours, 41 minutes into the flight. Our velocity is down to 5,162 feet per second [1,573 m/s]. We're 106,270 [nautical] miles [196,812 km] from home. And here's some conversation recorded in the last 20-minute time block.

a08_0255653.speaker: Collins
a08_0255653.text: Roger. At 26 hours GET, we'll be switching our antennas back again at Madrid, and you can expect a glitch on your comm system.

a08_0255653.speaker: Lovell
a08_0255653.text: I noticed that you skipped the IMU alignment for about 26 hours because we were still asleep. Do you want to include that again, or do you think it is required?

a08_0255653.speaker: Collins
a08_0255653.text: Roger, Jim. We think it's going to be required prior to the next set of P23 sightings, and we're suggesting that it be put in at 27:45. We'll have a Flight Plan - a more complete Flight Plan update in here shortly.

a08_0255653.speaker: Lovell
a08_0255653.text: Okay. Fine. We're in the process of having breakfast.

a08_0260406.speaker: Collins
a08_0260406.text: The tape dumps are complete; it's rewound. You can go ahead and record in low bit rate if you so desire.

a08_0264122.speaker: Collins
a08_0264122.text: Disregard. We were going to talk about the High Gain, but you beat us to it.

a08_0264122.speaker: Collins
a08_0264122.text: Rog, Jim. We would like to take control of the tape for a few minutes to make sure that we got all that last dump. Over.

a08_0264122.speaker: Anders
a08_0264122.text: Roger. I just noticed that I can hear those RTC's [Real Time Commands] coming through on normal voice. [Long pause.]

a08_0264122.speaker: Collins
a08_0264122.text: What does it sound like, Bill?

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Roger. I have a Flight Plan update for you sometime at your convenience.

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Were you calling? Over.

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Okay, Bill. This will be on page 2-22 of your Flight Plan. [Pause.] And for the Command Module Pilot - I've already mentioned it to him - but at the top of the page, at about 27:45, actually, we would like him to do a P52, an IMU alignment, and then the P23 should be done as scheduled. Those four stars, Procyon, Regulus, Alphard, and Spica: we realize Alphard may not be too good a star, Regulus is about 3° above the horizon, and Spica is at a 48° trunnion angle; so I guess what we are saying is if Jim has difficulty doing one set on each of those four stars, we suggest that he omit whichever o

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Alright. In the lower right hand corner of page 2-22, the Passive Thermal Control attitude should read "pitch, 224°; yaw, 020°."

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: And on the next page, at about 29 hours, you can resume the normal Flight Plan. We would like to make one addition; at 29:30, add a waste water dump. Even though one is not really required at that time, we would like to get the dump out of the way so we can track you uninterruptedly without any dumping, you know, as we are coming up on midcourse correction number 3. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: That's about all, Bill. You got any questions on this?

a08_0264634.speaker: Anders
a08_0264634.text: No. It looks pretty good. We've been saving up some water of our own to dump here, so that will work out all right.

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Very good. And don't ruin Jim's optics.

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Roger. We'd like P00 and Accept, please. We'd like to send you up a P27. It's a LM state vector, going to the LM slot only, and we do not want you to transfer it over to the CSM. [Long pause.]

a08_0264634.speaker: Collins
a08_0264634.text: Okay. We got it. We're sending you a LM state vector, and we would like you not to transfer that vector over to the CSM slot.

a08_0265100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0265100-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston at 26 hours, 51 minutes into the flight. We're a hundred - I'll have to estimate, based on the wall map, 112,000 [nautical] miles [207,400 km] out. And we've had this brief conversation in the last few minutes.

a08_0265536.speaker: Anders
a08_0265536.text: Apollo 8. Roger. Are you still planning an MCC-2 at 28 hours? Over.

a08_0265536.speaker: Collins
a08_0265536.text: Stand by one, Bill. [Pause.] Bill, negative. No, that midcourse correction number 2 has been cancelled. It's magnitude was less than 1 foot per second, so we decided not to do it. Over.

a08_0265536.speaker: Collins
a08_0265536.text: And you've got the computer again, if you go to Block.

a08_0265700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0265700-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control again, 109,900 - well let's make it 110,000 even - [nautical] miles [203,700 km] out. Our velocity; 5,028 feet per second [1,533 m/s]. Our spacecraft weight now is down to 63,000 pounds, 63,023 pounds [28,587 kilograms]. I think in the course of that conversation, you heard that we see no further need for any more midcourse corrections between now and their journey to the Moon. At 26 hours, 57 minutes; that's our status.

a08_0265829.speaker: Lovell
a08_0265829.text: Are you still computing the pericynthion time of 69:10?

a08_0265829.speaker: Collins
a08_0265829.text: Stand by. We will get an update for you.

a08_0265829.speaker: Collins
a08_0265829.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Your 69:10 pericynthion is still good plus or minus a minute, and we'll get it down to a fine map measurement [garble].

a08_0272608.speaker: Collins
a08_0272608.text: Okay, Bill. We just got your read-out on your voice tape, and we will be back with you shortly on it. Over.

a08_0272608.speaker: Lovell
a08_0272608.text: Houston, I'm going to be doing my alignment at this time. I'm in a good position for viewing the stars. [Pause.]

a08_0281813.speaker: Collins
a08_0281813.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston with a voice check. Over.

a08_0281813.speaker: Lovell
a08_0281813.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Reading you loud and clear now. How us?

a08_0281813.speaker: Collins
a08_0281813.text: Oh, good. Reading you loud and clear. One, two, three, four, five, five, four, three, two, one. Am I cutting in and out still? Over.

a08_0281813.speaker: Lovell
a08_0281813.text: Nope. All the numbers are coming up nicely.

a08_0281813.speaker: Collins
a08_0281813.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're going to switch antennas at 28:20. Stand by for a blitz.

a08_0281813.speaker: Borman
a08_0281813.text: Roger, Houston. And we have stopped Passive Thermal Control and we're maneuvering to P23.

a08_0281813.speaker: Collins
a08_0281813.text: Roger. Understand; maneuvering to P23; I understand.

a08_0282331.speaker: Anders
a08_0282331.text: Roger. You copying high bit rate now for this P23?

a08_0282331.speaker: Collins
a08_0282331.text: Negative, Bill. We're getting low bit rate now.

a08_0282331.speaker: Anders
a08_0282331.text: If you go high bit rate, we won't bother recording it.

a08_0282331.speaker: Collins
a08_0282331.text: Roger. We just went to high bit rate.

a08_0282900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0282900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 28 hours, 29 minutes into the flight. I want to clear up a velocity reading. Apparently I gave a reading earlier which either was in error, or I read it wrong. Our present feet per second is 4,875 [1,486 m/s]. I say again 4, 8, 7, 5; and our altitude is 114,000 nautical miles [211,000 km]. Within the last hour in a private conversation we've learned that there is some - a little nausea aboard. Frank Borman reported an upset stomach, but Chuck Berry tells me it's getting better. That's all we know about it right now. Here's some taped conversation just recorded.

a08_0282900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0282900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control again. I say again on the nausea, Frank Borman reported an upset stomach. He has taken some medication, and he is apparently feeling better, he so reported to Dr. Berry. And Bill Anders reported he wasn't feeling his best. We don't know whether it is some sort of virus or just what, but I'm sure Chuck Berry will have more for us at the change-of-shift briefing today. I say again the situation was reported to us within the last hour in a private voice tape down, that Frank Borman was reporting some stomach upset and not feeling particularly well. From strictly a layman's

a08_0282900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0282900-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston; at 28 hours, 55 minutes into the flight. Apparently our earlier report regarding velocity is still causing a great deal of consternation in the Press room, so we will go through it one more time. Through error either on our part or on the part of a chart, we apparently reported a discrepancy in the velocity. We want to correct that error. The present velocity we read on our Space Digitals Chart is 4,833.3 feet per second [1,473.2 m/s], and it is getting smaller as is proper. It will continue to get smaller until the spacecraft reaches the lunar sphere of in

a08_0290339.speaker: Lovell
a08_0290339.text: Roger. Cislunar Nav accomplished. We did two sets on star 16 [Procyon], two sets on 22 [Regulus], and one set on 21 [Alphard].

a08_0290339.speaker: Collins
a08_0290339.text: Roger. Understand P23 completed, two sets on 16, two on 22, and one on 21.

a08_0290339.speaker: Lovell
a08_0290339.text: Roger. It was getting a little late, so we didn't want to start on 26 [Spica].

a08_0290718.speaker: Anders
a08_0290718.text: Is our previous PTC attitude okay for the next session?

a08_0290718.speaker: Collins
a08_0290718.text: Roger, Bill. The one that we updated an hour or so ago, i.e., pitch, 224; yaw, 020, is a good one.

a08_0290718.speaker: Collins
a08_0290718.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'll be changing antennas in about 2 minutes. You can expect a glitch in your comm.

a08_0290718.speaker: Anders
a08_0290718.text: How are all of the systems looking down there, Houston? [Long pause.]

a08_0290718.speaker: Collins
a08_0290718.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're looking good here in all respects.

a08_0291752.speaker: Collins
a08_0291752.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_0291752.speaker: Collins
a08_0291752.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_0291800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
