We are reading the spacecraft loud and clear. No problem with communications across the 132,000 some odd miles between the spacecraft and Earth. The problem appears to be between Houston and Hawaii. Hawaii has b

a08_0353700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0353700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 35 hours, 37 minutes. We have reestablished our communications from the ground up to the spacecraft directly from Houston, and a preliminary assessment of the problem is that it originated at the Goddard Space Flight Center where all of our communication lines are routed through en route to Houston. Apparently we blew a fuse at Goddard and our communications circuit between Goddard and Hawaii was down. We were able to receive the spacecraft communications loud and clear here in Houston, and we were able to relay information through the station at Hawaii throu

a08_0354826.speaker: Borman
a08_0354826.text: Okay. The CMP is now up. We'll proceed with the 52 option and start on the - the cislunar navigation.

a08_0354826.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0354826.text: Okay. Thank you, and we'll start looking for some star data.

a08_0355358.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0355358.text: Okay. When you pick up your activities, I have a preferred alignment here that I want you to be in when you do your P52. And I'll have about four items to change on your timelines, so if you give me a call when you're ready for it.

a08_0355358.speaker: Borman
a08_0355358.text: We're ready right now. We were doing the P52. You want us to hold off and go to a particular alignment, is that right?

a08_0355358.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0355358.text: Okay. The attitude is pitch, 23.4; roll, 184.7; yaw, 14.3. And the reason we're doing the alignment in this attitude is, the next thing we'll be coming up with is the scanning telescope visibility test and that will be 70 degrees, Sun from Arcturus, with a shaft and trunnion of zero. And then we can go ahead with the P52 and then a trunnion bias followed by P23 with the same stars that we read to you before.

a08_0360032.speaker: Borman
a08_0360032.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We're maneuvering to the angles you - the angles you gave us.

a08_0360400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0360400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. We don't appear to have any more communication developing between the ground and the spacecraft at this time. During that previous conversation, part of the information that was passed up to the crew from the ground were routine updates to the backup information that is carried onboard the spacecraft to allow the crew to return to Earth at various points in the flight should it become necessary, and should at that point not be able to get updated information from the ground. This includes returns at 25 hours after, rather 35 hours after Translunar Injection, another poi

a08_0360945.speaker: Borman
a08_0360945.text: Houston, we've reached the preferred attitude, and we're proceeding with the P52.

a08_0360945.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0360945.text: Okay. Real fine, and I'll pass up some advice from your friendly Flight Surgeon. He says you're supposed to take one more Lomotil. [Pause.]

a08_0361320.speaker: Borman
a08_0361320.text: Houston, the P52 is completed. We're ready for your other data.

a08_0361320.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0361320.text: Okay. Understand that you've done the P52. The next item on the Flight Plan should be a scanning telescope visibility test, and this is the same one that was on your Flight Plan previously at 34 hours and about 12 minutes, and we'll be checking that 70 degree Sun on Arcturus. Following that, we need to make a trunnion bias check, and then we'll go into a P23, and I can read you those star numbers and sets if you don't have them from the last time I read them up.

a08_0361320.speaker: Lovell
a08_0361320.text: Roger. With such good visibility - or such good communications, let me just give you a verbal description without seeing the scanning telescope right now. Your angles for maneuver to Arcturus were quite good. I've got Arcturus centered in the scanning telescope. At this Sun angle, there is a shaft of light directly across the center of the scanning telescope and - yeah, band of light. It precludes seeing a lot of - a lot of stars around us, and although I kept my eye glued to the telescope now for some time, it's very difficult to see any star patterns or anything. I couldn't recognize that wi

a08_0361320.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0361320.text: Okay. I copy that. Can you tell us something about the orientation of this band? You mentioned that last night also - that you also had a band about 10 degrees wide that ran across. Is there an orientation that we can tie that to?

a08_0361320.speaker: Lovell
a08_0361320.text: I believe so, Ken. This band is parallel to the M-line [a horizontal line in the reticle], and I think it has something to do with the design of the optics, where we have that shaft or the rectangular entrance of the optics from the outside. At this particular Sun angle, it cuts right across. Now I noticed that both the Earth and the Sun do this to the scanning telescope. In the sextant, the same light band is there, although it covers the entire sextant's field of view. However, the magnification brings out the stars quite well, and it's possible to mark on them. But it's the identification o

a08_0361320.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0361320.text: Okay. Thank you very much. [Long pause.]

a08_0361320.speaker: Borman
a08_0361320.text: Ken, what stars did you want to use [for the navigation exercise]? Do you want to read them off?

a08_0361320.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0361320.text: Okay. First star will be 26 [Spica, Alpha Virginis], and we'll be making two sets of measurements, Earth near-horizon using star 26. Then we would like to have one set - we'd like to have one set on star 16 [Procyon, Alpha Canis Minoris], that's 16, using the Earth far-horizon. If it turns out that star 26, Earth near-horizon is not possible, then we'd like to have star 16 on the Earth far-horizon for one set, and star 22 [Alpha Leonis], Earth far-horizon, one set. Over.

a08_0361320.speaker: Borman
a08_0361320.text: You want star 26, Earth near-horizon, two sets; star 16, Earth far-horizon, one set; and star 22, Earth far-horizon, one set.

a08_0361320.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0361320.text: Okay. The star 22 is only in the event that 26 on the Earth's near horizon is not possible? Over.

a08_0361320.speaker: Borman
a08_0361320.text: We won't even do star 22 then unless we can't get 26 on the near horizon.

a08_0361320.speaker: Anders
a08_0361320.text: Comm sure is good all of a sudden, isn't it?

a08_0362300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0362300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 36 hours, 23 minutes into the flight. Apollo 8, at this time, is at a distance from the Earth of 134 - rather 135,042 nautical miles [250,097 km], and our current velocity is 4,236 feet per second [1,291 m/s]. Jim Lovell, who had been asleep for what appears to have been about 2 hours, is now up and we've heard from him aboard the spacecraft. At the present time, Lovell is involved in some midcourse navigation using the onboard Guidance and Navigation system. We have some of his comments made during the past few minutes in conversation with the ground on tape

a08_0362300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0362300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. It appears we'll have no further communications with the crew for the moment anyway. Shortly we would expect that Frank Borman would attempt to get a few hours rest. He indicated earlier that as soon as either Lovell or Anders awoke that he would attempt to get several hours of sleep. At the present time, Apollo 8 is at an altitude of 135,442 nautical miles [250,838 km] and our velocity is 4,225 feet per second [1,288 m/s]. This is Apollo Control at 36 hours, 33 minutes into the flight.

a08_0365052.speaker: Borman
a08_0365052.text: Okay, we've completed two sets on 26 and one set on 16.

a08_0365052.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365052.text: Rog. You're getting pretty speedy there.

a08_0365052.speaker: Borman
a08_0365052.text: Yeah, Jim - Jim is getting to know the optics.

a08_0365052.speaker: Lovell
a08_0365052.text: Are you receiving the data, Houston?

a08_0365052.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365052.text: Okay, Apollo 8. They looked at the data and it looks good and they feel like you can go back to PTC attitude anytime you're ready to. And if you can [interruption from spacecraft] - go ahead.

a08_0365052.speaker: Borman
a08_0365052.text: What attitude do you want to use? The same one?

a08_0365052.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365052.text: Okay, if you can reach over Bill there and get to panel 3, I believe we'd like to cycle the oxygen fans. And also like to get the Biomed switch over to CMP.

a08_0365052.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365052.text: If you have to bother Bill to do that, why, we can hold off on the cryo fans.

a08_0365052.speaker: Borman
a08_0365052.text: No, he moved. We already chased him under the seat. Okay, now you want just the oxygen fans on?

a08_0365052.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365052.text: That's affirm. One of it - turn one on for about 2 minutes and when we turn it off, then we will turn the next one on. We don't want to turn them on simultaneously though.

a08_0365052.speaker: Borman
a08_0365052.text: Yeah, I know that. I mean you don't want hydrogen though?

a08_0365052.speaker: Lovell
a08_0365052.text: Ken, just to recap a little explanation here on your maneuver PAD, something which I'm really not knowledgeable about, the way it was presented to us, you mentioned fast return P37 Delta-V of 8750, just briefly clarify that, will you please?

a08_0365500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0365500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 36 hours, 55 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. At the present time, we're in communication with the spacecraft. Jim Lovell is the only one of the three crewmen who is awake at the present time. Our indication at this time are that both Frank Borman and Bill Anders are resting. And here in Mission Control Center as well as onboard the spacecraft, activities have slowed down somewhat and it has become quite quiet here. At the present time, Lovell has just finished a series of star sightings for onboard navigation. And we're in the process of passing up some PAD data

a08_0365743.speaker: Borman
a08_0365743.text: Ken, can you give us a little report on how our trajectory looks and the tracking's going and things like that?

a08_0365743.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365743.text: Okay, sure will. I'll put a summary together here.

a08_0365743.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0365743.text: Rog, we'll get all that together for you in just a few minutes.

a08_0365743.speaker: Borman
a08_0365743.text: And we never did get the news.

a08_0365743.speaker: Borman
a08_0365743.text: Come off it, come off it. [Long pause.]

a08_0365743.speaker: Borman
a08_0365743.text: Okay, the fans have been cycled 2 minutes each and they're back off.

a08_0370607.speaker: Borman
a08_0370607.text: Houston, Apollo 8 is back in the PTC attitude, reads the MHPTC.

a08_0370607.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0370607.text: Okay, thank you. And in reference to your question about the P37 Delta-V, 8750, that's the number that goes into the option at P37 for your minimum-time return. That gives you a target for the Indian Ocean. And in this case, we're going to have to use the high-speed procedures that were worked out for you to use the minus number for the major axis.

a08_0370607.speaker: Lovell
a08_0370607.text: Roger. Understand. I'm going to give that a try, Ken, in a run through. I tried it yesterday, I wasn't getting too much in the way of results. I'll give it a try today.

a08_0370607.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0370607.text: Okay. And on the - your tracking that we have now, it still looks like the time we gave you last night for a time of pericynthion is still good, 69 plus 10 and right now your flyby pericynthion altitude - 65.8 [nautical miles, 121.9 km]. Looks like the midcourse number 3 is going to be something less than 1 foot-per-second. And all trajectory parameters are just holding real fine.

a08_0370607.speaker: Borman
a08_0370607.text: That's the things we'd like to hear. We'd like to keep those holding very fine.

a08_0371400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0371400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. There appears to be no further conversation with the crew at this time, so we'll take the circuit down for the time being. At the present, the mission appears to be going very well. Right on the Flight Plan, in most cases, and our crewmen reported earlier that they were feeling much better. A short while ago, the medics advised Frank Borman to take one additional Lomotil tablet. This is a pill to reduce bowel activity. We've heard no word from the crewmen of any physical problems they're having and the feeling here on the ground is that their condition is improving. We'

a08_0372100.speaker: Borman
a08_0372100.text: Roger. We're getting near - we're going to need to dump some urine overboard here. I wonder if that's going to foul your trajectory up. Or can we go ahead and do it?

a08_0372100.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0372100.text: No, that's okay. Something that's kind of interesting though is that last time you had your water dump, they noticed a change in the trajectory tracking at the same time and when they got through correlating it, they found some fellow that thought he knew the characteristics of a nozzle and how much water you're dumping and his estimates of the effect on the trajectory seemed to coincide with the tracked results. So I guess you have to stay honest on those things.

a08_0372100.speaker: Borman
a08_0372100.text: Rog. Okay, we'll go ahead and dump some, [garble].

a08_0372329.speaker: Lovell
a08_0372329.text: You planning on using our computer any time in the near future, I thought I'd do a little P37.

a08_0372329.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0372329.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You can go ahead and run that 37 and we're going to kind of watch that from the ground, too, and see how it works out. A couple of items that are just of general interest in the trajectory world. Looks like the uncertainty in position is about 12 miles. Your uncertainty in velocity is about a quarter of a foot per second. And the perigee [means pericynthion] altitude uncertainty is 5 miles.

a08_0372329.speaker: Lovell
a08_0372329.text: Rog. Understand. Just for information, perhaps you read it out on the ground. I ran our pericynthion altitude determination using first of all, P21 with our state vector that we navigated with, we have plus 84.7-[nautical] mile altitude. Then we ran out your state vector that you updated with us the last time. We got 64.2 and then I ran P30, using our state vector and got 82.6 nautical miles. These are all plus.

a08_0372329.speaker: Lovell
a08_0372329.text: What I'm going to attempt to do on P37 is to input your Delta-V on your TLI plus 44 and use that 44 burn time. I notice that the entry velocity is a little high. I think we might not be able to do a normal P37, but I'll give it a try

a08_0372329.speaker: Lovell
a08_0372329.text: Houston. One more question then before I start. Did you notice on this last update PAD, this minus MA, NC-1. Was that referring to the P37 fast return or the nominal maneuver which you gave me?

a08_0372329.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0372329.text: Apollo 8, that's referring to the fast return procedures.

a08_0373155.speaker: Lovell
a08_0373155.text: Are you following my procedures [That is, are they watching the DSKY displays as Jim is running P37]?

a08_0373155.speaker: Lovell
a08_0373155.text: Okay. This happened yesterday, too. I'm trying to load the Delta-V you gave us in the maneuver TLI plus 44 in P37, but I keep getting an operator error every time I try to load zeros for the termination of the middle and corner [R2]. Do you know what I'm doing wrong in my procedure?

a08_0373524.speaker: Lovell
a08_0373524.text: Okay, go ahead. I can take it.

a08_0373524.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0373524.text: Okay, looks like the decimal point in R2 under Noun 60 is on the extreme right-hand side so the proper load will be 06070. Over.

a08_0373524.speaker: Lovell
a08_0373524.text: Ah, so. Okay, fine. Thank you. [Pause.] I'll update my checklist. Don't know what I want to update it for. I can't read.

a08_0374200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0374200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 37 hours, 42 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. At this time, the spacecraft is 138,226 nautical miles [255,994 km] from the Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,148 feet per second [1,264 m/s]. It's continued to be relatively quiet here in Mission Control. The Flight Plan also shows relatively little activity onboard the spacecraft for the crewmen. Both Frank Borman and Bill Anders are scheduled to be sleeping at this time. The crew is following the ground advice that was passed up earlier today from Mission Control Center that they pace themselves and set

a08_0375424.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0375424.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're about to hand over to another site so you may lose lock momentarily.

a08_0375424.speaker: Lovell
a08_0375424.text: Roger, Houston. Did you receive the results of the P37?

a08_0375424.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0375424.text: Sure did. Looks pretty good here.

a08_0375714.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0375714.text: Apollo 8; Houston through Honeysuckle. The [ground station] switch is completed.

a08_0375823.speaker: Lovell
a08_0375823.text: Another comment on the optics. We're in PTC right now. We're passing the - we have the - a roll of about 182; we're about in 226 pitch and 18 in yaw. I can rotate the shaft all the way around at this particular attitude, and I get this band of light at about 10 degrees either side of the M-line. It - it varies in intensity with the shaft position. However, it's there at this particular attitude.

a08_0375823.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0375823.text: Jim, they've just been looking at your marks with respect to accuracy and they figure they're within a couple of thousandths of a degree of the theoretical optimum. And I guess the integrator seems to bear that out.

a08_0375823.speaker: Lovell
a08_0375823.text: Well, I hope they're enough to get us home if we have to use them.

a08_0375823.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0375823.text: Well, I am getting a lot of confidence in your ability to run that mystery show now.

a08_0375823.speaker: Anders
a08_0375823.text: Hey, Jim [means Ken]. We have to spend four more days up here with him. Will you take it easy. [Pause.] He's already talking about going back to MIT as a professor.

a08_0380600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0380600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 38 hours, 6 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. At the present time, the spacecraft is 139,151 nautical miles [257,707 km] from Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,122 feet per second [1,256 m/s]. In the last few minutes we had a conversation with Jim Lovell aboard the spacecraft. Lovell gave us another of the periodic updates that he's been passing down on the optics system used in conjunction with the onboard guidance and navigation equipment. Lovell again noted, as he has in the past, that he is getting a band of light through the field of view of his sca

a08_0380600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0380600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 38 hours, 41 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. We have had no communications with the crew in the past 20 minutes since our previous announcement. At the present time, Apollo 8 is at an altitude of 140,600 nautical miles [260,400 km], traveling at a speed of 4,083 feet per second [1,244 m/s]. We continue through a very quiet period, both here in Mission Control Center and on the Flight Plan. We've just gotten a call from the spacecraft and we will pick that up now.

a08_0384137.speaker: Borman
a08_0384137.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read Apollo 8?

a08_0384137.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0384137.text: You sure do sound wide awake. [Long pause.]

a08_0384137.speaker: Borman
a08_0384137.text: Hello, Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0384137.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0384137.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Read you loud and clear. How me? [No answer.]

a08_0384405.speaker: Network
a08_0384405.text: Honeysuckle, Network, GOSS Conference. How do you read?

a08_0384405.speaker: Borman
a08_0384405.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0384405.speaker: Borman
a08_0384405.text: Go ahead Honeysuckle. How do you read?

a08_0384405.speaker: Borman
a08_0384405.text: Well, I say hello to all of you in Australia. How's everything down there?

a08_0384405.speaker: Network
a08_0384405.text: Honeysuckle, Houston Network on GOSS Conference. How do you read?

a08_0384405.speaker: Honeysuckle
a08_0384405.text: Houston Network, this is Honeysuckle reading at 5, 5.

a08_0384618.speaker: Borman
a08_0384618.text: Roger, just checking with you. Hey, if you all start having ground switching problems, how about having some site that has comm come in and tell us about it. Will you please?

a08_0384618.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0384618.text: Roger. Apollo 8. That's what we have been trying to do. Some of our problem seems to be getting from here to that site.

a08_0384618.speaker: Borman
a08_0384618.text: Houston. Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0384618.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0384618.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Loud and clear. How me? [Long pause.]

a08_0384618.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0384618.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Read you loud and clear. [Long pause.]

a08_0384700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0384700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. We're apparently having some problems with direct communication from Houston to the spacecraft. We're reading them loud and clear. But at the present time we are having to relay information through the Honeysuckle maintenance and operations personnel to the spacecraft and we're checking into the lines between - connections between here and Honeysuckle, Australia to determine just where the problem lays.

a08_0384700-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_0384700-pao.text: Roger, just checking with you. Hey, if you all start having ground switching problems, how about having some site that has comm come in and tell us about it. Will you please?

a08_0385500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0385500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. Having reestablished two-way communication with the spacecraft, it appears that we won't hear any more from the crew at least for the time being. We did hear from Frank Borman that time that indicates that he is no longer resting, or at least is not asleep. Frank had indicated earlier that he would attempt to get some rest beginning at about 37 hours Ground Elapsed Time, and we heard from him there at about 38 hours, 45 minutes into the flight. We do not have a - an evaluation as to what the problem was with the uplink. The problem appeared to lie between Houston and th

a08_0385500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0385500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 39 hours, 10 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. We've had no further communications with the crew since our previous report. We do have a preliminary report on the cause of our communications problem through Honeysuckle. And it appears that the problem was with a control monitor panel at the Honeysuckle, Australia site. The exact nature of the problem with this piece of electronic equipment is not known at this time. It is associated with the unified S-band system at Honeysuckle. The problem, as we said, occurred at about 38 hours, 42 minutes Ground Elapsed

a08_0393802.speaker: Borman
a08_0393802.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0393802.speaker: Carr
a08_0393802.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Reading you weak but clear.

a08_0394300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0394300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 39 hours, 43 minutes, 15 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at the present time is at an altitude of 143,023 nautical miles [264,878 kilometres]; our current velocity reading, 4,019.1 feet per second [1,225 m/s]. As had been previously reported, we were undergoing a change of shift briefing. We have a change of shift here in Mission Control, I should say, we have done that. The Glynn Lunney team of - Black Team of flight controllers is now on duty. Glynn's first action, as he took over, was to bring up each member of his flight contr

a08_0394300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0394300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 39 hours, 53 minutes. This is a brief clarifying report on our last transmission. The conversation between the spacecraft Apollo 8 and Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr can perhaps be best identified by its brevity. Apparently it did not get recorded on tape, only some eight seconds in length. However this transmission was strictly an acknowledgement of communications between the spacecraft and the ground. We thought that you should know that at this time since it apparently did not play with our previous announcement. So at 39 hours, 54 minutes; this is Apollo Control,

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Go ahead, Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Roger, Frank. I've got a little news and some ball scores if you want them.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Go ahead.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Okay. The big news right now, on the wires, is that all 82 crewmen of the Pueblo have been returned. They walked across the Bridge of Freedom, Monday night.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Wonderful! [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Said it took about 30 minutes for all 82 men to come across the Bridge of No Return and that's the one separating North and South Korea. They started across about 11:30 am and were over by about noon, and they brought the body of the crewman who was killed, also. [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Okay, Frank. On ball scores, did you get the word on the Baltimore/Minnesota game today?

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Not the final one.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Okay. Final score was the [Baltimore] Colts 24, [Minnesota] Vikings 14. That gives them the western conference, so it looks like, for the NFL title, it's gonna be the Browns versus the Colts on the 29th.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: 29th?

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Rog. Slow return - you'll get it.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Say again.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Roger. Come back slow return and we'll get it.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: I'd rather come back fast and watch it on television.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Atta boy! Let's see, for the AFL: the big game today was Oakland [Raiders] and Kansas City [Chiefs] and Oakland dumped them 41 to 6, so it's looks the AFL [American Football League] title game will be the Raiders and [New York] Jets.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Righto! That's hard to believe, that score.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Amen! Okay. In yesterday's game, I don't know if you got the score on that. The Cleveland Browns and the [Dallas] Cowboys. The Browns dumped the Cowboys 31 to 20.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Yeah, we heard that.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Yeah, they're crying in Dallas. Basketball scores: Houston [University of Houston] didn't do so good this weekend. The Illinois beat Houston 97 to 84. And North Carolina took the Owls [Rice University]. The score was 85 - 77. [Long pause.] We had a couple of words in the paper, Frank, on the Oilers [Houston's pro football team]. The Oilers voted George Webster their most valuable player and - although Houston didn't make anybody on the All-AFL Offensive Team this year, they put Walt Suggs and Hoyle Granger on the second team.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Very good. [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: But although the [Houston] Oilers didn't do so well out on the field, they did great in the box office. Bud Adams, Don Klausterman and Wally Lemm were all - real pleased with it. By the way, they were at the Cape to watch the show. Houston, in 11 games - the Oilers attracted 460,628 people.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: That must be a record? For them? I don't believe they ever got that many in Rice [University] Stadium.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: I think so. Let's see, the regular season attendance was about half of that. This includes all the exhibition games. The paper says they averaged about 40,480 for the league games.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Great! [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Well, that's about it for now, Frank. We got some more news that they promised they'd bring over as soon as it comes off the wire. The only things of real interests were the - particularly was the Pueblo release. I think you've already been told about the - [Julie] Nixon-[David] Eisenhower wedding. And about the only other thing is the weather which is pretty clear around here. We've got high overcasts. But it's cold and good visibility, and it's beginning to feel like winter again.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Good time for Christmas, good weather for Christmas. [Long pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Who have you got up now, Frank?

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: The other two guys are pretty sleepy. They sacked out again. So I'm holding the fort down for a while.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Okay. Thanks.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Rog. Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: Frank, we had a little eggnog over at Charlie Duke's tonight.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Say again.

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: We had a little eggnog over at Charlie Duke's tonight. Val Anders dropped by. She's looking fine. Tell Bill she's doing real well.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Fine. [Long pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: How do you like shift work, Jerry? [Pause.]

a08_0400215.speaker: Carr
a08_0400215.text: It's great, Frank. You've got the Black Watch watching you tonight.

a08_0400215.speaker: Borman
a08_0400215.text: Yeah, that's what I figured.

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0401100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 40 hours, 11 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft is now 144,094 nautical miles [266,862 km] in altitude. Our current velocity; 3,991.2 feet per second [1,216.5 m/s]. Jerry Carr, the capsule communicator here in Mission Control, has just had a rather long chatty conversation with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman, in which, among other things, he passed on a bit of news and some ball scores and - and told Colonel Borman of the release of the 82 crewmen from the Pueblo today. As a matter of fact, they're still talking a bit here and we'

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_0401100-pao.text: Boy, Jerry. That old Earth is sure looking small. [Pause.]

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0401100-pao.text: Rog. I guess it'll get smaller, too.

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_0401100-pao.text: Yeah, we're getting along pretty good, though, now.

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0401100-pao.text: Real good. It looks like you're approaching 150,000 miles.

a08_0401100-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0401100-pao.text: Have you looked at the Moon lately?

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Boy, Jerry. That old Earth is sure looking small. [Pause.]

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Rog. I guess it'll get smaller, too.

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Yeah, we're getting along pretty good, though, now.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Real good. It looks like you're approaching 150,000 miles.

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: How's the Moon look, Frank?

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Say again.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Have you looked at the Moon lately?

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: No. [Long pause.] I saw it yesterday, but we haven't seen it today. [Long pause.]

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Frank, you've probably already been told this, but you looked great on TV today. One little homey item, though. In the El Lago area you were upstaged by Santa Claus. He came around on a fire engine just about the time you guys came on. So most of the little critters were all outside.

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: That's good. I wish we could have got that one lens working. I'd like to share the view we have here of Earth.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Frank, we've got some guys looking at it. We might be able to find a way to make it work for you. Hopefully, by a couple of hours before TV time tomorrow, we'll have an answer.

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Very good.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Jack Schmitt's working with us, too. [Pause.]

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Very good. That's Typhoid Jack.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: [Laughter.] [Long pause.]

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: This comm is so good we don't figure we'll have much to debrief.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Roger. [Pause.] Probably the biggest part of the debrief will be the medical part.

a08_0401117.speaker: Borman
a08_0401117.text: Roger. You're sure right. [Long pause.] Oh, we're all in fine shape.

a08_0401117.speaker: Carr
a08_0401117.text: Real fine, Frank.

a08_0402300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0402300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard Colonel Frank Borman, he is up at the present time by himself minding the store in Apollo 8 while the other two crewmembers, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders are taking a rest period. As to condition, he described the crew as all in fine shape, acknowledging certainly that the medical debriefing would be a significant one. As you heard, the conversation ranged a wide gamut of subjects but I guess when you're 44,548 [Means 144,548] nautical miles [267,702 km] away from home it is perhaps stimulating to occasionally have what would seem to be at least in a large m

a08_0404842.speaker: Borman
a08_0404842.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We just completed the canister change.

a08_0413731.speaker: Carr
a08_0413731.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We have a handover coming up in 2½ minutes to Guam. Over.

a08_0413731.speaker: Borman
a08_0413731.text: Okay, Jerry. Thank you. Hey, Jerry?

a08_0413731.speaker: Borman
a08_0413731.text: How about the long-range guess on what the weather is going to be like in the recovery area on Friday.

a08_0414452.speaker: Carr
a08_0414452.text: Apollo 8, Houston, with a weather watch. [Pause.]

a08_0414452.speaker: Carr
a08_0414452.text: Roger, Frank. For 7 degrees, 38 minutes north; 165 west landing area, we're showing 2,000 scattered, 12,000 broken, high over at 10; with the winds from the east at 12, 4-foot swells, about an 82-degree temperature. There'll be some rain showers in about 10 to 30 percent of the area with ceilings around 2,000. If there is - turns out to be a thunderstorm in the area, it'll probably have a ceiling around 500 feet.

a08_0414452.speaker: Carr
a08_0414452.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Did you copy that weather okay?

a08_0414452.speaker: Borman
a08_0414452.text: Roger. I said thank you. Do you read me now?

a08_0414452.speaker: Carr
a08_0414452.text: Roger. Reading you much better. We got the voice coming down through Honeysuckle now.

a08_0415200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0415200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 41 hours, 52 minutes, 35 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Our current altitude on Apollo 8, now 147,956.7 nautical miles [274,015.3 km]. Our current velocity on Apollo 8; 3,892 feet per second [1,186 m/s]. We've had a bit of a conversation with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman, and we'll pass that along now. Apollo Control Houston. As you heard, spacecraft Commander Frank Borman did request a weather advisory for his time of return to Earth and you certainly can't fault the spacecraft Commander for not planning his mission in advance. At the present time

a08_0415823.speaker: Carr
a08_0415823.text: Roger, Frank. Can you cycle the H 2 and O 2 cryo fans now for us?

a08_0415823.speaker: Borman
a08_0415823.text: Rog. Will start her now with H 2 . Manual, 2 minutes.

a08_0415823.speaker: Borman
a08_0415823.text: You may need to call us now and then. Everybody's a little drowsy.

a08_0420707.speaker: Borman
a08_0420707.text: That completes it, Jerry. They're all cycled through.

a08_0420707.speaker: Borman
a08_0420707.text: Did you get my message about the fans?

a08_0422100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0422100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 42 hours, 21 minutes, 32 seconds into the flight, Apollo 8. At the present time, Apollo 8 now 149,041.4 nautical miles [276,024.1 km] in altitude. Our - meanwhile our spacecraft velocity continuing to slow down. Our current velocity reading 3,864.7 feet per second [1,178.0 m/s]. Since our last announcement, we've had only one conversation with Apollo 8, and we'll pass that along now. And that concludes the conversation; a procedural one. And at 42 hours, 23 minutes, 15 seconds into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0424447.speaker: Borman
a08_0424447.text: Rog. The cabin temperature's down to 60[degrees Fahrenheit, 16°C], and it's getting pretty chilly. You got any approved solutions on how to bring it up without screwing up this nice thermal balance we've had?

a08_0424447.speaker: Carr
a08_0424447.text: Frank, do you have your cabin fans on?

a08_0424447.speaker: Borman
a08_0424447.text: We haven't had them on since we separated.

a08_0425622.speaker: Carr
a08_0425622.text: Roger, Frank. Midcourse number 3 looks like just a shade more than 1 foot per second, so we don't recommend that you do it. That leads us off into a midcourse 4 of only about 3 feet per second right now. Your trajectory is looking real good. Your height at pericynthion is 70 miles.

a08_0425622.speaker: Carr
a08_0425622.text: Roger. Roger, Frank. Little few thoughts on what's coming up now. The star sightings, when Jim gets up, looks right now like we've had enough of the Earth horizon. Everything looks real good; and we're ready to start on some lunar horizon sightings. So when Jim gets up, we'll pass the Flight Plan update to him for a set of stars with the Moon. Also, around 48 or after the star sightings is when we'd like to see your next water dump come up. So, if you can, I recommend you get a little shut-eye.

a08_0425622.speaker: Borman
a08_0425622.text: Rog. You got any answers on warming this place up a little bit?

a08_0425622.speaker: Carr
a08_0425622.text: Roger. They're still cranking around. They're talking about cabin fans, but that sounds like sort of a noisy proposition.

a08_0430400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0430400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 43 hours, 4 minutes, 22 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft is now past the altitude mark of 150,000 nautical miles. Our current reading here on the display is 150,634.6 nautical miles [278,974.7 km]. Our velocity is shown as 3,825.2 feet per second [1,165.9 m/s], continuing its slow-down process. We've had a conversation with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman, which began at the onset with Colonel Borman remarking about the chilly temperature inside the spacecraft. Our current temperature reading being 60 degrees. We'll play this con

a08_0430517.speaker: Carr
a08_0430517.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Got two methods for you to warm up the cabin there. The first one is a one-man job. About the best way would be to put one or both cabin fans on, and go full hot on the cabin heat exchanger. It'll be a fairly slow process of warming up, and you won't get a whole lot of heating. Your second method would be to adjust, with the mixing valve, your Radiator Out temperatures. This, again, is a two-man job. You have to be pretty careful.

a08_0430517.speaker: Lovell
a08_0430517.text: Rog. Well, Frank just went to bed, and Bill isn't up yet. I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll put on the fans and we'll - I'll go High on the cabin temperature and see what that does.

a08_0430517.speaker: Carr
a08_0430517.text: Okay, Jim. Remember, if you use just one fan, cover the other. [Pause.]

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0431000-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you no doubt surmized, Frank Borman did take Jerry Carr's advice and decided to grab some shut-eye. Jim Lovell, now awake, took the last part of that transmission. In our verbal update on the Flight Plan, as you had heard, our next set of star sightings, we use the Moon horizon as a reference rather than the Earth, this being for Program 23. Also our Flight Dynamics Officer, who was closely scrutinizing midcourse trade-offs, looking over a 1.1 foot per second Delta-V versus something on the order of 3 feet per second is strongly inclined toward recommending a midcou

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431000-pao.text: Roger. If I use just one fan - You mentioned about covering the other one - are you sure that's true in this spacecraft? [Pause.]

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431000-pao.text: I thought that was a Block I problem. [Pause.]

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0431000-pao.text: Stand by. Jim. We'll recheck on that one. [Long pause.]

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0431000-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Did you get the word from Frank on the star-sighting plan?

a08_0431000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431000-pao.text: Rog. I'll get out the Flight Plan if you have an update to it now, though. We can certainly update it right now.

a08_0431022.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431022.text: Roger. If I use just one fan - You mentioned about covering the other one - are you sure that's true in this spacecraft? [Pause.]

a08_0431022.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431022.text: I thought that was a Block I problem. [Pause.]

a08_0431022.speaker: Carr
a08_0431022.text: Stand by. Jim. We'll recheck on that one. [Long pause.]

a08_0431022.speaker: Carr
a08_0431022.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Did you get the word from Frank on the star-sighting plan?

a08_0431022.speaker: Lovell
a08_0431022.text: Rog. I'll get out the Flight Plan if you have an update to it now, though. We can certainly update it right now.

a08_0432842.speaker: Carr
a08_0432842.text: Roger. You ready for that Flight Plan update?

a08_0432842.speaker: Carr
a08_0432842.text: Okay. At time 47:15, delete the P23 sightings you're showing there; and at 45 minutes - correction, 45 hours, add one additional set of sightings to each star. [Pause.]

a08_0432842.speaker: Lovell
a08_0432842.text: Okay. You say at 45 hours we're going to add one set of sightings to each of the three stars. Is that correct?

a08_0432842.speaker: Carr
a08_0432842.text: That's affirmative. Everybody's real pleased with the Earth horizon work; and as far as we're concerned, you can knock that off, and just add one set to each one of your lunar horizon stars at about 45. This 45-hour time also is not hard. You can shift it as your - as you desire.

a08_0432842.speaker: Lovell
a08_0432842.text: Roger. As I see things coming up now, Jerry, we're going to get some block data around 44, and we'll do alignment around 44:30 and then we'll go into cislunar navigation.

a08_0432842.speaker: Carr
a08_0432842.text: Okay. Fine, Jim. Then remember after you do the sightings, we'll want you to go back to the PTC mode again. And a little curiosity, how's the water tasting, and how did you sleep?

a08_0432842.speaker: Lovell
a08_0432842.text: Water's tasting okay; no problems. And the sleep is getting better: We find it better to sleep underneath the couch now. I was up here with Frank, and I was dozing off periodically over the last several hours. Frank's now down below and Bill's below, too.

a08_0433300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0433300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 43 hours, 33 minutes, 8 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8's current altitude per our displays; 151,686.2 nautical miles [280,922.3 km]. Current velocity; 3,799.2 feet per second [1,158.0 m/s]. Capsule communicator Jerry Carr has just passed along some Flight Plan update numbers with regard to the Program 23 star sightings to Command Module Pilot Jim Lovell. And we'll pick up that conversation.

a08_0433700-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0433700-pao.text: Apollo 8, we've got a command handover from Guam to Honeysuckle coming up in about 2½ minutes.

a08_0433727.speaker: Carr
a08_0433727.text: Apollo 8, we've got a command handover from Guam to Honeysuckle coming up in about 2½ minutes.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8. This is Flight...

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: I might add that at this distance...

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Say again, Apollo 8.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: I might add that at this distance, there is no problem - there is no problem in seeing stars in the daylight at this distance.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Roger. Copy. [Long pause.]

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Apollo 8, Flight.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: This is 8; go ahead.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Jim, are you talking about out the window or out any of the - or out the telescope?

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: I'm looking out the window right now. I have the lights out in the spacecraft, the window covered where the Sun is, and I can see stars very well out the left rendezvous window.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Okay. I guess that window's still pretty good for you then, huh?

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: That's right. It's one of the few that is. The center window, unfortunately, is all fogged over; it looks like a coating of ice or coating of heavy fog. Bill claims it's something else, though.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Roger. [Pause.] By the way. I am just getting OJT (On Job Training) on this CapCom job while Jerry's out of the room.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: Well, we all have to learn sometime.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Yes sir. [Long pause.]

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: You picked a midnight shift, I see.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Yeah. Turning out to be kind of quiet, too.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: We like it that way.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Well, things will pick up here by tomorrow night, I think.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: I believe you're right. [Pause.]

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: We're starting to show cabin temperature at 70, so it may be warming up for you.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lovell
a08_0433922.text: Well, we can feel it warm up. I have both fans on and the - our gauge indicates about 70.

a08_0433922.speaker: Lunney
a08_0433922.text: Okay. And I got a real CapCom back now.

a08_0434500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0434500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, the star sighting results have been indeed well accepted on the ground. So we'll have here for the first time the lunar horizon becoming the prime reference point for these navigation exercises. At 43 hours, 37 minutes, 6 seconds into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0434500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0434500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 43 hours, 45 minutes, 15 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Our current altitude on Apollo 8; 152,125.2 nautical miles [281,735.3 km]. Current velocity reads 3,788.4 feet per second [1,154.7 m/s]. We just had an interesting conversation with Jim Lovell who called with regard to seeing stars in daylight. Glynn Lunney, incidentally, got on the line. Jerry Carr, the Capsule Communicator, was out of the room briefly. We thought we would pass along that conversation now. Apollo Control, Houston. Glynn Lunney's reference of course, to tomorrow night dealt with

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8 here.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Apollo 8. This is Houston, with a flyby, and a PC, pericynthion plus 2 hours maneuver PAD, when you're ready to copy. [Long pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Ready to copy.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Your TLI plus 44 maneuver PAD is good, requires no update.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: I am copying.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: I'm copying. Stand by. I'm going to switch Omni antenna.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Standing by. [Long pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. H A is not applicable, plus 0020.2; 0235.6, 022, 0228.0; 03, 039.3, 31.0; 013, up 04.8, right ze - 3.5 - I repeat, right 3.5. Copy?

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Copy.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Plus 14.18, minus 165.05; 1290.4, 36160, 146:29:11; GDC Align with your Sirius, Rigel set stars; 137, 311, 339; no ullage. Copy?

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: We are copying.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. I have two comments. Number one; requires realignment to preferred REFSMMAT; two, raises perilune to 554 miles. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Roger. I have it. Stand by for readback.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Standing by.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Flyby maneuver, SPS/G&N; 62954; minus 1.62, plus 1.29; 060:59:48.08; 953, 578 - those are 0095.3 and plus 0057.8, minus 0207.6; 000, 000, 000; not applicable, plus 0020.2; 0235.6, 0:22, 0228.0; 03, 039.3, 31.0; 013, up 04.8, right 3.5; plus 14.18, minus 165.05; 1290.4, 36160, 146:29:11; Sirius, Rigel; 137, 311, 339; no ullage, requires realignment to preferred REFSMMAT, raises perilune to 554 nautical miles.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Jim, that's correct. Let me know when you're ready for your PC plus 2. [Pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Okay. Let's go on PC plus 2.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Pericynthion plus 2, fast return, SPS/G&N; 61503; minus 1.58, plus 1.31; 071:36:12.44; plus 5957.8, minus 0008.6, minus 0528.7. Copy?

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: I am copying.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Copying.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Earth, up 00.5, right 2.7; plus 03.98, plus 065.00; 1321.5, 36961, 106:19.11; Sirius, Rigel; 137, 311, 339; no ullage. Copy? [Pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Roger.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Two remarks to go. Number four... [Pause.] Stand by [Pause.] number four: use P37 NC dash 4, steps 1 through 10 and NC-8, steps 3 and 4. Remark number five: average V 400K for corridor control chart equals 36531. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Copy.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. I have five remarks. Number one, assumes execution of flyby maneuver; number two, use same alignment as for flyby; number three, time of midcourse number 5 for GERU determination, GET of 83:38. Copy? [Pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Roger, Houston. PC plus 2, maneuver PAD as follows: SPS/G&N; 61503; minus 1.58, plus 1.31; 071:36:12.44. Copy?

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger. Copy.

a08_0435347.speaker: Lovell
a08_0435347.text: Plus 5957.8, minus 0008.6, minus 0528.7; 012, 080, 018; not applicable, plus 0020.3; 5981.3, 6:50, 5956.6; 11, 216.0, 33.2; Earth, up 00.5, right 2.7; plus 03.98, plus 065.00; 1321.5, 36961, 106:19:11; Sirius, Rigel; 137, 311, 339; no ullage, assumes execution of flyby maneuver, uses same alignment as for flyby; time of MCC-5 for GERU determination is 83 plus 38; use P37 NC-4 steps 1 through 10, NC-8 steps 3 and 4. Average V 400K for corridor control chart 36531.

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Roger, Jim. That's all correct. [Long pause.]

a08_0435347.speaker: Carr
a08_0435347.text: Apollo 8, Houston. That PC plus 2 is a fast return.

a08_0441100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0441100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 44 hours, 11 minutes into the flight, Apollo 8. At this time, Apollo 8 153,100.2 - 153,100.2 nautical miles [283,541 km] in altitude. Our current velocity reading; 3,764.7 feet per second [1,147.5 m/s]. Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr, has just passed along a - passed along block data information to Jim Lovell aboard the spacecraft. These come out as a long stream of numbers meaningful to the onboard computer. The numbers, by the way, are not part of the ongoing Flight Plan. These are for a contingency situation only. A means of assuring proper return data fo

a08_0441100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0441100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 45 hours, 1 minute, 24 seconds now into the flight. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time, 154,847.7 nautical miles [286,777.4 km] in altitude. Its slowing velocity now reading 3,722.7 feet per second [1,134.7 m/s]. We've had no conversational contact with Apollo 8 since our last announcement. Command Module Pilot Jim Lovell apparently continuing with his navigation task. At 45 hours, 2 minutes into the flight, Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0451450.speaker: Lovell
a08_0451450.text: Roger. Just some interesting things on the - just done a Nav with the Moon; the Sun is practically right in the way. I managed to get one set on Antares and was working on the second set, and the rim of the Moon just disappeared completely. The view through the sextant is a milky white, whether you're looking at black sky or the - or the Moon. The tint of the Moon is practically washed out by the brightness of the Sun. I'll try the next star and see what I can do with it.

a08_0451450.speaker: Anders
a08_0451450.text: Good morning, Houston. How are the systems looking here lately?

a08_0451450.speaker: Carr
a08_0451450.text: Mornin', sleepy head. Systems are looking Go.

a08_0451450.speaker: Anders
a08_0451450.text: Oh, off and on, Jerry. There was quite a bit of noise in here, and anytime somebody responds to a transmission, why, it tends to wake you up. But it was a reasonably good rest.

a08_0451450.speaker: Carr
a08_0451450.text: Real fine. We got a little work scheduled for you here. We've got an ECS redundant component check to run and some fuel cell purging to do.

a08_0451450.speaker: Anders
a08_0451450.text: Okay. How about if we wait until this nav[igation] exercise is over with?

a08_0451450.speaker: Carr
a08_0451450.text: Bill, what we have planned for you right after Jim gets finished is a waste water dump, a cryo fan cycle, redundant component check, and a fuel cell purge.

a08_0451450.speaker: Carr
a08_0451450.text: We'll be wanting an O 2 and H 2 fuel cell purge; we'll give you a 20-minute hack on the heater.

a08_0451450.speaker: Anders
a08_0451450.text: Okay. Want me to turn them on now or when you give me a hack?

a08_0452000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0452000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 45 hours, 20 minutes, 40 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8's current altitude at this time of 155,579.3 nautical miles [288,132.3 km] above the Earth. The velocity of the spacecraft now reading 3,705.1 feet per second [1,129.3 m/s]. We've had contact in the past few minutes with both Jim Lovell, and Bill Anders who has just awakened. We'll play that conversation now. Apollo Control, Houston. So you heard how the Sun, with its close relative proximity, tended to wash out the last of nav[igation] sightings for Jim Lovell. We expect we'll hear from h

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Bill, are you still eating?

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Doing what?

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Are you busy eating?

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Negative. I'm watching the store while Jim does his Nav sighting and then recording the data for him.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Okay. We have a correction to make to your TLI plus 44-hour PAD. If you've got a chance there, we'd like to fire it on up to you.

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Stand by.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Okay. Ready to copy the correction to TLI plus 44.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger. The correction is in the remarks at the end. Delete the reference to high speed procedure minus MA. [Pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Roger. Delete minus MA slash NC-1, Charlie.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: That's affirmative, and copy the following. This comment should read, "use P37 NC-4, step 1 through 11." Over. [Pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Rog. Use P37 NC-4, steps 1 through 11.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger. Then proceed to longitude control for no comm procedure, page NC-7. [Pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: You went a little fast. Say again the page.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger, That page is NC-7. I'll read that again. Then proceed to longitude control for no comm procedure, page NC-7. Average 400K - V 400K, for corridor control charts is 36253. I repeat, average V 400K for corridor control charts is 36253. Over.

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Roger. Say again. That's average G as in George.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Negative. Average Victor 400K for corridor control chart is 36253. [Pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Roger. Average V 400K for corridor control chart is 36253.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger. The minus MA procedure is okay after abort when the GERU is less than 07990. [Long pause.]

a08_0452513.speaker: Anders
a08_0452513.text: Roger. Minus MA procedure okay for abort when GERU less than 07990.

a08_0452513.speaker: Carr
a08_0452513.text: Roger. I'll read back the entire remarks now just to make sure we got it straight. Use P37 NC-4, steps 1 through 11; then proceed to longitude control for no comm procedure on page NC-7; average Victor 400K for corridor control chart is 36253; Minus MA procedure is okay after abort when GERU is less than 07990. [Long pause.]

a08_0453900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0453900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 45 hours, 39 minutes, 25 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8's current altitude, 156,242.7 nautical miles [289,360.9 km]. Our velocity now reading 3,689.4 feet per second [1,124.5 m/s]. Here on the ground we've passed along on a correction to the TLI plus 44-hour PAD already with the crew. We'll play back that report. Apollo Control, Houston. Taking down all that navigator talk was Systems Engineer Bill Anders

a08_0454224.speaker: Carr
a08_0454224.text: Bill, you can turn on the H 2 purge line heater now.

a08_0454500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0454500-pao.text: Here in Mission Control Center, our LOS clock now reading 23 hours, 12 minutes, indicating that we're now less than a day away from that time that the Apollo 8 spacecraft passes - starts its pass over the backside of the Moon and out of communications range with Mission Control Center. It's relatively quiet here in the Mission Control Center now. However, we don't expect this to be representative of what it'll be like in this room this time tomorrow. At 45 hours, 45 minutes, 40 seconds into the flight, Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0454741.speaker: Carr
a08_0454741.text: Jim, when you get a chance, either you or Bill, would you give us a crew status report on you and Bill?

a08_0454741.speaker: Lovell
a08_0454741.text: Rog. We're going to finish up this one set of stars for you, then we'll do that.

a08_0454741.speaker: Lovell
a08_0454741.text: Have you been getting this data down there in Houston?

a08_0454741.speaker: Carr
a08_0454741.text: Jim, so far we've only missed one point; we'll ask you to read it back a little bit later.

a08_0454741.speaker: Carr
a08_0454741.text: Apollo 8, Houston. What, we need is the third mark on the first set, star 33, trunnion only. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0454741.speaker: Anders
a08_0454741.text: Roger. That's the only one we're in doubt of. We think it was 12020.

a08_0455201.speaker: Lovell
a08_0455201.text: Houston, for information, the last two stars, 34 and 40, were shot at the very tip of the thin rim, and you practically have to imagine the rim continuing on past where it goes into the darkness.

a08_0455201.speaker: Carr
a08_0455201.text: Roger. Understand they were shot at the tip of the lit rim.

a08_0455201.speaker: Lovell
a08_0455201.text: That's affirmative, and the area around the entire Moon now, both the sky and the Moon itself, are all milky white because of the nearness of the Sun.

a08_0455201.speaker: Carr
a08_0455201.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You can reestablish PTC, same attitude, [pitch] 224 and [yaw] 20.

a08_0455201.speaker: Anders
a08_0455201.text: Roger, Houston. I'm heading that way now.

a08_0455800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0455800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 45 hours, 58 minutes, 20 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. We read Apollo 8's altitude at this time at 156,917.4 nautical miles [290,610.4 km]. The velocity reading shows 3,673.5 feet per second [1,119.7 m/s]. Jim Lovell has completed his program 23 navigation sightings and at this time the Apollo 8's spacecraft is being returned to a Passive Thermal Control attitude. We'll play the report that Command Module Pilot Lovell passed down to our capsule communicator Jerry Carr now.

a08_0460133.speaker: Carr
a08_0460133.text: We'd like to have you start your waste water dump...

a08_0460133.speaker: Carr
a08_0460133.text: We'd like to have you start your waste water dump as soon as you can; dump to 20 percent. We're doing this in order to get 71 percent at LOI. Over.

a08_0460300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0460300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. We picked up the last transmission as it was going on - the advisory that Apollo 8 should proceed with its waste water dump as soon as possible. So at 46 hours, 3 minutes, 3 seconds into the flight, Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0461432.speaker: Carr
a08_0461432.text: Roger. We see the waste water coming down now. While it's on its way down, how about a cryo fan cycle?

a08_0461432.speaker: Lovell
a08_0461432.text: Okay. Cryo fan cycle; I'll cycle the H 2 and O 2 fans, one at a time, 2 minutes each.

a08_0462156.speaker: Carr
a08_0462156.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're showing you at 20.0 percent now [left in the waste water tank]. [Pause.]

a08_0462156.speaker: Anders
a08_0462156.text: Roger. We're showing about 25. We'll shut it [the dump valve] off now.

a08_0462156.speaker: Carr
a08_0462156.text: Roger. Next on deck is the fuel cell H 2 , O 2 purge.

a08_0462500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0462500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 46 hours, 25 minutes, 22 seconds now into the flight, Apollo 8. We now read an altitude of 157,868.9 nautical miles [292,372.6 km] for Apollo 8. Velocity now reading 3,651.2 feet per second [1,112.9 m/s]. The waste water dump has been completed by the Apollo 8 crew. And here's a conversation regarding that sequence.

a08_0463034.speaker: Anders
a08_0463034.text: Okay. Houston, we're ready to start the purge.

a08_0463034.speaker: Carr
a08_0463034.text: Roger, Bill. While you're purging, can you give us a crew status report? [Pause.]

a08_0463034.speaker: Anders
a08_0463034.text: That's going to be O 2 and H 2 . Is that correct?

a08_0463034.speaker: Anders
a08_0463034.text: We're getting H 2 flow, Jerry, but we don't see any - any vapor particles anywhere. [Pause.] Some are starting now.

a08_0463034.speaker: Carr
a08_0463034.text: Roger. We confirm your flow and understand you're seeing particles now.

a08_0463034.speaker: Anders
a08_0463034.text: Yeah, not much, though. Okay. going to go to [fuel cell] number 2.

a08_0463034.speaker: Anders
a08_0463034.text: You know, it's really too bad these side windows are fogged up because we never see any Sun in the rendezvous windows, and we can't get very good pictures through these foggy ones.

a08_0463621.speaker: Carr
a08_0463621.text: Roger, Apollo 8. Apollo 8, this is Houston. Would you set for Accept for a P27 update, state vector to your LM side, and we'd like you to...

a08_0463621.speaker: Carr
a08_0463621.text: Roger, Bill. Would you set up to Accept a state vector update? We'll be putting it in the LM slot, and do not unzap. Over.

a08_0463621.speaker: Anders
a08_0463621.text: We're going to put the word "zap" back in the dictionary.

a08_0463621.speaker: Lovell
a08_0463621.text: Might be interesting to note that after nav sightings, we ran out P21, and we get a pericynthion now of 66.8 [nautical] miles.

a08_0463621.speaker: Anders
a08_0463621.text: I knew if he did it long enough, he'd finally get one that was close. [Long pause.]

a08_0463621.speaker: Carr
a08_0463621.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Your state vector update is complete and verified. You can have the computer back in Block. Over.

a08_0464000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0464000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 46 hours, 40 minutes, 20 seconds now into the flight of Apollo 8. Present altitude, 158,396.4 nautical miles [293,349.6 km]. Present velocity, 3,639 feet per second, 3,639 feet per second [1,109 m/s]. As we pick up this conversation, we find the crew undergoing one of the systems procedures, that of a fuel cell purge. Let's pick up that conversation.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay. Going to number 1, O 2 .

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger, Bill.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Old Helmut Kuehnel's kitchen timer's pretty nice. [Long pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger, Bill. You can turn off your H 2 heaters now.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Wilco. [Long pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Bill, we show you 168,000 [means 158,000 nautical miles, 293,000 km] out, and we're getting - still getting pretty good high bit rate off the 30-foot dishes.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay. I'm in Narrow Beam High Gain now. [Pause.] Were you getting good high bit rate on the Omni?

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: That's affirmative. We're back on High Gain now. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay, number 1 O 2 is off, and will you clarify your previous statement. Were you getting good high bit rate while we were on the Omnis about 10 minutes ago? Over.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Apollo 8, Houston. That's affirmative. We were getting fairly good high bit rate with a little bit of noise.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay. Thank you.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger. We only got two things left to do now. We need your crew status report and a redundant component check.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay. Jim will give you the latter - former, and I'll give you the latter.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Bill, EECOM says thanks for the good job of keeping the Omnis moving. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Roger. We'll make any sacrifice as long as they keep an eye on the systems. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Wilco. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Who's on the watch with you?

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: It's just me right now.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: How about EECOM?

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Oh, we have Clint. [Pause.] The Black Watch is watching.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Okay. Stay alert.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger. The Black Watch is watching.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Roger. I'll stay - Roger. I'll stay alert. [Long pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: Okay, Houston. Here comes the status report.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger. We're ready to copy.

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: For sleep - Roger. For sleep, each of us has had two sleep periods; Frank's in his third one right now. Bill's had 6 hours the last time; I had 4 hours the last time. Good to fair, both of us. Frank had 5 hours the last time, of fair [sleep]. And Frank, of course, is sleeping now. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger, Jim. How are the three of you feeling?

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: We're all feeling pretty good now; no problems. We've all had about between 40 and 60 ounces of - or clicks of water so far today.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Okay.

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: The food: we're up to - we've eaten day 2, meal 2 so far. [Pause.] And both of us have eaten the rehydratables and the juices and about half of the solids.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger. Copy. [Pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: The cabin's running slightly cold. We do have one cabin fan on, and we're in full heat, and it's running just slightly under 70. Might be a design note for future spacecraft.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger, Jim. That fan pretty noisy?

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: It's not as noisy as both fans when they're running; we cut it down to one fan.

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger. We keep thinking we hear it when you're talking to us.

a08_0464120.speaker: Lovell
a08_0464120.text: I wouldn't be a bit surprised.

a08_0464120.speaker: Anders
a08_0464120.text: Houston, we're showing a glycol Evap[orator] Out Temp around 44 [degrees Fahrenheit, 7°C], and a Rad[iator] Out Temp of about 28 [degrees Fahrenheit, -2°C]. I wonder if we might try some manual mixing here to raise the glycol Evap Temp Out a little bit? [Long pause.]

a08_0464120.speaker: Carr
a08_0464120.text: Roger, Bill. Stand by.

a08_0464500-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_0464500-pao.text: Who's on the watch with you?

a08_0464500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0464500-pao.text: Oh, we have Clint. [Pause.] The Black Watch is watching.

a08_0464500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_0464500-pao.text: Roger. The Black Watch is watching.

a08_0464500-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_0464500-pao.text: Roger. I'll stay - Roger. I'll stay alert. [Long pause.]

a08_0464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0464500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, we sent a load to the onboard computer to update this state vector. This was sent and verified. Also, that was Jim Lovell along with Bill Anders. Jim indicating that they had narrowed their pericynthion through additional Nav sightings down to 66.8 nautical miles [123.7 km]. Bill Anders obviously very good spirits as you heard through the course of that conversation. At 46 hours, 45 minutes, 5 seconds into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0465300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0465300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 46 hours, 53 minutes, 58 seconds into the flight. Our current altitude on Apollo 8 is 158,873.2 nautical miles [294,232.6 km]. Current velocity, 3,627.9 feet per second [1,105.8 m/s]. We've received a status report from the crew. And we'll pass this along now.

a08_0465415.speaker: Anders
a08_0465415.text: Okay. Houston, secondary loop is coming up.

a08_0465415.speaker: Anders
a08_0465415.text: Okay. We're boiling the secondary Evap, and the temperature's stabilized, and so we're gonna close up the Evap pressure valve.

a08_0465415.speaker: Carr
a08_0465415.text: Roger, Bill. Before you try the manual mixing, we'd like you to give it a whirl at the manual and increase on the cabin temp. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0465415.speaker: Anders
a08_0465415.text: We've done that. [Pause.] We're in full hot, and what is your - what's the lowest Rad Out - individual Rad Out Temp you seen here during our PTC?

a08_0465415.speaker: Carr
a08_0465415.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We saw 26[°F, -3°C] one time.

a08_0465415.speaker: Carr
a08_0465415.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Go ahead with your manual mixing. Suggest you set your Evap Out at about 55. Over.

a08_0465415.speaker: Anders
a08_0465415.text: Okay. We'll give that a try, and let us know if the Rad Out Temps get too low.

a08_0470000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0470000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We now read Ground Elapsed Time of 47 hours. Perhaps it's good to point out again that as we examined the data in the early hours of this morning, we chose not to do the midcourse correction burn at Ground Elapsed Time of 47 hours. The reason we chose not to do this; the data indicated that the burn would be in the magnitude of about one foot per second, This would be followed by a water dump which would have some perturbation on the trajectory and it appeared wise to pass this one by. So at 47 hours, 1 minute now; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0471018.speaker: Anders
a08_0471018.text: Rog. We have it stabilized about 53° [F, 12°C], and we will leave it there, but we'll go back Auto if you start having any concern about the radiators.

a08_0471018.speaker: Carr
a08_0471018.text: Roger, Bill. We are showing 51.4 [°F] here.

a08_0472300.speaker: Carr
a08_0472300.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We're going to have a command changeover to [means from] Honeysuckle in about 2 minutes. Over.

a08_0472300.speaker: Carr
a08_0472300.text: [Correcting himself.] Apollo 8, Houston. That was Honeysuckle to Madrid.

a08_0472434.speaker: Lovell
a08_0472434.text: Roger. Did you delete the cislunar nav exercise at 47:15?

a08_0472434.speaker: Carr
a08_0472434.text: That's affirmative, and we added the extra star sightings to the one at 45.

a08_0472500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0472500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 47 hours, 25 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8 now showing a velocity of 3,603.1 feet per second [1,098.2 m/s]. Current altitude just under 160,000 nautical miles. 159,968.9 nautical miles [296,261.8 m/s]. We have a short strip of conversation with the crew and we'll play that now.

a08_0472743.speaker: Anders
a08_0472743.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0472743.speaker: Carr
a08_0472743.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Buenas dias, muchachos.

a08_0472743.speaker: Anders
a08_0472743.text: Buenas dias. We're going to be answering your calls pretty quietly for a little while here. Try to let the CDR [commander] get to sleep. If you can't hear us, why, just tell us so.

a08_0472800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0472800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. That concludes our latest conversation with the crew. At the present time in Mission Control Center, some members of the Green Team are beginning to arrive. We will have a change of shift within the next hour. And during the Green Team's time aboard, we will cross that great divide in space; at 55 hours, 30 minutes - about 8 hours from now - where, for the first time in a manned space flight, the Earth's sphere of influence will be secondary to another celestial body. Apollo 8 will enter the Moon's sphere at about 55 hours, 30 minutes, At this time the attraction of th

a08_0473307.speaker: Anders
a08_0473307.text: Roger. My two cohorts are going to try and get some sleep here, so y'all might keep a good eye on the systems. I'm going to move over to the other side [of the cabin, to the left seat].

a08_0473307.speaker: Carr
a08_0473307.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're getting low bit rate now. We could do better with a High Gain Antenna [HGA] before you move over to the other side. Over.

a08_0474049.speaker: Anders
a08_0474049.text: Roger, you might just give me a call every now and then, Jerry, to just let me know you're still there, as we're switching antennas, or play some music or something.

a08_0474049.speaker: Carr
a08_0474049.text: Say again, Bill. You're kind of garbled.

a08_0474049.speaker: Anders
a08_0474049.text: I say you might just give me a call every now and then as we switch antennas, just let me know you're still there, or play some music or something, just to make sure we haven't lost comm.

a08_0474049.speaker: Carr
a08_0474049.text: Okay, Bill. Your antennas are looking good now. [Long pause.]

a08_0474049.speaker: Carr
a08_0474049.text: Hey, Bill. If you want music, I'll have Mike [Collins] sing.

a08_0474049.speaker: Anders
a08_0474049.text: Ask him to sing "Anchors Aweigh" will you?

a08_0474300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0474300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 47 hours, 43 minutes, 53 seconds into the flight of Apollo 8. Our current altitude reading, 160,614 nautical miles [297,457 km]. Current velocity in feet per second; 3,588 feet per second [1,094 m/s]. We've had additional conversation with the crew and we'll pass that along now.

a08_0474300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0474300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You no doubt gleaned that last comment when Jerry Carr offered a musical rendition by the oncoming CapCom Mike Collins. Mike just walked into the room a few moments ago. He will take over duties as Capsule Communicator shortly. So at 47 hours, 46 minutes, 50 seconds into the flight of Apollo 8, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0480745.speaker: Carr
a08_0480745.text: On your - on your secondary coolant loop, looks like your back-pressure valve might be slightly open. I suggest you go to secondary coolant loop Evap switch to the Reset position for 58 seconds. Over.

a08_0480745.speaker: Anders
a08_0480745.text: I did that again; I'll try it a third time.

a08_0481004.speaker: Anders
a08_0481004.text: That didn't do it any good, Houston.

a08_0481004.speaker: Anders
a08_0481004.text: Keep an eye on it. See if it starts dropping. It stabilized there right after I shut the evaporator off.

a08_0481004.speaker: Anders
a08_0481004.text: What might have happened [is that] Jim might have gotten the water control valve off before we completely had the back-pressure valve closed.

a08_0481004.speaker: Collins
a08_0481004.text: Roger. Understand Jim turned the water control valve off.

a08_0481004.speaker: Anders
