a08_0481004.text: Roger. We have the secondary water Evap control valve off, but he might have gotten it off on that return pump chart check prior to the time the evaporator back-pressure valve had completely closed, which might explain its lower-than-nominal state pressure.

a08_0483000-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0483000-pao.text: Roger, Bill. We see your secondary steam pressure coming back up slowly, and we would like to just sit and watch it for a while before doing anything else.

a08_0483000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0483000-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston. We're standing by of, or estimating right now a press conference from the previous should begin - a change of shift briefing in approximately eight minutes, shooting for 7:30 Houston time, we want to alert all press people to that fact. While that tape was playing, we did hear an analysis of - from the Surgeon's console here, and they said while they felt the crew was doing better with their little medical problems of yesterday, they didn't feel like they were completely out of the woods yet. They note that they are behind on water and they're apparently be

a08_0483017.speaker: Collins
a08_0483017.text: Roger, Bill. We see your secondary steam pressure coming back up slowly, and we would like to just sit and watch it for a while before doing anything else.

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: Roger. Just wanted to let you know we still have voice contact, and we have the morning news for you. We can give it to you now or some time later. Your choice.

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: Very good. This is the 23rd of December edition of the Interstellar Times a la Paul Haney...

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: Good. We had a big blizzard down here in the midwest; I don't know if you can see that from up there or not. And in Houston, as a matter of fact, it's getting pretty chilly, about 35 degrees [Fahrenheit, 2°C]. And we'd like to know who do you like next Sunday, Baltimore or Cleveland? Baltimore defense looked pretty tremendous yesterday. They put on a great pass rush, and it sounds to CapCom like Haney is trying to con you guys into a bet. Over.

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: I guess you don't if you don't give points.

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: Okay. That's about the size of the news. Houston, standing by.

a08_0491634.speaker: Borman
a08_0491634.text: How are the families doing, Mike?

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: They are doing just great, Bill; just talking to Valerie a few minutes ago.

a08_0491634.speaker: Collins
a08_0491634.text: Oh, well, likewise with Susan [Borman]. Haven't talked to her since last night.

a08_0492000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0492000-pao.text: Apollo Control here. We got a little lull on the conversation. That may be resumed. And in - we'll take advantage of the lull to give you the altitude which is 163,920 [nautical] miles [303,579 km] and our velocity; 3,514 feet per second [1,071 m/s]. If you take three-fourths of that, you can get the distance [means velocity in miles per hour] - I'd read that - it's something like 26 - 26 hundred miles per hour, call it. We'll stand by. Here's more conversation.

a08_0492116.speaker: Borman
a08_0492116.text: Mike, this is Frank again. You tell the doctors I got about 5 hours of good sleep last night?

a08_0492116.speaker: Collins
a08_0492116.text: Roger. Thank you, Frank; we were wondering about that. About 5 hours of good sleep.

a08_0492116.speaker: Collins
a08_0492116.text: How's everything going up there, Frank; y'all three of you guys feeling okay this morning?

a08_0492116.speaker: Borman
a08_0492116.text: Feel fine. Jim went back to sleep. Bill and I are having breakfast and everything seems fine.

a08_0493000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0493000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control here. Apparently we are wrapping up, the crew is now eating and we doubt that we'll get any additional conversation for at least the next few minutes. The eat period extends up to 50 hours [Ground] Elapsed [Time]. We're at 49 hours, 29 minutes. The spacecraft meanwhile has - is about to complete its second - let's put it - let's back off that statement and put it this way. The Earth is about to complete its second revolution under the spacecraft. The spacecraft now, in relation to the Earth, is over Africa and that is its second revolution since the second rev when sudde

a08_0500718.speaker: Collins
a08_0500718.text: Rog. Just checking in with you after about a 45-minute quiet break. Say, we notice on your High Gain Antenna, if you like, you can get a little bit more use out of it by switching to it from an Omni when you have a yaw angle of 90 degrees, 9-0, and a pitch angle of minus 45 degrees. We're noticing that you're staying maybe an extra 10 minutes on the Omni, which is fine; but you could get more use out of the High Gain if you use that procedure. Over.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: Okay, thank you. It's a lot simpler for us, as long as the Omni isn't working. We've got it all wrapped up here on the eight-ball with the roll [garble] pointing to an Omni number. We just switch it; it makes it a lot easier, if it is not bothering you.

a08_0500718.speaker: Collins
a08_0500718.text: Okay. That's fine. We're presently happy with the comm, Frank. We are just trying to be helpful.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: Thank you very much. It's unusual that Mike Collins tries to be helpful, but nevertheless, thank you very much.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: Say hello to Howard Tindall for us, will you? His procedures seem to be working.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: I hope you've got everybody looking this thing over very carefully. One thing we want is a perfect spacecraft before we consider the LOI burn.

a08_0500718.speaker: Collins
a08_0500718.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We concur, and we're doing that.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: And Houston, Apollo 8. The water is in the process of being chlorinated at this time.

a08_0500718.speaker: Collins
a08_0500718.text: Roger. Understand you're chlorinating the water at this time.

a08_0500718.speaker: Collins
a08_0500718.text: At your convenience, we'd like a readout of your Service Module RCS propellant quantities. We haven't gotten one of those so far this flight.

a08_0500718.speaker: Borman
a08_0500718.text: Alright. Stand by. We're just about to - need to change the antenna. I'll give them to you. [Long pause.]

a08_0501214.speaker: Borman
a08_0501214.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_0501214.speaker: Borman
a08_0501214.text: Okay. A, Service Module [quad] A. You ready?

a08_0501214.speaker: Borman
a08_0501214.text: The temperature is about 111 [degrees Fahrenheit], the helium pressure - Do you just want the quantity, or do you want the whole works?

a08_0501214.speaker: Collins
a08_0501214.text: Well, if you're reading, give us the whole works.

a08_0501214.speaker: Borman
a08_0501214.text: Okay. The helium pressure's about 37 [on quad A, that is 3,700 psi, 25.5 MPa], the [fuel] manifold [pressure] is about 182 [psi, 1,255 kPa] and the quantity is reading 80 [percent]. [Pause.] B has got the temperature about 112, the helium pressure about 36.5, the fuel pressure 180, and the quantity about 77. C has got the temperature of 140 - incidentally, those other temperatures should have been 120 instead of 110; I was looking at the wrong calibration here. The pressure is 37, the shield - the manifold shield pressure is about 182, and the quantity's 80. [Pause.] Temperature is - temperatu

a08_0501214.speaker: Collins
a08_0501214.text: Roger, Frank. I read you loud and clear. On the temperatures, quad A and B should both be 120. Roger.

a08_0501214.speaker: Borman
a08_0501214.text: I will trade all that good information for a readout of the actual quantities. If you give us a minute, we'll go ahead and chop - plot them up, Mike.

a08_0501214.speaker: Collins
a08_0501214.text: Roger. We'll stand by, we get them for you.

a08_0501634.speaker: Collins
a08_0501634.text: Apollo 8, Houston. I have your Service Module RCS quantities available. Over.

a08_0501634.speaker: Borman
a08_0501634.text: Roger. We're ready to copy at 50 hours, 16 minutes.

a08_0501634.speaker: Collins
a08_0501634.text: Okay. I have them both in percent and pounds; I'll give you both numbers. The pounds are slightly more accurate for plotting on your chart. Quad A, 72 percent, 219 pounds; quad B, 76 percent, 233 pounds; quad C, 70...

a08_0501634.speaker: Borman
a08_0501634.text: Take it a little slower, Mike; whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa.

a08_0501634.speaker: Borman
a08_0501634.text: Slow up. We just got quad A plotted. They're on separate charts.

a08_0501634.speaker: Borman
a08_0501634.text: Would you give us the O 2 and H 2 as long as we're plotting?

a08_0501634.speaker: Collins
a08_0501634.text: Roger. Stand by for O 2 and H 2 .

a08_0501958.speaker: Collins
a08_0501958.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We've got those numbers in percent. We're going to switch them over to pounds, and in the meantime, we're going to be changing our ground antenna in about another 2½ minutes. You can expect a comm glitch. Over.

a08_0502344.speaker: Collins
a08_0502344.text: Roger. I have your oxygen and hydrogen quantities when you're ready to copy.

a08_0502344.speaker: Collins
a08_0502344.text: Oxygen tank number 1, 270 pounds, 270; oxygen tank 2, 267, 267 pounds. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0502344.speaker: Collins
a08_0502344.text: Roger. On the hydrogen, hydrogen tank 1, 19.7; hydrogen tank 2, 20.1. Over.

a08_0502344.speaker: Collins
a08_0502344.text: Roger. A little bit low on the line on your graph due to the fact they started off low.

a08_0502700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0502700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. We've apparently got a lull in the conversation. We've been listening to the exchange between Mike Collins and Apollo 8 live now, for nearly half an hour. Our present position in relation to Earth, 166 thousand miles - 116, 166,116 [nautical] miles [307,646 km] from Earth. Our velocity in feet per second; 3,466 [1,056 metres per second]. And one-fourth [means three fourths, a quick means of converting feet per second to miles per hour] of that would be about 27 - 2,725 miles per hour. Velocity will continue to slow down to a value of 2,170 miles per hour - miles per hou

a08_0502700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0502700-pao.text: And at the point of lunar capture, or the point of lunar sphere of influence, which we're rapidly approaching; it - and we in fact reach, I believe, at 55 hours - we will begin to see a slight acceleration. I think the biggest unknown that we - we will experience today, at least we'll be filling in numbers in an unknown but at a predicted area, is in the range of temperatures that the spacecraft will be seeing. The - the Earth, even in Earth orbit, the Earth exerts a temperature factor over a spacecraft, even out at 100 or more miles. And the Moon, it's theorized, does the same thing because o

a08_0505446.speaker: Borman
a08_0505446.text: Houston, how do you read? Apollo 8.

a08_0505446.speaker: Collins
a08_0505446.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Loud and clear. How me? Over.

a08_0505446.speaker: Borman
a08_0505446.text: Loud and clear. I was just checking on you.

a08_0505446.speaker: Collins
a08_0505446.text: Roger, Frank. Your 51-hour update of block data will be omitted. The block data you have on board is satisfactory. Over.

a08_0505446.speaker: Borman
a08_0505446.text: Understand. The block data we have aboard is satisfactory.

a08_0505446.speaker: Collins
a08_0505446.text: Right. That's for the flyby and the pericynthion plus 2-hour block update.

a08_0505446.speaker: Borman
a08_0505446.text: Okay. Number - window number 1 and number 5 are clouded, but they may be partially useful. The hatch window is very badly clouded. Window number 2 and 4 are good.

a08_0505446.speaker: Collins
a08_0505446.text: Okay. Understand the hatch window is unusable, 1 and 5 are partially usable, and the rendezvous windows are both good.

a08_0505500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0505500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 50 hours, 55 minutes into the flight. We - Mike Collins just put in a - I take that back. Apollo 8 gave us a call a few minutes ago, I guess to check and make sure our antennas are all switched around, which I believe they have been. We can expect some communication very shortly. We've had a number of calls on conversion charts, and we'd like to pass on to you a few of these conversion tables. Earlier we'd estimated that to get a handy grab on statute miles per hour, simply take three-fourths of feet per second. Of course, the number is somewhere between three-

a08_0510000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0510000-pao.text: Apollo Control here. We'll take advantage here to go ahead and give you these conversion tables that we talked about earlier. If you have feet per second and you want statute miles per hour, you convert by multiplying feet per second times 0.6818. The resulting number gives you statute miles per hour. If you want knots, you take feet per second, and multiply by 0.5925, I repeat, feet per second times 0.5925 gives you knots per hour. If you want kilometers per hour, you take feet per second and multiply by 1.097, 1.097, and you get kilometers per hour. And one other factor to help, particularly

a08_0510000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0510000-pao.text: Apollo Control here. CapCom Mike Collins is sitting back in his seat and apparently we will not have any communication unless it's initiated by Apollo 8. So we will take the line down now at 51 hours, even, into the flight and we're a hundred and sixty - they are 167,000 [nautical] miles [309,000 km] from Earth, moving at a velocity of 3,441 feet per second [1,049 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0511313.speaker: Collins
a08_0511313.text: Roger, Frank. We'd like to ask you about the next few hours in the Flight Plan. We're inclined to let Jim go ahead and sleep and to slip the P23 that occurs at 52:15. On the other hand, we'd think it would probably be a good idea if he returned more to the normal sleep rest cycle; and if you got him up nominally to do the 52:15 work, then perhaps he would be ready to go back to sleep at about 61 hours, when he nominally is expected to do so.

a08_0511313.speaker: Borman
a08_0511313.text: Okay. He's up now, eating. We're planning to go to normal procedures on the Flight Plan.

a08_0511313.speaker: Collins
a08_0511313.text: Okay. That - that's fine then. If - you know, there's no - it's not time critical that P23 be done at 52:15, but if you get up to do it then, that's just fine.

a08_0511313.speaker: Borman
a08_0511313.text: Well, we thought we might give it a try.

a08_0511313.speaker: Borman
a08_0511313.text: This sleep cycle here is - we're just going to have to real-time it, I guess. I'm supposed to be asleep right now but, obviously - or I'm supposed to go to sleep here shortly, but I just got up. We're going to have to play this by ear.

a08_0511739.speaker: Borman
a08_0511739.text: Are the stars in the Flight Plan proper for this next exercise of P23?

a08_0511739.speaker: Collins
a08_0511739.text: We would like to talk to Jim about it when he's ready to copy.

a08_0511739.speaker: Lovell
a08_0511739.text: Good morning, Mike. How you doing?

a08_0511739.speaker: Collins
a08_0511739.text: Fine, fine, Jim. You're sounding good this morning. We'd like to give you a little rundown on these stars. As you can see in the Flight Plan, we've got you scheduled for a number 33, Antares, number 34, Atria, and number 40, old Altair. Now, the first of those, Antares, is in plane; the second two are out of plane. As you know, we would like to get a mixture of the in and the out of plane. Antares, number 33, is close to the Sun, and we expect that you're going to have difficulty getting those measurements on number 33. We'd like very much for you to try, but if you're unable to do number 33,

a08_0511739.speaker: Lovell
a08_0511739.text: Roger. Understand. I'll - we'll go to Antares first and try it. You know, we tried it last time, but I got one set before I lost the Moon completely in the white haze. I'll give it another try, and if it doesn't work out, we will go to Peacock and give it...

a08_0511739.speaker: Collins
a08_0511739.text: That, that's affirmative, Jim, and if neither Antares nor Peacock work, well then, we just will be happy to go with Atria and with Altair. We'd like then to increase the number of sets and do three on Atria, that's, number 34, and two on Altair, number 40; but that's only in the event that you can get neither Antares nor Peacock. [Long pause.]

a08_0511739.speaker: Lovell
a08_0511739.text: Roger. This is 8. Copied. We'll increase the number 34 to three and the number set of 40 to two if we cannot get 33 or 42.

a08_0514755.speaker: Collins
a08_0514755.text: Roger. We're getting low bit rate from you now, rather than high, and on this P23 work, for us to get our data, you're going to have to delay the DSKY display about 10 seconds when it comes up with Noun - Noun 87. Over.

a08_0514755.speaker: Collins
a08_0514755.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're past that [Noun] 87 display now. Did you write down what your trunnion bias was? [Pause.]

a08_0514755.speaker: Lovell
a08_0514755.text: Houston, we haven't started [P]23 yet. Our Cal is zero.

a08_0514755.speaker: Lovell
a08_0514755.text: We're in the process now to - to go to P23 attitude.

a08_0515342.speaker: Collins
a08_0515342.text: Rog. Our downlink data shows that on star 33, Jim's using the lunar far horizon when he should be using the lunar near horizon. Over.

a08_0515342.speaker: Borman
a08_0515342.text: You want the far horizon now, Houston?

a08_0515342.speaker: Lovell
a08_0515342.text: We have far horizon in now, Mike, on 220. I'll check again, though.

a08_0515342.speaker: Collins
a08_0515342.text: Yeah, the - that's right. We're requesting the lunar near horizon as per the Flight Plan, the lunar near horizon. We show that you are using the lunar far horizon.

a08_0515342.speaker: Lovell
a08_0515342.text: Okay. Roger. I thought that you had copied up 220 to me. I'll put it in the near horizon.

a08_0515850.speaker: Anders
a08_0515850.text: Mike, it's getting kind of damp - we're getting a playback, Mike. It's getting kind of damp in here. It might be a good idea to go back into Auto on the temp in - the glycol temp in for a while to try and get some of this moisture out of the cabin.

a08_0515850.speaker: Collins
a08_0515850.text: We concur. We'd like you to go back to Auto on the glycol temp inlet valve. Over.

a08_0515850.speaker: Anders
a08_0515850.text: Okay. And, what was our lowest radiator Out Temp during the last couple of hours while we have been in Manual?

a08_0515850.speaker: Collins
a08_0515850.text: Roger. Back in Auto, and 29 degrees (F, minus 2° C) is as low as we've seen.

a08_0515850.speaker: Anders
a08_0515850.text: Okay. We're showing a cabin temp of about 76. It's very comfortable, but we're getting a lot of condensation on the walls now.

a08_0520500.speaker: Lovell
a08_0520500.text: Roger, Mike. While we are waiting for the spacecraft to maneuver to the Moon, I might note that as we get closer to the Moon, the light from the Sun comes right into the scanning telescope, and it's impossible to use. You have to rely on the sextant alone. [Long pause.]

a08_0520500.speaker: Collins
a08_0520500.text: Roger, Jim. Understand that light from the Sun is coming into the scanning telescope making it impossible to use, and you have to rely on the sextant alone. Can you attach any angle to that? [Pause.]

a08_0520500.speaker: Lovell
a08_0520500.text: Well, Mike, I'm right now at the substellar point of [star] 33 [Antares] and I don't know where the Sun is exactly from there, but that's about the angle. We're - the optics are pointed right at the Moon now.

a08_0520847.speaker: Collins
a08_0520847.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're going to be changing our antennas in a couple of minutes. You can expect a comm switch-over.

a08_0521922.speaker: Anders
a08_0521922.text: Rog. The LMP is going to take a little snooze here for a while. I'm wondering, can you give me a quick - your view of the system status here before I depart, and also give me an idea of when the next cryo stir is due?

a08_0521922.speaker: Collins
a08_0521922.text: Roger, Bill. Will do; stand by. [Long pause.]

a08_0521922.speaker: Collins
a08_0521922.text: Roger. Your systems remain unchanged. They're all looking good. You can go ahead and stir up the cryo starting right now.

a08_0522100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0522100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. 52 hours, 21 minutes into the flight. We have a little tape backed up from the last 20-minute time period since we talked to you, and we'll play that for you. Very shortly we expect to query the crew on their medical status. We've had some communication regarding the system status. Now that's reported to be in excellent shape. Dr. Berry, and his people on the medical console are wondering about the water intake and the food intake which seems to be off, and we don't completely understand the sleep cycle. The crew are grabbing naps or better when they can, and w

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0522519.speaker: Borman
a08_0522519.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Roger. Before Jim makes his next mark [his last on Antares], could he call up Verb 1 Noun 1 [sic]? We missed the last trunnion. Over.

a08_0522519.speaker: Borman
a08_0522519.text: Roger. The last trunnion was 10660.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: 10660. Thank you.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0522519.speaker: Borman
a08_0522519.text: Go ahead.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Roger. Before Bill gets his snooze, we'd like him to give us a PRD read-out on all three crewmembers. Over.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Rog. [Long pause.] CDR is 0.06, CMP is 0.64, and LMP is 0.64.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Roger. Thank you, Bill. [Pause.]

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Looks like I'm the only one that's radioactive.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Understand. [Long pause.]

a08_0522519.speaker: Borman
a08_0522519.text: Okay. Houston, we got three sets [of marks] on 33 [the star Antaries]; we are going now to 34 [the star Atria] lunar far horizon for one set. Don't you agree?

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: We agree. Star 34, lunar far horizon, for one set.

a08_0522519.speaker: Borman
a08_0522519.text: Okay.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Houston, the cryos have been stirred, and could you also give me a quick rundown on how the SPS line temps are doing?

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Roger, Bill. Understand you've stirred the cryos. Last time we checked, the SPS line temps were excellent; they were nice and warm. We'll give you another number right now.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: And - and a PU valve. [Long pause.]

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Go ahead.

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Roger. On your SPS system, your oxidizer is running 75 degrees (F, 24°C); fuel, 74 degrees (F, 23°C); and the PU valve between 78 and 82 (°F, 25.5°C and 28°C) depending on where we measure it. Over.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Real good. Everything really is working fine, Isn't it?

a08_0522519.speaker: Collins
a08_0522519.text: Yeah, it's really humming along, Bill.

a08_0522519.speaker: Anders
a08_0522519.text: Okay. See you later.

a08_0523300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0523300-pao.text: Okay. Apollo Control, Houston here; 52 hours, 33 minutes. We'll just shut it [the line] down. Save wear and tear on the eardrums.

a08_0523757.speaker: Borman
a08_0523757.text: I understand you want two sets on [star] number 40 [Altair], lunar near horizon. Is that right?

a08_0523757.speaker: Collins
a08_0523757.text: That's affirmative. Two sets on number 40, lunar near horizon.

a08_0524225.speaker: Collins
a08_0524225.text: Roger. We missed your last trunnion angle, Frank.

a08_0524225.speaker: Collins
a08_0524225.text: Roger. 21450, and Paul tells me Valerie is over here and wishes Bill a happy nap.

a08_0524225.speaker: Borman
a08_0524225.text: Okay. Thank you. Tell her that he makes us tired sometimes too, will you? [Pause.]

a08_0524225.speaker: Collins
a08_0524225.text: Rog. I'll deliver a modified version of that message.

a08_0524225.speaker: Collins
a08_0524225.text: Roger. On star number 40 that you're doing now, the Flight Plan only calls for one set of marks. You called down two sets, and it's really your choice. Only one is required. We're glad to have the data if you do a second set. Over.

a08_0524225.speaker: Borman
a08_0524225.text: We'll only do one then, if you want to. Our Flight Plan has been updated to include two sets. That is why I called it down.

a08_0524225.speaker: Collins
a08_0524225.text: Roger. One set is - will suffice.

a08_0524728.speaker: Collins
a08_0524728.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We missed the last trunnion [angle].

a08_0524728.speaker: Borman
a08_0524728.text: Very well, I will read it to you; 21455.

a08_0524728.speaker: Collins
a08_0524728.text: 21455. Thank you. Just a matter of interest: it's taking your voice about 1.6 seconds to get down to us.

a08_0524728.speaker: Borman
a08_0524728.text: I'm a little hoarse, that's why. [Long pause.]

a08_0524728.speaker: Borman
a08_0524728.text: Okay. Houston, do you want us to go back to the PTC attitude now and start the rotisserie again?

a08_0524728.speaker: Collins
a08_0524728.text: That's affirmative, Frank. We'll have the PTC attitude for you in just a second here. [Long pause.]

a08_0524728.speaker: Collins
a08_0524728.text: Roger. Those PTC attitudes remain pitch, 224 degrees; yaw, 020 degrees. On the next page, page 2-39 of your Flight Plan, those PTC numbers should be changed to reflect that.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: When you've got a few minutes, we'd like to get a detailed crew status report from you.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Like what?

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Well, like we'd like to know, in the last 24 hours, has anybody had any symptoms similar to Frank's. We'd also like to know - You know, we told you the other day to take Marezine if you like - we'd like to know if anybody had taken any drugs, and then we'd like to talk over there about sleep, rest and water and such.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Okay. Nobody's taken any other drugs; nobody took any Marezine; nobody's sick. Bill took one of those pills, sleep Seconal pills, last night. We - everybody had breakfast this morning and ate most of a meal - 1 day 3 - meal A day 3. What else do you want?

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Well, we'd like to tell you to drink plenty of water. We think your water intake may be down. We copied your dosimeter readings. The only other thing is we just were wondering how you - in general how you feel. We show you'd had about 15 hours sleep total - Frank or Bill about 10 and Jim about the same, and we were wondering just how you're feeling in general.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: We all feel fine; we're going to fix it now so that we all have one more rest period before the LOI.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Roger. Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Lovell
a08_0525223.text: Happiness is bacon squares for breakfast. [Pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: If you don't eat them all, bring them back. We'll polish them off here. [Long pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Okay, Houston. Apollo 8 here. I stand corrected, William had one Marezine. He didn't tell me about it; he snuck it.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Roger. Understand Lovell sneaked the Marezine. Understand.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: That's Bill Anders, though, he took one when he took the - with the Lomotil, when the doctors told him to.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Roger. We copy that. Thank you.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Okay. We're back in the barbecue attitude, starting PTC.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Roger, Apollo 8. Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Mike, we ran the latest state vector we have through the P21, and it showed the pericynthion at 69.7 miles.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: Yeah, we're all having big talks about that down here. It looks like you're giving us a real good comparison on our system. Looking - looking extremely good.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: We've got the navigator, par excellence , here.

a08_0525223.speaker: Collins
a08_0525223.text: I believe. [Long pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Aldrin
a08_0525223.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Go ahead.

a08_0525223.speaker: Aldrin
a08_0525223.text: Rog. What was the time you used on that P21?

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: 69:10 [GET] there, Mr. Slide Rule.

a08_0525223.speaker: Aldrin
a08_0525223.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Mike, I wonder if Buzz wants us to change the time?

a08_0525223.speaker: Aldrin
a08_0525223.text: No, that's fine.

a08_0525223.speaker: Borman
a08_0525223.text: Oh, okay. Thank you.

a08_0530307.speaker: Borman
a08_0530307.text: Roger. Are you going to give us an update for a maneuver PC plus 2 that does not assume a flyby maneuver?

a08_0530500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0530500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 53 hours, 5 minutes into the flight. The spacecraft's 171,360 odd [nautical] miles [317,358 km] from Earth. Its velocity, in feet per second; 3,356 [1,023 m/s]. We've heard from the crew in the last 20 minute time period, a rather complete medical status. They reported that Bill Anders had taken 1 Marezine. They say they're all feeling quite well now as opposed to yesterday. And they also explained their sleep and rest cycle. As a general reference, the spacecraft is proceeding on sort of a nose-down - in a nose-down attitude. If you consider in your mind's eye

a08_0530803.speaker: Aldrin
a08_0530803.text: Rog. Here's a rather brief summary of the updates that you'll be getting. The one that you have now for PC plus 2 following an LOI minus 8 flyby maneuver is still good. That will not be updated. The next update you'll get will be MCC [Mid-Course Correction]-4. After that, you'll get two PC plus 2 maneuvers that assume MCC-4 completed. One will be a minimum Delta-V, and the other'll be a fast return. Do you copy?

a08_0530803.speaker: Lovell
a08_0530803.text: Roger. Understand, and also I take it for MCC-4 you're going to give us a new alignment. Is that correct?

a08_0531600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0531600-pao.text: Apollo Control here. That was Jim Lovell who came back with that snappy line, "happiness is having bacon cubes for breakfast." Our present distance, 171,699 [nautical] miles [317,986 km]. Velocity, in feet per second, 3,349 [1,021 m/s]. An update on the passage into the lunar gravitational field. That event to occur at an Elapsed Time of 55 hours, 38 minutes, 46 seconds. And the - our present weight of the spacecraft is 62,915 pounds, Earth pounds [28,538 kilograms]. At 53 hours, 16 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Roger, Frank. I've got a lot of talking to do regarding TV cameras and brackets and what not. I'd like to start in on it whenever you are ready to talk about it.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Let me get a piece of paper out.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Go ahead.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. First a question. Are you planning to show us TV pictures of the Earth today?

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Well, that's what we wanted to do. It seems to us that's the most interesting thing that we can show you, but we - you know, we had trouble with the lens.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. Well, that's good. All this procedure that I'm going to give to you here is relative to what we hope are fixes to the lens and for looking out your - your rendezvous window at the Earth, and all the gimbal angles and all that good stuff is based toward looking out the window at the Earth rather than at the Moon. Over.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. First, unstow the red filter, the polarizing filter, the red and blue filter holder, and some tape. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Okay. Let me write this down.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Roger. I'd suggest that. I've got a whole page full. [Long pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Okay.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Alrighty. Tape the red filter to the telephoto lens. That red filter is the 25A red filter, not the one that is in the red and blue filter slider.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Attach telephoto lens to camera.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Hey, that - we can figure out how to do that. Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Ensure that the automatic light control, the ALC switch on the camera, is in the In position. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: ALC In. Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Rog. Attach camera to the adjustable TV bracket and attach the bracket to the TV mounting point on the Commander's side of the hatch to point out the rendezvous window number 2. [Pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. And there's a note here that says, 'use dovetail on top of camera.' That's rather than the side dovetail. Use the dovetail on the top of camera for mounting to bracket and place the locking nut on the bracket down, and down means toward your minus-X direction. [Long pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. They say this is - this step I just got through giving you is somewhat complicated. You might want to get the cameras set up early using the instructions I just gave you. When it's properly...

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: We are not reading you.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Roger. I say again, the instructions that I just gave you should end up having the camera looking out the window and about 30 degrees yawed left from your plus X-axis, so I suggest you get the camera set up that way early; and if there are any problems, come back to us; we will talk them over. These mounting instructions are sort of complicated.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Roger.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. The next step: dim the interior lights. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Dim interior lights.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Roger. Next, stop Passive Thermal Control at gimbal angles pitch 224, yaw 020, roll 270. Over.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Pitch 224, yaw 020, roll 270.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Roger. Next, acquire on High Gain Antenna, switch to Auto Track, Narrow Beam upon acquisition. Over.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Got it.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. Yaw spacecraft left to get good view of Earth in your rendezvous window number 2. And you may have to pitch slightly as well, but primarily a left yawing maneuver to get a good view of the Earth.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Got it.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. This maneuver is going to put you very close to your scan limit for the High Gain Antenna, so while you're making the maneuver, you know, check your lights. If your scan limit light comes on, you still have got 15 degrees to play with. But the only message is, should you break lock, then you are going to have to go back and reacquire and do that maneuver over again, because you're going to be very close to the edge of your High Gain Antenna capability.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Thank you.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Okay. And then finally, now that you've got the spacecraft over there, aim the camera as required to include the Earth in the field of view, and do not touch the body of the lens while televising. Apparently, if you put your hands on the lens itself, it causes electrical interference. Over. [Pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Okay. Aim camera and do not touch lens while televising.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Right. And in all this stuff, in all these pictures using the ALC, it's important that you let the camera stabilize for at least 10 or 20 seconds, to let the ALC do its thing. [Long pause.]

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Stabilize for 10 to 20 seconds. Thank you.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: Right, now. We have some additional instructions in case this does not work. They say a full 20, Frank, on that ALC. It requires a full 20 seconds undisturbed for the ALC to properly do its thing. Now if these procedures that I've given you do not work, then we'll be giving you some more, and they have to do with other filters and various combinations thereof. So I'd have the polarizing filter and the red and blue filter holder at hand because we'll be attempting to use those in addition to the red filter if - if this procedure doesn't work.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: All very well, Mike.

a08_0532631.speaker: Collins
a08_0532631.text: That's all we have right now. We'll have a few more remarks on the TV coming up to you later. But I'd suggest that you get set up for this early, and if you have any questions on it, shoot them down to us. We have a bunch of experts down here eager to help out.

a08_0532631.speaker: Borman
a08_0532631.text: Thank you; will do.

a08_0533400-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0533400-pao.text: Right, now. We have some additional instructions in case this does not work. They say a full 20, Frank, on that ALC. It requires a full 20 seconds undisturbed for the ALC to properly do its thing. Now if these procedures that I've given you do not work, then we'll be giving you some more, and they have to do with other filters and various combinations thereof. So I'd have the polarizing filter and the red and blue filter holder at hand because we'll be attempting to use those in addition to the red filter if - if this procedure doesn't work.

a08_0541850.speaker: Collins
a08_0541850.text: Rog. We would like some high bit rate data when you can get us locked up on the High Gain. We haven't had any of that for a while.

a08_0541850.speaker: Collins
a08_0541850.text: Thank you. How's that camera bracket thing working out?

a08_0541850.speaker: Borman
a08_0541850.text: We are doing it right now. [Long pause.]

a08_0541850.speaker: Borman
a08_0541850.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8 transmitting to you on the High Gain. How do you read?

a08_0541850.speaker: Collins
a08_0541850.text: Read you loud and clear, Frank. Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0541850.speaker: Borman
a08_0541850.text: Apollo 8 transmitting on the High Gain Antenna.

a08_0541850.speaker: Collins
a08_0541850.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're loud and clear. Thank you for the High Gain.

a08_0542500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0542500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 54 hours, 25 minutes into the flight. We have some conversation that's come in recently from the crew, we'll play it for you now.

a08_0542500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0542500-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston back. During their television pass this afternoon, we can ex - we don't know exactly what the crew is going to do, but you know from the earlier discussion, they're going to work with the telephoto lens again with a filter application which we hope will enhance the image of the Earth and it's also entirely possible they will swing it around - swing that camera around and take a picture of the Moon. If we are successful, we should see approximately about a quarter Moon - the eastern limb of the Moon - and in what detail, it's impossible for us to estimate. Bu

a08_0543259.speaker: Borman
a08_0543259.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. Are you getting the high bit rate all right? [Pause.]

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: That's affirmative, Apollo 8. We are getting good high bit rate.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: Rog. I've got some more talking to do about the TV any time it's convenient for you.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: Okay. First thing, we've made no provisions in these instructions for taking pictures of the Moon. If you could get some Moon shots after it's all over by looking out a different window or by making some small maneuver, of course, we'd be happy to have them, but the show as scheduled is just out the window at the Earth only. Over.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: The second point is, of course, when you stop your Passive Thermal Control, you're about 90 degrees to the Earth line, so when you make that yaw left, you're going to have to yaw left until your middle gimbal angle is in the vicinity of 60 degrees. You'll get the additional 30 degrees by the offset between where the camera is pointed and your plus-X axis. But the two together are going to total up around 90. We just wanted to make sure that you understood you were going to be working with a large middle gimbal angle. Over.

a08_0543259.speaker: Borman
a08_0543259.text: Roger. We understand that. We also are looking at the Earth right now, and there is a spectacular long thin band of clouds. Looks like it may be a jet stream. It's absolutely spectacular - going almost all the way - or halfway around Earth.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: Roger. Well, you might want to repeat that during the - during the TV narrative, and we also would like you, if possible, to go into as much of a detailed description as you poets can on the various colors and sizes of those things and how the Earth appears to you, in as much detail as you possibly can muster. Over.

a08_0543259.speaker: Borman
a08_0543259.text: Roger. I figure we'll have to do that because I'll bet you - I won't bet, but I bet the TV doesn't work.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: Well, we won't take that bet, but anyway, we are standing by for a nice, lurid description, and we would suggest that you talk a little bit slower than you did yesterday. Over.

a08_0543259.speaker: Collins
a08_0543259.text: And the only other thing on this TV is that the experts tell us that, do not point - with the wide angle lens on the camera, do not point at either the Earth or the Moon. It comes close to damaging the interior of the instrument due to the fact that it's too bright. Over.

a08_0543500-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0543500-pao.text: Roger. Well, you might want to repeat that during the - during the TV narrative, and we also would like you, if possible, to go into as much of a detailed description as you poets can on the various colors and sizes of those things and how the Earth appears to you, in as much detail as you possibly can muster. Over.

a08_0544123.speaker: Anders
a08_0544123.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We're going to have to switch to an Omni.

a08_0545257.speaker: Collins
a08_0545257.text: Roger. Just checking the voice comm, Frank.

a08_0545400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0545400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 54 hours, 50 - almost 54 minutes into the flight and the spacecraft presently 174,800 [nautical] miles [323,700 km] from the Earth. A word or two here on a change in our charts and a change in our reporting procedure which will come up following the passage of what we call MSI or Moon Sphere of Influence. That event to take place in about a half an hour from now. With the reading - the reporting we've given you on distance and velocity is coming from a chart called the Command Service Module Space Digitals and it presently uses, as a reference, the Earth. Now a

a08_0545739.speaker: Collins
a08_0545739.text: Rog. We'll be switching antennas from Madrid to Goldstone in another 3 minutes. You can expect a glitch on your comm.

a08_0550238.speaker: Borman
a08_0550238.text: Houston, how do you read? Apollo 8.

a08_0550238.speaker: Collins
a08_0550238.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're reading you loud and clear through Goldstone. Over.

a08_0550238.speaker: Borman
a08_0550238.text: Okay. We have the television On now, and we're trying to maneuver to the - to the Earth.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Roger. We're maneuvering to position now for the TV. Bill's got it set up in Frank's left rendezvous window, and I'm over in Bill's spot looking out the right rendezvous window, and the Earth is now passing through my window. It's about as big as the end of my thumb.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: About as big as the end of your thumb at arm's length, huh?

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: That's right. And I think what we see now is South America down below us.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Is the TV camera pointed about 30 degrees yaw left from the plus-X axis?

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Stand by a moment. We're checking it. We think we've got it in the right position. We're going into position now.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Houston, are you getting any sort of a picture? [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Negative; not yet. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Okay. Houston, Apollo 8. We should have...

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Hello, Houston; this is Apollo 8. We have the television camera pointed directly at the Earth now and have followed the instructions you gave us.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger, Frank. We're picking something up on our TV. It's not very good so far, but let it sit for a second, and we'll have more instructions for you. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Okay. It[Earth]'s coming into view now, Frank.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: It is?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Yes. We have it in the corner of our screen. You're slightly off on your pointing, but we're getting a darn good look at the corner of it. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's moving off, Frank. It's moving off our - 3 o'clock on our TV screen. I have no idea what to tell you about which way to point. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's moving further away. We've lost it now. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Receiving nothing now. Over.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We're - we're - we're receiving the picture; we're just not seeing the view of the Earth.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Roger. I got you.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Okay. We're just picking it up at 3 o'clock on our screen.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's moving up toward 1 o'clock and in toward the center; keep it going in that direction.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's looking better. You're holding it about 1 to 2 o'clock. Looking better.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: And it's disappeared off to our 3 o'clock. There, it's coming back in now. It's headed toward the center of our screen.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Mark.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's right in the center of our screen. And just hold her - hold her steady. It's really looking good. Okay. We have...

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: What you're seeing, Mike, is a - Houston, what you're seeing is the Western Hemisphere. Looking at the top [left in this image] is the North Pole; in the center - just lower to the center is South America, all the way down to Cape Horn. I can see Baja California and the southwestern part of the United States. There's a big, long cloud bank going northeast, covers a lot of the Gulf of Mexico, going up to the eastern part of the United States, and it appears now that the east coast is cloudy. I can see clouds over parts of Mexico; the parts of Central America are clear. And we can also see the w

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Could you give us some ideas about the colors, and also, could you try a slight maneuver? It's disappearing. We're seeing about half of it. It's going off to our 12 o'clock. Now it's going off to our 3 o'clock. That is the wrong direction. Ya, that's a good direction. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We need another small correction to bring it to our center screen. If you could maneuver toward the terminator; we're - that's the part of it we're missing. We're getting the lighted portion. There you go; that's fine. Stop it right there.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Okay. For colors, the waters are all a sort of a royal blue. Clouds, of course, are bright white; the reflection off the Earth is - appears much greater than the Moon. The land areas are generally a brownish - sort of dark brownish to light brown in texture. Many of the vortices of clouds can be seen of various weather cells, and a long band of - it appears cirrus clouds that extend from the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico going straight out across the Atlantic. The terminator, of course, cuts through the Atlantic Ocean right now, going from north to south. Southern hemisphere is almost complet

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Could you maneuver toward the terminator again, please? [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: A little bit more. Stop right there and hold it. [Pause.] It keeps slipping up a little bit; could you maneuver slightly more toward the terminator? [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: How's that, Houston?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We're getting about half of the Earth, Frank. The top half of it - our top half which includes the dark portion, is obscured. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: How's the definition on the picture?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Looks pretty good.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Can you see cloud patterns at all?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That's affirmative.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Good.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Are you still seeing it, Houston?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Yeah, we're seeing it. We're missing the portion of the Earth that's over toward the terminator. The dark portion of the Earth is - we're not picking up. We're getting about three-quarters or four-fifths of the rest of it.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Roger. I'll move it, and tell me when I'm getting better or worse please.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Good. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Stop right there. That's - that's worse, Bill. Go - go back where you were. You made it disappear to our 3 o'clock. Now it's coming back. [Pause.] Okay. Stop right there. Now you're back where you were, and we need a motion that's about 90 degrees to that last one you gave us. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That's the wrong 90 degrees. 180 degrees away from that one. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Stop right there. [Pause.] Okay. Now we've lost a different half of it. I need a motion 90 degrees to that last one. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That - that's good right there, Bill. That's good right there. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Apollo 8, Houston. If you can stick your polarizing filter in front of the camera without disturbing anything else, it might improve the quality slightly. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Stand by.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger, Bill. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Okay. The polarizing filter's in front. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: How's it now, Mike?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's still looking good. That didn't make much of a change one way or the other, but in general, considering how far away, it's looking excellent. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Well, I hope that everyone enjoyed the picture that we're taking of themselves. How far away from Earth now, Jim, about?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We have you about 180,000 [nautical miles].

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: You're looking at yourselves - [Garble] Jim. You're looking at yourselves as seen from 180,000 miles out in space. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Mike, what I keep imagining is, if I'm a - some lonely traveler from another planet, what I think about the Earth from this altitude, whether I think it'd be inhabited or not.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Don't see anybody waving; is that what you are saying?

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Well, I was just kind of curious whether I would land on the blue or the brown part of the Earth.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: You better hope that we land on the blue part.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: So do we, babe.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Jim is always for land landings.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. This picture is drifting off center again. If you could make another correction to bring it back. I couldn't tell you which direction, but that - you're going the right way, you're going the right way. A little bit more; a little bit more. Ah, whoa, stop right there. That - that's the best centering we've had, Apollo 8. If you could just hold that, that's perfect.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: To give you some idea, Mike, of what we can see: We can - I can pick out the southwest coastline of the Gulf and where Houston should be, and also the mouth of the Mississippi; I can see Baja California and that particular area. I'm using a monocular which we have aboard.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Rog. Understand.

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: This is an 8-power instrument I have.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Right. Well, we are seeing the entire Earth now including the terminator. Course we can't see anything past the terminator at all. Are you able with your binoculars to see the dark horizon? Anything past the terminator?

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: Negative. Mike. We can't see anything past the terminator with the binoculars or without them. This Earth is just too bright, and it cuts down the night adaptation to see anything on the dark side.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Rog. Understand.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Since this is winter - since this is winter time in the northern hemisphere, we can see all of the South Pole and the southern ice cap, and not too much of the North Pole.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Hey, you and Jim better get together. Jim just said he saw the North Pole.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: He is looking out a different window.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: That's what makes it different.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Do you still have the...

a08_0550411.speaker: Lovell
a08_0550411.text: [Garble] the monocular upside down.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Do you still have the polarizing filter in front of the camera?

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: Negative.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Okay.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Try putting it back in front of the camera one more time.

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: [Garble.] Okay? [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: And once again, we need a small attitude correction. Our Earth is disappearing up and to the right. Our Earth and your Earth. The wrong way, wrong way. [Pause.] A little bit more. [Pause.] Okay. That's fine if you can hold it right there. Oops! No, it's slipping back off again. [Pause.] Okay. Keep coming a little bit more, a little bit more. Okay. Ninety degrees to that direction; that's the wrong 90, the other way. There we go. A little bit more. Nope, no, wrong way, wrong way; I'm sorry. Keep coming in that direction. [Pause.] No, it is gone up at our 12 o'clock, to that last - There we go,

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: I hope that the next camera has a sight on it.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Anders
a08_0550411.text: How's that?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Well, that has disappeared, just practically. We're wondering if there was any chance of your looking out one of the other windows and seeing the Moon? Hey, it's coming back in now, Bill. Okay. Hold it right there. That - that - that's fine for the Earth right where you are. That - that's extremely good on the Earth if you can just hold that.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: I don't think we have - It has the polarizing filter in front of it now, Mike.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Thank you, and it's centered very well. We get a very slight improvement with this, but in general, it is very good considering the distance.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: How about the Moon, Frank? Is it visible through one of your other windows? Could you get it visible with a small maneuver?

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Negative. I think we have to save the Moon for another time.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Understand. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: It's still very well centered with your picture. We noticed a couple of jumps in the apparent intensity. Did you make some filter changes?

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Roger. We tried to put that other red filter in front of it, but it didn't seem to fit.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We'd - On a final test when you get down to the end of your allotted time here, we'd like you to remove all filters and let us see how it looks with all filters removed, and then we would like to get several spotmeter readings at the very end after the test. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay. We will be removing the red filter now.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Do you still have us, Mike? The lens [means filter] is off now.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Roger. We have it, and if you could maneuver toward the terminator slightly, we - you would again center our picture. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay. Stand by. [Pause.] How's that? Is that the right direction?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That's the right direction. Keep coming. [Long pause.] Now that's the wrong direction, Frank. Did you...

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: How is it now, Houston?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Well, negative. I need another maneuver toward the terminator. [Pause.] It's drifting off the screen to our 11 o'clock. We appear to need a maneuver toward the terminator, Frank.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: No, that is apparently the wrong way, Frank. We're starting to lose the picture. There you go. That - that's the correct way. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay, Houston. How's that for today?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That's just fine, Frank. That's great. We would like to, at the conclusion here, take three spotmeter readings. You can do that at any time at your convenience. We'd just like to get some after-the-fact readings on the Earth's intensity.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Roger. Jim has got the spotmeter on now.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Thank you.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Is it centered now, Houston?

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Not quite, Frank. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: That's good right there. Hold that right there. That's good. That's perfect. [Pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Okay, Earth. This is Apollo 8 signing off for today.

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: Good show, Apollo 8. We appreciate it. See you mañana.

a08_0550411.speaker: Borman
a08_0550411.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_0550411.speaker: Collins
a08_0550411.text: We got Haney down here following your trajectory, so all's well. He says you're 10 minutes from the Moon's sphere of influence.

a08_0550800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0550800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. And Frank Borgan - Borman has come up a little bit earlier - a little earlier than anticipated, but let's buzz this picture out. It is - The bright blob on the upper right of the screen is the Earth.

a08_0550800-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0550800-pao.text: Okay. It[Earth]'s coming into view now, Frank.

a08_0550800-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0550800-pao.text: Yes. We have it in the corner of our screen. You're slightly off on your pointing, but we're getting a darn good look at the corner of it. [Pause.]

a08_0550800-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0550800-pao.text: It's moving off, Frank. It's moving off our - 3 o'clock on our TV screen. I have no idea what to tell you about which way to point. [Pause.]

a08_0550800-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0550800-pao.text: It's moving further away. We've lost it now. [Long pause.]

a08_0551400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0551400-pao.text: That's the North Pole at the lower left portion of the Earth at about 8 o'clock.

a08_0551400-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0551400-pao.text: We're getting about half of the Earth, Frank. The top half of it - our top half which includes the dark portion, is obscured. [Pause.]

a08_0552400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0552400-pao.text: Our present distance from Earth is 175,803 [nautical miles, 325,587 km] - 175,803.

a08_0552400-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_0552400-pao.text: Negative. I think we have to save the Moon for another time.

a08_0552600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0552600-pao.text: The spacecraft is almost directly over dead center South America. This picture is being - beamed and received simultaneously through our antenna at Madrid and at Goldstone, California.

a08_0552600-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_0552600-pao.text: Okay. Stand by. [Pause.] How's that? Is that the right direction?

a08_0552600-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_0552600-pao.text: That's the right direction. Keep coming. [Long pause.] Now that's the wrong direction, Frank. Did you...

a08_0553000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0553000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We think that wraps up our television viewing for the day. The pictures started - I have to go back and get a hack on it. I would estimate about 5 minutes off 2 [o'clock]. Stand by and we'll get an exact start time. We'd not anticipated the starting of the pass until about 5 or 6 minutes after the hour. The crew moved in on us a little early as they did yesterday. I guess maybe we should have anticipated it, and when we began receiving a signal through Goldstone. Stand by one. We've had word from our station on Goldstone that they suspect their reception may be

a08_0553328.speaker: Borman
a08_0553328.text: Houston, Apollo 8's returning to the PTC mode.

a08_0553328.speaker: Collins
a08_0553328.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Understand; returning to PTC. Thank you.

a08_0553328.speaker: Collins
a08_0553328.text: You can tell Jim he's getting pretty ham-handed with that P21; he got a perilune altitude three-tenths of a mile off what we're predicting down here.

a08_0553328.speaker: Collins
a08_0553328.text: Rog. Apparently, he got 69.7 [nautical miles], and the RTCC [Real Time Computer Complex] says 70.

a08_0553328.speaker: Borman
a08_0553328.text: Are we going to leave it at that, or we going to correct it to make it lower?

a08_0553328.speaker: Collins
a08_0553328.text: We're - we're talking about it, Frank. [Long pause.]

a08_0553328.speaker: Borman
a08_0553328.text: We got a lumen riding - reading [of the Earth] of about between 1 and 1.25 thousand - 1.25 K.

a08_0553328.speaker: Collins
a08_0553328.text: Rog. Understand; between 1 and 1.25 K. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_0553328.speaker: Lovell
a08_0553328.text: Roger. If you put your CM TLM to Accept, we'll send you our state vector.

a08_0553800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0553800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 55 hours, 38 minutes into the flight. And we've been asked for a reaction here in the Control Center during that television passage. I think the remark from Lovell that got the most reaction was in his description of the blue and brown Earth and not being sure whether he would land on it. This triggered a tremendous spike of laughter, the likes of which I can't recall, which immediately settled down to business. And in general, the room the - there was just zero talking going on in the room at the time, except what we all heard from Mike Collins in an exchang

a08_0553800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0553800-pao.text: And that wraps it up from - from Apollo 8. Now - now presently 33,681 [nautical] miles [62,377 km] from the Moon and moving in a Moon related velocity, 3,989 feet per second [1,216 m/s]. At 55 hours, 42 minutes into the mission; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_0554503.speaker: Borman
a08_0554503.text: How does everything look, Mike, all our systems and everything? See any switches out of place?

a08_0554503.speaker: Collins
a08_0554503.text: Negative. I'll take a check around here, but it is looking good. Just a second.

a08_0554503.speaker: Borman
a08_0554503.text: We're all over the cabin, and like monkeys, and I wanted to make sure we didn't hit anything. [Long pause.]

a08_0554503.speaker: Collins
a08_0554503.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Everything's looking good down here. All switches and systems are Go.

a08_0555025.speaker: Borman
a08_0555025.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How are you reading on Omni D?

a08_0555025.speaker: Collins
a08_0555025.text: We're reading you loud and clear, Frank.

a08_0555025.speaker: Borman
a08_0555025.text: Okay. We're reading you loud and clear also. Thank you.

a08_0555025.speaker: Collins
a08_0555025.text: We're having a playback of your TV show. Still enjoying it down here. [Pause.] It was better than yesterday because it didn't preempt the football game.

a08_0555025.speaker: Borman
a08_0555025.text: Thank you. Don't tell me they cut off a football game; didn't they learn from Heidi?

a08_0555025.speaker: Collins
a08_0555025.text: Well, you and Heidi are running neck and neck in the telephone call department.

a08_0560300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_0560300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here. 56 hours, 3 minutes into the flight. And in the last 15 to 20 minutes, we had a most interesting discussion with the crew. Like getting Frank Borman's reactions primarily to the television pass. He was advised by Mike Collins that fortunately today, those spectacular views of the Earth had no competition - had no football games to compete with and Borman allows as how he hopes that a football game wasn't stopped to see the view from space. That pretty well sums up Frank Borman's extraordinary interest in the game of football. Here's the conversation.

a08_0561006.speaker: Borman
a08_0561006.text: Hey, Jerry, how much water does this - the water dispenser in the Lower Equipment Bay, the one that puts out hot and cold water - how much comes out of that with each shot?

a08_0561006.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0561006.text: Stand by. I'll take a check on that. And, by the way, welcome to the Moon's sphere.

a08_0561006.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0561006.text: The Moon's sphere - you're in the influence.

a08_0561006.speaker: Borman
a08_0561006.text: That's better than being under the influence. [Long pause.]

a08_0561006.speaker: Borman
a08_0561006.text: My handy LMP had his schematics out at the drop of a hat and informs me that it's one ounce per cycle. [Long pause.]

a08_0561006.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0561006.text: Apollo 8, looks like the flying EECOM and the ground EECOM [Charles Dumis] came to a dead heat on that one.

a08_0561006.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0561006.text: Rog. We got the same answer at the same time. [Pause.]

a08_0561006.speaker: Borman
a08_0561006.text: I'll have Bill put it - I'll have Bill put it on the tape recorder and send it down to you.

a08_0563705.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0563705.text: Okay, 8. We want to run a little exercise on the ground here to ensure that we're able to dump the tape and bring the voice portion back to Houston in a timely manner. So we plan to dump your tape, and we're going to exercise the procedures on the ground to get it back here and take a listen to it. We believe that we have something on the tape already unless you have recorded over it after the last dump. Just to make sure, we'd like to have you just say a few words, give us a short count or something on the tape and anything else that you might want to put on there. And we're going to do this

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: ...hazy, so we haven't really taken too many pictures on the way out. Every now and then we have taken a shot with the 70-millimeter camera and 80-millimeter lens at f/11, 1/250th, but it's questionable how good these will be, because of the haze on the windows.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Another problem has been trying to record the development of the smear on the windows. Seemed to come pretty quick on window number 3. And the technique of - of taking a picture when the Sun is 85 degrees incidence is not possible, because the window frames are so thick that you can't get any Sun on them with an 85-degree incidence. What pictures have been taken, have been taken about 60 to 70 degrees incidence with various f-stops.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Anybody else have anything for the record?

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Yeah, you might mention about this hard thing to open here.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: One point we might mention is that the foodbox doors are hard to close. Looks like the foodbox has split out a little bit on the left....

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: ...left side. And in - look's like we've gotten the handle bent in trying to close the door. We're able to lock it on one side now, on the right side, but not on the left. The food has generally been good, particularly the last meal: butterscotch pudding, beef stew, grapefruit drink, and chicken soup. Notable...

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_0563944-onboard.text: ...the notable, mainly notable ones were the grapefruit drink and the butterscotch pudding.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Well, Bill, you might mention the hot water makes a big improvement, too.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Jim Lovell says the hot water makes a big improvement. The meals I've had have been quite tasty though none of us have really gone overboard for the little bread cru - cubes and cereal cubes.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Also, I'd like to suggest that if they ever fly one of these TV cameras again, they put a - some kind of a sight on it. Sort of ridiculous to have a 9-degree field-of-view lens with no way of aiming it except for looking down the side or putting some chewing gum on the top.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Also might tell Doc Frome that his toothpaste tastes pretty good. I don't know what kind of job it does on your teeth, but it's nice for settling your stomach after dinner.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard.text: We used it for frosting on the fruitcake.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard.text: Jim Lovell is be - engaged in an activity which I shan't describe, so I think I'll cut this short and get my oxygen mask.

a08_0563944-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard.text: But that could be improved, also [laughter].

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: ...hazy, so we haven't really taken too many pictures on the way out. Every now and then we have taken a shot with the 70-millimeter camera and 80-millimeter lens at f/11, 1/250th, but it's questionable how good these will be, because of the haze on the windows.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Another problem has been trying to record the development of the smear on the windows. Seemed to come pretty quick on window number 3. And the technique of - of taking a picture when the Sun is 85 degrees incidence is not possible, because the window frames are so thick that you can't get any Sun on them with an 85-degree incidence. What pictures have been taken, have been taken about 60 to 70 degrees incidence with various f-stops.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Anybody else have anything for the record?

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Yeah, you might mention about this hard thing to open here.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: One point we might mention is that the foodbox doors are hard to close. Looks like the foodbox has split out a little bit on the left....

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: ...left side. And in - look's like we've gotten the handle bent in trying to close the door. We're able to lock it on one side now, on the right side, but not on the left. The food has generally been good, particularly the last meal: butterscotch pudding, beef stew, grapefruit drink, and chicken soup. Notable...

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Borman
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: ...the notable, mainly notable ones were the grapefruit drink and the butterscotch pudding.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Well, Bill, you might mention the hot water makes a big improvement, too.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Jim Lovell says the hot water makes a big improvement. The meals I've had have been quite tasty though none of us have really gone overboard for the little bread cru - cubes and cereal cubes.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Also, I'd like to suggest that if they ever fly one of these TV cameras again, they put a - some kind of a sight on it. Sort of ridiculous to have a 9-degree field-of-view lens with no way of aiming it except for looking down the side or putting some chewing gum on the top.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Also might tell Doc Frome that his toothpaste tastes pretty good. I don't know what kind of job it does on your teeth, but it's nice for settling your stomach after dinner.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: We used it for frosting on the fruitcake.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Anders
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: Jim Lovell is be - engaged in an activity which I shan't describe, so I think I'll cut this short and get my oxygen mask.

a08_0563944-onboard-notch.speaker: Lovell
a08_0563944-onboard-notch.text: But that could be improved, also [laughter].

a08_0564420.speaker: Anders
a08_0564420.text: Houston, Houston, this is Apollo 8. Over.

a08_0564420.speaker: Anders
a08_0564420.text: Okay. Ken, we put a few comments on the last of the tape after we heard from you, and it's being rewound now, and you can have it as soon as we get it back to the beginning.

a08_0564420.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0564420.text: Okay. We'll have to wait. It looks like you are going out of the attitude to use High Gain. We'll catch it next time around and then dump it.

a08_0564420.speaker: Anders
a08_0564420.text: Okay. I notice it's been in high bit rate, so it will probably take quite a while.

a08_0571644.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0571644.text: Rog. Do you think you're in a position where we could use the High Gain?

a08_0571905.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0571905.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're dumping at this time.

a08_0571905.speaker: Anders
a08_0571905.text: We ought to also get a check on it at low bit rate for DSE voice, Ken.

a08_0571905.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0571905.text: Apollo 8, are you saying that everything that's on there now is in high bit (rate)?.

a08_0571905.speaker: Mattingly
a08_0571905.text: Okay. We'll take a look at it then. If there wasn't anything that was previously recorded in low bit, why, we'll come back and maybe take a look at that, too.

a08_0571905.speaker: Anders
a08_0571905.text: Okay. We might get - wait 'til - wait until we get in a little closer to the Moon to put as big a strain on it as we can.

a08_0573200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
