a08_1073837.text: Rog. You should have flashing 37 on your DSKY now, and without releasing that flashing 37, go ahead with the Verb 25, et cetera .

a08_1073837.speaker: Lovell
a08_1073837.text: Oh, Roger. Okay. I see what you mean. Okay. We'll insert Verb 25, Noun 07 Enter, 77 Enter, 40 Enter, Enter, then reinsert Verb 37 Enter, 00 Enter.

a08_1073837.speaker: Collins
a08_1073837.text: That's all correct. And if you've got any questions about that, we would be happy to answer them.

a08_1073837.speaker: Lovell
a08_1073837.text: Roger. Are we cleared to do that now?

a08_1073837.speaker: Collins
a08_1073837.text: That's affirmative, Jim.

a08_1073837.speaker: Lovell
a08_1073837.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_1073837.speaker: Borman
a08_1073837.text: Hey, Mike, this is Frank.

a08_1073837.speaker: Collins
a08_1073837.text: Go ahead, Frank.

a08_1073837.speaker: Borman
a08_1073837.text: Is there any danger that this might have screwed up any other part of memory that would be involved with entry or anything like that? [Pause.]

a08_1073837.speaker: Collins
a08_1073837.text: Frank, all indications are that there is absolutely no problem with anything in the computer memory other than the W-matrix. However, we are continuing to look at it, and if there is any doubt in our mind, we will ask you to dump the memory locations for us later. Over.

a08_1073837.speaker: Borman
a08_1073837.text: Okay. Fine.

a08_1074400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1074400-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 107 hours, 44 minutes into the flight. And the exhaustive business of checking the onboard computer continues. We're 157,989 [nautical] miles [292,596 km] from home, moving at a velocity of 4,464 feet per second [1,361 m/s]. Our weight is down to 31,679 pounds [14,369 kg]. Here's how the conversation's been running.

a08_1075641.speaker: Collins
a08_1075641.text: Roger, Jim. We thought you might be interested in knowing, based on 2½ hours worth of track after your last midcourse, and looking ahead, we're predicting that the midcourse correction at 122 hours will be less than 1 foot per second. And keeping on going to Entry Interface minus 2 hours, we're predicting a 2-foot-per-second midcourse at that time. Now those numbers will be refined; we'll get about another 8 hours of track on you before we amend them. Over.

a08_1075641.speaker: Lovell
a08_1075641.text: Sounds like we're on a pretty good trajectory.

a08_1075641.speaker: Lovell
a08_1075641.text: After we do these next P23s, I'll see what our P37 gives us. What's that midcourse, 122 hours, that has practically zero?

a08_1075641.speaker: Collins
a08_1075641.text: Yeah. It's looking to be less than 1 foot per second, about four-tenths of a foot per second right now. And then the one before entry, at 2 hours before Entry Interface, is looking to be about 2 feet per second. [Pause.]

a08_1075641.speaker: Lovell
a08_1075641.text: Roger. Okay. Well, I'll - I'll run a P37, and we can just compare the difference.

a08_1080759.speaker: Anders
a08_1080759.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Over. [No answer.]

a08_1080759.speaker: Anders
a08_1080759.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Over.

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1080759.speaker: Anders
a08_1080759.text: Roger. You got the J.O.D. back on watch again. We want to make sure we don't overdo the star sightings at the expense of thermal control, so you might keep an eye on us and give us a No-Go if we start getting too hot on one side.

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Roger. Will do, Bill. Has Jim gone to bed?

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: No, I'm right here, Mike. We're going to start doing cislunar nav right now, and Bill's up in the left-hand seat.

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Rog. Understand you're going to do some P23s now, huh? We thought you were going to take a rest and do them later.

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: No, Frank's asleep now. We'll get these out of the way. So I'm going over to do a trunnion alignment at this time, and then we'll go into the P23. [Pause.]

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Okay, Jim. There's one thing before you get started on the P23. What we told you before, we still think is absolutely correct. The only thing in the computer memory that is changed by that P02 [means P01] is the W-matrix. However, as an additional precaution, we'd like to dump the computer memory and go through it and check it bit by bit and make sure everything is exactly copacetic. Over.

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: Okay. Do you want to do that now?

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Affirmative. We're getting Goldstone configured for it; it'll be just a minute. And while we're doing that, I can read you the procedure if you're ready to copy.

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: Okay. Stand by one, and I'll be ready to copy pretty soon.

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: Go ahead.

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Okay. We'd like a Verb 01 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, and then we'd like you to read us register 1. Register 1 we expect will be a 10000, 1 0 0 0 0. And if register 1 is equal to that, then what that means is that the computer will dump its erasable memory twice. That's 10,000 numbers, twice number for the erasable memory dump. If it's not reading 10000, then we'll ask you to make it read 10000 by going Verb 21 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, 10000 Enter. And after you've done that, then the dump Verb is Verb 74 Enter, and that will automatically dump the total erasable memory twice, and return you to

a08_1080759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1080759.text: Okay. The procedure will be Verb 01 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, and read out register 1. If it's 10000, the memory - the computer will then dump the memory twice if properly configured. If not, we have to load in 10000, and we do that by going Verb 21 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, 10000 Enter, and Verb 74 Enter. Now if register 1 does read 10000, we'll still have to do the Verb 74 Enter, is that correct?

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: That's affirmative. That Verb 74 Enter is what starts the dump. Then we, just prior to that, want to make sure we got 10000 in register 1. And just hang loose one on Goldstone here; we're getting it configured.

a08_1080759.speaker: Anders
a08_1080759.text: Roger. You need the High Gain, Mike?

a08_1080759.speaker: Collins
a08_1080759.text: Negative. We won't need the High Gain.

a08_1080759.speaker: Anders
a08_1080759.text: Okay.

a08_1081200-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1081200-pao.text: Okay. The procedure will be Verb 01 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, and read out register 1. If it's 10000, the memory - the computer will then dump the memory twice if properly configured. If not, we have to load in 10000, and we do that by going Verb 21 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, 10000 Enter, and Verb 74 Enter. Now if register 1 does read 10000, we'll still have to do the Verb 74 Enter, is that correct?

a08_1081521.speaker: Collins
a08_1081521.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Goldstone is all ready, and you can go ahead with that procedure, Jim.

a08_1081521.speaker: Lovell
a08_1081521.text: And do you want the Verb 74 now?

a08_1081759.speaker: Collins
a08_1081759.text: Roger. Have you done the Verb 74 Enter yet?

a08_1081759.speaker: Lovell
a08_1081759.text: No, I'm waiting for your command.

a08_1081759.speaker: Collins
a08_1081759.text: Okay. I'm sorry; you must have missed it. You can go ahead right now, Jim; we're all set.

a08_1081900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1081900-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston at 108 hours, 12 minutes into this flight. Frank Borman is now retired for a night's sleep. Jim Lovell is still going through his computer check with the ground, and Bill Anders is up and about. Refers to himself as the JOD, which I believe means Junior Officer of the Day. Here's some conversation.

a08_1081900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1081900-pao.text: Apollo Control here. Spacecraft's 156,460 [nautical] miles [289,764 km] from Earth, moving now at a speed of 4,493 feet per second [1,369 m/s]. And at 108 hours, 19 minutes; that's our status.

a08_1082018.speaker: Collins
a08_1082018.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Jim, the dump is complete. You can go ahead and do whatever you like with your computer now.

a08_1082018.speaker: Anders
a08_1082018.text: We're going to be restricted to P23 for a while.

a08_1082018.speaker: Collins
a08_1082018.text: Just don't let Anders touch the computer.

a08_1082018.speaker: Anders
a08_1082018.text: I haven't yet, and I don't plan to.

a08_1082018.speaker: Collins
a08_1082018.text: Roger. We concur with that decision.

a08_1082217.speaker: Collins
a08_1082217.text: Oh, we've just been honored by the presence of Mr. Neil Armstrong who is now standing by the CapCom console, alert and eager.

a08_1082217.speaker: Lovell
a08_1082217.text: Roger. Ask him how the stock market's doing.

a08_1082217.speaker: Collins
a08_1082217.text: Tears are rolling down his face.

a08_1082625.speaker: Collins
a08_1082625.text: Roger. Well with the computer, we sort of got behind in our promise of music. are you still wanting it?

a08_1082625.speaker: Anders
a08_1082625.text: Just so Neil doesn't accompany it.

a08_1082625.speaker: Collins
a08_1082625.text: Neil says you're in luck; he has a cold today. [Long pause.]

a08_1082928.speaker: Anders
a08_1082928.text: Must be the wrong speed. [Long pause.]

a08_1082928.speaker: Anders
a08_1082928.text: Roger, Mike. That's real nice, but if you don't mind, you'd better hold it off until we get this tracking test done. [Garble].

a08_1082928.speaker: Anders
a08_1082928.text: Sounds like it is [was] being run at the wrong speed. [Pause.]

a08_1082928.speaker: Collins
a08_1082928.text: It doesn't sound very good to us either.

a08_1082928.speaker: Anders
a08_1082928.text: Coming through nicely, though, Mike. You're coming through nicely, Mike; maybe you could just sing a little bit. [Pause.]

a08_1083400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1083400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 108 hours, 29 minutes. The crew has asked for some music to pass away the hours on this Christmas evening. Here's how the conversation is going and here's - here's what we're piping up.

a08_1083400-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1083400-pao.text: Coming through nicely, though, Mike. You're coming through nicely, Mike; maybe you could just sing a little bit. [Pause.]

a08_1083400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1083400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control here. Apparently, the music didn't sound at just the right speed to Bill Anders, or it may have somehow interrupted the other activities on board. Whatever the reason, he gave us a call and asked us to stop it with the music, so we have. At 108 hours, 34 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1083400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1083400-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 108 hours, 54 minutes into the flight. Since our last report we've had no communications with the crew. Very, very quiet. These hours this afternoon, as you might have assumed, might be contrasted with the last several revs, perhaps earlier than that. Maybe the last 10 or 12 hours of a long-duration mission. The crew feels - senses that it is all down hill, which of course, it is. The only thing that is different here is, that we still have 37 hours to go, and - before splashdown. But subjectively, it's very much like the - the last revs of an Earth orbital miss

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Roger, Mike. How are our temperatures looking across the Service Module? Could it be Go here for a shoot in another couple sets on this next start?

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Yeah, I'm monitoring them. They look real good to me, Bill. Just a second and I will check with the experts. [Pause.] Yeah, you're just fine, Bill, on your quad temps.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: And SPS is okay?

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Affirmative. SPS is looking good also.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Apollo 8.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Go ahead, Mike.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Roger, Bill. Because of this W-matrix thing, we'd like to add some more star sightings when Jim gets through with the series that he's currently on. And I have the information relevant to them when you're ready to copy.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Go ahead.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Okay. This is - we'd like him to do them, as I say, whenever he is through the series he's on now, and they're the same ones that are printed on your Flight Plan page 2-86. The first one, we'd like to increase to two sets; the second one, we'd like to increase to two sets, making a total of five sets on those stars on page 2-86. Do you copy?

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Okay. The other change...

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders (talking over Collins)
a08_1085636.text: How come we have to...

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: ...is on an elapsed time of 120 - a hundred and twenty hours: we'd like to increase that P23 work, the first star, change from one set to two sets. The second star from one to two...

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute, Mike.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Okay.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Okay. Looking for the page; I got it now.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Okay. The first star, make two sets; second star, two sets; for a total of five sets.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Okay.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: And if you're in a copying mood, I have, would you believe, a couple of changes to your entry checklist which I'd like to read up to you sometime today or tomorrow.

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Okay. Why don't we get them here after this one set of stars.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Very good. [Long pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Roger, Bill. I was just given a new one here. While you've got your Flight Plan out, this would be 130 hours GET, and you got that page?

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: I just put it away, but I'll get it out again. Wait a minute.

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Yeah, I'm sorry about that. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: We're neat up here. Not sloppy. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Roger. At 130 hours GET, star 02: Where it is printed two sets, we'd like to make that only one set; and then we would like to add star 11, star one - one, lunar far horizon, two sets. Over. [Pause.]

a08_1085636.speaker: Anders
a08_1085636.text: Okay.

a08_1085636.speaker: Lovell
a08_1085636.text: Hey, Mike. Is MIT slipping in the back door?

a08_1085636.speaker: Collins
a08_1085636.text: Not - Not really, Jim. It has to do with - with this W-matrix. You remember that we reinitialized it in lunar orbit, and then we worked on it as you came back on the previous sightings you made, and now we've - we've gone and reinitialized it again at this point. And we'd like to restore it to its former size and shape and what-not.

a08_1085636.speaker: Lovell
a08_1085636.text: Okay. I understand.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: Mike, I've got the entry checklist out now. You want to give me that update?

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Okay, Bill. Thank you. The first one is on page E-7.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: Okay, Mike. Ready to go. Now I know why Neil was over there.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: No. You can't blame it on him. Page E-7 under CM RCS preheat, halfway down where it says "Up Telemetry, Block" - Are you with me?

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Okay. After Up Telemetry, Block, insert "RCS CM heaters, circuit breakers, two, Close." [Long pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders (talking under Collins)
a08_1091212.text: Let me get them on both [garbled] we're ready.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: ...they are doing there is just making sure you get your heater circuit breaker closed. The next one is on page E-9. [Long pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Roger. On E-9 up near the top under "terminate CM RCS preheat" in the middle there, after "CM RCS heaters, Off, LMP confirm," insert "RCS CM heaters, circuit breakers, 2, Open." That's just opening those two breakers back up.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: And the last change is on page 14. [Long pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: This one should be a favorite of yours. Near the top where it says "tape recorder, Record, Forward" - Are you with me?

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Insert between "tape recorder" and "Record, Forward," insert "Command Reset, high bit rate." Over. [Long pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: How's it going? Do you want any systems dope?

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: Yeah, they hanging together? I haven't even looked at them for the last half an hour. I've been over here in the Sun.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Yeah, they sure are, Bill. They can get you any specific numbers, what-not, if you're interested. [Pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: Well, I hate to say I wasn't interested, but I don't need any specific numbers right now.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: On second thought, how's the evaporator outlet Temp doing? [Long pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Lovell
a08_1091212.text: I'm getting a crossed eye looking at this thing. Hey, Mike, as a matter of interest, I've been just looking at the Earth for the last hour and a half and there's two tremendous storms down there. Not too sure where they are, but the vortexes are - are huge.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: That's your first space weather report. That's a manned weather forecast from space, and he's not so sure where it's raining, but it is raining somewhere.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: I'd like to point out that Magellan is not a good analogy. I'd also like to point out that Magellan is not a good analogy. I don't think he made it around.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: I don't know how much detail you can see, Jim, but your sub-spacecraft point is out in the middle of the Pacific Ocean about halfway between Australia and South America. [Pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Lovell
a08_1091212.text: Rog. Okay. The next time I take a look, I'll see what I - I see we're maneuvered to the Moon now. [Pause.] We'll see if we can see our shadow. [Pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: Seriously, has anyone been able to see the spacecraft from Earth, Optically? [Pause.]

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: We don't think so, Bill. We haven't been able to confirm that they have.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: You're coming right down the center line of the airways. If you see the airliners going the other way, you better move over.

a08_1091212.speaker: Anders
a08_1091212.text: That's the first time old Lovell's been on track for a long time.

a08_1091212.speaker: Lovell
a08_1091212.text: Mike, an interesting viewpoint of the nav sightings: maneuvering with the minimum impulse controller on the way home is a lot more difficult than going out because of all the fuel we don't have now. Every little pulse really moves the spacecraft around.

a08_1091212.speaker: Collins
a08_1091212.text: Rog. Understand you have too much control authority.

a08_1091700-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1091700-pao.text: On second thought, how's the evaporator outlet Temp doing? [Long pause.]

a08_1092348.speaker: Collins
a08_1092348.text: Roger, Jim. Dick Underwood's over here. They're getting their film processing all prepared for your film when you get back and tentatively, can you give us some idea of how much you exposed?

a08_1092348.speaker: Lovell
a08_1092348.text: Let me introduce you to the great film man. He'll tell you all about it.

a08_1092348.speaker: Anders
a08_1092348.text: Tell him I hope he can account for haze through the windows. We - on our departure from the Moon, we tried to burn up as much as - of what we had left over, which was quite a bit, and tell him I hope he can develop the high-speed film taken at normal film settings. [Long pause.]

a08_1092348.speaker: Collins
a08_1092348.text: Roger. Understand you used just about everything and a lot of the high speed; you used it to normal settings.

a08_1092348.speaker: Anders
a08_1092348.text: Roger. We got it in the wrong bucket there a couple of times.

a08_1092348.speaker: Anders
a08_1092348.text: We never did have a chance to do any night Earthshine stuff. [Pause.]

a08_1092348.speaker: Collins
a08_1092348.text: Say again about the Earthshine, Bill.

a08_1092348.speaker: Anders
a08_1092348.text: We never did have a chance to do any Earthshine photography.

a08_1092600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1092600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 109 hours, 17 minutes into the flight. And we have had a little chatter with the crew, Bill Anders primarily sitting over in the driver's seat. Here's how that is going.

a08_1092600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1092600-pao.text: And so we get a good something of a wrap-up on our film situation, which we've been wondering about now for about a 24-hour period. And at 109 hours, 26 minutes; with the spacecraft 153,504 [nautical] miles [284,289 km] from home; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1095551.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1095551.text: How are you coming along with your P23 marks?

a08_1095551.speaker: Lovell
a08_1095551.text: My eyeballs are getting square. That's what we've been doing most of the day, Ken. Are you receiving the data down below?

a08_1095551.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1095551.text: Rog. Looks like you're getting some pretty good marks there. We have a pretty good hack on the vector and the matrix, and looks like if you wanted to terminate at this point, that we do have good data.

a08_1095551.speaker: Lovell
a08_1095551.text: Sounds good. I'll terminate after this.

a08_1095551.speaker: Anders (speaking over Mattingly)
a08_1095551.text: We should just as soon not try to do star 01 again.

a08_1095920.speaker: Lovell
a08_1095920.text: Ken, did you have a nice Christmas? [Pause.]

a08_1095920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1095920.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Did you call? [No answer.]

a08_1100500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1100500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 110 hours, 5 minutes into the flight. At the present time here in Mission Control Center, we have just completed a shift change. Our Flight Director at this time is Milton Windler and our Capsule Communicator is astronaut Ken Mattingly. Apollo 8 at this time is at an altitude of 151,789 nautical miles [281,113 km] from Earth and it's traveling at a speed of 4,584 feet per second [1,397 m/s]. Since our last report we've had something under a minute of conversation with the crew. We'll play that back for you now.

a08_1100500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1100500-pao.text: This is Mission Control. At the present time, we understand Bill Anders is flying the spacecraft, occupying the Commander's couch, the left-hand couch, and Frank Borman is getting some sleep. The medic advises that he has been sleeping now for about 2 hours. We expect that shortly, Jim Lovell will also begin a sleep period and we would also expect that Frank Borman would be waking up. At 110 hours, 10 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control.

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Who is this, Ken or Gerry?

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Okay, Ken. We're getting back to the PTC attitude. Would you like us to do this High Gain Reacq test now on the first roll?

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Okay. Look, how about if I just went to Reacq right now? [Long pause.]

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Matter of fact, I'm in Reacq. If you want me to stay here, why, we'll just press on. [Pause.]

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: I guess this step about stopping in roll 150 then really doesn't matter too much then. [Long pause.]

a08_1101552.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1101552.text: That's right, Bill. That was just to let you acquire.

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Man, we can acquire on the run here.

a08_1101552.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1101552.text: Hey, you're getting good at that.

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: That's all they'll let me do. [Pause.]

a08_1101552.speaker: Anders
a08_1101552.text: Okay. We'll keep it here for two revs, Ken. Mike and - Frank and Jim are asleep, and just keep nothing else to do so I'll just keep it going here for two rolls.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Over.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Go ahead, 8. [No answer.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Go ahead, 8.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Well, the Reacq didn't work as advertised. It looked like it went on by the scan limit and into the mechanical limit and followed MSFN around looking out of the corner of its eye on wide beam. And when MSFN came back underneath the spacecraft, why it snapped back on into Narrow Beam. It apparently never broke lock; or if it did, it was only instantaneously. [Pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Rog. It looked like we did break lock there for about 8 minutes.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Well, we might have broken two way lock, but I was still having about AGC right at the noise level, at the minimum reception level.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: When we get out here in the clear zone, when we're definitely out of the scan limit, why, I'll go ahead and go through the Manual and Auto lock-on sequence and switch over to Reacq and see what it does next time around.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Houston. You able to get high bit rate from the omnis now, by the way?

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The omni high bit rate capability is noisy, but usable.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Okay. I think what we'll do here is, if I see the High Gain definitely going past the scan limit before it gets the mechanical limit, I'll go ahead and - if it has - if the Reacq feature hasn't taken over I'll just go ahead and shut it down so it doesn't go bang in the stops. [Long pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: How's that sound?

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: We are talking about it now, Bill.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Okay. [Pause.] It's my understanding that the scan warning limit of this thing is supposed to stop tracking; and it break off lock, and snap on over to the - to the thumb-wheel settings. [Pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Rog. That's my understanding, Bill. We're talking about it right now. I'll let you know in just a second.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Yeah. Probably, Ken, we are not ever losing the Earth present signal.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: That's correct.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Say, Bill. Could you tell us what angles this went through? The curve that we have plotted is apparently the RF limit rather than the mechanical limit; and discussing the function of the Auto Reacq mode, it looks like it's supposed to shift when it hits the RF limit, which is your - should be your Enter set of numbers as opposed to the scan warning limit. And if it went inside of that number, could you tell us about what kind of numbers it did go to?

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Roger. It went past the caution/warning limit to the scan or RF limit, as I understand it. And let me give you a rundown on what it did here.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Okay. Say it slow so I can copy it.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders (talking over Mattingly)
a08_1103559.text: We switched to - we locked on...

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Okay. [Pause.] The antenna went to about 330 to 270 yaw, plus 60 to 80 pitch. [Pause.] Copy?

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Rog.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Okay. The AGC dropped off to what I call our noise level, that was the voltage level on the AGC measured at - integrated when the noise broke in. It was about 11 o'clock position on the gauge, and it looked like it was switching beam widths there off and on. It would pulse up and down, and a couple of times dropped to full-scale low very briefly. [Pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: You got some marks on that AGC that should register in volts, I believe. Do you have an indication other than 11 o'clock?

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Okay.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Copy?

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Well unfortunately, the numbers never got on here. If you look on that chart that Fred Haise has, it shows one at 11 o'clock position which is the noise level. I don't remember what the voltage was. I might have it on my systems book, though.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Bill,..

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Another bit of information. When the antenna... [hears Ken] When the antenna did snap back in, it went to yaw, 80; pitch, minus 5; with Verb 64 reading plus 67 for yaw and minus 10 for pitch.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Okay. Copy all that. I think you have four or five marks on that power meter, don't you? From what you're saying, I take it, it's between marks 2 and 4.

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Yes. Stand by a second. [Long pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Stand by, Ken. I'll tell you what that volt is.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_1103559.speaker: Anders
a08_1103559.text: Okay. It went to about - hovering around 2.4 to 3 volts.

a08_1103559.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1103559.text: Okay. Thank you.

a08_1105011.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1105011.text: Okay. It's not real clear that it did, in fact, get to the mechanical stop, and if it does, the back room people say we can stay up against that stop for a maximum of 15 minutes without doing any damage. And we'd kind of like to track it through one more time as is. We do have the high bit rate capability on omnis. So we'd like to follow through that same configuration for one more rev. [Pause.]

a08_1105011.speaker: Anders
a08_1105011.text: Well, since we're not sure that it didn't get up against the mechanical stop the last time for 10 minutes or so, I don't think it would be too smart to do it this time because we may end up having a switch fail the High Gain position and have lost the High Gain too. [Pause.] Still a long way from home.

a08_1105011.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1105011.text: I'm sorry, Bill. You didn't come through. Say that again, please.

a08_1105011.speaker: Anders
a08_1105011.text: Well, since we're not - it's not clear to me that we weren't up against the mechanical stop for a while the last time around. That might account for 10 minutes of that 15 minutes, and there's no sense in pushing our luck. I think we ought to - if it starts dropping off again, we just - we ought to go and put it back into Manual and take it back where it belongs. [Pause.] We're still a long ways from home, and if that antenna switch fails, it's going to fail the High Gain position, and that's all we got.

a08_1105011.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1105011.text: Rog, Bill. And we'll be making a hand-off on stations here at 55.

a08_1105011.speaker: Anders
a08_1105011.text: Ken, we're going to switch comm carriers here for a second.

a08_1105011.speaker: Anders
a08_1105011.text: Belay that. We'll hold this configuration for a while.

a08_1110600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1110600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 111 hours, 6 minutes. Since our previous report, we've had about 8 or 9 minutes of conversation with Bill Anders aboard the spacecraft. It appears that both Frank Borman and Jim Lovell are getting some rest at this time. We'll bring you up to date on the conversations that have developed, and then stand by briefly for any live conversations with the crew.

a08_1110724.speaker: Anders
a08_1110724.text: It did the same thing that time, Ken. This time the voltage AGC did drop to full-scale low for several seconds, but the antenna does seem to have the capability to look right through the spacecraft, and I guarantee you, the Earth went where the antenna's not supposed to be able to go.

a08_1110724.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1110724.text: Okay. I would just like to confirm with you that it never did go back to the preset numbers.

a08_1110724.speaker: Anders
a08_1110724.text: No, it apparently never lost Earth present signal. It's always - it had - sounds like it was trying to pick up one-way lock all the time, and we usually hovered around 2-volts AGC except for brief periods.

a08_1110724.speaker: Anders
a08_1110724.text: It looks like if they'd had - they should have not had the feature switch into Wide Beam until after it had gone to those preset limits. [Long pause.]

a08_1110724.speaker: Anders
a08_1110724.text: We're back in Auto on the omni.

a08_1111259.speaker: Anders
a08_1111259.text: Houston, CDR is up and manning the helms. We're going to switch comm carriers. We'll be off the air for a little bit.

a08_1111624.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1111624.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8. Loud and clear.

a08_1111624.speaker: Borman
a08_1111624.text: How far are we from home, Ken?

a08_1111624.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1111624.text: Oh, about 152, looks like. That's pretty gross; I'll get you a real number in just a minute.

a08_1111624.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1111624.text: 148,550 [nautical miles, 275,115 km]; that's a good number. [Pause.]

a08_1111624.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1111624.text: And your velocity is about 4,650 [feet per second, 1,417 m/s]. [Pause.]

a08_1112200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1112200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 122 - rather 111 hours, 22 minutes; and at the present time we're standing by for a status report - a crew status report which we anticipate to be coming up from the crew shortly. In that past conversation we heard from Frank Borman for the first time in about three hours and we should be getting a report in that crew status summary from Frank on just how much sleep he did get. We'll continue to stand by for that call to the crew from capsule communicator, Ken Mattingly.

a08_1112200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1112200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. We've been advised that, that the crew status report will probably be a little bit delayed in coming. At the present time Borman is scheduled to be eating and we plan to wait until sometime after he has had a chance to complete his eat period before requesting that status report. At the present time Apollo 8 is traveling at a speed of 4,657 feet per second [1,419 m/s] and our current altitude reading is 148,210 nautical miles [274,485 km]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1113121.speaker: Anders
a08_1113121.text: Say, we're trying to get back on our normal sleep cycle, and I just woke up here a little while ago, so I'm going to try to hit the hay again. It'd probably be a good idea to try another Seconal to try to get with it. What do you guys think down there? [Pause.]

a08_1113121.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1113121.text: Okay. Sounds like a good idea, and if we can get Frank to tell us how much sack time he got, why, that'll go in the log, too. [Pause.]

a08_1113121.speaker: Borman
a08_1113121.text: I was in bed for 7 hours, Ken, and I probably slept for about 4½ to 5 hours of it, anyway.

a08_1113121.speaker: Borman
a08_1113121.text: If you - if you're interested in further reports, we've all had three meals today, and we have drunk a lot of water, and Jim's asleep now. He worked pretty hard this afternoon, but I think we're all in pretty good shape now.

a08_1113121.speaker: Borman
a08_1113121.text: Well, Ken, that just leaves you or I - how about you and I - did anything exciting happen today?

a08_1113121.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1113121.text: Oh, I think you know about all the things that are exciting up on your end, and it's real quiet down here. Everybody is smiling; Santa was good to most of the folks in the world, and everything is pretty calm, like it should be on Christmas.

a08_1113121.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1113121.text: Milt says we're in a period of relaxed vigilance.

a08_1113500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1113500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 111 hours, 35 minutes. At the present time, we're in communication with Frank Borman aboard the spacecraft. Frank has just advised us that he is the only one up at the present time. A short while before that, Bill Anders came on. Said that he planned to get a little bit of sleep. Requested permission to take a Seconal tablet, one of the short-acting sleeping pills carried aboard the spacecraft, and was given a go-ahead to take a tablet. We also received a crew status report from Borman and he reported that all three crewmen had eaten three meals today, said they had b

a08_1113724.speaker: Borman
a08_1113724.text: Hey, Ken, has anybody got any good idea why that quad A tank is running hot, hotter than the rest by so much?

a08_1113724.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1113724.text: Okay. I didn't have an answer when I came on; just a second and we'll check again.

a08_1113944.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1113944.text: Okay. [Pause.] Okay, Apollo 8. Let me tell you what the subjects are that we're going over down here: number one, we're making a review of all the entry procedures and this type of information, and we're going to actually go through and review the entry checklist. We have people that are still working on verification of your erasable memory. We're looking at the EMS problem, and we're discussing the quad temperature, so I'll feed up some of these pieces of information to you as they come along, and right now we're just sort of having a status review.

a08_1113944.speaker: Borman
a08_1113944.text: I don't think the EMS is much of a problem; it just jumps when you go into Auto. I don't believe it'll bother us for entry. I - I'm doing the same thing; I am looking over my entry checklist. One of the first things I see here is a cold-soak, and I don't think we want to evaporate between the last midcourse and entry, do we?

a08_1114500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1114500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. In that previous conversation with Frank Borman, we heard CapCom Ken Mattingly review activities here in Mission Control Center, including a comment on the quad temperatures. These are the temperatures in the Reaction Control System engine quads, of which there are four on the spacecraft Service Module, and we have been observing the temperature of quad A for several hours now. That quad is running about 83 degrees [F, 28°C] compared with 60 or 70 degrees [F, 15.5 or 21°C] for the other three. The assessment here in Mission Control Center is that that is not a problem.

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: Roger. Looking at the Flight Plan, you have a P52 coming up at a 115 hours, and we'll have to do another one at 119:45 in preparation for the P23. And it's acceptable with the ground procedures if you'd like to delay that 115-hour alignment, and do it just once at 119:45, or you can do it there in Flight Plan location. If you want to skip the 115-hour alignment, we could go ahead and start in on the pitch and yaw free PTC mode at this time.

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: Okay. We have a DTO that requests that we do a PTC and go ahead and do it in a minimum impulse mode so that we're not putting any attitude hold corrections in. And we're going to be tracking the attitude excursion, and they want this for something like 6 hours - or until we reach a limit.

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: Cabin's running a little bit warmer today than normal.

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: I say the cabin is running a little bit hotter today than it has been. It seems like this particular PTC alignment gets more Sun in the cabin than the PTC before.

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: Rog. What kind of temperature are you recording now?

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: I just put the window shades up. That'll cool it down.

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: Do you want me to take the pitch and yaw out of Rate Command, right?

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: That's affirmative. You just put it in Minimum Impulse, and then we'll watch it. [Pause.]

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: Rog. And on that quad temperature, the upper limit of that thing is 105 degrees [F, 40.6°C] on the bottle, so we're well below that. We've been watching it, and it is tracking, although it's tracking very slowly as you roll the spacecraft. The temperature excursions seem to be a little sluggish, but it isn't a frozen sensor, and talking a little bit more about that one right now. You might tell Jim the next time he goes to work with the optics, when he works on the trunnion, if he'll go ahead and recycle the Zero Optics switch, he can avoid the problem we had prior to midcourse correction 4. A

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: Midcourse correction number 6 right now looks like zero, and midcourse correction number 7 is approximately 2 feet per second.

a08_1120933.speaker: Borman
a08_1120933.text: Okay, Ken. Now, because we've got on the checklist to initiate cabin cold-soak. This involves evaporating, and I don't think we wanted to do that.

a08_1120933.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1120933.text: Okay. We've talked that over with FIDO, and at 12 hours out, everyone seems to think that we don't need to do it there. But in close, it doesn't seem to have any effect on the trajectory, and what's been suggested if you'd like - we can go over the Entry Checklist and just kind of walk through it on the air with all the people on the console. Right now, you have the team that'll be performing the entry session with you, so we can go over the checklist and run down any questions that you might have. That's up to you.

a08_1121900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1121900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 112 hours, 19 minutes. Apollo 8 is at an altitude of 145,758 nautical miles [269,944 km] and traveling at a speed of 4,709 feet per second [1,453 m/s]. Since our previous report we've had about 6 or 7 minutes of conversation with Frank Borman aboard the spacecraft. He reported that his cabin temperature was running a little bit higher than normal, about 80 degrees at the present time and indicated that apparently the higher temperature is due to the fact that the current spacecraft attitude allowed more sunlight into the windows. We'll playback the tape of t

a08_1122223.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1122223.text: Okay. We've drifted off about 25 degrees now in pitch. I'd like to have you take it back and set up the PTC pointing again at pitch of 10 and yaw, 45; and set up the PTC under control, and then turn your pitch back to minimum impulse. And give us a mark when you've done that, and we'll time the drift rates down here.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: Okay, Ken. I've got them all damped out about as low as I can get them.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: I'll put in a roll right now.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: Takes three actuations to get about - that's about a degree and a half, or a tenth of a de - 0.15 degrees per second.

a08_1122501.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1122501.text: Okay. And give me a mark when you release the Rate Command in pitch and yaw.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: I haven't even got them on.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: When I gave you - when I gave you that mark, that was it.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: It's much more sensitive today than it was when it was heavy.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: Well, the old Earth is getting bigger.

a08_1122501.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1122501.text: Good show. Going in the right direction, then.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: Yeah. I was beginning to get worried.

a08_1122501.speaker: Borman
a08_1122501.text: Ken, be sure and call me if you see the gimbal angles start to get near gimbal lock or anything. I'm a little drowsy still and I don't want to end up with another null attitude, like one's enough.

a08_1123100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1123100-pao.text: This is Mission Control. There doesn't appear to be any further conversation developing at this time. We do have some figures for you on the half-way point in the spacecraft's return to Earth. We anticipate that that will be reached at a time of 126 hours, 3 minutes, 9 seconds in the flight. At that point Apollo 8 would be 103,002 nautical miles [190,760 km] from Earth and would be traveling at a speed of 5,870.6 feet per second [1,789.4 m/s]. At 112 hours, 31 minutes into the flight; our velocity is 4,720 feet per second [1,439 m/s] and the spacecraft at this time weighs 31,649 pounds [14,356

a08_1124257.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1124257.text: Okay. Would you reinitialize the PTC attitude, and let's try that one more time.

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: Is it sleepy out down there, too?

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: I say, is it sleepy out down there?

a08_1124522.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1124522.text: Rog. It's getting pretty good now. I figure it's getting sleepy up there, though.

a08_1124522.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1124522.text: Okay. Well, would you believe that the North beat the South, three to nothing, and they did that all with a first-quarter field goal. [Pause.]

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: Very good. When was the East-West game? [Pause.]

a08_1124522.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1124522.text: And, Frank, we're going over the checklist right now and I'll get back with you on the entry checklist in a few more minutes.

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: Okay, Ken. I think it's a pretty good one; that's one thing we've practiced a lot. But we might as well let everybody know what we're doing.

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: Ken, while we're just killing time here, there are a couple of anomalies we've noticed. The booties, you know, for these inflight coveralls,...

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: ...mine have frayed very badly, and I had to take them off. Also, we had one Y adapter with an open [circuit] in it, and the lightweight headsets were kind of useless.

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: I take that back. I really didn't mean to say that. The lightweight head... - what I really meant to say was - the lightweight headsets are useless.

a08_1124522.speaker: Borman
a08_1124522.text: But these Snoopy hats are pretty comfortable. We've worn them the whole time.

a08_1124522.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1124522.text: Yeah. I noticed that on TV.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: Ken, one thing we're gonna do on these suits, we're going to stow them one under each seat, the way North American suggested.

a08_1125158.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1125158.text: Roger. And you'll be putting the helmets in the food stowage.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: Yeah, I think we'll put the helmets in the food stowage; and any stuff we have to take out of there, we'll just stick in the suits.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: Is the weather still good out there?

a08_1125158.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1125158.text: Oh, it's not quite as clear as it was yesterday, but sure is nice and balmy.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: No, I mean out at 165 west.

a08_1125158.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1125158.text: Okay. Frank, we've got a weather picture here. Their forecast shows 2,000 scattered and 4,000 broken with a high overcast. You might see that as you come down through it, and wave heights 4 feet, wind about 070 at 12 with a 10-mile visibility and perhaps some scattered showers in the area, and this is forecast for the twenty-seventh at 16:00 Zulu.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: I don't think those waves are too high. We're going to have to sit in this heap for about 45 minutes.

a08_1125158.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1125158.text: Okay. We'll - we'll put in a kit for some small waves.

a08_1125158.speaker: Borman
a08_1125158.text: Tell Jerry Hammack that if the waves get high, it's his fault.

a08_1125800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1125800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 112 hours, 58 minutes. At the present time both here in Mission Control Center and aboard the spacecraft it's a relatively a quiet period. Frank Borman continues to be the only one of the three crewmen who is awake at the present time and he's reported on a couple of occasions that he is getting sleepy. Earlier, Frank reported, that he had gotten about four and a half to five hours of sleep and had been in the sleep station for about seven hours. Since our previous report, we've accumulated about five minutes of taped conversation. We'll play that back and th

a08_1125800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1125800-pao.text: This is Mission Control. Apparently a small segment of Borman's remarks during that past conversation were at a low enough level that they did not trip the recording mechanisms for our release circuits. We will have those on a backup tape and they'll be included in the transcript. Generally, those remarks consisted of brief comments on anomalies encountered. Borman summarized about four or five items that constituted minor problems and I'll run through those for you now. He mentioned that the inflight coverall booties that the crew was wearing had become frayed and that they had removed them,

a08_1130951.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1130951.text: Okay. Why don't you drive it back over to the PTC attitude and put it back in Attitude Hold for the roll, and we're going back in and reviewing the DTO requirement. You had about the same result, it looks like, on a cursory analysis all three times. So we're going to take another look and see if there's any reason to do it again. If so, why, we'll call you. But you go ahead and put it back in Attitude Hold now.

a08_1134503.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1134503.text: Rog. It's taking us a little longer to go through and rehash all of the entry checklist than I thought, and we're just about to wrap it up now.

a08_1134503.speaker: Borman
a08_1134503.text: No problem. Just watch - keep an eye on the gimbal angles for me, and give me a call if they get too close.

a08_1141919.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1141919.text: We'd like to look at a couple more Delta-V tests on the EMS, and the general consensus is that we don't think there's any particular problem. We'd like to go ahead and take a look at what you get by running four or five more Delta-V tests. And prior to that, we'd like to run one of these null bias tests; and since we don't have any way of monitoring any of this stuff on the downlink, like to have you tell us each step when you turn the switch and different orders and things like that. [Pause.]

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: Alright. I'll run a test now.

a08_1141919.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1141919.text: Okay. The first thing we want is this null bias for 100 seconds.

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: Okay. Stand by then. I'll do a null bias for 100 seconds. You just want me to put in Delta-V and Automatic and let it alone for 100 seconds?

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: Went to one-tenth and back to zero.

a08_1141919.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1141919.text: Understand; that's a plus one-tenth and back to zero.

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: One-tenth, now it's a minus one-tenth and back to zero; no, it's not zero yet; wait a minute. [Long pause.]

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: It's up to a minus 4; 0.4, that is.

a08_1141919.speaker: Borman
a08_1141919.text: Minus 0.7, and there is 100 seconds; minus 0.7 at 100 seconds.

a08_1141919.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1141919.text: Okay. If we go back to mode switch to Stand by and Function switch, Off. [Pause.]

a08_1141919.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1141919.text: Okay. Now we'd like to do a couple of Delta-V self-tests.

a08_1142446.speaker: Borman
a08_1142446.text: Going to a Delta-V test now. Counting down.

a08_1142847.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1142847.text: Okay. We got caught in a station handover there. I didn't copy anything after you said you were putting it to Delta-V test.

a08_1142847.speaker: Borman
a08_1142847.text: I ran - I ran three tests during that handover. Two over minus 19.6 - two of them are minus 19.8; and one of them, minus 19.6.

a08_1142847.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1142847.text: Okay. The other thing that - sometime prior to entry, and we're going to be looking at it, is the normal entry test pattern, and it's called out presently in the checklist as something we do around an hour. And we'd like to check if you can read the number on the scroll that's up now so we can see where we are in the test pattern sequence. We're considering taking a look at one of these test patterns before we get into an hour so we can have more time to think about it in the event that there should be something anomalous in it.

a08_1142847.speaker: Borman
a08_1142847.text: Why don't we do it right now? We're on number 8.

a08_1142847.speaker: Borman
a08_1142847.text: Roger. It takes an awful long time to run them over there anyway. It won't hurt to do one.

a08_1142847.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1142847.text: Okay. If you'll stand by just a second; we're checking to see where we stand in the sequence of events if we're on pattern 8.

a08_1143258.speaker: Borman
a08_1143258.text: Another little thing about this EMS: you know, we had it set up when we separated from the booster..

a08_1143258.speaker: Borman
a08_1143258.text: ...and the shock of the separation - the shock of the pyro's blowing in separation knocked it up to 100 and something.

a08_1143258.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143258.text: Was the pyro separation enough that the - you felt a sensible g in the bird?

a08_1143258.speaker: Borman
a08_1143258.text: Rog. Let's just say there wasn't any question we were separating.

a08_1143258.speaker: Borman
a08_1143258.text: While you are checking the scroll, find out which entry pattern I should be using this bird in.

a08_1143900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1143900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. During the past few minutes the conversation has concerned the Entry Monitoring System. We've been running some tests on this system to - stand by, here's a call to the crew.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Go ahead.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. While we are verifying that scroll position - they're talking it over in the back room about that now - I'd like to go ahead and run down the checklist with you for entry.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Go ahead.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Looking on entry 1: the second item there is the 12-hour cabin cold soak, and in discussions here and preflight, I think it's agreed that we don't want to do the cold soak there. So we're gonna delete that step 2. And what it amounts to is, I think we do want to do a cold soak, and we certainly want to exercise the water boilers prior to entry in order to ensure that we don't have one that's dried out, in the same manner that we had one dried out prior to LOI. And we're working on some procedures for that, and we'll have to come back to you with those a little bit later, and we'll try to

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. I guess maybe I have that backwards. They copy - you folks copied the VHF out to 20k, and we're checking on the - on the downlink into that now. But in any event, this 4 hours and 35 minutes will get it well in advance of that.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay, 8. We just got an answer back on the test patterns. We thought it was - We had 25 test patterns which are allocated to ground test, and these are the ones we've been looking at. Then there's five more that are allocated to flight, and the only difference in these patterns is that the flight patterns have the instructions actually written on them; so if we're looking at test pattern 8, that means that we're still working on the ones that were allocated to ground test, so there was no problem there. And I'll get you a number for which pattern we should be using for entry; working on that o

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I don't mean the..

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Say again, Frank.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I don't mean the test pattern. I say, I don't mean the test pattern. We asked them to put the supercircular on the number, the first place on the scroll; I'm sure they did. I'm sure it's the first pattern, but I just want to make sure that's right.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Rog. That's what we're trying to verify. So..

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: You want me to run through a test pattern?

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Yes, sir. If you would, please. And if you'd tell us each...

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: ...step as you go through it.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Going through step 1; EMS test 1: [Long pause.] wait 5 seconds. There's 5 seconds. Going Auto. [Pause.] Okay. The indicator lights are all Off, and the range is zero, zero. [Pause.] I'm gonna slew the hairline over the notch. [Pause.] Okay. And now [laughs] we go in EMS test 2.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Got the 0.05g light; all others are out.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Roger.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Go on test 3. [Long pause.] Far side lower light's on, 10 seconds; going to set the range counter to 58. [Long pause.] Okay. It's set at 58; going test 4.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Beautiful. It's perfect. It's right in the corridor. It comes down and stops at zero, zero.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Very good. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Go in test 5. [Pause.] Perfect again. [Long pause.] Okay. Now I go to range set.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: In Standby.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. That was perfect.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Real fine. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay, Apollo 8. I'd like to run one more null bias and looks like we will have exercised everything we can get to.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Delta-V Auto. [Pause.] All zeros. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Minus 2.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Rog. Understand minus 2. [Pause.] Alright. Is that minus 2 or minus two-tenths?

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Two-tenths, three-tenths now.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Real good. That looks like we..

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: It looks like we had a lot of noise on the circuit for a while there, Ken.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Yes, we did, too; all those electronic glitches I guess.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. A hundred seconds. It's minus four-tenths.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Real fine. That looks like that's about all of the functions that we can check, and looks like everything is just down the line.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. We still owe you confirmation that you can expect your high speed scroll to be the first pattern you come to, and I'll let you know as soon as they come in with an answer on it.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: I'd like to go ahead and finish going through the...

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: ...entry book if you're ready.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. We've reviewed most of the book up here, and we will have to come back and suggest a way that we can check out the water boiler prior to getting to the entry area. We've reviewed all of the last minute changes that were put in - pen and ink type things - and they're all looking good. On page E-7, like to add a couple of items.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: What's that?

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. On step 34 under final stowage, which is a sort of catch-all area, there's a step that says Secondary Glycol to Radiator, and it says Bypass, Verify. While we're down in this area, we'd like to go to panel 382, the water control panel, and set up the evaporator water control valve, both primary and secondary, to Auto. Now this is something we would have done had we done the cold-soak at minus 12 hours, but since we weren't doing it there, we'd like to go ahead and make sure we have these in Auto, and this will enable automatic controls from the panel. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Can we just make this part of the procedure when we test out the water boilers beforehand?

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Yes, sir. If we get that checked out earlier, we can just leave them in Auto.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I'd rather do that.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. I'm just going to make a note here, and we can do it the other way, too. The other item that was pen-and-inked in..

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Yeah, [garble].

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: You may already have this down as step 35. It says Up Telemetry to Block, Verify, and there's a step right after that that says RCS Command Module heaters, two circuit breakers, Closed.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I have that.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. I guess that one was sent up to you this afternoon. And when you turn the page over to E-8, it shows the EMS entry check being run at minus an hour, and you know it's a short test. There's really no reason to wait for an hour; might as well go ahead and do that as soon as you get through with step 35 on page E-7 because we're coming up...

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: ...on a pretty busy period.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I agree with you.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I say that's fine; we'll do that. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Houston, are you still there?

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Rog. We got a discussion going, and be right back.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay, Apollo 8. On page E-9.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: At the top of the page, you have step 38, and right underneath that, prior to step 39, we want to have a primary glycol loop activation. What we're gonna do is to get the glycol evaporator water switch to Auto and the glycol evaporator steam pressure switch to Auto. This will get your primary water boiler on the line prior to entry, or at least it'll enable it.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Tell me what to write in, Ken.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. It's Glycol Evaporator Water to Auto. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You there? [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Glycol evaporator water switch to Auto.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. And the second switch is the Glycol Evaporator Steam Pressure to Auto. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. So that takes care of getting the primary water boiler enabled, and it's my understanding that we were going to make the actual entry with both the primary and the secondary water boilers on the line.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: I'm not reading you now, Houston.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Rog. How now?

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Loud and clear.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. There's some question from reading the checklist. It's my understanding that both the primary and secondary water boilers would be On for the actual entry, and I don't find a place in the checklist where it's actually turned on. So we'd like to get confirmation of that, and we'll make sure that we have all the proper switching put in the checklist.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Alright. Still on page E-9 and under step 39 at the bottom of the pyro circuit check, there's a step that says panel 8, all circuit breakers closed except, and then it lists five that are printed, one that was pen-and-inked prior to launch. It says EDS power circuit breakers, 3, Open, and to be complete we ought to add the RCS heater circuit breakers. There's two of those, and they should also be Open. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Alright. The rest of these pages look good; I'm coming over through the graphs. [Pause.] And on page E-11... [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger. I'm with you.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. On step 5 on E-11, there's - the first subtitle there is Helmets and Gloves, and the items that follow beneath that are affected by whether you wear suits or come in shirt sleeves, but they do have to be accomplished. And the suit return air valves would actually be Open for a shirt-sleeve entry. And you should have a line penciled in of Optics Power to Off between an emergency cabin pressure valve and the time when the CMP moves to the couch.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Right.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. And the step shows the tape recorder to Rewind at minus 30. Now that's an onboard step rather than a ground step, just to verify that. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Under step 6, almost at the bottom - in fact, it's three lines from the bottom of the step 6 - there's a section that says secondary coolant loop evaporator to Reset, and should be a note there that that's 58 seconds if you hold it in Reset prior to moving the pump Off.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: That's it; that's in it.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Pause.] Okay. The next comment is on page E-13. [Pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. I'm there.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: All right. This is a general comment that refers to any time you're working around P62 or when you're going between P62 and P63, and you should be careful not to call an extended Verb during this time. This is in the program notes, and it is just a reminder. What'll happen if we get into an extended Verb such as an 83 or an 82? We may get hung-up in P62 and have to recycle through it in order to get the 63, and neither of these displays are normally used, and it's just a good practice. And we're just trying to remind you that we don't want to call an extended Verb while we're in P62.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Okay. Neither do we. That's right.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: Okay. In going through the rest of it, we didn't find any other things we wanted to make comments on. You have all the latest corrections in your checklist.

a08_1143939.speaker: Borman
a08_1143939.text: Roger. The main thing, that is to come up with a way to determine that the boiler - water boiler is not dry and make sure that Bill gets it activated at TMS 7.

a08_1143939.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1143939.text: That is correct, and we'll talk to you some more about that next time we catch both you and Bill up.

a08_1150641.speaker: Borman
a08_1150641.text: Ken, this is Frank. I'm going to be off the headset for about 5 minutes here.

a08_1150641.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1150641.text: Okay. Fine. When you come back, I'll have a systems rundown for you.

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. Loud and clear.

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Back with you.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. I've got a few good words for you. The erasable memory has been taken completely apart and looked at, and it looks like it's all okay. Your P01 didn't have any effect. The one thing that might be questionable is if you use a Verb 67 when you get to the Noun 99 display, you may find that one to be unreliable, and what you're going to get there is the - that's an error display for the W-matrix. And it's something that you probably won't be using again anyhow; and if the occasion arises, why, we can - we can update that one, but it's not a normally used display and everything else, all the

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Very good.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. As of 114 hours, your batteries - you had battery A with 39.32 amp-hours, battery B had 35.21, and battery C 38.46. Your cryo quantities remaining at Sep were the same we gave you the last time, 180 pounds of oxygen per tank and 11 pounds of hydrogen per tank. At present, the Service Module RCS, using the computer values for the quantities, you have quad A with 55 percent, Bravo with 50, Charlie with 58, and Delta at 48. What we plan to do with the secondary tanks is to go ahead and turn them on at 37 percent actual, and in the event of lost comm or something like that, recommend that yo

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Rog.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. A couple of items I want to check up on: I'd like to confirm that the hatch dogs will be taken off while you're on the chutes if you can. If not, you're going to do that in the water. Is that affirm? [Pause.]

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: [Garble] didn't even put them on [garble]. [Pause.]

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. Now we've got a little better signal. Like to confirm that the hatch clamps on the side hatch will be taken off either on the chutes or in the water, whichever you can get to. Is that affirm?

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Roger. That's affirm. As a matter of fact, we didn't even put - didn't even put them on.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. Do you plan to put them on for an entry?

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: I don't think so. It's held pretty well so far. I don't think - everybody tells me it wouldn't help much anyway.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. And we realize we never did find out what happened to the Mae West. Did you leave it blown up, or did you dump it?

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: We dumped it.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. Who was the lucky guy?

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: The same guy that tried to launch us this afternoon again.

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Okay. And just as a gee whiz item: you're now 137,915 [nautical miles, 225,419 km] out, and you've only accelerated the 4,883 [fps, 1,488 m/s]. You might check to make sure you don't have a speed brake hanging.

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Uh-oh. That good or bad?

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: Those are nominal values.

a08_1151712.speaker: Borman
a08_1151712.text: Rog. 137,000 [nautical] miles [254,000 km] out, huh?

a08_1151712.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1151712.text: That's affirm.

a08_1151900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1151900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 115 hours, 19 minutes. At the present time our spacecraft is at an altitude of 137,374 nautical miles [254,417 km] from Earth and traveling at a speed of 4,895 feet per second [1,492 m/s]. Capsule communicator Ken Mattingly has just received the call from Frank Borman. We'll pick up that conversation now.

a08_1153318.speaker: Anders
a08_1153318.text: Good morning, or good afternoon, or whatever it is. The JOD's back at the Con; CDR went back to bed.

a08_1153318.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1153318.text: Looks like all the junior guys have the midwatch.

a08_1153318.speaker: Anders
a08_1153318.text: I know what you mean. [Pause.] I had a little sleep earlier, so I'm pretty well rested. We want to make sure Frank gets a good snooze here prior to entry. [Pause.] This might be a good time to try out your background music again. See if you have any better luck.

a08_1153318.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1153318.text: Okay. We'll try that a little later.

a08_1153748.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1153748.text: Okay. I guess we should start off with a little dialogue about sleep. How much did you have?

a08_1153748.speaker: Anders
a08_1153748.text: Well, let's see; whenever it was I told you I went to bed last time until now. Just a second and let me check the Flight Plan.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Have you got it logged in when it was I asked for that last Seconal?

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. I guess we can figure that out for ourselves, can't we?

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Yeah. Why don't you let me know. I've kinda lost track of what time it was when I went to bed. But it was about - I went to sleep about 15 minutes after that and woke up about 10 minutes ago. Good sleep.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. So I see it is now 142 hours. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Who do you think I am, Rip van Winkle?

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Just trying to find out how soundly you really slept. I guess you're not that sleepy.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: I may be confused but not that confused.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. It's really about 4 hours ago. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Okay. Good. [Long pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Have you got somebody under the left couch, or could you get down to the water control panel?

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: I can get down there. Frank hasn't quite gone to sleep yet.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Well, what we were thinking about doing was boiling a little out of the secondary evaporator to check it out, just as a component check, something we need to do; but if there's somebody down there in the way, why, we can do that some other time. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Well, if it boils, we're gonna to know it before - it won't take long to find out if it won't boil. Not a heck of a lot we can do about it, so why don't we wait until someone else wakes up here, till Frank wakes up again. How will that be?

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Yes. That would be fine. There is something you can do; you can reservice it. And it's a kind of a tedious process, and that's the reason why we just want to kind of keep our eyes on it so we'll have some idea prior to entry if we can count on having two loops or one. Which kind of leads us into another question we're trying to pin down, two questions, in fact. Number one, we'd like to verify that you do plan to use both primary and secondary boilers during the actual entry, and we're also looking for a way of checking the primary boiler to make sure it isn't dried out prior to entry. And that

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: The answer to the question is yes, we do plan to use both. Before we get into the water boiler pump though, CDR would like to take a Seconal also; make sure he can get off to sleep here. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. That's a Go.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Okay. [Pause.] On the - on the water boilers: [Pause.] it's interesting that I get -I get my own [Pause.] I was going to say anytime you have your mike keyed, I can hear myself talk with about a 2-second time delay. With respect to the primary and secondary boilers checks, I think it's a good idea to make sure we got them both prior to entry and have the reservicing procedures handy. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Rog, Bill. You know the secondary - well, in fact, both reservicing procedures are available in a malfunction book, and sort of the problem with checking out the primary boiler is finding a way to make it boil on the way in. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Yeah. Just a second, I got another little chore going here. [Long pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Rog. Looks like the only way we'd be able to do it would be to shut off the radiators.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: We were looking for a little more docile way to do that.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
