a08_1154048.text: Roger; That - that would be agreeable to me too, a little more docile way, but they shouldn't freeze up if we did it quickly.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Rog. We're talking over several things, you know, like putting the ten-pin valve to Manual or partially closing it or some of these different ideas, and something you can think about while you're laying there with nothing else to do.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Yeah. We've noticed that it had gotten rather warmer in the cockpit coming back than it was going out. And I remember going out when we manually positioned the ten-pin valve, but we had pretty good control over the glycol evap outlet temperature. So possibly that would be the thing to try first rather than the radiators.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. We've got the back room boys looking at it too. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: I guess if we do pick a time, though, we ought to pick a time that if something did go haywire, we could afford to boil hencefo... - the rest of the way in, but still leave us enough time to make sure we got the evap serviced if they didn't work.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: That's affirm, and we're factoring in things like trajectory considerations and all that sort of thing, too.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Right. I think that the second derivative of the water boiler versus time plot will give us the optimum time to do it. [Long pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: EECOM's copying that. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: There's also speculation you have a chart on board that gives that information. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Well, if I don't, I'm sure those guys can ship one up. They've shipped up some other pretty good ones.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: It's also been suggested that perhaps if you don't have a chart, it's on the tape recorder. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Well, if I don't have a chart, I'll put it on the tape recorder. [Pause.]

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Okay. I think, unless you guys got some - some more comments along those lines, maybe we ought to give these guys a chance to get to sleep, and I'll hold down the replies here for a while. If you've got something to brief me on, go ahead; but I'd like to keep my answers to yesses and nos and whatever else you think you really need.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay. Real fine, Bill, and I'll check with you like every 30 minutes, just to make sure we still have voice contact.

a08_1154048.speaker: Anders
a08_1154048.text: Okay. I've got some - I've got some log writing to do and whatnot. So keep an eye on the systems and the gimbal angles, and we'll be all right.

a08_1154048.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1154048.text: Okay.

a08_1154600-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1154600-pao.text: Yeah. Just a second, I got another little chore going here. [Long pause.]

a08_1154600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1154600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 115 hours, 46 minutes; and just about 10 minutes ago we had a change of watch aboard the spacecraft. Bill Anders, who had been sleeping for about 4 hours, awoke and came on the circuit to advise that Frank Borman was now attempting to get a bit of rest. We're in conversation with Anders at the present time, We'll pick that up for you now.

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: And, Ken, if your EECOM there wants to play the omni-switch game, why, we're on Dog - Bravo at this time, actually on Bravo but also configured for D, so - correction, we are on D and also configured for Bravo. If you want to switch, why, go ahead.

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: Okay, we'll give that a try, and we're cranking up some background music for you.

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Okay. The last time they did that, it sounded like they were running at the wrong speed on the tape, but we're a little closer now. Maybe it'll be a little better.

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Might be another way to range. [Pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Problem is, if it was Doppler shift; we're heading back out again. [Long pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: Looks like we can use your humming for a backup ranging in case everything else fails.

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You don't need to answer this transmission, but doctors observe that it looks like your - some of your sensors may be working loose, so you might just kind of push on them and see if they are in place. [Long pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: No, it looks like it's one of your sternals, Bill. [Long pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: Apollo 8. We can't handle the omni switching for about thirty more minutes, 'til we get back to an 85-foot dish, so you'll have to watch the antenna store for a few more minutes. [Long pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Okay. I don't see any loose sensor - the upper, upper st... [Pause.]

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Are you trying to call, Houston?

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: No, I didn't. It sounded like you were getting an echo, and I checked, and I hadn't held the key down at the time either.

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: Okay. I don't see any loose sensors, but the upper sternal is beginning to irritate a little bit, but not badly; and possibly there's something going on there.

a08_1155217.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1155217.text: Okay. And did you copy about the antennas?

a08_1155217.speaker: Anders
a08_1155217.text: They really disappoint me, but I'll keep that in mind.

a08_1155900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1155900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. That appears to be all the conversation for now. We'll stand by to come back up when next we hear from the spacecraft. At 115 hours, 59 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; our velocity is 4,940 feet per second [1,506 m/s] and our altitude is 135,462 nautical miles [250,876 km]. This is Mission Control, Houston.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. I'd like to make a voice check with you. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Roger. Reading you five by [five].

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: I don't hear the music until you start talking, though. [Pause.] And I don't hear it now.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Roger, Ken. Read you loud and clear. If you're trying to play background music, I do not hear it.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Houston, read you loud and clear.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Loud and clear.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Loud and clear, Ken.

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Loud and clear.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [No answer.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston in the blind now. We're not receiving down-voice. We have data, and it appears it's probably a ground problem. [Long pause.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Roger, Houston. Read you loud and clear.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Okay. I got you that time. I take it you were able to copy us with the music? Is that affirm?

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: I was able to copy you all the time, Ken, but I could only hear the music when you were trying to transmit. And I wondered if you'd noticed cycling on my suit power switch when you - when you called me. I'm hearing an echo now.

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: Rog. I copy your echo. And what switch were you cycling?

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: I was cycling the suit power which turns off the Biomed periodically. I figured that would wake the doctors up. [Pause.]

a08_1160202.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1160202.text: It appears we have more than one communications problem.

a08_1160202.speaker: Anders
a08_1160202.text: Rog.

a08_1161125.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1161125.text: Oh, that was an inadvertent cut-in.

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: You need the High Gain, Houston, or will the omnis be okay? [Long pause.]

a08_1161834.speaker: Windler
a08_1161834.text: 8, Houston. That's negative. The omni is okay.

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: Roger. Be advised that about 50 - I am hearing these echoes quite a bit of the time, and if you're trying to play the music, I'm not hearing it.

a08_1161834.speaker: Windler
a08_1161834.text: Rog. We understand, and we're not trying to play music right now.

a08_1161834.speaker: Windler
a08_1161834.text: This is - Ken's only human. This is his substitute; this is Flight Director.

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: Oh, I didn't recognize your voice there.

a08_1161834.speaker: Windler
a08_1161834.text: I don't get to talk often.

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: Who is substituting for you now, Flight?

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: Okay. [Pause.] Things are looking pretty good from here. How about from down there?

a08_1161834.speaker: Anders
a08_1161834.text: You guys are doing a great job. I really appreciate it.

a08_1162100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1162100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 116 hours, 21 minutes. At the present time we're talking with Bill Anders aboard the spacecraft, A short while ago we attempted to play up some background music, as requested by the crew and met with marginal success. On that, we will pick up the conversation ensuing, following that attempt.

a08_1162323.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1162323.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Going to be handing over sites at 25. I'll make a voice check with you when we come up on the new site, and the ground says thank you for your kind words.

a08_1162536.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1162536.text: Okay, Bill, and our biomed data still looks a little bit squirrelly. How about checking the blue signal conditioner on your biomed harness. You have one connector, should be the center package, has a blue connector on it. You kind of check that, and I don't know if you have changed the biomed harness leads recently; if you have, this might have caused our problem. [Pause.]

a08_1162536.speaker: Anders
a08_1162536.text: Roger. I was just cracking open some acorns here for breakfast. Let me put them down, and I will check my biomed leads.

a08_1162536.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1162536.text: There is no rush on it.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Apollo 8, Houston. [No answer.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Go, Houston.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Okay, Bill. We're ready to try this music on a different kind of lash-up this time. What I'd like to do in order to make sure that we maintain voice comm is when you get it if you would, give us a call and tell us you have the music and any comment about its relative volume or anything like that. And if I get your call, then I'll call you back and tell you. And we're going to - what'll happen is, when I go to talk to you, we'll drop the music link. And we can go ahead and take over the switching of the antennas if you like. [Pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Okay. I'm in Bravo/Dog switch configuration, and go ahead with the - with the music. And be advised last time the fidelity was low, and the volume was too high.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Okay. And if you give us the same sort of comment, hopefully not the same comment but the same type of evaluation when you pick it up this time.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Okay. Well, play it a little bit, and we'll talk about it. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: I can barely, barely hear it. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Can't hear it at all. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Needs to be just a hair louder. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: That's good. [Pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: That'll keep me awake. [Pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Maybe you ought to crank it back down just a little bit. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Good. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Apollo 8, Houston. How was that?

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: That's real good for background level type, Ken. Maybe you - I'm trying to do some logging in here so that's real nice [at] about that level; maybe, if you didn't have anything else to do, you might want it a bit louder, but that's good for now.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Okay. That's about the max volume we can take down here; so if you want to talk to us, you may have to call us once or twice. You're just barely equaling it.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Okay. Try it again, and I'll give you a little louder call; I've been trying to keep it quiet.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Oh, yeah, that's alright. Don't - I was aware that you were calling; I just didn't make out what you said. And from now on, any time you call, why, we'll drop the music, and I'll talk to you.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Roger. Don't hesitate to inhibit it.

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: And, Bill, we're going to have to wait until we get around to Bravo before we start switching. Our margin is still a little bit low.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Okay. I'll just go ahead and switch it and [garble].

a08_1164926.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1164926.text: Okay. Thank you. I'll put the - our midnight DJ sho's back on the air.

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_1164926.speaker: Anders
a08_1164926.text: It's really great now.

a08_1170500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1170500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 116 hours, 52 minutes. CapCom Ken Mattingly has just put in a call to the crew. We'll pick up that conversation now.

a08_1170500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1170500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 117 hours, 5 minutes. We'll take the circuit down for the time being and come back up the next time we reestablish communications with the spacecraft. At 117 hours, 5 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Check your yaw gimbal angle.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: You must be reading my mind.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Thank you.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: ...the DSKY's.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Oh, okay. [Pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: When you go to High Gain, don't you tell me? [Long pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Ken. Do you want me to use the High Gain when we come around, or is the Omni sufficient? It doesn't matter to me.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: Okay. The Omni's doing fine. I just was watching your middle gimbal angle there; it was getting a little far out.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Oh, okay. I thought you - I was, too. I thought you said check the DSKY, and I thought you were talking about the High Gain Antenna.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: No, I'm sorry. I was just watching your middle gimbal.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Yeah, this thing really slops around in deadband, but it's really nice flying otherwise.

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: Glad to hear that. [Pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: All I have used the whole trip is pulse. [Pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: You just woke the doctor up. You said pulse, and he came alive. And he'd like to know if you did, in fact, check out the biomed harness.

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Yes, I tightened down on all the plugs and checked all the leads, and everything looked in order. And when the other fellows wake up, if you remind me, why, I'll give it a more thorough going over. [Long pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: Okay, Bill. It's been suggested that they'd like to see you try switching the two leads, you know, a yellow and a blue one, and just go ahead and switch them, and they'll sacrifice their pneumogram because they'd rather have the EKG. [Long pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: Do they need it now, or can they wait until somebody else wakes up? [Pause.]

a08_1171457.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1171457.text: I guess we can wait, Bill. Is that a hard thing to get to?

a08_1171457.speaker: Anders
a08_1171457.text: You got to take your pants off and about everything else - stand by.

a08_1171900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1171900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 117 hours, 19 minutes. At the present time the spacecraft is at an altitude of 131,548 nautical miles [243,627 km] and our velocity, continuing to increase, now up to 5,035 feet per second [1,535 m/s]. We're in communication with the spacecraft. At this time here's how that conversation is going.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: How's that, Houston? [Pause.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Okay. Stand by, Bill. We'll take a look at it. [Long pause.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Rog. Read you. We're looking at data now. [Off-mike voices in Mission Control.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: The other possibil - the other possibility; my heart's quit beating.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders (speaking over Mattingly)
a08_1172207.text: The other possibility is my heart's stopped beating.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: We couldn't argue with you. That doesn't help at all. That's pretty bad. [Long pause.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Is the pneumogram No-Go for entry?

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: One thing you might be interested in: we listened to that low speed information that you taped on the first couple of revs that we thought was going to be unusable. And it must have been a ground problem because it's coming through loud and clear now.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Hey, that's great 'cause I was just writing a long dissertation on why we got - got problems and we can't use that DSE in low bit rate. So that's real good.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Yeah, it's coming in loud and clear. It's pretty interesting.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Let me tell you, it was a hectic revolution.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: If you've got the music going, I'm not hearing it, Ken.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: No, I was waiting to see what we did on that before I started it up again.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Okay. If they could hold off here for a couple of hours, if they've got anything at all, just tell them, I'm alive, why, I'll give them a real good going over here when I get done. I might even make a statement to the world that I haven't noticed that their little amplifiers had gotten hot.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: You say it did get hot?

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: No, I hadn't even noticed it until I started changing the lead.

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Oh, okay. Okay. I'm going to crank the music up again then.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Okay. Are they - have they got anything at all down there?

a08_1172207.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1172207.text: Well, we're on low bit rate right now, so it'll be a few minutes before we get a chance to take another look at it. We'll let you know if you get sick.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Oh, well, we can hold off for a little bit.

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: Rog. [Long pause.]

a08_1172207.speaker: Anders
a08_1172207.text: I can't hear it, but it sounds like something I'd rather not hear anyway.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Hello, Apollo 8. We interrupt this program of music to bring you the late evening status report.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Good. What's up?

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. We're getting ready to have a shift turnover, and I wanted to go over a few items before we do. On the midcourse correction number 6: right now, it looks like that's about at most three tenths a foot per second, so there will be no burn at midcourse number 6. Midcourse number 7 is a little larger, and we'll make a decision on that later. [Pause.] Your weather in the landing site still reported as being good and the forecast to be about 2,000 scattered and 12,000 broken, about the same numbers they gave Frank earlier. Visibility will be about 10 miles; wave height, 4 feet. And I guess the

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Just my kind of weather.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Rog. Got a couple of Flight Plan things to consider. Now number 1 at 119:30: we've got a P52 IMU realignment which we need to slip in ahead of the P23 sightings, and that'll be an option 3 REFSMMAT. [Pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Some of the folks, in sitting back and looking at the TV business, have some ideas about things they would like to see tried with the filters. And I'd like to read you what they have here and let you think about it; and in the next 10 hours, why, you can decide whether or not you think it's worth the effort. Basically, they'd like to try using a whole different series of filters...

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Stand by one, Ken. [Long pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay, Ken. I got something to write on. Was that P52 at 18:30 or 19:30?

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Before you copy, let me read it all through to you here so you'll get the feel for what it is we're talking about. The title of this little epistle is "TV and Film Photography Correlation Experiment," and what they want to do is mount the TV camera with the telephoto lens on a bracket in the rendezvous window and take a TV picture of the Earth through the red and blue filters, 1 minute per filter; that means red and blue filters individually. Then they'd like to take a TV picture of the Earth through the red, in this case, the 25 Alpha filter combined with the polarizing filter. Rotate t

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: And I'm ready to copy on the TV.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: One minute.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. I'm standing by.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Were those - when you were talking about pictures through the polarizing filter, is that the TV pictures through the polarizing filter?

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: That's affirmative. All above was TV.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Now the only - the only problem here is it - it's darn near impossible to aim that television camera; the field of view is so narrow that it took three men and a boy up here to get the thing pointed in the right direction. And we tried using chewing gum for a sight and everything else, and let me tell you that the odds of getting that thing getting the Earth are pretty small.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. I think we weren't too clever in our ground call-up as to how to point the spacecraft for one thing. I think we can do that a lot better next time now that we have stumbled through it once. I agree with you.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: It's not the spacecraft; it's not the spacecraft that's hard to point, it's the camera. The bracket has sufficient slop in it that it can take the camera out of field of view when configured through the window. And it took a lot of microadjustments with a lot of coaching from the ground to get the thing in, and it was a real tough job. So I think you ought to take all this in mind; and if you could possibly use the wide angle lens, you might be better off.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying now. I'll run that back by the TV guys and see what they have to say about that. In conjunction with the above, they wanted to take some Hasselblad pictures of the Earth through the rendezvous window with the red and blue filter and black and white film, and then again through the polarizing filter, and this is all gonna be used in order to try and correlate the TV and the regular film photography. So if you think this is a worthwhile thing, and you'd like to give it a try, I'll run this by Jack and the TV cats and see if they would like to get something o

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Another thing to keep in mind is that we haven't seen the Moon - we didn't see it all the way - all the way out and we rarely see it going back. We have seen it once since we left, but we have maneuvered the wrong way from a sighting attitude to the shortest way to PTC; so to go from an Earth view to a lunar view will take quite a bit of time and some RCS. So you might keep that in mind, too.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Now - I just wanted you to be aware of this and see - think about it, what its implications to the Flight Plan might be, and I'll run this wide angle and comment about the Moon back by and see which sections they think would be most appropriate. Okay. On the EMS scroll, Frank wanted us to verify the order that he could expect to see the entry profile, and the first profile that comes up is labelled "Nonexit Number 2" and that's the short-range high-speed entry. The second thing that will come up is entitled "The 3,500-Mile" which is also a high-speed entry, but it is the one you would us

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Let me ask you one thing then. Do you want a cold-soak sometime prior to the midcourse correction for 1 hour. Is that what you're telling me?

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Not really. I think we're looking at that prior to the midcourse correction as being the time when we would like to check out the water boilers. The cold-soak does involve some water boiling too, but that's going to be done right before entry when these things aren't gonna be very sensitive, and if we don't do it at 12 hours, it's not real clear where the cold-soak takes place or where you turn on the secondary water boiler. In looking through the entry checklist tonight, we didn't find a place for that.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Is it really clear that you need the cold-soak? We've kind of figured on sometime prior to Sep bringing up the secondary evap, and also having the primary at that going sometime prior to that based on your suggestion.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. We're talking about doing that like an hour prior to SEP; but in the pre-SEP check, one of the things we power down is the secondary loop. And they won't need to turn it back.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: We do that to save.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Right. We're doing that to keep our power profile where we want it. And then we're going to be turning it back on sometime prior to entry. And the time to turn it on in entry, of course, isn't specified because as you turn it on, the voltages show that they can hack it.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Hopefully, right after separation.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: That sounds like a real good place. Okay. I'm sure we're going to discuss that one a little bit more, Bill. But right now those are the kind of things we're talking about doing. And on the High Gain, there's still a lot of discussion about just exactly what we saw and what it means. And I think it's a little too early to tell you anything about that one.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Roger. I think it's got X-ray eyes. [Pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: That's as good as some of the explanations. [Pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Yeah, I think that's one to hash out on the ground, Ken.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. I think we all agree that we don't want to try experimenting with it if we really don't know what it is we're looking at.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Roger. I've written down some numbers here that I hope will be helpful.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. Fine.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: And I'll give them to you in the debriefing.

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Real fine.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: I don't think it's any great big deal, because the antenna switching is not hard at all and if the Reacq - if it is required it will work; and if it doesn't work as advertised, at least it works in a reasonable manner. [Long pause.]

a08_1181740.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1181740.text: Okay. And we're looking at 120 hours for the next water dump, Bill.

a08_1181740.speaker: Anders
a08_1181740.text: Okay. [Garble.]

a08_1181800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1181800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 118 hours, 43 minutes - rather 118 hours, 18 minutes. And after almost 45 minutes of relatively quiet, we've received a call from the spacecraft. We're in communications right now with Bill Anders aboard Apollo 8. We will pick that up from the beginning.

a08_1183341.speaker: Anders
a08_1183341.text: Ken, is it my imagination, or have you got the music running?

a08_1183341.speaker: Anders
a08_1183341.text: Is it my imagination, or do you have the music running?

a08_1183341.speaker: Anders
a08_1183341.text: Uh-oh. Don't let the doctors hear that.

a08_1183341.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1183341.text: It's too late; he already heard you:

a08_1183341.speaker: Anders
a08_1183341.text: I must be getting that detached feeling.

a08_1183649.speaker: Anders
a08_1183649.text: Roger. Just to make sure the urge to get red/blue filter shots of the Moon haven't crept into this TV test. We have got red and blue filter shots of the Moon, so you needn't worry about that.

a08_1183649.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1183649.text: Okay. I don't think that would throw it away. I think we're trying to come up with something definitive so that postflight we'll have some real good data to compare with what we do on the ground for future work. We would like to have you go over and take a look at battery Charlie, please. [Pause.]

a08_1183649.speaker: Anders
a08_1183649.text: Okay. Battery Charlie is about 36.8 volts.

a08_1183649.speaker: Anders
a08_1183649.text: Also with respect to the TV test, I would think that we could probably get a pretty good handle on the operation just by taking red, blue and polarizing shots of the Earth independent of the TV, but within the same time frame or at about the same range we had the TV last time.

a08_1183649.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1183649.text: Okay. That's what the second portion of this really is asking that we do this with the Hasselblad, and again we're going to be using the red and blue filters so that we have a baseline.

a08_1183649.speaker: Anders
a08_1183649.text: Taking a picture of the Earth with the Hasselblad is no big deal because it does swing by there every now and then. But trying to get the TV and the Hasselblad all pointed to Earth at the same time would really be tough.

a08_1185300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1185300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 118 hours, 53 minutes. And at the present time our spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 5,152 feet per second [1,570 m/s], at an altitude of 126,944 nautical miles [235,100 km]. Here in Mission Control we're in the midst of a change of shift. Flight Director Glynn Lunney is coming on to replace Milton Windler. At the present time Bill Anders is the only crewman aboard the spacecraft who is awake at the present time, and he has had the watch for several hours now as Frank Borman and Jim Lovell have apparently been getting some well-earned rest. We've had a very quiet

a08_1185915.speaker: Anders
a08_1185915.text: We're going to hold up on the LiOH change for about a half an hour. The PCO 2 count - reading is low, and we don't want to wake up the CDR. It's right by his feet.

a08_1190246.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1190246.text: Okay, Bill. We're coming up on the P52 and then the P23 sightings, and there's some concern that if we just go directly to the P23 attitude that we're liable to overheat quad Charlie. So we'd like to have you maneuver to place the minus X-axis towards the Sun now. And I've got some gimbal angles here for you. And if we take it over there and point minus-X at the Sun between now and the time we have to start into the alignment, then the P23 business, why, we'll tend to cold-soak Charlie, and then we'll be able to go through the P23 operations without worrying about the temperatures.

a08_1190246.speaker: Anders
a08_1190246.text: Actually, we worked out up here on Lovell's slide rule and got 183.25 roll.

a08_1190615.speaker: Anders
a08_1190615.text: Houston, you wanted to go to this cold-soak attitude prior to the P52, did you not?

a08_1190615.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1190615.text: We'd like to go to the cold-soak attitude now.

a08_1190615.speaker: Anders
a08_1190615.text: And that was to keep from heating up quad D, was it?

a08_1193352.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1193352.text: Roger. The P23 that's coming up next; we'll want to do a water dump as soon as we're through with that P23. We'll dump down to 30 percent, and this ought to be the last dump of the mission. Over.

a08_1193352.speaker: Anders
a08_1193352.text: Okay. You think that we'll end up generating enough water to fill her up prior to entry.

a08_1193352.speaker: Anders
a08_1193352.text: Okay. We are at that attitude you gave us, so we stopped the roll a little bit short. We're more like 150 degrees roll right now.

a08_1193352.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1193352.text: Okay, Bill. On that water dump, we expect to have 90 percent.

a08_1194154.speaker: Anders
a08_1194154.text: Roger. We're done with the P52 and ready to start on the P23. Was there any constraint you wanted, or length of time you wanted to stay in this attitude? [Pause.]

a08_1194154.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1194154.text: Negative, Bill. When you're - when you're finished with P23; we'll go back into PTC.

a08_1194154.speaker: Anders
a08_1194154.text: Okay. We're going to maneuver for P23 now.

a08_1194154.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1194154.text: Roger. We're watching your tank pressures.

a08_1194154.speaker: Anders
a08_1194154.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll do an optics cal first and then do the P23.

a08_1194451.speaker: Carr
a08_1194451.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're handing over to Madrid in about 15 seconds. Over.

a08_1194451.speaker: Lovell
a08_1194451.text: Roger. And good morning, Jerry, or good afternoon, or whatever it is.

a08_1194451.speaker: Carr
a08_1194451.text: Morning, Jim. It's about 6:30 in the morning [of December 26]. [Long pause.]

a08_1194451.speaker: Carr
a08_1194451.text: Apollo 8, Houston. How do you read?

a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 120 hours, 18 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8 at the present time; 122,637 nautical miles [227,124 km] away from Earth. Our current velocity now 5,267 feet per second [1,605 m/s] on Apollo 8 as it returns to Earth. We've had conversation with Apollo 8 and we are going to pick up that conversation now.

a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.speaker: Carr
a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.text: Morning, Frank. Looks like we've lost the transducer on the Primary Radiator Out temperature. We're showing an off-scale high. The rest of the loop looks real fine, though. When you get a chance, would you take a look at it. See if you're in the same position. Over.

a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.text: Ours is showing 100 off-scale high, also.

a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1200000-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, all three crewmembers; Borman, Lovell, and Anders now awake and ready for business. Apollo 8 has completed its platform alignment and as you heard, the cislunar star sighting operation has begun; this matching the stars with, now at this phase of the mission, the Earth's horizon. Jim Lovell, now awake, handles these activities. Following P23, the cislunar navigation exercise, Apollo 8 will return to its Passive Thermal Control attitude. A bit earlier, we performed - just prior to the G&N exercises, put one of our Reaction Control System quads into a cold-

a08_1201749.speaker: Carr
a08_1201749.text: Morning, Frank. Looks like we've lost the transducer on the Primary Radiator Out temperature. We're showing an off-scale high. The rest of the loop looks real fine, though. When you get a chance, would you take a look at it. See if you're in the same position. Over.

a08_1201749.speaker: Borman
a08_1201749.text: Ours is showing 100 off-scale high, also.

a08_1201800-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1201800-pao.text: Ours is showing 100 off-scale high, also.

a08_1201800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1201800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, all three crewmembers; Borman, Lovell, and Anders now awake and ready for business. Apollo 8 has completed its platform alignment and as you heard, the cislunar star sighting operation has begun; this matching the stars with, now at this phase of the mission, the Earth's horizon. Jim Lovell, now awake, handles these activities. Following P23, the cislunar navigation exercise, Apollo 8 will return to its Passive Thermal Control attitude. A bit earlier, we performed - just prior to the G&N exercises, put one of our Reaction Control System quads into a cold-

a08_1202000-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1202000-pao.text: Roger. About this rad outlet temp: does your telemetry show that it happened all of a sudden?

a08_1202127.speaker: Anders
a08_1202127.text: Roger. About this rad outlet temp: does your telemetry show that it happened all of a sudden?

a08_1202400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1202400-pao.text: That was our final exchange with Apollo 8, the conversation with Bill Anders. And at 120 hours, 24 minutes; we'll continue to monitor. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1202525.speaker: Carr
a08_1202525.text: Roger. Frank, all of your primary loop temperature readings look just fine. Your Evap In temperatures are normal and indicate you're getting normal mixing.

a08_1202744.speaker: Carr
a08_1202744.text: Roger. For the P23 attitude that you're in right now, your quad tank temperatures are better than we expected. We're still monitoring, and it's looking good.

a08_1202744.speaker: Borman
a08_1202744.text: Thank you. [Pause.] After we complete this, do you want us to return to the PTC attitude? Is that correct?

a08_1202744.speaker: Borman
a08_1202744.text: Would you have someone get up the gimbal angles for us to point the X-axis at the Earth at the TV time, please?

a08_1202744.speaker: Borman
a08_1202744.text: Also, Jerry, I'd like to know our range and velocity at that time.

a08_1202744.speaker: Carr
a08_1202744.text: Roger, Frank. You want the range and velocity at TV time.

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: Roger. At 128 hours, your altitude is 97,413; your velocity is...

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: Roger. That's TV time. Your altitude is 97...

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: Your altitude is 97,413; velocity is 6,072; roll is 1 degree, pitch is 58, yaw 0.

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: I just got a newspaper, Frank. I'll go through it and pick out some news items for you.

a08_1203333.speaker: Borman
a08_1203333.text: Good. That'll be great. We're just eating breakfast.

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: How are you having your eggs this morning?

a08_1203333.speaker: Anders
a08_1203333.text: Bacon. All except Lovell. He's having eggs Benedict, he says.

a08_1203333.speaker: Anders
a08_1203333.text: That Timber Cove crew, you know, they...

a08_1203333.speaker: Lovell
a08_1203333.text: Jerry, in doing these P23s, we were just about over Africa most of the time. At least, it was in view; nice weather over there this time of year.

a08_1203333.speaker: Carr
a08_1203333.text: Roger. You want to go down there?

a08_1204243.speaker: Borman
a08_1204243.text: Jerry, Jim Lovell just checked the P30, P21, and says you're right, 97,800 [nautical miles, 181,100 km].

a08_1204243.speaker: Carr
a08_1204243.text: We ought to have these computers flight qualified in another couple of missions.

a08_1204243.speaker: Lovell
a08_1204243.text: Roger. Was MCC-6 determined for exactly 122 hours, when you came up with that six-tenths of a foot per second? [Long pause.]

a08_1204243.speaker: Carr
a08_1204243.text: Roger. Jim, at exactly 122 we were figuring 0.5.

a08_1204243.speaker: Lovell
a08_1204243.text: Roger. I'll try it again now at the same time using the P37 with MA. The last time we did it, before the last sightings, I got 2 feet per second. I'm going to see what I come up with this time.

a08_1204300-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1204300-pao.text: We ought to have these computers flight qualified in another couple of missions.

a08_1204800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1204800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 120 hours, 43 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8 at the present time; 121,351 nautical miles [224,742 km] away from Earth. Current velocity on the spacecraft; 5,302 feet per second [1,616 m/s] and accelerating. As we pick up the Apollo 8 crew, we find during the conversation that spacecraft Commander Frank Borman is interested in Apollo 8's final television appearance scheduled for this afternoon, the final appearance prior to return to Earth. We'll pick up the conversation now.

a08_1204800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1204800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We repeat those altitude and velocity numbers. At 128 hours Ground Elapsed Time - that time for the final television transmission for Apollo 8 prior to return. At that time, the altitude is to be 97,413 nautical miles [180,409 km]; velocity, 6,072 feet per second [1,851 m/s]. As you heard, we do expect some news items to be passed on to the crew shortly. And so at 120 hours, 48 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Apollo 8, Houston. [No answer.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We're ready for you to start your waste water dump anytime now. And could we have a crew status report?

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: You may! We had a good night sleep. Everyone slept at least 7 hours yesterday, and we're just finished breakfast, drunk a lot of water, and I think we're in very good shape; just used the exerciser.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Roger, Frank.

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: What would you like to know about?

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: That's about it. You ready for some morning news?

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Yup!

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Okay. There's really not a whole lot in the news this morning. Things are kind of quiet. I guess the biggest news is the accident rate - the holiday deaths - which is certainly not very pleasant news, but we had 233 people killed nationally, and 9 of them were in Houston on Christmas Eve and Christmas. In the world news, the families made the news again. This is Associated Press: "The families of Apollo 8 crew sent a Christmas message to Navy Commander Lloyd Bucher, Captain of the USS Pueblo crew, released this week by North Korea. The message, addressed to Commander and Mrs. Bucher, at San Di

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Thank you.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Let see. Elsewhere in the national news, the newlyweds, David and Julie Eisenhower, came away from their secret honeymoon hideaway to have Christmas dinner with President-elect Nixon and his family. In New York city, the world's busiest harbor was reduced to almost complete inactivity Christmas day, due to a 5-day old longshoreman strike and a rare hiatus in shipping schedules. No ships arrived or left the harbor. Ferries, running on reduced holiday schedule, provided the only marine activity. [Pause.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Here's an interesting little feature item that's kind of good to hear. It seems that up in Ann Arbor, Michigan, they have a new youth gang. It's called the Gilnet Gang. It roams the streets of Ann Arbor, acting in secret, and sometimes bypassing the law. They call themselves the Guerrillas for Good. Some of the things they've done is, painted a bridge that was covered with obscenities. They painted it one night. A condemned house with - it's popular with neighborhood children, but dangerous, was boarded up. Downtown planters unfilled because of a debate over which group was responsible, busine

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: That's about it as far as the world and national news and the features is concerned. On the sport page, Hank Stram of the Kansas City Chiefs was named as the AFL coach of the year. This is the second time for him in three seasons. The voting was done by an Associated Press panel of 30 sports writers and sportscasters, three from each city. And the nearest one to him was Weeb Ewbank. Other coaches that received votes were Sid Gilman of San Diego, and Lou Sabin of Denver. As for the Shriners College All Star game yesterday, the North cooled the South 3 to 0. Michigan State's Dick Berlinsky boote

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Roger. We're dumping the water now, Jerry.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Okay, Frank.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: For the big Astro Blue Bonnet game, the big basketball classic followed by the Blue Bonnet Bowl in the Dome: SMU and Oklahoma have arrived. They are getting ginned up for the big game. [Pause.] Doesn't say here, I don't believe, which are favored. I'll look that up and let you know later, if there is a favor here. The Davis Cup is underway now, down in Australia, and the US is bidding to recapture that again, and apparently we're favored to recapture the supremacy today. Another item in the news, is 0. J. Simpson; he was named player of the year in college football for the second consecutive s

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Well, I guess that is about it, Frank.

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: Thank you, Jerry. Appreciate that. [Pause.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Lovell
a08_1205259.text: Jerry, this is Jim. We concur on that midcourse 6. Two tenths of a foot per second is what we get.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: Real fine, Jim. [Pause.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: You want to just turn off your radios and come back without us?

a08_1205259.speaker: Borman
a08_1205259.text: No. We can't read out the amazing erasable memory if we'd have to go into Program 01 again.

a08_1205259.speaker: Carr
a08_1205259.text: [Laughter.]

a08_1205259.speaker: Lovell
a08_1205259.text: I'd tried to get us back on the launch pad a little bit earlier.

a08_1210300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1210300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 120 [means 121] hours, 3 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at present; 120,309 nautical miles [222,812 km] away from Earth. Its present velocity; 5,331 feet per second [1,625 m/s]. We received a status report from the crew, and Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr, a sometimes newscaster here in Mission Control, passed along the news to Apollo 8. We'll pick up at this point.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Frank, one other little item in the news here, I thought might be interesting is - Stand by. [Pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Go ahead. You're loud and clear.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Okay. I got interrupted there for a minute. Bob Hope's back out in Vietnam again with his troupe, doing a great job as usual. One little name in the news story here is from the USS New Jersey. Bob Hope joked from atop a huge gun turret yesterday - or Wednesday - to delight the 1,500 men aboard the battleship New Jersey on its 20th Christmas entertaining US troops abroad. Hope and his 27-member troupe entertained the New Jersey seamen after attending a Christmas mass aboard the carrier Hancock, both off Vietnam. "This must be the biggest Chris Craft in the world," Hope told the seamen. "It look

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Did you say that was his 20th trip over there at Christmas time, or overseas at Christmas time?

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: That's right, it's the 20th time he has been over - overseas for Christmas with the troops.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: He's as old as Jack Benny.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Roger. Hey, you can turn off the water dump now.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: We're in the process, or as we say in the aerospace business: that's in work.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Roger. You do good work. [Long pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: That other aviator that's going around the world, Max Conrad with his light plane. He spent Christmas day in the Antarctic, at Puento Arenes in Chili; he's waiting for good weather so he can continue his flight down to the South Pole. He hopes to get around the world. He is going around both Poles, and he's going to fly from Palmer to Byrd, from Byrd to the South Pole, and then return home to the United States by way of New Zealand, Australia, and Hawaii.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Brother. He'd better take some No Doze with him.

a08_1210355.speaker: Lovell
a08_1210355.text: I tried to talk Frank into the same trip. [Long pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: You can give him a weather report from Apollo 8. The South Pole was really clobbered - or at least it was the other day.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: I don't imagine there's many alternates down there.

a08_1210355.speaker: Lovell
a08_1210355.text: No, I don't think so.

a08_1210355.speaker: Lovell
a08_1210355.text: We have some pretty clear weather up here.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: No fog, huh?

a08_1210355.speaker: Lovell
a08_1210355.text: Not outside. [Pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Actually, it's snowing outside right now with that waste water dump that Bill just did.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Roger. Does it look a little bit like Christmas?

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Right. [Long pause.]

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Jerry, do you have a decision on what we're going to do about this next midcourse?

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: No, Frank. We don't need it.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure officially we'll scrub MCC-6?

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Affirmative.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: I guess - Jim says that was already official. I was sleeping at the time. I didn't hear it.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Okay. Frank, by the way, how do you feel about your EMS now? You feel like you've got all the answers to the little funnies you saw earlier?

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Yeah. The answer is don't turn it into Auto, fast. It seems to be very sensitive to jerks, or separation.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: Okay. You figure it's all pretty much just a switch throwing anomaly and if you - if you play it by the numbers and then slow and deliberate, you'll be okay?

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Yeah. I'm getting - I'm getting razzed up here because I said it was sensitive to jerks.

a08_1210355.speaker: Carr
a08_1210355.text: [Laughter.] We thought of that, too, down here.

a08_1210355.speaker: Borman
a08_1210355.text: Yeah, I figured you did. I told Ken last night at separation after TLI, when we separated from the S-IVB, we got a nice bang out of the pyros and the EMS jumped over 100 feet per second.

a08_1211120.speaker: Borman
a08_1211120.text: Jerry, do you want to - I've got here in the Flight Plan to start charging battery B. Do you want that started at 100 now also?

a08_1211120.speaker: Carr
a08_1211120.text: Frank, we expect it'll take about 3 or 4 hours.

a08_1211120.speaker: Borman
a08_1211120.text: And we're happy to report the Earth is getting larger.

a08_1211120.speaker: Carr
a08_1211120.text: Roger, that's comforting. Looks like you are going to make Earth instead of Venus, huh?

a08_1211120.speaker: Carr
a08_1211120.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Your friendly guidance officer has got a LM vector update for you and a CMC time update. Over.

a08_1211120.speaker: Borman
a08_1211120.text: Okay. We'll go to P00. [Pause.] P00 and Accept.

a08_1211800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1211800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. Well, you heard Apollo 8 crew in extremely good spirits this morning. We have a well rested Apollo 8 crew. From the status report, indicated that each crew member had about 7 hours sleep; breakfast complete, the water dump in progress while you listened, and then completed. Jim Lovell confirmed that onboard numbers for midcourse corrections coincided very closely with those on the ground. And at 121 hours, 18 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; continuing to monitor, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1211956.speaker: Carr
a08_1211956.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. The updates are complete. The computer is yours. You can go to Block.

a08_1211956.speaker: Borman
a08_1211956.text: Houston. We won't transfer that state vector, since we're not going to do this MCC. Is that all right?

a08_1215627.speaker: Carr
a08_1215627.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Biomed switch to Center, please.

a08_1215627.speaker: Borman
a08_1215627.text: Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one.

a08_1223056.speaker: Borman
a08_1223056.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read?

a08_1223056.speaker: Borman
a08_1223056.text: Okay, thank you, we're starting P23.

a08_1223241.speaker: Carr
a08_1223241.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. We have lost all CMC data on you. The last data we had showed a high middle gimbal angle. Over.

a08_1223241.speaker: Borman
a08_1223241.text: No. I'm fine. How come you lost those CMC data?

a08_1223241.speaker: Carr
a08_1223241.text: I think maybe it was just your movement - movement out of PTC.

a08_1223241.speaker: Borman
a08_1223241.text: I see, fine. Thank you, it was high. I was watching it though.

a08_1224700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1224700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 122 hours, 47 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8's altitude above the Earth at the present time, 114,904 nautical miles [212,802 km]. Its present velocity as it's coming back to Earth; 5,487 feet per second [1,672 m/s]. Here's a replay of the last conversation that we've had with Apollo 8.

a08_1224700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1224700-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; and as you heard, this reading on the middle gimbal angle explained by maneuvering from - the spacecraft from a Passive Thermal Control attitude to an attitude for the star sighting that navigation the program 23. And so at 122 hours, 48 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1225033.speaker: Borman
a08_1225033.text: We're noticing our quad A helium tank is starting to go up again. You got any ideas on that?

a08_1225033.speaker: Carr
a08_1225033.text: Yeah. We're watching it to, Frank. So far, it's still okay and we're talking about it.

a08_1225033.speaker: Carr
a08_1225033.text: Roger, Frank, this helium tank in quad A - it looks like we may have lathered you up unnecessarily on this thing. It appears to be no problem now, as best we can tell. We got a few of the minds together talking about it, and it's been down-rated quite a bit. Also there - the folks down here monitoring the P23 suspect that Jim is shooting on star number 22 rather than star 02, so he may be having some problems.

a08_1225033.speaker: Lovell
a08_1225033.text: Oh no. We've changed; we're on star 02, on the Moon.

a08_1225033.speaker: Carr
a08_1225033.text: Frank, I may have to add some names to my chicken list.

a08_1225033.speaker: Borman
a08_1225033.text: Rog. I just don't want to be the one that proves the fracture mechanics people are right.

a08_1225033.speaker: Borman
a08_1225033.text: This attitude is going to have us right square into the Sun, too.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Go ahead.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're going to need some data from your last P23 marks. We missed some items, and so don't put it away and when you finish this next P23 we'll get it all together.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Okay.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger. Got some information for you on this PTC that we'll be going to, right after this next P23 exercise. We'd like you this time to try the nose north attitude, that's a pitch of 180, and a yaw of 315, and also we'd like to give another look at this mode free type of PTC and we think maybe we'll get a little bit of spin stabilization if we try it at 0.3 degrees per second on the roll rate rather than 0.1. So if you figure on doing that at 124:30 we'll see what kind of information we get out of it.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Okay. You know what I think of that, don't you? I'll be happy to do it, but I think it's playing games.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger. Frank, you're burning right now 1.4 pounds per hour with attitude hold in pitch and yaw. We're kind of interested to see if 0.3 degrees per second will reduce your RCS usage due to spin stabilization.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Yeah, I know. I predict that it will not.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Okay.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Jerry, I'm a little concerned about the temperature. We're getting kind of warm in here, and also the evaporator outlet temperature is up around 45 degrees. Do you have any trend that we're getting less efficient operation of the radiators now? [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Frank, EECOM says everything looks nominal down here. You might try a change in your cabin temperature heat exchanger there.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: No, we don't have the fans on, but what we have done is put up the window shades. That seems to help it. We've been getting a lot more sun in the cabin this way.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger. We'll keep a close eye on things and keep you posted.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Roger. I don't mind playing games because, you guys have been very nice in the five and a half days. If you want to play games in the next half hour, we'll play.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger, Frank. [Long pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Jim is trying this set with the eye relief optics so we can give you some information on that.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: I think it would be very difficult to extrapolate anything that you're getting out of this spin business to a LM-Command Module combination, because the spacecraft handles quite a bit different just with the change of fuel load, including the difference in drifting off in roll.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger, Frank. We just got finished discussing that, too. We agree with your point of view on that one. I think this is more of a curiosity thing than anything at all.

a08_1232208.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232208.text: I think it's fine. No sweat. We don't have anything else to do here for about another 10 hours.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232208.text: Jerry, what I'm kind of curious about is the fuel usage. Now with P23 and what we were doing, we have a lot more fuel. [Long pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Jim, we'll take a look at that fuel usage bit. Right now, the trend looks like it is getting better as we would expect with a lighter weight. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: We'll try to get a little more definitive for you here.

a08_1232208.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232208.text: Okay.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: We really - we shouldn't complain about the fuel usage on that SPS engine though, because we're sure getting a lot of miles per gallon out of it. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger, Frank. [Pause.] Frank, we'll enter you in the Shell road test on that.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Yeah, but we don't have any TCP in it, or what is that, TCP? Yeah. That's the problem. If we'd had that, we would have probably used only half the fuel.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Oh, you mean Platformate?

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: That's right, Platformate. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: If you will get the people to spread out one of those banners around the target area, we'll try to break it, you know, and coast through it.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Okay. We'll call some of the paper companies and see if they can find a roll big enough.

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: It won't take a big roll, just about 30 feet.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232208.text: Onboard nav. [Pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: You tell the doctors that we put William to sleep.

a08_1232208.speaker: Carr
a08_1232208.text: Roger. You won't leave any scars will you?

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: No. No, he's got his tape recorder with him. [Long pause.]

a08_1232208.speaker: Borman
a08_1232208.text: Bill said to call Valerie and have her to rewind the tape recorder - his tape recorder at home.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1232500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Jerry Carr's reference to the chicken list - this reference brought about on the Quad A temperature - it appears now that our tolerances are even better than we had previously thought. Since our last report, we've talked with our Retrofire officer here in Mission Control, Jerry Bostick, who has passed along some preliminary entry numbers to us, both assuming no midcourse correction at Entry Interface minus 2 hours or - correction - midcourse correction at Entry Interface at minus 2 hours. We will pass along both sets of numbers and emphasize that they are preli

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1232500-pao.text: Jim is trying this set with the eye relief optics so we can give you some information on that.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1232500-pao.text: I think it would be very difficult to extrapolate anything that you're getting out of this spin business to a LM-Command Module combination, because the spacecraft handles quite a bit different just with the change of fuel load, including the difference in drifting off in roll.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1232500-pao.text: Roger, Frank. We just got finished discussing that, too. We agree with your point of view on that one. I think this is more of a curiosity thing than anything at all.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232500-pao.text: I think it's fine. No sweat. We don't have anything else to do here for about another 10 hours.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1232500-pao.text: Jerry, what I'm kind of curious about is the fuel usage. Now with P23 and what we were doing, we have a lot more fuel. [Long pause.]

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1232500-pao.text: Jim, we'll take a look at that fuel usage bit. Right now, the trend looks like it is getting better as we would expect with a lighter weight. [Pause.]

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1232500-pao.text: We'll try to get a little more definitive for you here.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1232500-pao.text: We really - we shouldn't complain about the fuel usage on that SPS engine though, because we're sure getting a lot of miles per gallon out of it. [Pause.]

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1232500-pao.text: Roger, Frank. [Pause.] Frank, we'll enter you in the Shell road test on that.

a08_1232500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1232500-pao.text: Yeah, but we don't have any TCP in it, or what is that, TCP? Yeah. That's the problem. If we'd had that, we would have probably used only half the fuel.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Go ahead.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: I hate to tell you this, Frank, because Jim probably won't even be able to wear his comm carrier anymore, but that last set of marks put your state vector right on top of the MSFN state vector.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Come off that, Jerry. Come on; you promised.

a08_1233055.speaker: Lovell
a08_1233055.text: I'll get you that bottle of brandy when I get home, Jerry.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Maybe we can get him to go to Program 01 again today, too.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger. That sounds good. [Long pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Also, on the Flight Plan for l24:30, we'd like for you to run an O 2 purge on the fuel cells.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Okay.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Hey, Jerry. We were going over the checklist on entry here, you know?

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger, Frank.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: I've got a question. Is John Harpold around? [Pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger. He's listening.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: John, I can't remember. Is the lift vector up head-down or... [Pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Lovell
a08_1233055.text: Jerry, I'm beginning to worry up here.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger. It depends on which way your nose is pointing.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Touché. [Pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Right. You might note for the people at MIT that the next series of stars will be shot by the master navigator with a space helmet on and long eye relief eyepieces.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger. That ought to cut his speed down a little bit.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Right. [Long pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Frank, while you're talking about the entry checklist, this cold-soak, have you decided exactly where you want to do it there prior to entry?

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Well, I understood that EECOM talked that over with Bill, and we do it 1 hour prior to entry. We'll do it wherever you say is the best.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Okay. One hour is fine. It's just a matter of finding time in the timeline to do it.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: I think we can initiate it 1 hour before Sep.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Okay. Fine. Sounds like a winner.

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Really got all zeroes with that helmet on.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger. We just noticed that. [Long pause.]

a08_1233055.speaker: Borman
a08_1233055.text: Jim's going to leave the helmet off now for the rest of them. It gets a little anoxic in there. These helmets don't have face plates, and we have a difficult time breathing with that on.

a08_1233055.speaker: Carr
a08_1233055.text: Roger.

a08_1233300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1233300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 123 hours, 33 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8's altitude at this time above the Earth; 112,413 nautical miles [208,189 km]. Our current velocity; 5,563 feet per second [1,696 m/s]. Through Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr, we've had a rather healthy exchange with Apollo 8 crew. And we'll play that now.

a08_1233300-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1233300-pao.text: Hey, Jerry. We were going over the checklist on entry here, you know?

a08_1233300-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1233300-pao.text: I've got a question. Is John Harpold around? [Pause.]

a08_1234200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1234200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. The ground readings do show that the cabin temperature is a bit on the high side. We read 79 degrees Fahrenheit [26°C], a little warmer than normal. You heard the crew make a remark about miles per gallon on the Service Propulsion System engine. The reference here, obviously to the Trans-Earth Injection burn, which put them on their path back to Earth after orbiting the Moon. We haven't had a chance to check our numbers to see what the mile-per-gallon figure might be, but we rather suspect it is a world's record. So at 123 hours, 42 minutes into the flight of A

a08_1240226.speaker: Borman
a08_1240226.text: Okay. Jerry, that completes the P23. Did you have something else you want us to do now? You wanted to check on something from the last Sep.

a08_1240226.speaker: Carr
a08_1240226.text: Roger, Frank. We need to get some numbers that we weren't able to copy down here. Stand by just one. [Pause.] Frank, on your first P23, we missed three marks on star number 2. We missed mark number 3 runnion - trunnion.

a08_1240226.speaker: Carr
a08_1240226.text: Okay, 05650. Then star number 1, mark 2. We need the trunnion on that one, too.

a08_1240226.speaker: Carr
a08_1240226.text: And on star number 1, mark 3, the Delta-R and Delta-V.

a08_1240226.speaker: Carr
a08_1240226.text: Roger. Four balls 6 and four balls 1. Okay. Frank, your PTC attitude is pitch 180, yaw 315, and roll rate 0.3 degrees per second. The reason for wanting to point it north is not because we are concerned at all about any changes due to venting; there's been, as far as we can tell, no effects on your trajectory by venting. They just want to try out that direction on it.

a08_1240226.speaker: Borman
a08_1240226.text: That's fine. We're going to stay in for about two more seconds while Jim takes the pictures through the sextant for the optics people.

a08_1240226.speaker: Carr
a08_1240226.text: Okay, Frank. And then, also, we're looking for a fuel cell O 2 purge when you get a chance.

a08_1240226.speaker: Borman
a08_1240226.text: That's right. At - I got the word now; it's supposed to be at 124:30.

a08_1241114.speaker: Carr
a08_1241114.text: Roger. For your P37 that's coming up that you're going to run, use a midcourse 7 time of l44:46. Also just a little note here, the trajectory is looking so good, it looks like you could probably make the corridor without even making a midcourse 7.

a08_1241340.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241340.text: We're going to set this up for the normal PTC mode for a few minutes until Frank gets through with the - another step of the call.

a08_1241340.speaker: Carr
a08_1241340.text: Roger, Jim. When the time is auspicious, would you shift the Biomed switch over to left side?

a08_1241340.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241340.text: I think we ought to shift it over right now.

a08_1241340.speaker: Carr
a08_1241340.text: Okay. No, they say hold it up for a little while.

a08_1241340.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241340.text: So you can see the medical data... [pause] So you can see he has the same data that Dr. Berry got on me in Gemini VII is also good for Frank on Apollo 8.

a08_1241900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1241900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 124 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. Apollo 8's current altitude reads 109,929 nautical miles [203,589 km] above the Earth. Our current velocity reading; 5,641 feet per second [1,719 m/s]. Since our last report we've talked to the Apollo 8 spacecraft - spacecraft Commander Frank Borman and Jim Lovell on a range of subjects, and we'll pass those along.

a08_1241900-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241900-pao.text: Do you see that Program Alarm we got when we went through P37, 1302?

a08_1241900-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241900-pao.text: I'll run through it again and see what happens here.

a08_1241925.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241925.text: Do you see that Program Alarm we got when we went through P37, 1302?

a08_1241925.speaker: Lovell
a08_1241925.text: I'll run through it again and see what happens here.

a08_1242133.speaker: Carr
a08_1242133.text: Looks like you loaded the wrong time there in P37. You should load 144:46 for your midcourse time; looks like you loaded 146:46.

a08_1242133.speaker: Lovell
a08_1242133.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Yeah, I have it here. I wrote it down, 146:46. Okay.

a08_1242133.speaker: Lovell
a08_1242133.text: I guess the best way to terminate this is by going back to P00, is that right?

a08_1242400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1242400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. The midcourse correction number 7 referred to in the conversation exchange [at 124:11:18] is that Entry Interface minus 2 hours, or 2 hours before the spacecraft is due to reenter the Earth's atmosphere. And this would [be] consistent with an Entry Interface time of 146 hours, 46 minutes - would read 144 hours, 46 minutes, so the reference to POO is program 00 aboard the computer, the onboard computer. So at 124 hours, 24 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1242802.speaker: Lovell
a08_1242802.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Looks like a plus 2.8 foot per second correction at midcourse 7.

a08_1244125.speaker: Borman
a08_1244125.text: Started the fuel cell purge, and I'm going to 183:15, and I'll start that three-tenths of a degree per second roll stabilization test for you.

a08_1244125.speaker: Borman
a08_1244125.text: Okay. There we are, and we are going to start rolling now.

a08_1244125.speaker: Carr
a08_1244125.text: Frank, on this free pitch and yaw, if either one of them gets outside of 15 degrees from the nominal values, we'll call it off.

a08_1244500.speaker: Carr
a08_1244500.text: Apollo 8, Houston. I would like to have the Biomed switch left now, if you can.

a08_1244700-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1244700-pao.text: Houston, fuel cell purged to complete, O 2 . [Pause.]

a08_1244739.speaker: Borman
a08_1244739.text: Houston, fuel cell purged to complete, O 2 . [Pause.]

a08_1245000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1245000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 124 hours, 47 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The altitude of Apollo 8, at this time; 108,386 nautical miles [200,731 km] above Earth. Present velocity; 5,690 feet per second [1,734 m/s]. The Apollo 8 spacecraft now returning to a Passive Thermal Control attitude, this one of three-tenths of a degree per second. We will play conversation with Apollo 8 now.

a08_1245000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1245000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, the purge of the fuel cells, part of our nominal time lines in the Flight Plan, has been completed. The latest roll in the Passive Thermal Control a bit above the nominal mission plan, but is being done more to acquire additional data in this mode. The nominal mission plan being one-tenth of a degree per second, this some variance from that roll rate. Apollo 8 has passed that point in the mission, incidentally, for possibilities of an Atlantic Ocean splash or an Indian Ocean splash. Therefore, recovery in Mission Control Center is now passing alon

a08_1245000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1245000-pao.text: Looks like you've exceeded your 15 degrees offset PTC attitude, so you can go to attitude hold in pitch and yaw.

a08_1245000-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1245000-pao.text: Okay. I'll go back to the attitude. We didn't even get around once, did we?

a08_1245000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1245000-pao.text: Doesn't look like it. So much for spin stabilization.

a08_1245050.speaker: Carr
a08_1245050.text: Looks like you've exceeded your 15 degrees offset PTC attitude, so you can go to attitude hold in pitch and yaw.

a08_1245050.speaker: Borman
a08_1245050.text: Okay. I'll go back to the attitude. We didn't even get around once, did we?

a08_1245050.speaker: Carr
a08_1245050.text: Doesn't look like it. So much for spin stabilization.

a08_1245050.speaker: Borman
a08_1245050.text: Well, we tried it last night several times at 0.15 to 0.2 degree per second. [Long pause.]

a08_1245050.speaker: Borman
a08_1245050.text: I think there's the phenomena known as inertial coupling that has something to do with that, huh?

a08_1245050.speaker: Borman
a08_1245050.text: Put a bigger rudder on it.

a08_1245050.speaker: Carr
a08_1245050.text: Apollo 8, Houston. On the P37 comparison; using the MSFN vectors, we get a minus 1.4 on that midcourse, compared to your 2.8.
