We ran your solutions through our computer and we also get a 2.8, so your P37 looks good. We are busy still fiddling with the vectors and comparing them and we'll keep an eye on the difference.

a08_1245050.speaker: Lovell
a08_1245050.text: Roger. Looks like we came up with a plus 2.8 though, and you say you came out with a minus one point something.

a08_1245050.speaker: Lovell
a08_1245050.text: Still quite a bit of difference, isn't it there? Isn't it? [Long pause.]

a08_1245050.speaker: Carr
a08_1245050.text: Jim, that 4 feet per second difference is worth 0.28 degrees on the flight path angle.

a08_1250710.speaker: Carr
a08_1250710.text: Roger, Frank. How is your cabin temperature looking now?

a08_1250710.speaker: Borman
a08_1250710.text: It's getting cooler, thank you. We put those shades up, and that really helps.

a08_1250710.speaker: Carr
a08_1250710.text: Okay. The primary loop down here still looks real good, so it looks like you are in fine shape. Your battery B charge ought to be done by about 127 hours, and we think you shouldn't even try to charge battery A, since it looks like, at Entry Interface, it's going to have 38 amp-hours on it.

a08_1250710.speaker: Borman
a08_1250710.text: How is the weather down there, Jerry?

a08_1250710.speaker: Carr
a08_1250710.text: No, it's pretty balmy around here today.

a08_1250710.speaker: Carr
a08_1250710.text: Yeah, the temperature's about in the 70's here. It's a real nice day.

a08_1250710.speaker: Borman
a08_1250710.text: Say, Jerry, last night, Ken was saying something about turning on VHF Simplex A about 20,000 miles [37,000 km] out. I agree. I wrote it down, but I can't seem - I can't remember where I put it. You still want to do?

a08_1250710.speaker: Carr
a08_1250710.text: Roger, Frank. We've got it in the checklist here as right around 4 minutes - 4 hours before EI, right after your nominal P23, P37 onboard comparisons, page E-1.

a08_1251900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1251900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 125 hours, 19 minutes into the flight, Apollo 8. Apollo 8 continuing its descent, its trip back to Earth. The altitude now registering 106,615 nautical miles [197,451 km] away. Velocity now reads 5,748 feet per second [1,752 m/s]. We have had some discussions with Apollo 8, which we'll pipe up now.

a08_1251900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1251900-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. So there we have it. That was Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr carrying on conversations both with spacecraft Commander Frank Borman and Command Module Pilot Jim Lovell. The Passive Thermal Control test referred to, this at three-tenths of a degree per second roll, showed perhaps greater deviation in pitch and yaw than the slower rate did. We did the exercise at 0.3 versus the nominal 0.1 to see if we would get greater spin stabilization out of it. We did not. We terminated the test within 10 minutes after it started. As you heard Frank Borman reported that he had tried

a08_1253000.speaker: Carr
a08_1253000.text: Roger. We're showing some garbage on your computer. If you'll hit Error Reset, we can clear that Program Alarm so the next one can be identified. Over.

a08_1253000.speaker: Borman
a08_1253000.text: We don't have any Program Alarm.

a08_1253000.speaker: Carr
a08_1253000.text: I think this - this is a carryover from your last Program Alarm there on that P37.

a08_1253000.speaker: Borman
a08_1253000.text: Okay. Error Reset. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_1253000.speaker: Carr
a08_1253000.text: Stand by. Okay. Thank you, Frank. That did it.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Roger. Your battery is full; you can terminate charging. You've got 40 amp-hours on it now, and we've got a couple of requests for data here.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Roger.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: ...requests.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Okay. We were just talking about that. I tell Bill stop. Okay. What are your requests?

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: The first one is - the first time somebody is down in the equipment bay, we would like to get another reading on your RCS temperatures, those six temp meter readings, and the other one is of the boys in the back...

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: We just read them again.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Beg your pardon?

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: We just read the RCS qua - thruster temperatures again, and they're all pegged high.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Okay. Good deal, Frank. The other one is - the boys in the back room would like some time when everybody's awake - if you would fire up both cabin fans for about 5 minutes, they would like to see what the Delta-temperature is on the telemetry when you get the stagnation broken down and get some flow going over it. So if you can see your way clear to do that, we'd like to see it some time when everybody is up.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: We had that running before in the flight. Did they check it then?

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: You mean early in the game, when you were cool?

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Yep. When we were cool. Right.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Yeah. They got that data, and they were kind of interested in seeing what it looks like when the cabin is nice and warm and the temperature indicator is reading on the high side, to see how the Delta[-T] works in the other direction.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Okay. Coming on.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Okay. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: What else, Jerry?

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: That's it, Frank.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Another thing, Frank, is we just want to remind you that there's no charge needed on A battery.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Hey, listen, these cabin fans - one of them sounds like it's got a bad bearing. We're going to turn it off. It's got a real squeal to it.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Okay, Frank.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Sounds like it's got something in it. [Pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: That must be Bill's teddy bear.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Say again.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: That must be Bill's teddy bear.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: I don't know, but there's something in there. [Long pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: We'll try them again, one at a time. See if we can determine which one's got the noise.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Number 2 is really bad. It's got a bad bearing, and it whines like mad, so we're not going to turn it on.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Roger. Thank you.

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: We are not going to try number 1 either; there may have - something might have got in both of them, Jerry.

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: Okay, Frank. That's fine. [Long pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Borman
a08_1263828.text: Sounds like that MG starter of yours. [Pause.]

a08_1263828.speaker: Carr
a08_1263828.text: I'm afraid to turn my starter on now. It's been so long.

a08_1265200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1265200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 126 hours, 52 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 8. The current altitude above the Earth of Apollo 8 now reads 101,319 nautical miles [187,643 km]. Present velocity now 5,929 feet per second [1,807 m/s]. We've had some conversation with Apollo 8 which we're going to punch up now.

a08_1265200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1265200-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. So Frank Borman reports a noisy cabin fan. Incidentally on the ground, we're not necessarily surprised by this report. Noisy fans have shown up in some of the earlier spacecraft. And at 126 hours, 56 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Go.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Roger. We'd like to leave the PTC long enough to go orient toward the Earth for a TV shot to see if this TV thing is going off on 128. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Roger, Frank. That is fine. Do you have the gimbal angles you need?

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Yes, thank you. I got them earlier today.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: I'd keep this kind of short because we're trying to get some sleep earlier [garble] earlier.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Say again, Frank. You're getting pretty garbled. [Pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: How's that antenna?

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Loud and clear, Frank.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: I said, will this be a short one? We're going to - we're trying to hurry things up a little bit to see if we can get as much sleep as possible.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Would you put the Biomed switch on the right side now, please?

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Frank, do you intend to start your TV before 128? [Pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Negative.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Roger.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: That's what you wanted, isn't it? I thought - I thought that's when it was all squared away for.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Affirmative.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Are you planning on using the wide angle lens?

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: I think that'd be best.

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Okay. Jack says you want to be sure and use the red filter and the filter holder for that one. It takes a little darker filter.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Do you want to take both red filters on there or just the one for the filter holder? [Pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: He thinks just the red one on the filter holder will do, but might not hurt to have the other one ready, just in case. [Long pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: How about if we use the telephoto? It will be a little harder to focus, but it might end up a better picture. [Pause.]

a08_1271436.speaker: Carr
a08_1271436.text: Roger, Frank. If you want to use the telephoto lens, you ought to use the same combination you used going out, the 25A.

a08_1271436.speaker: Borman
a08_1271436.text: Okay.

a08_1271900-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1271900-pao.text: He thinks just the red one on the filter holder will do, but might not hurt to have the other one ready, just in case. [Long pause.]

a08_1271900-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1271900-pao.text: How about if we use the telephoto? It will be a little harder to focus, but it might end up a better picture. [Pause.]

a08_1272212.speaker: Borman
a08_1272212.text: Ask your EECOM how many gallons of fuel we burned for TEI, will you?.

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Roger. In work. [Long pause.] He's breaking out his sathometer now. [Long pause.]

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We will be handing over to Goldstone in 2 minutes. Over.

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Frank, the doctors say they're not getting anything on Bill yet. He's apparently not plugged up.

a08_1272212.speaker: Borman
a08_1272212.text: He is down underneath the couch getting some stuff out; he doesn't have his umbilical on.

a08_1272212.speaker: Borman
a08_1272212.text: Tell them to look at the stuff they got yesterday. He hasn't changed at all. Just as mean as ever.

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Hey, Frank, this simulation has really been great. What do you say after these photos we recycle back to TLI again?

a08_1272212.speaker: Borman
a08_1272212.text: That's fine. Bring on the backup crew.

a08_1272212.speaker: Lovell
a08_1272212.text: Hey, Jerry, yesterday I tried to cycle back to the pad with 01 Program but it didn't work.

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Jim, we missed that. Say it again when you get a better antenna.

a08_1272212.speaker: Borman
a08_1272212.text: Don't blame your antenna problems on us [garble].

a08_1272212.speaker: Lovell
a08_1272212.text: Jerry, yesterday I tried to cycle [garble] 01 [garble].

a08_1272212.speaker: Carr
a08_1272212.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We are not reading you; stand by one.

a08_1272300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1272300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 127 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft, at this time, less than 100,000 nautical miles [185,000 km] away from Earth. We read 99,802 nautical miles [184,833 km], the distance that separates Apollo 8 from Earth. Current velocity; 5,983 feet per second [1,824 m/s]. We've been talking and are still talking to spacecraft Commander Frank Borman, regarding his upcoming TV pass at 128 hours GET. And we're going to switch over to that conversation now,

a08_1272300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1272300-pao.text: It appears that the discussion at present is going a little slow. That was Frank Borman, reconfirming by the way, our television time at a Ground Elapsed Time of 128 hours, our... [brief interruption by CapCom]

a08_1272300-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1272300-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We will be handing over to Goldstone in 2 minutes. Over.

a08_1272300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1272300-pao.text: Goldstone will acquire in 2 minutes. That's a prime site for this television period. We're about 37 minutes away from our time for television. Standing by, continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1272650.speaker: Borman
a08_1272650.text: I say, Bill will be ready in a minute; he is cycling back and forth under the couch trying to get the TV stuff out.

a08_1272650.speaker: Carr
a08_1272650.text: Backup crew says they're ready to go.

a08_1272650.speaker: Borman
a08_1272650.text: Great. [Pause.] That was a fantastic voyage. [Pause.]

a08_1272650.speaker: Borman
a08_1272650.text: Now we're - now we're not through yet. We've still got 100,000 [nautical] miles [185,000 km] to go. You know, we kind of feel like it was all over with TEI, but we're still a long way. [Pause.]

a08_1272650.speaker: Lovell
a08_1272650.text: Jerry, what I was saying before: I tried to hurry up the voyage home by - by calling up Program 01 to get us back on the pad, but it didn't work.

a08_1272650.speaker: Carr
a08_1272650.text: Well, that's the best excuse I've heard so far, Jim.

a08_1273300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1273300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. 127 hours, 29 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The spacecraft is presently 99,211 [nautical] miles [183,739 km] above the Earth; its velocity, 6,005 feet per second [1,830 m/s]. We are just exceeding the 6,000 feet per second mark. We've have had further discussions with Apollo 8, Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr talking with both Frank Borman and Jim Lovell. ...

a08_1273300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1273300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. Bill Anders apparently now unstowing the television gear for the upcoming period of TV. I have some of the earlier communications on that discussion - they were a bit noisy and you may have missed an earlier comment made by Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr when he said, 'Gee, the simulation is really great. Why not recycle back to TLI?' referring, of course, to the reignition of the S-IVB which sent the Apollo 8 spacecraft to lunar distance. Apollo 8 retorted, 'Send the backup crew.' A later report indicated that the backup crew was indeed ready. So at 127 hours, 33 min

a08_1273935.speaker: Carr
a08_1273935.text: Roger, Frank. On TEI, you burned 1,480 gallons.

a08_1273935.speaker: Carr
a08_1273935.text: Frank, you going to need Jim's slide rule for that calculation?

a08_1273935.speaker: Lovell
a08_1273935.text: Rog. This is one of those rare occasions where Bill left his seat and I'm now sitting in it, and for the first time, I can see the Earth. I'm looking through his monocular; it's pretty nice.

a08_1273935.speaker: Lovell
a08_1273935.text: You had a little weather today it appears.

a08_1273935.speaker: Carr
a08_1273935.text: Last word from the weather guys here was that it was clear.

a08_1273935.speaker: Lovell
a08_1273935.text: Well, we can see South America and Florida and through the lower part of the U.S. Looks like there is a weather front going over into the central part of the United States, lot of clouds over the northwest area. Florida is clear; it looks like the east coast is pretty clear.

a08_1273935.speaker: Lovell
a08_1273935.text: Lot of clouds up in Canada. [Pause.]

a08_1273935.speaker: Carr
a08_1273935.text: Maybe the geese'll go home. [Long pause.]

a08_1273935.speaker: Borman
a08_1273935.text: Jerry, we are going to turn it on and see how the picture is.

a08_1274400-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1274400-pao.text: Takes a while to warm up, I think.

a08_1274400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1274400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 127 hours, 44 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time; 98,361 nautical miles [182,165 km] above Earth. Its velocity exceeding 6,000 feet per second [1,830 m/s]. We have had some conversations with - further conversations with both Frank Borman and Jim Lovell, Bill Anders apparently still out of his seat - getting ready for television and we're going to pass those on now.

a08_1274400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1274400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We're...

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: We got a picture now, Frank. It's twitching. [Long pause.]

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: The Earth is on now, Frank.

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: We are seeing about half of it. You moved in the wrong direction. Okay. It's coming back, a little more. Good, now a shade toward the terminator. [Pause.]

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: A little bit more toward the terminator and in the same direction you were moving it before. [Long pause.] Right; you have got it centered right in the middle. [Long pause.]

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: Now move it away from the terminator just a bit. [Pause.]

a08_1274503.speaker: Borman
a08_1274503.text: Okay. You want us to wait until 128, right?

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: Affirmative. Frank, move your camera to the right; I want to see which way the Earth moves on my screen.

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: Okay. Moving your camera to the right moves the Earth to the left on our screen. [Pause.] On our screen, the terminator is almost parallel to the horizontal direction, and the dark part is on the top.

a08_1274503.speaker: Borman
a08_1274503.text: Okay. We'll turn it back on at 128 then.

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Are you on a High Gain Antenna?

a08_1274503.speaker: Carr
a08_1274503.text: What beam width are you on, Apollo 8? [Pause.]

a08_1274503.speaker: Anders
a08_1274503.text: This is Apollo 8. Do you read?

a08_1274503.speaker: Anders
a08_1274503.text: Houston, Apollo 8. How do you read now? Over.

a08_1274757-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1274757-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We've just picked up a final dress rehearsal for the actual television scheduled at 128 hours Ground Elapsed Time. We will be back in about 12 minutes with that picture.

a08_1274757-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1274757-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Are you on a High Gain Antenna?

a08_1274757-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1274757-pao.text: What beam width are you on, Apollo 8? [Pause.]

a08_1275100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1275100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 127 hours, 51 minutes. At the present time, we're about 9 minutes away from when we have the full scale television show. You had a preview of what we might see, mainly a very good view of the Earth. We've had a few additional conversation - very limited conversation I should say, since that picture came on your screen, and we'll play that conversation now.

a08_1275100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1275100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Our current altitude on Apollo 8 is 97,847 nautical miles [97,847 km] above the Earth. Current velocity is 6,055 feet per second [1,846 m/s]. So at 127 hours, 53 minutes; standing by, this is Apollo Control.

a08_1275259.speaker: Carr
a08_1275259.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're in the scan limit right now on the High Gain Antenna; although you may have narrow beam width selected, you're in wide. To improve the situation would take a pitch down and a yaw left, and we'll have FAO check it and give you some angles if we need to change it.

a08_1275259.speaker: Borman
a08_1275259.text: We just got out of the scan limit by pitching up and yawing right. [Long pause.]

a08_1275259.speaker: Borman
a08_1275259.text: Are we still in wide band, or are we in narrow band now?

a08_1275259.speaker: Carr
a08_1275259.text: Apollo 8, Houston. EECOM says you're in good shape now.

a08_1275700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1275700-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 127 hours, 57 minutes. We've had some updated conversations with the crew which we're going to put on before we pick up the next television.

a08_1275700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1275700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Our current altitude reading, 97,507 nautical miles [180,583 km] above Earth. Current velocity; 6,068 feet per second [1,850 m/s]. This coincides very closely with the numbers we passed up earlier to Frank Borman this morning when he asked about the television pass. It was indicated at that time at an altitude of 97,413 nautical miles [180,409 km] should be our time - should be our distance at time of acquisition, and a velocity of 6,072 feet per second [1,851 m/s]. We're very close to reaching both of those marks. We're less than a minute away now from our ant

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Roger. The picture is on the lower right hand of our screen. [Pause.]

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Camera should go down away from the terminator and to the right. [Long pause.]

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Still down and about the same place; a little worse; now it's coming in.

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280000-pao.text: Are you getting it now, Jerry?

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Roger. We've got most of it; keep moving off to the right. Good. You have it centered right now.

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280000-pao.text: Well, the Earth looks a little bigger to us today, not much, but it's somewhat bigger. I'm sitting over in the right hand seat now; Bill's got the TV camera; Frank's helping him out aiming it directly to hit the Earth. I hope we have a good picture. Can you see the clouds?

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Affirmative. We sure can. Move it up toward the terminator - correction, away from the terminator just a shade.

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280000-pao.text: At the tip of South America, there's a great swirl of clouds down there. It looks like a great storm. I wonder if you can see it.

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1280000-pao.text: Roger. We see a large swirl just to the south of the terminator.

a08_1280000-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280000-pao.text: Rog. And then up to the left hand side, or towards the north, we can see the light waters around the West Indies, and we can actually see Florida. I'm looking through Bill's monocular, and I can see the various land masses, South America and the central part and southern part of the United States.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're getting television.

a08_1280113.speaker: Borman
a08_1280113.text: Roger. How's the picture?

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger. The picture is on the lower right hand of our screen. [Pause.]

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Camera should go down away from the terminator and to the right. [Long pause.]

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Still down and about the same place; a little worse; now it's coming in.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: Are you getting it now, Jerry?

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger. We've got most of it; keep moving off to the right. Good. You have it centered right now.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: Well, the Earth looks a little bigger to us today, not much, but it's somewhat bigger. I'm sitting over in the right hand seat now; Bill's got the TV camera; Frank's helping him out aiming it directly to hit the Earth. I hope we have a good picture. Can you see the clouds?

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Affirmative. We sure can. Move it up toward the terminator - correction, away from the terminator just a shade.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: At the tip of South America, there's a great swirl of clouds down there. It looks like a great storm. I wonder if you can see it.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger. We see a large swirl just to the south of the terminator.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: Rog. And then up to the left hand side, or towards the north, we can see the light waters around the West Indies, and we can actually see Florida. I'm looking through Bill's monocular, and I can see the various land masses, South America and the central part and southern part of the United States.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger. Move a little bit away from the terminator now. [Pause.] Little left with the camera and a little further away from the terminator.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: Say again, Jerry.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Okay. You're moving it toward the center of the screen now, and the Earth is off on the left side of our screen.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Real fine. That's good. [Pause.] Hold it right there.

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: What we're thinking about right now, Jerry, is hitting that wedge angle, about 2 degrees their limit. When we come back, the Earth looks pretty small right from here.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a08_1280113.speaker: Lovell
a08_1280113.text: You got it, Bill. [Pause.]

a08_1280113.speaker: Anders
a08_1280113.text: As I look down on the Earth here from so far out in space, I think I must have the feeling that the travelers in the old sailing ships used to have: going on a very long voyage away from home, and now we're headed back, and I have that feeling of being proud of the trip, but still - still happy to be going back home and back to our home port. And that's - that's what you're seeing right here.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger, Bill. We'll sure be glad to get you back, too. [Pause.]

a08_1280113.speaker: Borman
a08_1280113.text: This is Frank Borman. We've enjoyed the television shows, and we'd like you to stay tuned in, in the future, because there'll be flights and rendezvous in Earth orbit; and then, of course, there'll be television from the lunar surface itself in the not too far distant future. So, until then, I guess this is the Apollo 8 crew signing off, and we'll see you back on the good Earth very soon.

a08_1280113.speaker: Carr
a08_1280113.text: Roger, Frank. Adios.

a08_1280600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1280600-pao.text: That, our last television transmission before the Apollo 8 crew returns to Earth, at 128 hours, 5 minutes at the present time. And right now we show an altitude above Earth of 97,073 nautical miles [179,779 km]. The velocity as the spacecraft, Apollo 8, now on its return trip, a velocity of 6,084 feet per second [1,854 m/s]. So at 128 hours, 6 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1280653.speaker: Carr
a08_1280653.text: We'd like you to go back to PTC. Pick either attitude that's easiest to fly to.

a08_1281126.speaker: Carr
a08_1281126.text: Roger. Your PTC attitude ought to be either a 1045 or a 18315. We'd recommend 18315. That will keep your windows out of the Sun.

a08_1281126.speaker: Borman
a08_1281126.text: 180, that's right. I got them mixed up, didn't I? It's 18315.

a08_1281703.speaker: Carr
a08_1281703.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. You're unreadable due to background noise. Over.

a08_1281703.speaker: Borman
a08_1281703.text: I say we're starting to stow the spacecraft and get all squared away and then be sleeping and eating. We'll be all thinking about entry from now on.

a08_1281703.speaker: Carr
a08_1281703.text: Roger, Frank. And now that Bill's up, we'd like to get a redundant components check.

a08_1281703.speaker: Borman
a08_1281703.text: All right. He's putting helmets in the food boxes. Just a minute, I'll get him to do it for you.

a08_1281703.speaker: Carr
a08_1281703.text: Roger. There is no great hurry, Frank. We're...

a08_1281703.speaker: Borman
a08_1281703.text: What do you want it for?

a08_1281703.speaker: Carr
a08_1281703.text: We're mostly interested in looking at the secondary loop.

a08_1281703.speaker: Borman
a08_1281703.text: That's what I was going to say. I can't see any reason to check anything other than the secondary loop, can you?

a08_1281703.speaker: Borman
a08_1281703.text: Now in that cabin cold-soak, we won't have any cabin fans.

a08_1281952.speaker: Lovell
a08_1281952.text: Roger. I just got on the sextant and now looking at Texas, and the weather man is right, it looks like a pretty good day. Full of clouds down there, but not bad.

a08_1281952.speaker: Carr
a08_1281952.text: Real fine, Jim. Can you see the kids out in the yard waving?

a08_1281952.speaker: Lovell
a08_1281952.text: Would you tell Pete Conrad to get his kids off my roof?

a08_1281952.speaker: Carr
a08_1281952.text: Jim, do you see the bright spot out in the Pacific Ocean through the sextant?

a08_1281952.speaker: Lovell
a08_1281952.text: I'll try. We saw it, of course, through the windows and through the monocular. I'll see if I can spot it.

a08_1281952.speaker: Lovell
a08_1281952.text: Yes, Jerry, I can see the bright spot. It's - I guess it's the subsolar point. It's off of South America, it appears to me. It is a grayish spot compared to the blue waters surrounding it. It's undefined in diameter, though, I mean, it's not a clear round spot at all; it's just a raggedy one.

a08_1281952.speaker: Carr
a08_1281952.text: Roger. That showed up real well on the TV's picture. [Long pause.]

a08_1281952.speaker: Carr
a08_1281952.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'd like to belay that request for a secondary loop check to a little better point as far as thrusting is concerned.

a08_1281952.speaker: Borman
a08_1281952.text: Fine. We can wait for a long time on that.

a08_1282100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1282100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 128 hours, 21 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft now 96,149 nautical miles [178,068 km] above Earth. Its velocity now reading 6,119 feet per second [1,865 m/s] and accelerating as it returns at an increasing velocity towards the Earth. Among those interested viewers in Mission Control Center watching the television pass, or perhaps we should say passes, was Mrs. Marilyn Lovell, along with two children, Jay and Barbara. We've had discussions with Apollo 8 since that time. Since the time of the television transmission and we'll pas

a08_1282100-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1282100-pao.text: Yes, Jerry, I can see the bright spot. It's - I guess it's the subsolar point. It's off of South America, it appears to me. It is a grayish spot compared to the blue waters surrounding it. It's undefined in diameter, though, I mean, it's not a clear round spot at all; it's just a raggedy one.

a08_1282100-pao.speaker: Carr
a08_1282100-pao.text: Roger. That showed up real well on the TV's picture. [Long pause.]

a08_1282410.speaker: Carr
a08_1282410.text: Roger. Jim, we've got some bird watchers in the viewing room.

a08_1282410.speaker: Lovell
a08_1282410.text: Oh, well, good. Say hello to her for me.

a08_1282410.speaker: Carr
a08_1282410.text: Yeah, and she's got a few troops with her, too. [Pause.]

a08_1282410.speaker: Lovell
a08_1282410.text: Did she see the TV, I wonder?

a08_1282410.speaker: Carr
a08_1282410.text: Affirmative. Barbara and Jay are with her.

a08_1282638.speaker: Carr
a08_1282638.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're replaying your television pictures now. We can see the Chilean coast and Florida.

a08_1282638.speaker: Anders
a08_1282638.text: That's a pretty good little television camera, isn't it?

a08_1282638.speaker: Carr
a08_1282638.text: It sure is. With the right filters on it, it's great. That was a Schmitt input. [Pause.]

a08_1282638.speaker: Lovell
a08_1282638.text: He must be a Jack of all trades.

a08_1282700-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1282700-pao.text: He must be a Jack of all trades.

a08_1283001.speaker: Borman
a08_1283001.text: Bill would like to ask the friendly Flight Surgeon's permission to take a Seconal so he can sleep.

a08_1283237.speaker: Carr
a08_1283237.text: Roger. Before Bill falls asleep, we'd like to have him go ahead and do that secondary evap check now at any time at his convenience, and if we don't happen to be able to monitor it with high bit rate, just let us know when you did it.

a08_1283237.speaker: Lovell
a08_1283237.text: Roger. I'll tell him that evaporator check at any time.

a08_1284038.speaker: Carr
a08_1284038.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Biomed switch to the CDR. Over.

a08_1284600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1284600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 128 hours, 46 minutes now into the flight, Apollo 8. The Apollo 8 spacecraft at this time; 94,676 nautical miles [175,340 km] above the Earth. Velocity at this time 6,176 feet per second [1,882 m/s]. We have a couple of minutes conversation with the crew that we'd like to play to you now.

a08_1284800.speaker: Anders
a08_1284800.text: Okay. Somebody said something about checking out the evaporator, or evaporators. What do you want to do?

a08_1284800.speaker: Carr
a08_1284800.text: Roger. Before we get too far along, we'd like to see, essentially with the secondary evaporator check, that we've got a redundant components check.

a08_1284800.speaker: Carr
a08_1284800.text: Roger. EECOM says to be sure and let it go for at least 5 minutes.

a08_1284800.speaker: Anders
a08_1284800.text: Roger. Now you want to check out the primary evaporator also, or did you decide it's not necessary?

a08_1284800.speaker: Carr
a08_1284800.text: I guess they decided it's not necessary, Bill.

a08_1284800.speaker: Anders
a08_1284800.text: Okay. Secondary glycol loops coming on the line.

a08_1284800.speaker: Anders
a08_1284800.text: And the secondary evap's coming on the line.

a08_1284800.speaker: Anders
a08_1284800.text: And it's stabilized the leg, oh, for about 5 minutes.

a08_1284900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1284900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 128 hours, 49 minutes into the flight. We're coming up on a change of shift here very shortly. The Black Team change of shift briefing now scheduled for 4:15 pm in the big auditorium. Participants for this news conference will include Flight Director Glynn Lunney, his Retrofire Officer Jerry Bostick, Major General Vincent G. Houston, DOD Manager for Manned Spaceflight Support Operations, and Mr. Jerome Hannick, chief of the landing and recovery division of the Manned Spacecraft Center. And this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1284900-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1284900-pao.text: Okay. Secondary glycol loops coming on the line.

a08_1285329.speaker: Anders
a08_1285329.text: All right. What do you have in mind here in the way of activating the secondary loop prior to separation? It looks like if we do have a cabin fan problem, we won't be able to do a full-blown cold-soak. Is there anything that we can do that'll do any good?

a08_1285329.speaker: Carr
a08_1285329.text: Well, right now, Bill, in the checklist, we're showing this activation at about minus 1 hour. Let me check with EECOM for a minute and see if they got any more words considering the cabin fan situation.

a08_1285329.speaker: Carr
a08_1285329.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Looks like a good time. One hour before Sep - Entry Interface would be fine.

a08_1285329.speaker: Anders
a08_1285329.text: Okay. It won't do any good, then, seems to me, to fool around with these cabin temp valves. [Garble] primary and secondary [garble].

a08_1285329.speaker: Carr
a08_1285329.text: Bill, stand by. You're - got a lot of background noise. [Long pause.]

a08_1285329.speaker: Anders
a08_1285329.text: Okay. This cold-soak is built around the premise that you've got a cabin heat exchanger, in my view; and if you haven't got a cabin heat exchanger, I'm wondering just what you can do. [Pause.]

a08_1285329.speaker: Carr
a08_1285329.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We think it'll still do a little bit of good so we'd just as soon go through with it.

a08_1285329.speaker: Anders
a08_1285329.text: Okay. Even bypassing the suit heat exchanger and that part of it too, huh?

a08_1285329.speaker: Carr
a08_1285329.text: Also, Bill, your secondary loop is looking good.

a08_1285329.speaker: Anders
a08_1285329.text: Okay. We just had 5 minutes. I'll deactivate it now.

a08_1290500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1290500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 129 hours, 5 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 8. Here in the Mission Control Center, the Green flight control team coming aboard very shortly. The previous shift, or our shift I should say, the members of the Black Team currently briefing their counterparts on what our status is as of this time. At the present time the Apollo 8 spacecraft, 93,527 nautical miles [173,212 km] away from Earth. Current velocity reads 6,221 feet per second [1,896 m/s] and accelerating. We'll switch now to some conversations between our Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr and the

a08_1290801.speaker: Anders
a08_1290801.text: Hey, Jerry. When do you want to crank up the VHF, anyway?

a08_1290801.speaker: Carr
a08_1290801.text: Roger. VHF Simplex - well, we had that on the checklist for about minus 4 hours.

a08_1290801.speaker: Anders
a08_1290801.text: Okay. We wanted - we wanted to put it out prior to max range, don't you think? Get an idea of when we're picking it up?

a08_1290801.speaker: Carr
a08_1290801.text: Roger. Stand by, Bill. They're talking about it.

a08_1291100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1291100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Well that's the first we've heard from Lunar Module Pilot Bill Anders for a while. He was obviously preoccupied during the television pass. And at 20 - 129 hours, 11 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1291100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1291100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We are breaking shift at this time. Flight Director Clifford Charlesworth and his Green Team are now aboard. We do want to announce again that the change of shift briefing for Glynn Lunney, Flight Director, is scheduled for 4:15 pm. 4:15 pm [December 26]. And at 129 hours, 12 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1291244.speaker: Carr
a08_1291244.text: Roger. Entry Interface minus 4 hours is just about right for the VHF. That's about - oh, around 142 GET

a08_1291244.speaker: Carr
a08_1291244.text: Next voice - next voice you hear will be that of the smiling Irishman [Mike Collins].

a08_1292239.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292239.text: Oh, it's Michael Collins, is it? Good morning to you.

a08_1292239.speaker: Collins
a08_1292239.text: Righto. And we're looking at your pitch CDU read-out down here and looks to us like you are about 25 degrees off the 180 for your PTC, and we were just wondering how come?

a08_1292239.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292239.text: We've been looking at that, too. It keeps wandering off in pitch for some reason more than yaw. I was just about ready to go back to it again. I had to go back one time, and I was just seeing how far she'd drift. I thought it would drift out a ways and come back by itself, but it is not doing it.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We're in the process of doing the trunnion bias check; then we'll go to P23.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger. Thank you, Frank. [Long pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Houston, Apollo 8.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Go.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger. We'd like to have the PTC attitude to comply with P23 requirement.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger, Frank. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Go ahead.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Any time you want to start on those P23s is just fine.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay. I was just checking. I just wanted to know how our thermal control was going before we left. [Long pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Your temperatures are looking good, Frank. There's still a differential temperature between quads, but nothing that would cause us in the slightest to worry about doing P23.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger. Understand.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Go ahead.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger, Jim. We've been looking at these stars that we gave you this time for P23. It looks like the second star, number 11, has a trunnion angle right out near the limit, about 49.7 degrees. And we're thinking it might be a better idea to switch you over to star 1, which has a much smaller trunnion angle. What do you think? Star 1 is Alpheratz.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Fine with me; I would just as soon take star 1.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay. That will be then; in place of star 11, star 1; and in place of lunar far horizon, lunar near horizon; and it remains two sets. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger. Star 1, lunar near horizon, two sets.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Thank you.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Roger, Frank. Old golden fingers there is getting so swift we missed some marks on the downlink, and I wonder, if you hand recorded them, could you read us your three marks, trunnion angles, your three trunnion angles on star 2 and the last four trunnion angles on star 1. Over. [Pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Do you read me still, Mike?

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Stand by. We're not reading you good enough, so we'll wait until you get a better Omni.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: That ought to be a good one.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: That is a good one. That's loud and clear.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay. Star 2 trunnion angle, first one 05245, second one 05243, next one 05241; last 4 trunnion angles 04133, 04133, 04132, 04132.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Thank you kindly. [Long pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Can you give me some idea of the updates from the midcourse that we might need, and all that good stuff, Mike?

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Yeah, I sure can, Frank. Stand by.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Go ahead, Mike.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay. We're predicting at the nominal time of your next midcourse, which is Entry Interface minus 2 hours - we're predicting a 1.4 foot per second burn which changes your gamma at Entry Interface by a tenth of a degree. Right now, with no further maneuvers, your gamma is minus 6.39 degrees. And we're going to steepen it up very slightly to hit the center of the target line, and it will be, after the maneuver, minus 6.51. Over.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Very good.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Anything else you want like that?

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: No. I just wondered. We hadn't heard whether we were going to do it or not and so on.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Rog.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: When we get the PAD data, we'll get it all out here.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Yeah. We'll be sending the PAD data up to you in about another 2 hours, Frank; about 132 hours GET.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay. We - this will be the last set of star sightings we do now nominally, and even if we lose comm, we'll just come on in with what we got.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Okay, Frank.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Incidentally, that comm has been fantastic. I don't know how you've heard us, but boy, it was just like you're next door even at lunar distances.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Yeah. It really has been great there, with the rare exception is when you are on a bad Omni right before you switch. Then we get an awful lot of background noise, but in general, it's been excellent, and boy, we're really thankful for it because reading all these updates would be bad news with bad comm, as you know.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Right.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Say, Mike, have you noticed the confidence the Captain has in his navigator?

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: He hasn't called you Goldfinger yet.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: No. He is disregarding anything that I can do. We're coming in anyway. [Pause.]

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Collins
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: I suspect he is right on that point.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Lovell
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: Well, back to the drawing board.

a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.speaker: Borman
a08_1292400-pao-press-conference.text: As usual, we are all a little pooped. I've got Bill sleeping now, and then Jim and I will swap just as soon as we get through with these stars.

a08_1293211.speaker: Borman
a08_1293211.text: Houston, Apollo 8. We're in the process of doing the trunnion bias check; then we'll go to P23.

a08_1293211.speaker: Borman
a08_1293211.text: Roger. We'd like to have the PTC attitude to comply with P23 requirement.

a08_1293211.speaker: Collins
a08_1293211.text: Any time you want to start on those P23s is just fine.

a08_1293211.speaker: Borman
a08_1293211.text: Okay. I was just checking. I just wanted to know how our thermal control was going before we left. [Long pause.]

a08_1293211.speaker: Collins
a08_1293211.text: Your temperatures are looking good, Frank. There's still a differential temperature between quads, but nothing that would cause us in the slightest to worry about doing P23.

a08_1294722.speaker: Collins
a08_1294722.text: Roger, Jim. We've been looking at these stars that we gave you this time for P23. It looks like the second star, number 11, has a trunnion angle right out near the limit, about 49.7 degrees. And we're thinking it might be a better idea to switch you over to star 1, which has a much smaller trunnion angle. What do you think? Star 1 is Alpheratz.

a08_1294722.speaker: Lovell
a08_1294722.text: Fine with me; I would just as soon take star 1.

a08_1294722.speaker: Collins
a08_1294722.text: Okay. That will be then; in place of star 11, star 1; and in place of lunar far horizon, lunar near horizon; and it remains two sets. Over.

a08_1294722.speaker: Lovell
a08_1294722.text: Roger. Star 1, lunar near horizon, two sets.

a08_1301324.speaker: Collins
a08_1301324.text: Roger, Frank. Old golden fingers there is getting so swift we missed some marks on the downlink, and I wonder, if you hand recorded them, could you read us your three marks, trunnion angles, your three trunnion angles on star 2 and the last four trunnion angles on star 1. Over. [Pause.]

a08_1301324.speaker: Borman
a08_1301324.text: Do you read me still, Mike?

a08_1301324.speaker: Collins
a08_1301324.text: Stand by. We're not reading you good enough, so we'll wait until you get a better Omni.

a08_1301324.speaker: Borman
a08_1301324.text: That ought to be a good one.

a08_1301324.speaker: Collins
a08_1301324.text: That is a good one. That's loud and clear.

a08_1301324.speaker: Borman
a08_1301324.text: Okay. Star 2 trunnion angle, first one 05245, second one 05243, next one 05241; last 4 trunnion angles 04133, 04133, 04132, 04132.

a08_1301324.speaker: Borman
a08_1301324.text: Can you give me some idea of the updates from the midcourse that we might need, and all that good stuff, Mike?

a08_1301324.speaker: Collins
a08_1301324.text: Yeah, I sure can, Frank. Stand by.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Over.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Go ahead, Mike.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Okay. We're predicting at the nominal time of your next midcourse, which is Entry Interface minus 2 hours - we're predicting a 1.4 foot per second burn which changes your gamma at Entry Interface by a tenth of a degree. Right now, with no further maneuvers, your gamma is minus 6.39 degrees. And we're going to steepen it up very slightly to hit the center of the target line, and it will be, after the maneuver, minus 6.51. Over.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Very good.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Anything else you want like that?

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: No. I just wondered. We hadn't heard whether we were going to do it or not and so on.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Rog.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: When we get the PAD data, we'll get it all out here.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Yeah. We'll be sending the PAD data up to you in about another 2 hours, Frank; about 132 hours GET.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Okay. We - this will be the last set of star sightings we do now nominally, and even if we lose comm, we'll just come on in with what we got.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Okay, Frank.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Incidentally, that comm has been fantastic. I don't know how you've heard us, but boy, it was just like you're next door even at lunar distances.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Yeah. It really has been great there, with the rare exception is when you are on a bad Omni right before you switch. Then we get an awful lot of background noise, but in general, it's been excellent, and boy, we're really thankful for it because reading all these updates would be bad news with bad comm, as you know.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Right.

a08_1301755.speaker: Lovell
a08_1301755.text: Say, Mike, have you noticed the confidence the Captain has in his navigator?

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: He hasn't called you Goldfinger yet.

a08_1301755.speaker: Lovell
a08_1301755.text: No. He is disregarding anything that I can do. We're coming in anyway. [Pause.]

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: I suspect he is right on that point.

a08_1301755.speaker: Lovell
a08_1301755.text: Well, back to the drawing board.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: As usual, we are all a little pooped. I've got Bill sleeping now, and then Jim and I will swap just as soon as we get through with these stars.

a08_1301755.speaker: Collins
a08_1301755.text: Well, you're sounding real good, and you are doing good work.

a08_1301755.speaker: Borman
a08_1301755.text: Thank you.

a08_1302400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1302400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 130 hours, 24 minutes. During our change of shift press briefing, the crew has been primarily involved in some guidance and navigation activities onboard the spacecraft. Frank Borman reported that Bill Anders is sleeping at the present time. And at the present time our spacecraft is traveling at a speed of 6,417 feet per second [1,956 m/s]. Our current altitude is 88,706 nautical miles [155,024 km] and this is how the conversation's been going up to now.

a08_1305640.speaker: Collins
a08_1305640.text: Roger, Frank. If you get a chance to, we'd like for you to read us down your trunnion calibration number. We missed that one on the downlink, and we have an update for your Passive Thermal Control attitude.

a08_1305640.speaker: Borman
a08_1305640.text: Okay. The trunnion calibrations were all zeros.

a08_1305640.speaker: Collins
a08_1305640.text: Roger. Thank you, and on page 2-104, the PTC attitudes should read zero pitch and 45 degrees yaw. Over.

a08_1305640.speaker: Collins
a08_1305640.text: Roger. And we'd like some PRD readings for those of you who are up and around. [Long pause.]

a08_1305640.speaker: Borman
a08_1305640.text: I'm asking that. I didn't - I wasn't sure I copied it right.

a08_1305640.speaker: Collins
a08_1305640.text: Yeah. That's affirmative, Frank. Zero pitch, 45 degrees yaw.

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: This is 8. Loud and clear. How us?

a08_1313339.speaker: Collins
a08_1313339.text: Roger. You're loud and clear, Jim. We'd like to get your PRD reading while we've got you up and a Flight Plan change we're suggesting on page 2-107 when you're ready to copy.

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: I'm the only person up, and my PRD is reading 0.15.

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: And I'll bet that Bill's is still reading 0.64.

a08_1313339.speaker: Collins
a08_1313339.text: That's okay; don't bother him with it. He's asleep. [Long pause.]

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: Okay. Go ahead with your Flight Plan change. [No answer.]

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Go ahead with your Flight Plan change.

a08_1313339.speaker: Collins
a08_1313339.text: Okay, Jim. On page 2-107, we're recommending that you delete that P52 and just stay in PTC attitude. Your platform is real good, and we don't feel that alignment's necessary. One is coming up again at 139 hours anyway. And also, on that same page, we'd like to delete the "begin cabin cold-soak." Over. [Pause.]

a08_1313339.speaker: Lovell
a08_1313339.text: Righto. We'll delete the "begin cabin cold-soak," and we'll delete the P52.

a08_1320457.speaker: Collins
a08_1320457.text: Roger, Apollo 8. This is Houston. Over.

a08_1320457.speaker: Lovell
a08_1320457.text: Roger. Mike. Are you still planning to send up these updates at 132 hours?

a08_1320457.speaker: Collins
a08_1320457.text: Yes; affirmative, Jim. We're getting them together now.

a08_1320457.speaker: Collins
a08_1320457.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Would you please go to P00 and Accept, Jim, and we'll send you a P27. [Long pause.]

a08_1320457.speaker: Collins
a08_1320457.text: Okay. Sending up a state vector to the LM slots.

a08_1320900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1320900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 132 hours, 9 minutes. Apollo 8 is at an altitude of 1 - or rather, 82,111 nautical miles [152,070 km] and our current velocity is 6,712 feet per second [2,046 m/s]. It continues to be very quiet here in Mission Control and aboard the spacecraft. We've had one or two very brief conversations with the crew and we're anticipating a call up to the spacecraft, shortly, from Mike Collins, so we'll pick that up and - and then stay tuned.

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: Roger, Jim. You can go back to Block; we got the P27 in and verified. It was a state vector update to the LM slot, and I'm standing by for the midcourse correction number 7 and the entry PAD at your convenience. Over.

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: Okay. Midcourse correction number 7; RCS/G&N; 31600; not applicable, not applicable; 144:45:57.99; minus 0001.4, plus five zeros, plus 0000.1. Are you with me so far? Over.

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: Hey, Mike, hold it. Hold it, Mike.

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: You said not applicable for H A . And H P , I started to copy it down, and then I didn't get the right number sequence. Did you skip down to what, V T ?

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: No. Let's go back to apogee is not applicable, and then I just started reading the numbers again. From there, I've got a perigee and then a Delta-V T and then a burn time and so forth. Over.

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: Okay. I didn't hear a plus or minus on the H P , and I only got four numbers off of it. So could you start with H P again?

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: Okay. Going back to apogee, not applicable; perigee, plus 0019.1. And you weren't hearing things; it was my mistake. Over.

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: Okay. Picking up with Delta-V T ; 0001.4, 0:04, 0001.4; 45, 045.9, 22.5; Shaula, up 23.6, 00.0; plus 08.13; minus 165.03; 1220.2, 36301, 146:46:41; north set of stars, Sirius and Rigel; roll, 308; pitch, 209; yaw, 357; remarks: perigee in P30 equals plus 22.2 nautical miles. Over.

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: Roger. Midcourse number 7; RCS/G&N; 31600; not applicable, not applicable; 144:45:57.99. Are you with me?

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: That's all correct, Jim, and I have the entry PAD at your convenience.

a08_1321003.speaker: Collins
a08_1321003.text: Okay. Entry PAD: the area, mid-Pacific; 357, 152, 359; 146:29:13; 268, plus 08.13, minus 165.03; 068, 36221, 651, 1220.2, 36301, 146:46:13, 0028, not applicable four times, in other words, D L MAX, D L MIN, V L MAX, and V L MIN - all not applicable. Starting with D 0 : 4.00, 02:07, 00:25, 03:33, 08:16; 16, 059.0, 31.2. And your boresight star, Zeta Persei, which is half way between Mirfak and Aldebaran, up 16.5, right 3.4, up. Remarks: use non-exit EMS pattern. Over. [Pause.]

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: Entry as follows: mid-Pacific, 357, 152, 359; 146:29:13; 268, plus 08.13, minus 165.03; 068, 36221, 651, 1220.2, 36301, 146:46:13, 0028, N/A 4 times, with D 0 4.00, 02:07, 00:25, 03:33, 08:16; 16, 059.0, 31.2; Zeta Persei, up 16.5, right 3.4; up. And remarks: use non-exit EMS pattern. And Zeta Persei is between Mirfak and Aldebaran, and Frank can never find it anyway.

a08_1321003.speaker: Lovell
a08_1321003.text: We certainly don't waste much time getting down to drogue deploy, do we?

a08_1323441.speaker: Collins
a08_1323441.text: Roger, Jim. In your computer, we'd like to do an erasable memory dump again, like we did the other day, and the reason we'd like to do it is, when you did that P37 about 8 hours ago, and you remember you put that EI time in for T IG and got that P00-doo thing; we'd like to - We don't think there's anything in the world wrong with it. We think everything is just perfect inside the computer, but we'd like to do an erasable dump as we did the other day; go through it bit by bit. Give us something to do down here. Over.

a08_1323441.speaker: Collins
a08_1323441.text: And I have the procedures for you when you're ready to copy.

a08_1323441.speaker: Collins
a08_1323441.text: Okay. Verb 01 Noun 01 Enter, 333 Enter, and then read out register 1, and that register 1 should be 10000, 1 0 0 0 0. And then if it's not, I can give you a procedure for getting it to 10000. If it is 10000 as we expect, then Verb 74 Enter, and that'll do the dump. Over.

a08_1323441.speaker: Lovell
a08_1323441.text: Roger. When do you want it? [Long pause.]

a08_1323441.speaker: Collins
a08_1323441.text: And, Apollo 8, you can do the first part of that now at your convenience to verify that register 1 is reading 10000, but would you hold up on the dump itself until we get our ground stations configured, please. Over.

a08_1323800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1323800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 132 hours, 38 minutes. At the present time we're in touch with the spacecraft. We'll pick up that conversation for you and then stand by to follow it as it develops.

a08_1323837.speaker: Collins
a08_1323837.text: Jim, we're getting noisy down here. Could you switch Omni antennas, please? [Pause.]

a08_1323837.speaker: Collins
a08_1323837.text: That works pretty well, doesn't it?

a08_1323837.speaker: Lovell
a08_1323837.text: Not bad. I was amazed at the communication at the Moon, too. [Pause.]

a08_1323837.speaker: Collins
a08_1323837.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're configured for the dump. Verb 74 Enter at your convenience.

a08_1323837.speaker: Collins
a08_1323837.text: Apollo 8, Houston. The dump is complete, and it's your computer. Thank you.

a08_1330633.speaker: Anders
a08_1330633.text: Good morning, Mike. We had a little change of the guard here.

a08_1330633.speaker: Collins
a08_1330633.text: You sound all bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. How's it going up there?

a08_1330633.speaker: Collins
a08_1330633.text: Apollo 8, Houston. How about giving us a countdown to PRD. reading. Over?

a08_1330633.speaker: Collins
a08_1330633.text: Yes, just on you, Bill. We got the other two while you were sacked out. [Pause.]

a08_1330633.speaker: Anders
a08_1330633.text: The one that I have now, and the one that Jim took off, which is obviously broken, it's still at 0.64.

a08_1331138.speaker: Collins
a08_1331138.text: Roger, Bill. On your PTC attitude, we're requesting a pitch angle of zero, and we're showing you about 27 degrees pitch and increasing. Over.

a08_1331138.speaker: Anders
a08_1331138.text: Roger. I've been trying to work it down to Enter again.

a08_1331138.speaker: Collins
a08_1331138.text: They're letting you drive, after all, huh?

a08_1331138.speaker: Anders
a08_1331138.text: I have to every now and then just to square this thing away.

a08_1331138.speaker: Anders
a08_1331138.text: Mike, I'll just give you my status here before the rest of them go to sleep; had about 3 hours sleep, another meal, and everybody is doing fine.

a08_1331200-pao.speaker: Collins
a08_1331200-pao.text: They're letting you drive, after all, huh?

a08_1331200-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1331200-pao.text: I have to every now and then just to square this thing away.

a08_1331200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1331200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 133 hours, 12 minutes. At this point, Apollo 8 is traveling at a velocity of 6,914 feet per second [2,107 m/s], and our current altitude reading is 77,946 nautical miles [144,356 km]. We've just heard from Bill Anders for the first time in about 3 hours. Bill has been getting some rest and we anticipate that at this time both Borman and Lovell are resting while Bill is on watch. We'll pick up that conversation for you now.

a08_1343650.speaker: Collins
a08_1343650.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_1343650.speaker: Anders
a08_1343650.text: Roger, Mike. How do you read?

a08_1343650.speaker: Collins
a08_1343650.text: Reading you loud and clear now, Bill. I wasn't hearing here for a couple of calls. How're you reading me?

a08_1343650.speaker: Anders
a08_1343650.text: I had my hands full; I was putting something down. I read you fine.

a08_1343650.speaker: Collins
a08_1343650.text: Okay. Understand. If it'll be any help to you in your PTC driving, we've computed that as you look out plus-X in the COAS or just out the window, you should be pointed right at Acrux when you're in a perfect PTC attitude. We don't know whether that's a help to you or not, but we thought you might enjoy trying an alternate mode of keeping the attitude under control.

a08_1343650.speaker: Anders
a08_1343650.text: Okay. From my present position, we're going to have to move Acrux a little bit. [Pause.]

a08_1343650.speaker: Collins
a08_1343650.text: Well, whatever you think. We just thought you might appreciate knowing. [Pause.]

a08_1343650.speaker: Anders
a08_1343650.text: I'll give it a try, Mike. I can see Acrux...

a08_1343650.speaker: Collins
a08_1343650.text: Can you see it all right?

a08_1343650.speaker: Anders
a08_1343650.text: Yeah, I think so. There's a star out there anyway.

a08_1344058.speaker: Anders
a08_1344058.text: Actually, Mike, it's so easy to do it with the eight-ball within a reasonable sloppy limit that it's hardly worth the trouble to scootch way up to the seat to look out the COAS, and it's enough light in the cockpit where the star really isn't too easy to see. So I'm kind of inclined to use the IFR technique here where you can see the rest of the instrument panel.

a08_1344058.speaker: Anders
a08_1344058.text: I thought you were an all-weather pilot.

a08_1344058.speaker: Collins
a08_1344058.text: Well, you just caused Flight down here to get a "Gotcha" on CapCom and FAO. [Pause.]

a08_1344058.speaker: Anders
a08_1344058.text: Give me a little warning next time.

a08_1345400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1345400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control; 134 hours, 54 minutes into the mission. At the present time we are some 11 hours, 52 minutes from the time of re-entry. Apollo 8 is traveling at a speed of 7,289 feet per second [2,222 m/s] and the current altitude of the spacecraft is 70,989 nautical miles [131,472 km]. Since our last report, we've had very little communication with the spacecraft. We'll play back for you what we - what communication we have, and then stand by for any calls to the spacecraft or any calls down from the spacecraft.

a08_1345400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1345400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control. It appears we'll have no further conversations at this point. We'll take the circuit down. At 134 hours, 58 minutes.

a08_1350708.speaker: Collins
a08_1350708.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Could you give us a better Omni, please? [Long pause.]

a08_1350708.speaker: Collins
a08_1350708.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'll be changing the antennas in 3 minutes. You can expect a comm glitch. Over.

a08_1352110.speaker: Collins
a08_1352110.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Could you switch us to Omni Charlie, please. [Long pause.]

a08_1360121.speaker: Collins
a08_1360121.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over.

a08_1360121.speaker: Anders
a08_1360121.text: I was just seeing if you were still there, Mike. Old Gray Eagle has taken over the Hail Mary. [Pause.]

a08_1360318.speaker: Collins
a08_1360318.text: Roger, Bill. We had an erasable memory dump, few hours back. I think it was while you were asleep, but anyway we've checked the computer's erasable memory bit by bit, and everything agrees 100 percent. Over.

a08_1360318.speaker: Anders
a08_1360318.text: Mighty fine. Glad to hear it, Mike. Thank you.

a08_1360318.speaker: Collins
a08_1360318.text: Rog. [Pause.] You gonna brief Frank on your tape recorder before you go to sleep?

a08_1360318.speaker: Anders
a08_1360318.text: He can't handle it. It's too complicated.

a08_1360400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1360400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control; 136 hours, 04 minutes into the flight of Apollo 8. At the present time, we're in conversation with the crew. Frank Borman just came on the line. Indicated that he had gotten some sleep and was now joining Anders. Apparently, Jim Lovell is still sleeping at this time. We'll pick up that conversation and stand by to follow it.

a08_1360400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1360400-pao.text: This is Mission Control. At the present time, our spacecraft velocity is 7,598 feet per second [2,316 m/s], and we're traveling now at an altitude of 65,851 nautical miles [121,956 km]. Noting that the velocity is beginning to increase more rapidly now and our altitude decrease. At the present time we show 10 hours, 39 minutes, 25 seconds until Entry Interface. We'll continue to stand by briefly for any further conversation from the crew.

a08_1361325.speaker: Collins
a08_1361325.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Give us a different Omni, please. [Pause.]

a08_1363423.speaker: Collins
a08_1363423.text: Rog. We're going to switch our ground antennas in about a minute and a half. You can expect a comm glitch, Frank.

a08_1363423.speaker: Borman
a08_1363423.text: Were you transferring from Honeysuckle, Mike?

a08_1363709.speaker: Collins
a08_1363709.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston through Carnarvon. Were you calling a minute ago, Frank? [Pause.]

a08_1363709.speaker: Borman
a08_1363709.text: Y'all in Australia, do you hear us?

a08_1363709.speaker: Collins
a08_1363709.text: Yeah, we're reading you loud and clear now. [Long pause.]

a08_1363709.speaker: Borman
a08_1363709.text: Carnarvon, how do you read Apollo 8?

a08_1363709.speaker: Collins
a08_1363709.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Reading you loud and clear through Carnarvon. [Long pause.]

a08_1363709.speaker: Borman
a08_1363709.text: We're just listening to all the guys around the net.

a08_1363709.speaker: Borman
a08_1363709.text: I could that time, all the way from Carnarvon to Texas. [Pause.]

a08_1363709.speaker: Borman
a08_1363709.text: How'd they ever get an old maintenance officer on the midnight shift? [Long pause.]

a08_1363709.speaker: Collins
a08_1363709.text: Frank, you're on GOSS Conference if you'd like to debrief. Over.

a08_1365047.speaker: Collins
a08_1365047.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Omni Bravo, please. [Long pause.]

a08_1365200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1365200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 136 hours, 52 minutes. Since our past - our last report, activity here in Mission Control and on the spacecraft has been minimal. We have had a few communications checks with the spacecraft and some routine housekeeping chores being done by the crew. Very little Flight Plan activity scheduled at this time. At the present time, Apollo 8 is at an altitude of 62,413 nautical miles [115,589 km] and our velocity reads 7,825 feet per second [2,385 m/s]. We have one bit of interesting information from our Flight Dynamics Officer, which illustrates the rapid velocity increase

a08_1371148.speaker: Collins
a08_1371148.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a08_1371148.speaker: Borman
a08_1371148.text: Have you noticed how long I've stayed locked in in this PTC mode? [Long pause.]

a08_1371148.speaker: Collins
a08_1371148.text: Just about an hour and a quarter looks to us like, Frank.

a08_1371148.speaker: Borman
a08_1371148.text: I haven't even touched the hand control here for about 20 minutes, and it just hasn't moved outside that zero; I've never seen it like this before. [Pause.]

a08_1371148.speaker: Borman
a08_1371148.text: Be sure and have your troops give me a call if it gets close to gimbal lock, will you? I'm snoozing a little bit now and then up here.

a08_1371148.speaker: Borman
a08_1371148.text: And if you'd switch the antennas, you'd really be good guys.

a08_1381846.speaker: Collins
a08_1381846.text: Apollo 8, this is Houston. Over. [Long pause.]

a08_1381846.speaker: Collins
a08_1381846.text: Roger. Just a check on the radio, and if it's practical, Biomed switch, left, please.

a08_1381846.speaker: Anders
a08_1381846.text: Okay, Mike. We got a new change in the watch again.

a08_1381846.speaker: Collins
a08_1381846.text: Yeah, that was quick. Did you decide you didn't want to sleep after all?

a08_1382128.speaker: Collins
a08_1382128.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'll be changing antennas in about 2½ minutes; you can expect a comm glitch.

a08_1382128.speaker: Anders
a08_1382128.text: Roger. What are you changing to? [Pause.]

a08_1382128.speaker: Collins
a08_1382128.text: We're switching from Carnarvon to Honeysuckle, Bill.

a08_1390818.speaker: Collins
a08_1390818.text: Roger, Apollo 8. Your Green Team will be signing off in a few minutes, and before we do, Charlesworth and the rest of us would like to say we've enjoyed it and look forward to seeing you back in Houston. Over.

a08_1390818.speaker: Anders
a08_1390818.text: We have sure enjoyed it, too, troops, and you guys have really done a good job. Really do appreciate it.

a08_1390818.speaker: Collins
a08_1390818.text: Well, nice words there. We'll be seeing you, Bill.

a08_1390818.speaker: Anders
a08_1390818.text: Okay, Mike. We'll see you, Buddy. [Pause.] Tell old Cliff adios for me, too.

a08_1391904.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1391904.text: Apollo 8, we'd like to have you, before you get in a P52 going here, we'd like to have you re-zero the optics and read us the mechanical CDUs. We're trying to collect a little data for troubleshooting.

a08_1391904.speaker: Anders
a08_1391904.text: What's the trouble you're trying to troubleshoot?

a08_1391904.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1391904.text: This goes back to some of the problems we had prior to LOI; trying to see if the software readouts we're getting down here compare with the mechanical readouts. It's not a current problem as far as we know.

a08_1392127.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392127.text: Okay. Why don't you just read me the mechanical CDUs there now, and then it looks from the ground like you're clear to go ahead with the P52.

a08_1392127.speaker: Anders
a08_1392127.text: Okay. We'll get the navigator squared away here in just a minute.

a08_1392127.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392127.text: This'll be a P52 out of a deep sleep. Okay, stand by one. [Long pause.]

a08_1392127.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392127.text: The trunnion mechanical CDU looks like it's reading about one one-hundredth.

a08_1392127.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392127.text: And the shaft mechanical C - OCDU looks like it's reading about four hundredth below zero, which would be about, what, 364. Yeah.

a08_1392127.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392127.text: Understand, Jim. That's four hundredth below zero on the shaft; is that affirm?

a08_1392127.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392127.text: Yes. Stand by one. [Pause.] About 35996 I get.

a08_1392127.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392127.text: Okay. Thank you. And you can go ahead with P52 now.

a08_1392536.speaker: Anders
a08_1392536.text: I always said he did better in his sleep. [Long pause.]

a08_1392628.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392628.text: Okay. It looks like we're getting down on the Service Module RCS to the place where we ought to go ahead and activate the secondary Service Module RCS propellant.

a08_1392830.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392830.text: Okay. We've got a new PTC attitude. For the pitch, 180; and the yaw, 315.

a08_1392830.speaker: Anders
a08_1392830.text: Could you pick one a little further away?

a08_1392830.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392830.text: Not in our normal sphere. [Long pause.]

a08_1392830.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392830.text: Aren't we still a little high on the quantity side to activate the secondary?

a08_1392830.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392830.text: Negative. We have - let's see, we have quad Bravo and quad Delta which are getting right down, according to the calculated numbers, next to where we ought to be activating them. The numbers you're reading are going to be a little bit high, but the computer data on the ground shows that you have about 134 pounds in Bravo and Delta, and about 130 pounds is where you ought to be on the secondary.

a08_1392830.speaker: Lovell
a08_1392830.text: Okay. Roger. We'll activate the secondary and turn off the primary.

a08_1392830.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1392830.text: Okay. It's just to keep you from running one of them out.

a08_1393500-pao-press-conference.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1393500-pao-press-conference.text: Apollo Control here at 139 hours, 52 minutes; and a good, good morning from the Maroon Team. We're 48,000 [nautical] miles [89,000 km] from home, moving at nearly 9,000 feet per second [2,750 m/s]. And in the last half hour we've had these bits and pieces of conversation with the crew. Among other items of interest, Jim Lovell awakened, which you may already know. He awakened a little bit earlier than his planned seven-hour sleep period; he was awake at least a half an hour ago. Here's our recorded conversation.

a08_1402811.speaker: Borman
