a08_1402811.text: Ken, on this maneuver, MCC-7, are you going to - are we going to burn the PAD data that we got sometime ago, or is there a new maneuver coming up, or what's going on in that regard? [Pause.]

a08_1402811.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1402811.text: Okay, Apollo 8. If required, we'll give you a new one. Right now, we are looking at not making a maneuver burn at all.

a08_1402811.speaker: Borman
a08_1402811.text: You're saying we may not even have that one now?

a08_1403103-unanswered-calls.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1403103-unanswered-calls.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Could you try another omni? [No answer.]

a08_1403103-unanswered-calls.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1403103-unanswered-calls.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Try another omni, please. [No answer.]

a08_1403547.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1403547.text: Okay. Read you loud and clear now. Just wanted to remind you that in the event of a loss of comm, we don't want you to burn MCC-7. Your present entry PAD is good. We'll be updating your landing point at the same time that you would have gotten MCC-7, and I'd like to have a crew status report from you when it's convenient. [Long pause.]

a08_1403547.speaker: Borman
a08_1403547.text: Okay, Ken. I understand now, if we would lose comm, you do not want us to burn MCC-7, just go ahead and use the entry PAD that you've given us?

a08_1403547.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1403547.text: That's affirmative. You'll be within 0.06 degrees of your entry angle target line.

a08_1403547.speaker: Borman
a08_1403547.text: All right. The crew status is, everybody has gotten real good rest last night, and everybody's in good shape. Jim is just waking up, Bill's starting the initial stowage, and we're - we all feel very well.

a08_1403547.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1403547.text: Okay. And we'd like to - guess we need a PRD reading from you. And we'll be needing one in the neighborhood of 145-hour period, somewhere when it's convenient in there again.

a08_1404000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1404000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 140 hours, 40 minutes into the flight and we just had a chat with the crew which was significant in two respects. They were advised that we would not have another midcourse. None was necessary. And we heard from Frank Borman that the crew is up now, and alert and awake, and Frank said they had a real good night's rest. And they are all set for the re-entry. Here's the conversation.

a08_1404520.speaker: Borman
a08_1404520.text: Roger. Could you give us our range - correction, our velocity and range from the Earth now?

a08_1404520.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1404520.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, Houston. At time 51, your velocity will be 9,526, altitude 42,946. Over.

a08_1405500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1405500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 140 hours, 55 minutes into the flight. And before we get all wrapped up in the entry process, why don't we take a final look at our onboard system quantity readings? Our cabin pressure remains, as it has now for some days, at 4.9 pounds per square inch [33.8 kPa]; cabin temperature, 78 degrees [F, 26°C]. The amount of waste water on board right now is 69.5 percent of the tank capacity or 38.9 pounds [17.6 kg]. The potable drinking water quantity remains as it has throughout most of the mission at slightly over 100 percent, it is constantly being refilled from the

a08_1405500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1405500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston here at 141 hours, 29 minutes. It's been at least a half an hour since we've heard from the crew but no concern here. Things are very quiet obviously in the spacecraft. They're very quiet here in the Control Center. I suppose the two most active areas are the recovery forces. They're working very hard to ensure the adequacy of their communications circuits. They're running almost constant checks. And the retro people, who work very hard over this final entry-into-atmosphere maneuver. And all the members associated with it; they're working and comparing and talki

a08_1413343.speaker: Borman
a08_1413343.text: Negative, this is Apollo 8. We did not call you.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Apollo 8, Houston.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Go ahead, Houston. Apollo 8.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. I've got some weather and recovery force status and a couple of last minute items to run down any time it's convenient for you.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: All right. It's convenient right now.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. For the mid-Pacific, the general condition is good. You can expect cloud bases 2,000 foot scattered, visibility 10 miles, wind 070 at 12, wave heights 4 feet, altimeter 2974. [Long pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay, sunrise will be 17:10 Zulu, and first light, 16:49 Zulu. Recovery forces: ship will be Yorktown; the aircraft will be Airboss number 1 and 2, and Recoveries 1, 2, and 3. [Pause.] The estimated time to a target point: the ship is - Yorktown is on the target point; Airboss aircraft, 15 minutes and will be on-scene commander. Recoveries 1, 2, and 3 are SH3 Alphas, and they go with the Yorktown, so they're at the target point. All of them have swimmers aboard. If the recovery aircraft do not hear from the spacecraft, they'll go ahead and put swimmers in the water, and if you're in good shape

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Roger. Say again the sunrise and first light time for me, would you, please?

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Say again, 8. [Long pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Notice the rather large middle gimbal angle. Over.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Thank you. [Pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Would you say again the daylight time, please; sunrise, and first light.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. Sunrise is 17:10 Zulu, and the first light is 16:49 Zulu. [Pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Thank you.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay, 8. Looking over the weather I gave you was the 2,000 foot scattered at the target point. May have a 6,000 foot broken layer above that. At the max lift point, you have about the same thing, and altimeter's the same down the range. As you go further to the east, the weather should improve slightly; there's no problem with thunderstorms or rain showers in any of your recovery area.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Very good; thank you. [Pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: The items that we still need will be a PRD reading as late as you can do it conveniently prior to a final stowage. And we don't have any numbers on the last crew sleep period. I'd like to verify that the secondary RCS was activated on all four quads. And I have about five comments on the entry checklist procedures to verify.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: It was activated on all four quads; that's correct. Our final stowage is completed. We'll read out the PR - we'll read out the PRDs for you now.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: All right. Thank you.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: The LMP's reads 0.64; I believe it's been that way throughout the flight. [Pause.] CMP's reads 0.11, that's 1.11.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Roger.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Stand by a minute while we look at it closely. That's 0.11.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Roger. 0.11.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: And the one I ended up with reads 3.10.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Okay. Go ahead, Ken. What else do you want to talk about?

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. To make everybody happy, we can use an estimate of the number of hours sleep that people got.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Oh. Okay, sorry.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Just a minute, I'll give you that; I forgot.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Thank you.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Bill Anders got about 5 hours, [pause] and Jim Lovell got about five, and I got about five and a half or six.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Sounds good.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Right.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. We went through an exercise with the mockup on the pre-entry preparations, and we noticed that in the LMP's checklist on page S-12, when you go to top off the repress bottles, I believe it's a misprint; it should read the PLSS fill valve rather than the Repress valve, and we should be going to the fill position as opposed to going to On.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Roger. That's what we do.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. And on - go ahead. [Pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Go ahead. We agree that's what we do.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. On page E-7 of the entry checklist and under step 34, as long as you have panel 382 open, that's a convenient time to go ahead and have the evaporator water controls, both primary and secondary, to Auto, and the suit heat exchanger for the secondary glycol to Flow.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Those items are already accomplished.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Very good. On page E-9, when you're getting ready to transfer the RCS to the Command Module position, if you want to avoid having the engines fire as a result of attitude correction, you might want to take the manual attitude switches to Accel Command or Minimum Impulse. And again on E-9 Alpha at step 41 Bravo, if you want to go back to attitude hold, bring the manual attitude switches back to Rate. [Pause.]

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: What was that last step?

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Step 41 Bravo on page E-9 Alpha. It's if you decide to use either Minimum Impulse or Accel Command on page E-9, step 41 Bravo would be a good place to go back to Rate Command.

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: Okay. We do - that's where we do it.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay, fine. And...

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: I don't...

a08_1414131.speaker: Borman
a08_1414131.text: I didn't put all those control configurations changes in the checklist, but that's exactly what we do, use Minimum Impulse.

a08_1414131.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1414131.text: Okay. Real fine.

a08_1415200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1415200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, and everything seems to be proceeding very nicely. Ken Mattingly's been running through a entry - pre-entry checklist with Frank Borman. We're content, so are they. At the news conference a little while ago, numbers were passed to the press based on a final maneuver of something on the order of one or two feet per second. As you know, we scrubbed it, there is no need for such a maneuver, and has been terminated, but the fact that we are not going to have the maneuver matters almost not at all on the numbers. For instance, it changes the splash time by one secon

a08_1420051.speaker: Borman
a08_1420051.text: I'd like to confirm one item on the PAD message, please.

a08_1420051.speaker: Borman
a08_1420051.text: Time to retro the drogues, reference your last time to drogues, please.

a08_1420051.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1420051.text: Okay. I'll check that one out.

a08_1420051.speaker: Borman
a08_1420051.text: And also, Ken, we're going to turn on our VHF now, about 4 hours before entry.

a08_1420051.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1420051.text: Real fine. Thank you. I'll let you know when we pick it up.

a08_1420051.speaker: Anders
a08_1420051.text: Ah, we're listening on VHF now too, Ken.

a08_1420300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1420300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 142 hours, 3 minutes into the mission. A word or two on some of the congratulatory message traffic that we've experienced during this mission. I would call it unusually high. Probably associated with the general interest in the mission. The fact that it is the holiday season and more people have more time to express themselves. In general, far and away, the comments have been extremely laudatory, praiseworthy, and of course, there has, as there always is, a very small but an extremely vocal minority who thinks we shouldn't have done the mission or if we shoul

a08_1421733.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1421733.text: Okay. We have checked into your drogue time, and the number of 08:16 on your entry PAD is correct. We'll be giving you an updated entry PAD on the scheduled time of 143:30. At the same time, we'll be giving you an update of your state vectors for the LM and CSM.

a08_1421733.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1421733.text: The midcourse correction number 7 was less than seven-tenths foot per second, and we will not execute it.

a08_1421733.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1421733.text: You have a - You have a P52 scheduled at 143:30 which is not required. Your option. However, if you decide to delete the P52, the CMC self-check and DSKY condition light test are still requirements. Over.

a08_1421733.speaker: Borman
a08_1421733.text: What - what do you mean, they're still requirements? We weren't planning to do the CMC self-test. [Long pause.]

a08_1421733.speaker: Borman
a08_1421733.text: On that DSKY check, for goodness sake, that's...

a08_1422107.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1422107.text: Apollo 8, Houston. That's my mistake on the CMC self-check and DSKY condition light. That's an optional test. Over.

a08_1422107.speaker: Borman
a08_1422107.text: That's what we thought, Ken. Gosh, that's been working perfectly for 6 days, I don't - I don't see any reason to test it.

a08_1422107.speaker: Lovell
a08_1422107.text: Morning, Ken. How's Houston this morning?

a08_1423400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1423400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 142 hours, 34 minutes. In the last few minutes we recorded this conversation.

a08_1423400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1423400-pao.text: And that was Jim Lovell you heard chime in at the end, he's up and sounding perky this morning. At 142 hours, 37 minutes; that's our status.

a08_1425128.speaker: Anders
a08_1425128.text: I'm just - It's my understanding we're going to bring up the secondary loop at 1 hour prior to Sep, is that right?

a08_1425128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1425128.text: And Bill, Rod suggested that if we have the water boiler going on the primary loop, that you - you might wait about 5 minutes or so before you initiate the secondary loop. [Pause.]

a08_1425128.speaker: Anders
a08_1425128.text: Wait 5 minutes from what? From the time the primary loop starts or from 1 hour?

a08_1425128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1425128.text: From the time the primary loop starts; this'll give you a check to see if it had a chance to dry out or not. [Long pause.]

a08_1425128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1425128.text: And for your own information, we already have a VHF downlink. It's poor quality, but we do have contact.

a08_1425128.speaker: Anders
a08_1425128.text: Okay. We haven't turned anything over to VHF yet.

a08_1425128.speaker: Anders
a08_1425128.text: We tried to call you on the VHF though, Ken.

a08_1425128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1425128.text: Rog. I say, the quality's pretty poor; they may not be able to understand you.

a08_1425659.speaker: Anders
a08_1425659.text: Ken, we got two things going here which make this suit heat exchanger flow a little different. One of them is we're not doing a cold-soak, and the other one is we're powering down the secondary loop prior to Sep. And I wonder if it's a good idea to have the suit heat exchanger only on a secondary loop in that case. And plus the fact that we haven't got any cabin heat exchanger.

a08_1425659.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1425659.text: I don't think that was the intent, Bill. What they had in mind, we'd have both loops - have the suit heat exchanger on both loops; and if they got too cold, you could use the panel switching to shut down the primary loop through the heat exchanger. But in any event, you'd always have something going to the suit heat exchanger. I recognize that we are going to be shutting down the secondary heat exchanger pre-Sep and then turning it back on prior to entry, but the idea was to have both primary and secondary loops on the suit heat exchanger simultaneously.

a08_1425659.speaker: Anders
a08_1425659.text: Yeah, my checklist doesn't reflect that, but I think that's a good idea since we're a little suspect of our cabin fans and don't plan to use them.

a08_1425900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1425900-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 142 hours, 59 minutes into the flight. And the velocity increase we're seeing is now becoming dramatic. We're up to 11,298 feet per second [3,444 m/s] and it's really building. We're at 30,424 [nautical] miles [56,345 km] from home. Here's the conversation with the crew.

a08_1430154.speaker: Anders
a08_1430154.text: Roger. What's Rod's estimate of our post-separation main bus voltage?

a08_1430400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1430400-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here. That brings us up to date. And to amplify one remark I think you heard Bill Anders say, he'd try to call on VHF. If it was received, it was badly garbled. If I recall correctly, on the way out, and they're quite a way from the Earth, we - they heard us broadcasting on VHF out to about 22,000 [nautical] miles [41,000 km]. They've got just about the reverse situation here where it's slightly more than 29,000 [nautical] miles [54,000 km] out. At 143 hours, 4 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1431241.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1431241.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We're making a handover from Carnarvon to Honeysuckle at 15.

a08_1431616.speaker: Anders
a08_1431616.text: I'm still a little bit confused on this - activate the secondary loop. You indicated in - activating it at 1 hour or 5 minutes after the primary evaporator comes on the line. My checklist shows that the primary evaporator probably won't come on the line until we bypass the radiators. Have you got something else in mind that I don't know about? [Pause.]

a08_1431616.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1431616.text: Okay, Bill. We passed up an update some time back on page E-9, step 38, right at the beginning; and you've got a final GDC drift check. And then between there and the - and the step 39 where it says to terminate CM RCS preheat, that was the place we wanted to activate the primary loop by putting the glycol evaporator water switch to Auto and the glycol evaporator steam pressure to Auto. [Long pause.]

a08_1431616.speaker: Anders
a08_1431616.text: Roger. I don't expect it to boil, though. Do you?

a08_1431616.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1431616.text: Okay, Bill. We're hoping that it will there. It looks like we'll have had a stable attitude for some time, and we anticipate that it will be warm enough to make it boil. That is the reason it's suggested if it is boiling, that you wait. If it isn't, go ahead and turn on the secondary loop.

a08_1431616.speaker: Anders
a08_1431616.text: Okay. Well, that's where I was confused. I'm waking up. Thank you.

a08_1432006.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1432006.text: Okay, Apollo 8. We'd like to update your LM state vector, CSM state vector, and target point. And if it's convenient now, why, we'll go ahead and do that if you'll go to P00 and Accept. [Pause.]

a08_1432920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1432920.text: Okay. The loads are in and verified, and the computer is yours.

a08_1432920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1432920.text: You can take it back to Block, and for Bill's information, latest guess on the main bus post-Sep voltage to 27.5 [volts].

a08_1432920.speaker: Anders
a08_1432920.text: Guess?! [Pause.] You mean the EECOMs are guessing? [Pause.]

a08_1432920.speaker: Anders
a08_1432920.text: At least, they're honest for a change.

a08_1432920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1432920.text: That's more than you can say for the computers.

a08_1433600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1433600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 143 hours, 36 minutes into the flight. And we've been chatting more with Bill Anders primarily on how things look. The spacecraft is now 26,458 [nautical] miles from Earth [49,000 km], moving in a velocity of 12,075 feet per second [3,680 m/s]. The weight of the spacecraft is 31,600 pounds [14,300 kg]. Now that weight will change dramatically 15 minutes before we reach the 400,000-foot mark when the Service Module leaves us and it will go from 31,600 down to about 12,000 pounds [5,400 kg] and will hold close to that on in. Here's the conversation.

a08_1433640.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1433640.text: Okay, 8. We have an entry PAD for you.

a08_1433640.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1433640.text: Okay. This will be the mid-Pacific; 357, 152, 359; 146:29:00; 268, plus 08.13, minus 165.03; 06.5, 36221, 6.45, 1212.2, 36301, 146:46:14, 00:28. The next block is November Alpha: D O 4.00, 02:12; 00:25, 03:34, 08:14; 16, 059.0, 31.2; Zeta Persei, up 16.5, right 3.4; up. Use non-exit EMS pattern, GDC Align; primary star Sirius, secondary Rigel; roll, 308; pitch, 209; yaw, 357. This entry will not involve P65. Over. [Pause.]

a08_1433640.speaker: Lovell
a08_1433640.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Entry PAD as follows: mid-Pacific; 357, 152, 359; 146:29:00; 268, plus 08.13, minus 165.03; 06.5; 36221, 6.45, 1212.2, 36301, 146:46:14, 00:28, next block not applicable, 4.00, 02:12; 00:25, 03:34, 08:14; 16, 059, 31.2; Zeta Persei, up 16.5, right 3.5, up. Use non-exit EMS pattern, backup alignment; Sirius, Rigel; roll, 308; pitch, 209; yaw, 357; and we won't see P65.

a08_1433640.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1433640.text: Okay, Apollo 8. I'd like to verify sextant star shaft 0590, and the boresight star.

a08_1433640.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1433640.text: The last one is right 3.4. Over.

a08_1433640.speaker: Lovell
a08_1433640.text: Roger. Boresight star is right 3.4. And I have the sextant shaft; that's 059.0.

a08_1434700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1434700-pao.text: Apollo Control here, and that brings us up to the point where we are now. For those newsmen watching the projection on monitors in our MSC Auditorium news area, you'll be able to see very shortly the spacecraft do a long loop-the-loop kind of maneuver against a flat map such as we're viewing. The maneuver will be quite similar to that that we saw the other day after the TLI burn when we did a big loop before we started tracing a steady flight path away from the Earth. Of course, we are going to see this morning the mirror image of that maneuver, only in this case it will be performed almost di

a08_1435937.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1435937.text: Okay, Apollo 8. Can you tell us if you've done anything with your potable water? We've noticed our readout has gone from 100 percent down to 56 in the last couple of minutes. [Pause.]

a08_1435937.speaker: Lovell
a08_1435937.text: We're reading about 50 percent right now.

a08_1435937.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1435937.text: Roger. That correlates with what we see. Have you done anything to change configuration? Over. [Long pause.]

a08_1435937.speaker: Lovell
a08_1435937.text: Yeah, we noticed we're venting here, too, Houston. [Long pause.]

a08_1435937.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1435937.text: Jim, did you mean you could visually see it?

a08_1435937.speaker: Lovell
a08_1435937.text: Yeah, we're - we're - oh, stand by, Ken. Bill just dumped urine, so that might have been urine we were seeing. [Long pause.]

a08_1435937.speaker: Lovell
a08_1435937.text: Bill just shut the potable inlet, Ken.

a08_1440444.speaker: Lovell
a08_1440444.text: Roger, Houston. We're still showing about 52 percent here, and we had our switch on waste so we don't know whether it dropped from a higher value or not. Has yours been stabilized now?

a08_1440444.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1440444.text: That's affirmative; ours has stabilized now. And it was reading full just a few minutes ago.

a08_1440444.speaker: Lovell
a08_1440444.text: Roger. I don't think - we can't account for any sudden drop in water.

a08_1440444.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1440444.text: Okay. We looked in the malfunction procedures, in number 28. And [it] doesn't reveal anything very startling.

a08_1440800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1440800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 144 hours, 8 minutes into the flight. And things are continuing to rock along. We're - In the last few minutes, we had a little surprise here with a not-yet-completely-explained water dump. We chatted with the crew about it and, apparently, Bill Anders had dumped some waste matter, some urine overboard earlier, which had collected for a while. We still don't completely understand it. We're talking a little about this and here's how the conversation goes.

a08_1440853.speaker: Anders
a08_1440853.text: Okay. I'm looking at malfunction 28, and it takes you to box 6, but I don't really think that's the problem because the waste tank quantity hadn't changed any. Over.

a08_1440853.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1440853.text: Okay. I concur. We're watching the same thing.

a08_1440853.speaker: Anders
a08_1440853.text: Look, we don't care about the potable tank, but we do about the waste tank, so I'm just gonna - just in case there is a problem somewhere, I'm going to shut the potable tank off and leave the waste tank inlet valve open. How's that sound to you?

a08_1440853.speaker: Anders
a08_1440853.text: If I see any water floating around, I'll give you another call.

a08_1441300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1441300-pao.text: So much for our water situation. It's apparently been laid to rest now. As Anders said, not - not really a problem. Just not immediately explainable so he turned off the potable tank. There are two tanks here; a potable tank - the drinking water, and the waste water tank. He had vented the waste water tank to some degree but apparently had not - they saw some kind of action on the potable meters. In any case, it's been adjusted. Our present distance; 22,276 nautical miles [41,255 km] from Earth. This puts the spacecraft at the synchronous orbital altitude and it will now begin to sink its dire

a08_1441830.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1441830.text: Roger. We had a momentary loss of comm on the ground then. Read you loud and clear.

a08_1442713.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1442713.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're loud and clear. We've taken a look at this water...

a08_1442713.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1442713.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, Houston. Read you loud and clear. We've taken a look at your potable water quantity problem, and it appears to be a transducer problem. Suggest that you leave the potable tank isolated. You have sufficient water in the waste tank to continue the entry. Over.

a08_1442713.speaker: Anders
a08_1442713.text: Does that mean we're Go for entry? [Long pause.]

a08_1442713.speaker: Borman
a08_1442713.text: Roger. Is our thermal stability good enough we can leave the PTC attitude and go to entry gimbal angles now?

a08_1443203.speaker: Borman
a08_1443203.text: Houston, how do you read? Apollo 8.

a08_1443203.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1443203.text: Read you loud and clear, Apollo 8, and we're checking on the PTC problem now. [Pause.]

a08_1443203.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1443203.text: Apollo 8: Houston. You're cleared with entry attitude at this time.

a08_1443800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1443800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 144 hours, 38 minutes into the flight. Apollo 8 is 19,000 [nautical] miles [35,188 km] from the Earth; it's moving at 14,029 feet per second [4,276 m/s]. Present combined weight of the Command Module and Service Module: 31,600 pounds [14,300 kg]. We have some conversation - we've had some conversation. Let's hear it now.

a08_1445646.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1445646.text: Apollo 8, loud and clear. Go. [No answer.]

a08_1445646.speaker: Anders
a08_1445646.text: Roger. We've completed the checklist down to the 1-hour point, and we'll stand by for 1 hour.

a08_1445646.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1445646.text: Just for information, did you folks end up having to use any Command Module RCS heaters?

a08_1445646.speaker: Lovell
a08_1445646.text: Negative. All our indicators are pegged either high or at 5 volts.

a08_1445646.speaker: Network
a08_1445646.text: Carnarvon, Network. GOSS conference voice check. How do you read?

a08_1445646.speaker: Carnarvon Comm Tech
a08_1445646.text: Network, Carnarvon. Read you weak but clear.

a08_1445646.speaker: Network
a08_1445646.text: Roger, Carnarvon. I read you loud and clear.

a08_1445646.speaker: Carnarvon Comm Tech
a08_1445646.text: You're loud and clear now. Thank you.

a08_1445646.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1445646.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Stand by for hand over to Carnarvon.

a08_1450205.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1450205.text: Okay, Apollo 8. If you'll go to P00 and Accept, we'd like to update your LM and CSM state vectors. Over.

a08_1450500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1450500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 145 hours, 5 minutes into the flight. Some brief conversation with the crew since we last talked. Here it is.

a08_1450618.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1450618.text: Apollo 8, Houston. State vector load is complete. Verify the computer is yours. [Long pause.]

a08_1450618.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1450618.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, Houston. State vector load is complete; the computer is yours. [Pause.]

a08_1450618.speaker: Borman
a08_1450618.text: Roger, Houston. We're going to Block.

a08_1450900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1450900-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here. And the spacecraft is now a mere 15,256 [nautical] miles [28,254 km] from the face of the Earth. Its velocity is almost a match in feet per second; 15,459 feet per second [4,712 m/s]. Its weight; 31,600 pounds [14,300 kg]. The Service Module, or approximately 20,000 of those pounds [9,000 kg] will be jettisoned abruptly at 15 minutes before we reach the 80-mile high, the 400K, 400,000-foot mark. At - one other mention, the viewing room as we've said earlier is beginning to fill with visitors and among them is Dr. Kurt Debus, director of the Kennedy Space Center, a

a08_1451054.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1451054.text: Okay. Two fast items: number one, it's been suggested that since Marezine takes some time to take effect, you might consider whether you'd be interested in taking some now. And I have an entry PAD which has some very small updates to go on it if you would like to copy that.

a08_1451054.speaker: Borman
a08_1451054.text: Okay. Stand by, and we'll get out the entry PAD. [Long pause.]

a08_1451054.speaker: Lovell
a08_1451054.text: Okay. Go ahead with the entry PAD, Houston.

a08_1451054.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1451054.text: Okay. We're still going to the mid-Pacific; 357, 152, 359; 146:29:13, 267; plus 08.13, minus 165.03; 06.6; 36221, 6.47; 1216.6, 36301; 146:46:13; 00:28; the next block is November Alpha; D 0 4.00, 02:10; 00:25, 03:35, 08:16; 16, 059.0, 31.2; Zeta Persei, up 16.5, right 34; up. Non-exit EMS pattern; Sirius and Rigel: roll, 308; pitch, 209; yaw, 357. No P65 involved. Over. [Long pause.]

a08_1451054.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1451054.text: Apollo 8, Houston. You're clear to initiate cabin cold-soak at your discretion. Over.

a08_1451054.speaker: Lovell
a08_1451054.text: Roger, Houston. We're starting that now.

a08_1452313.speaker: Anders
a08_1452313.text: Okay. It doesn't appear that we are going to be able to trigger the primary evaps, so I'm going to go ahead and start up the secondary loop. [Pause.]

a08_1452643.speaker: Borman
a08_1452643.text: Roger. Since we're going as smoothly as we are here, we've got good comm, let's start this pyro circuit check about 10 minutes early. What do you say? [Long pause.]

a08_1452643.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1452643.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. We can conduct the pyro check at any time.

a08_1452643.speaker: Borman
a08_1452643.text: Alright. Why don't we do it here just momentarily then?

a08_1452643.speaker: Borman
a08_1452643.text: We'll give you a call when we're ready.

a08_1452643.speaker: Borman
a08_1452643.text: Houston, we're ready to proceed with the pyro circuit check.

a08_1453107.speaker: Borman
a08_1453107.text: MSFN, are you monitoring the sequential test now? [Pause.]

a08_1453107.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1453107.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. Loud and clear. Affirmative we are monitoring.

a08_1453107.speaker: Anders
a08_1453107.text: Standing by for Go for Pyro Arm.

a08_1453107.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1453107.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. You have a Go.

a08_1453200-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1453200-pao.text: Standing by for Go for Pyro Arm.

a08_1453200-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1453200-pao.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. You have a Go.

a08_1453200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1453200-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 145 hours, 32 minutes into the flight, and the trajectory of Apollo 8 is programmed against the - our flat wall map here is carrying it on a path up the west coast of India. It will proceed northerly - northeasterly in a very few moments, and curve, and start in an easterly direction carrying it across China, perhaps before then it will see a little of the southern extremities of the Soviet Union, the Himalayas, China and then down across Guam. Present velocity is 17,272 feet per second [5,265 m/s]; the spacecraft is only 11,626 [nautical] miles [21,531 km] from

a08_1454141.speaker: Borman
a08_1454141.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8; How's your tracking looking?

a08_1454141.speaker: Borman
a08_1454141.text: Okay. Everything went fine with the check. We're all armed and ready to go here.

a08_1454141.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1454141.text: Okay. If you're not doing anything else, how about let's make a VHF check.

a08_1454141.speaker: Borman
a08_1454141.text: Okay. I'll turn off my S-band; the other two will stay on S-band.

a08_1454141.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1454141.text: Roger. I'll give you a count in just a second. [Long pause.]

a08_1454141.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1454141.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Simultaneous VHF and S-band. Over.

a08_1454141.speaker: Borman
a08_1454141.text: Rog. I'm not reading you on VHF.

a08_1454141.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1454141.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Simultaneous VHF and S-band. Do you verify that you are on the left hand VHF antenna? Over. [Pause.]

a08_1454141.speaker: Borman
a08_1454141.text: We can verify the antenna, but we can't verify reading you on S-band or on VHF.

a08_1454141.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1454141.text: Okay. We're receiving some downlink, although it's considered to be poor quality.

a08_1454500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1454500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 145 hours, 45 minutes into the flight. And all is continues to operate quite satisfactorily. We tried a VHF check with the spacecraft a few minutes ago. It didn't work out so well. Neither Carnarvon nor Guam picked up on VHF; that from about 10,000 miles out. We're now 9,600 [nautical] miles [17,800 km] from the Earth. The velocity is up to 18,532 feet per second [5,649 m/s]. And we have a little conversation backed up on us, let's hear it now.

a08_1454500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1454500-pao.text: Apollo Control here. Some may be wondering what happens to the Service Module. Well, it's jettisoned at 15 minutes before we reach our Entry Interface or entry point. And there's a preset burn of 90 feet per second [27 m/s] cranked into the Service Module. It departs from the Command Module at that rate. The burn continues for some period of time, exactly which period, I don't have in front of me; but at any case, the new trajectory of the Service Module carries it about 100 miles or more south of the track of the Command Module. It's not known exactly what will happen to the Service Module. S

a08_1455134.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455134.text: Apollo 8, Houston. We'd like to try the right VHF antenna, if you have time. [Pause.]

a08_1455134.speaker: Anders
a08_1455134.text: We're on ri - we're on right, Ken.

a08_1455134.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455134.text: Okay. This is a simultaneous VHF and S-band transmission: one, two, three, four, five. How do you read on VHF? Over.

a08_1455134.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455134.text: Understand that's on VHF. Is that affirm? [Long pause.]

a08_1455134.speaker: Borman
a08_1455134.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. I answered your call on VHF. Did you receive?

a08_1455134.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455134.text: Okay. It's not piped back here. MOCR'll have to check and see if they have it on the ground station.

a08_1455134.speaker: Borman
a08_1455134.text: You were loud and clear, Ken.

a08_1455134.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455134.text: Okay, Apollo 8. We received you loud and clear on VHF through Carnarvon. [Pause.]

a08_1455721.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1455721.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Stand by for handover from Carnarvon to Guam on the hour. We should have continuous contact except for the blackout period beginning at 146:51.

a08_1461200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1461200-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 146 hours, 12 minutes into the flight. I think all the consoles here have been reconfigured for this re-entry effort now. Probably the most noticeable item, leaving the consoles, are the lunar maps. They're being replaced by maps which rested right under the lunar maps, which were simply projections of good old Earth. A few minutes ago, the crew checked some of the events that will take place in the re-entry process and here's what we passed them.

a08_1461200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1461200-pao.text: Apollo Control here. And now the velocity acceleration pickup is quite dramatic. Our display here integrates a new value every 12 seconds, I believe. Let me give you a sample of how it is building; 23,303 feet per second [7,103 m/s] right now; altitude, 4,950 [nautical] miles [9,167 km]. Still reading 23,353, 23,403. It's been stepping up here in these last few minutes in increments of 50 to 60 feet per second. For reference purposes, the peak velocity previously reached prior to this mission by a manned vehicle was the Gemini 11 spacecraft, at perigee after its high altitude burn, which was t

a08_1461200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1461200-pao.text: PAO release line test. 1 2 3 4 5 - 5 4 3 2 1 - the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog's back. Test out.

a08_1462600-pao.speaker: Anders
a08_1462600-pao.text: Houston, this is Apollo 8. We're Go for Pyro Arm. [Long pause.]

a08_1462600-pao.speaker: Lovell
a08_1462600-pao.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Confirm Go for Pyro Arm.

a08_1462600-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1462600-pao.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, Houston. You're Go for Pyro Arm. [Long pause.]

a08_1462654.speaker: Lovell
a08_1462654.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Confirm Go for Pyro Arm.

a08_1462654.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1462654.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, Houston. You're Go for Pyro Arm. [Long pause.]

a08_1462654.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1462654.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. You're Go for Pyro Arm. Everything's looking good.

a08_1462654.speaker: Anders
a08_1462654.text: Roger. Everything's looking good here, Ken.

a08_1462800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1462800-pao.text: Recovery is advising the Flight Director of their good status, saying he has good weather out there. They're on station. The route of flight, in case you're not looking at a map, will be over northeast China, Peking, and over Tokyo, then we start a southeastern slant. The ship Redstone is parked at 24° north, 169° east. And the next listening point will be the ship Huntsville, tracking the ship at 172 west, 12° north, and the landing point just a few hundred miles southeast of there at 165 west, approximately 8 north. That point, by the way, is just 600 miles northwest of Christmas Island, whi

a08_1462910.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1462910.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. It appears that your primary evaporator may have dried out. If you get a chance, go ahead and give it a try to reservice. Over.

a08_1463128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463128.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. Ground data indicates the primary evaporator may have dried out. If you have a chance, you might try reservicing. Over.

a08_1463128.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463128.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8. Your secondary loop looks good.

a08_1463200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1463200-pao.text: The crew has been advised that their primary evaporator has dried out, a fact that I'm sure they couldn't care less about. They're about to say goodbye to that entire system in the Service Module in about two minutes.

a08_1463200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1463200-pao.text: And the spacecraft is now - we see our systems here show that they have gone to ring 2; the Reaction Control System. The system looks quite good, it's operational at 200 pounds of propellant available in that system. It is a redundant system. A few of the events, as we plan to clock them here: the point of - the 400,000 foot point, which is that point when many of our events begin to happen, we call it, the area of reaching some little small amount of atmosphere, is to occur at 146 hours, 46 minutes. The blackout period should begin about 25 seconds later. The maximum heating point would be 14

a08_1463300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1463300-pao.text: The Flight Director has confirmed separation - separation of the Command Module and the Service Module. We've been looking at data on the Command Module alone and all the values look quite good. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Looking good; both primary and secondary loops look good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Apollo 8, through the Redstone. You're looking good; both primary and secondary loops are holding good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Rog. Read you loud and clear. You're looking good.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Apollo 8, Houston. One minute to RRT.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1463600-combined.text: Houston, Huntsville. We have not established contact with the spacecraft at this time.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1463600-combined.text: Huntsville, AOS through S-band. [Pause.] Houston, Huntsville. Stand by. No contact.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, this is Houston through ARIA.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Unknown speaker, may be Lovell's call
Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8. Read you broken and loud.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Borman
a08_1463600-combined.text: Roger; this is a real fireball. It's looking good.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Borman
a08_1463600-combined.text: We're in real good shape, Houston.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Yorktown has radar on you.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463600-combined.text: If you get a chance, we'd like to have your DSKY readings before drogues.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463600-combined.text: Roger. DSKY's reading plus four balls 7, plus two balls 812, minus 16522.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB1
a08_1463600-combined.text: Roger, this is Airboss 1. You're sounding very good, very good. You have been reported on radar as, southwest of the ship about 25 [nautical] miles [46 km]. Go ahead.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB1
a08_1463600-combined.text: This is Airboss 1. Negative. Welcome home, gentlemen, and we'll have you aboard in no time. Go ahead.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: R3
a08_1463600-combined.text: This is Recovery 3. I have a flashing light, my 4 o'clock position, almost level.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB2
a08_1463600-combined.text: Recovery 2, Airboss 2. You are cleared to dispatch for your altitude over clouds. Over.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: R2
a08_1463600-combined.text: Roger this Is Recovery 2. I see the chutes, I see the light almost directly over Yorktown, level with me at 4,000 feet [1,220 metres] precisely.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB1
a08_1463600-combined.text: Yorktown, Airboss I - received a message that he sees the chutes, sees the flashing light almost over Yorktown, descending 4,000 [garble] very, very [garble] Out.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1463600-combined.text: All aircraft, this is Yorktown - have capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB1
a08_1463600-combined.text: Yorktown, this is Airboss 1. We consider recovery splashdown in your area. Take control recovery helos and vector them.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: R3
a08_1463600-combined.text: This is Recovery 3. Have lost sight of visual light

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: AB2
a08_1463600-combined.text: Recovery 2. Roger. Passing 1,500 feet [450 metres], descending

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1463600-combined.text: This is Yorktown. Affirmative, we do have him in - capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1463600-combined.text: Recovery 3, Yorktown. The capsule bears 147; 5,000 yards [4.6 km]. Yorktown, over.

a08_1463600-combined.speaker: Recovery 3
a08_1463600-combined.text: The spacecraft is down to 1,000 [300 metres].

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: ROT Control Power Direct, both, Main A/Main B.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Pitch needle error goes toward zero approaching zero at 0.5g time.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Don't forget Manual Attitude, three, to Rate Command.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes. Okay, but tell me that later, okay?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You've got to do it in checklist... as we go.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I've got to have that; just tell me later, okay?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: It's - it seems to be hanging in there, but it's awfully low steam pressure. I'll - I'll manually feed it if I have to.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: See where this baby wants me to fly? The pitch is way up.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: See if [garble] of the alpha meter.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Now, as we come close to the horizon we're going to [garble].

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: As we come closer to the...

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes. This thing came in long before. I thought it was going to at 45 degrees, where 152 is the nominal entry attitude.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Boy, it did come in wrong, didn't it?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Sure. See, I was waiting for that thing to come in. I didn't think it would come in until about 200 degrees.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: How come we came in so soon?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I keep wanting to yaw off the right here; It must be because we're boiling.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, all - We're standing by now - You've got Manual Attitude, three, Rate Command when you get time. That's - We're down to there, and we are going to have a CMC Go or No-Go check. We've got two things to do: either the DAP's No-Go, which we'll find out when he flies it; If the CMC is No-Go, he'll fly the EMS.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You got the 0.05g and EMS Roll, On.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, it looks like we got the evaporator.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I wish you'd keep checking my yaw for me there, will you?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I will. You're a little bit left now, or a little right - Go left, just a little bit.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I think you're slightly rolled - Roll right. Frank.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I don't care about the rolls.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay. We don't need any of that, Houston.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Roger; looks like we got it reserviced.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: And we've got a good horizon.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Looks like you are yawing to the left or something.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I've got two separate sources in here that tell me my yaw's zero don't I? Actually, I can just fly those needles, now.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: The control harmony is not too good in this. You get a lot more pitch than you do yaw and roll.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Hey there, you're yawing my way.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Look who's coming there, would you?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: At 6 minutes before, just like it says.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Are you still Min Imp, Frank?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: That's where we stop, Man Attitude, three, Rate Command.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Well, I'm going to give her to the DAP anyway when we get down.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: As soon as you see that needle starts going off the peg, huh?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes, I would, too. Better see what she does.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Make sure the BMAG's are not changed - they're not. It'll be [garble] If they are.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: We may end up losing our horizon here when that Moon goes down.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: That's probably what makes your horizon so good is the Moon background - before it rose.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I wonder if [sounds like Dimlight Dunkleman] would like me to do a little airglow photography right now?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Check - double check both balls for me, Jim, so...

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: We're not just reading one ball, okay?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes, this ball's agreeing with that one.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Check your other (RCS) ring, just for sure, Jim.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: There goes a washer; can you grab it?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes, I've been trying to get that washer...

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Now's the - how high's the voltage?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, 152 will be the entry PAD. Pitch?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay. You're about to lose your Moon.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Got a lot of lightning down there, so you - you'll probably have something.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I got the old - Bill never saw that.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Oh, did you notice? That's the haze level.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I'll look at the airglow next time.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: That's right, you've never seen the airglow. Take a look at it.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You can't get your [astronaut] pin without seeing the airglow.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I see it! I see it! [Laughter.]

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Let's see, is this where I'm supposed to ask how many g's, Lovell?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: That's right [laughter], you ask how many g's.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Now that horizon's getting harder to find.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You're within 30 degrees of - of the attitude.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Well, 152 is it, and you're coming up on it now.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: It's getting a, little hazy out here; does that mean anything - every time you fire a thruster.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: We're starting to get some reflection off the Earth, I guess.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Did anybody ever see the service module?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I'm going there now, but - Now the CMC has got us.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Did you check out the horizon?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You've got the checklist again, Bill.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: CMC in Auto; Well, you don't need Auto, but I'll put it there and make everybody happy.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I'll call 0.05 - I'll tell you when the g starts going...

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I've got to start this thing automatic - manually, if you don't give it to me, Jim.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yes. God, it is hazy out there, isn't it? That's a different lighting effect. I think.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: That's the airglow we are starting to get; that's what it is, gentlemen.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: God damn, this is going to be a real ride; hang on.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I've never seen it this bright before.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Cabin temperature is still holding real good.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: V I 's still high. Okay, we're [Program] 67.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Gemini was never like that, was it, Jim?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: No, it was a little faster than this one.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I assure you I've never seen anything like it.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Cabin temperature's holding real good - up 1 degree.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Primary evaporator's crapped out; secondary's still working.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Temperature's coming up in the primary loop okay.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Drogues at - You got then there? 8:16.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: It's a real glow. I can see our gegenschein.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: How much will this one go up, do you think?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Don't let me forget those - boost entry.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: It's almost all over but the shouting now, men.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I think he's going to take Paul Haney's job. [Laughter.]

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Don't go to boost entry yet.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Alright. Watch your altimeter, that's going to come up in a hurry here.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I'll - I'll give you warning on the steam pressure, if I can see it.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Looks like we're overshooting, according to the EMS.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Yeah, I'm getting steam pressure. Okay.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Make sure your heels are locked.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: We got a - we got a minute to drogues.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, anything on the altimeter, yet?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, we've got 15 seconds from where - from 90K [27,500 metres].

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Coming up on 40K. You should be at 40K now.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Stand by for RCS disable. Stand by on the apex cover.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: There goes the apex cover; there go the drogues.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Should be approaching 10K [3,050 metres]. Standby with the mains in 1 second.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: It should reef pretty soon. [Means unreef - the mains come out reefed, and unreef in two phases.]

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Float Bag, three, circuit breakers Closed.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: VHF antennas, recovery; VHF AM, simplex.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Beacons going On. Get your light On.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: you got your - you got it, Jim.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: You got the call - give them a call.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, standing by for the (RCS) dump.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Roger, Air Force 1. We indicate 8,000 [2,440 metres]. We can't see the chutes, but we're going down very slow.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Roger. We are now indicating 7,000 [2,130 metres].

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Ask him if he sees our beacon.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Airboss, do you see our flashing beacon?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Stand by for the dump, Frank.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, ready for the dump, Frank?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Cabin Pressure Relief valves, both, Closed.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Stand by. Stand by for Earth landing!

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Dump - purge the cabin at 3,000 feet [900 metres].

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Turn him down. Christ, we can't get anything done.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Negative; just stand by to release the mains.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Stand by for the Main Bus ties.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Well, wait; we've got 2,000 feet [600 metres], yet.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Lovell
a08_1463653-onboard.text: I don't know if we have or not. They - reporting us as lower.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Who was worried about getting hot?

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Only because I cooled you down.

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Borman
a08_1463653-onboard.text: He called it 1,000. Maybe we better get these...

a08_1463653-onboard.speaker: Anders
a08_1463653-onboard.text: Okay, Frank, you put them Close whenever you want. I'm turning the Main Bus ties Off now.

a08_1463900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1463900-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here. We continue to look good on all sources. We - in 11 minutes from now, we will be at the 400,000-foot mark and the velocity of the crew at this point will be 36,220 feet per second [11,040 m/s], we estimate. That converts to 24,530 [statute] miles per hour, which is - which is nearly, it's more than 500 miles per hour faster than the crew was moving only 2½ days ago [means 6 days] at Translunar Injection. Their burnout speed at that point 180 miles above the Earth was 35,556 feet per second [10,837 m/s] or 24,080 miles per hour. Today, as we come back to tha

a08_1463900-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463900-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Looking good; both primary and secondary loops look good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463900-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463900-pao.text: Apollo 8, through the Redstone. You're looking good; both primary and secondary loops are holding good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1463900-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control here. We've put in a call through the Redstone.

a08_1463900-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463900-pao.text: Rog. Read you loud and clear. You're looking good.

a08_1463920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463920.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Looking good; both primary and secondary loops look good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463920.text: Apollo 8, through the Redstone. You're looking good; both primary and secondary loops are holding good. [Long pause.]

a08_1463920.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1463920.text: Rog. Read you loud and clear. You're looking good.

a08_1464200-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464200-pao.text: And they were advised by Ken Mattingly that they were looking good, which they certainly are. The cabin pressure is 4.9 pounds per square inch, the cabin temperature is down a little bit, purposely, so it's down to 61. Most of the flight it ran between 77 and 78 degrees. We're estimating that the crew are still head down and tracking the horizon visually out their rendezvous - out the windows, any handy window, and letting the G&N system do its work. At 146 hours, 41 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. One minute to RRT.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1464500-pao.text: Roger.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston; 146 hours, 45 minutes. And we're very nearly at that 400,000-foot point. We just gave the crew a call and here's how it sounded: [brief communication with the spacecraft]. In the course of this blackout period, which we'll be into very shortly here, the comm control will be handed over from the Redstone to the Huntsville, and we have lost signal, our network controller says we lost signal at 146:46 minutes and with very nearly 46 seconds. And our estimate is that this blacked-out period will - will continue - oh, let's see, three minutes. And right about no

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: And our curves put the spacecraft down about 35 to 36 miles above the Earth and elevating slightly, perhaps up to 40.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1464500-pao.text: Good point, too. [Long pause.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Radio check. [Long pause.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston through Huntsville. Over.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1464500-pao.text: Houston, Huntsville. We have not established contact with the spacecraft at this time.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Roger. Thank you, Huntsville.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1464500-pao.text: Huntsville, AOS through S-band. [Pause.] Houston, Huntsville. Stand by. No contact.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Roger.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: Ken Mattingly just put in a call and just frankly labeled it a radio check. He's gotten no response as yet.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: And Ken tries a second call through the Huntsville. Our estimates say that the crew, along about now should be emerging. The Huntsville advises they have not established contact with the spacecraft at this time. About three and a half minutes since we went into the blacked-out area. And now the Huntsville is handing over communication checks - communication authority to one of the range aircraft, they call them AIRA. And the Huntsville - the Huntsville says they have acquired an S-band signal, at 51 minutes, 4 seconds; and they immediately called back and said no contact, they negate that firs

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, this is Houston through ARIA.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Unknown speaker, may be Lovell's call
a08_1464500-pao.text: [Garble.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Say again, 8. [Pause.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1464500-pao.text: Houston, Apollo 8. Over.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8. Read you broken and loud.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1464500-pao.text: Roger; this is a real fireball. It's looking good.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Outstanding! [Long pause.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: One of the recovery helicopters reported seeing something, but those kind of reports at these critical moments aren't unusual. Ken Mattingly puts in another call and there's Jim Lovell! He says, 'We're looking good.' I can't tell whether it's Borman or Lovell. Let's try to cut it in.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Borman
a08_1464500-pao.text: We're in real good shape, Houston.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Real fine. [Long pause.]

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1464500-pao.text: Now one of the range ships is reporting a radar contact. The first communication was extremely broken up, but the two words that did come through were 'looking good'. Another one of the flight controllers here in the control center heard the crew mention, something like 'a real fire ball'.

a08_1464500-pao.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464500-pao.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Yorktown has radar on you.

a08_1464515.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464515.text: Apollo 8, Houston. One minute to RRT.

a08_1464915.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1464915.text: Houston, Huntsville. We have not established contact with the spacecraft at this time.

a08_1464915.speaker: Comm tech (Huntsville)
a08_1464915.text: Huntsville, AOS through S-band. [Pause.] Houston, Huntsville. Stand by. No contact.

a08_1464915.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464915.text: Apollo 8, Apollo 8, this is Houston through ARIA.

a08_1464915.speaker: Unknown speaker, may be Lovell's call
Mattingly
a08_1464915.text: Go ahead, Apollo 8. Read you broken and loud.

a08_1464915.speaker: Borman
a08_1464915.text: Roger; this is a real fireball. It's looking good.

a08_1464915.speaker: Borman
a08_1464915.text: We're in real good shape, Houston.

a08_1464915.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464915.text: Apollo 8, Houston. Yorktown has radar on you.

a08_1464915.speaker: Mattingly
a08_1464915.text: If you get a chance, we'd like to have your DSKY readings before drogues.

a08_1464915.speaker: Lovell
a08_1464915.text: Roger. DSKY's reading plus four balls 7, plus two balls 812, minus 16522.

a08_1464915.speaker: AB1
a08_1464915.text: Roger, this is Airboss 1. You're sounding very good, very good. You have been reported on radar as, southwest of the ship about 25 [nautical] miles [46 km]. Go ahead.

a08_1464915.speaker: AB1
a08_1464915.text: This is Airboss 1. Negative. Welcome home, gentlemen, and we'll have you aboard in no time. Go ahead.

a08_1464915.speaker: R3
a08_1464915.text: This is Recovery 3. I have a flashing light, my 4 o'clock position, almost level.

a08_1464915.speaker: AB2
a08_1464915.text: Recovery 2, Airboss 2. You are cleared to dispatch for your altitude over clouds. Over.

a08_1464915.speaker: R2
a08_1464915.text: Roger this Is Recovery 2. I see the chutes, I see the light almost directly over Yorktown, level with me at 4,000 feet [1,220 metres] precisely.

a08_1464915.speaker: AB1
a08_1464915.text: Yorktown, Airboss I - received a message that he sees the chutes, sees the flashing light almost over Yorktown, descending 4,000 [garble] very, very [garble] Out.

a08_1464915.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1464915.text: All aircraft, this is Yorktown - have capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1464915.speaker: AB1
a08_1464915.text: Yorktown, this is Airboss 1. We consider recovery splashdown in your area. Take control recovery helos and vector them.

a08_1464915.speaker: R3
a08_1464915.text: This is Recovery 3. Have lost sight of visual light

a08_1464915.speaker: AB2
a08_1464915.text: Recovery 2. Roger. Passing 1,500 feet [450 metres], descending

a08_1464915.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1464915.text: This is Yorktown. Affirmative, we do have him in - capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1464915.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1464915.text: Recovery 3, Yorktown. The capsule bears 147; 5,000 yards [4.6 km]. Yorktown, over.

a08_1464915.speaker: Recovery 3
a08_1464915.text: The spacecraft is down to 1,000 [300 metres].

a08_1464915.speaker: Recovery 3
a08_1464915.text: Yorktown, Rec 3. At this time, the Command Module is in the water. Over.

a08_1465500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465500-pao.text: We estimate here we're about one minute to drogue deploy. Drogue chutes out at 23,000 feet, and the time plot says 146 hours, 54 minutes. The Yorktown is reporting and confirming a radar contact, the bearing is being passed to the recovery room, here in Houston.

a08_1465500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; at 146 hours, 55 minutes. According to our numbers we should have main chute deploy, we should have had it within the last minute. We've heard nothing but a lot of noise on the circuit for the last minute or so. It is understandable at these low level relays, everyone is passing it. And here comes something from Apollo 8: "Over" he said.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465700-pao.text: The transmission from Apollo 8, no follow up. In a simulation yesterday we had extremely good communication from the recovery area and we see - we're hopeful that that situation will be duplicated today.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465700-pao.text: 146 hours, 57 minutes; and according to our estimates, they should be hitting the water just about 147 hours even. If and when we get some intelligible comm, we'll come back up on the line. This is Apollo Control, Houston; standing by.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: AB2
a08_1465700-pao.text: Recovery 2, Airboss 2. You are cleared to dispatch for your altitude over clouds. Over.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: R2
a08_1465700-pao.text: Roger this Is Recovery 2. I see the chutes, I see the light almost directly over Yorktown, level with me at 4,000 feet [1,220 metres] precisely.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: AB1
a08_1465700-pao.text: Yorktown, Airboss I - received a message that he sees the chutes, sees the flashing light almost over Yorktown, descending 4,000 [garble] very, very [garble] Out.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465700-pao.text: All aircraft, this is Yorktown - have capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1465700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465700-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston; 146 hours, 58 minutes. Recovery II, within the last minute, has reported they have a flashing light in sight, and they followed that with, 'We have voice contact with the crew.' I repeat, they said, 'We have voice contact with the crew.' At 146 hours, 58 minutes; we're going to try to patch that conversation into our consoles here. Right now, we've not heard it.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465800-pao.text: All aircraft, this is Yorktown - have capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465800-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston; 146 hours, 58 minutes. Recovery II, within the last minute, has reported they have a flashing light in sight, and they followed that with, 'We have voice contact with the crew.' I repeat, they said, 'We have voice contact with the crew.' At 146 hours, 58 minutes; we're going to try to patch that conversation into our consoles here. Right now, we've not heard it.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465800-pao.text: The lookout - a lookout on the Yorktown now reports a visual sighting. They must be close at hand. The helicopter nearest them is piloted by Lt. Kenneth Owen of Pensacola, Florida. There are three swimmers in that helicopter. And the Flight Director has advised us to bring up a special circuit, which we hope will bring us the - any communication that develops out there.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB1
a08_1465800-pao.text: Yorktown, this is Airboss 1. We consider recovery splashdown in your area. Take control recovery helos and vector them.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465800-pao.text: : This is Yorktown. Roger, out.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: R3
a08_1465800-pao.text: This is Recovery 3. Have lost sight of visual light

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB1
a08_1465800-pao.text: [Garble]. Yorktown.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB2
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 2, 'boss 2. You're 22 out.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB2
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 2. Roger. Passing 1,500 feet [450 metres], descending

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465800-pao.text: This is Yorktown. Affirmative, we do have him in - capsule in sight. Out.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: R2
a08_1465800-pao.text: ... is Recovery 2. Passing 1,000 feet [300 metres].

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 3, Yorktown. The capsule bears 147; 5,000 yards [4.6 km]. Yorktown, over.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: R3
a08_1465800-pao.text: Roger.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Recovery 3
a08_1465800-pao.text: The spacecraft is down to 1,000 [300 metres].

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: R2 (from DSE)
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 2 is at level 1,000.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Yorktown
a08_1465800-pao.text: Re ready for code 3.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1465800-pao.text: We've - We have an estimate here now, that the splashpoint may be as close as 5,000 yards [4.6 km] from the Yorktown. I repeat, 5,000 yards from the Yorktown. That's a very rough estimate. Now, we've gotten a second estimate of 5,000 yards from the Yorktown.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB1
a08_1465800-pao.text: Roger, 2. This is [garble] 3.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: R2
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 2, descending through cherubs 5.

a08_1465800-pao.speaker: AB1
a08_1465800-pao.text: Recovery 1, this in Airboss...

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, and if you've been listening to that circuit, you can tell why we can't be too sure of these events. It's a little ragged, but I have talked to the - to our Public Affairs Officer on the carrier. He assures me the spacecraft is 5,000 yards [4.6 km] away. And the general plan was to wait [for] a little more daylight before attempting a pickup. Intermittently we have been able to pick Borman's voice out of the noise and he seems to be carrying on the routine kinds of conversations that pilots use when they talk to each other in these kinds of situations. Very unruffled an

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; 147 hours, 8 minutes. We have had several things confirmed or reverified in the last few minutes. The crew condition number 1 is okay, and that came through loud and clear, just as I was talking, crew condition okay. We have thought we monitored several conversations between the crew and local helicopters, airplanes, and what not. We do have it back now, crew condition okay. The estimate from the Yorktown is the swimmers will wait approximately 20 to 25 minutes before deploying, this as per planned that as long as the crew is in satisfactory condition and in fact

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here at 147 hours, 13 minutes. We have been advised by the recovery forces that recovery helicopter 3 is hovering over the spacecraft, 50 feet [15 metres] above it, and they estimate they are 6,000 yards [5.5 km] away from the Yorktown. The helicopter pilot is Commander Donald S. Jones of Madison, Wisconsin. When the swimmers get the signal to deploy, the first man in the water will be a Sonar Technician from Columbia, South Carolina, named Chester Coogin. Two other swimmers will follow him: Lt. J.G. Richard Flanagan of Oklahoma City, and Donald L. Schwab of Imperial Be

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here. Two new reports. The inflation bags around the spacecraft are inflated and there have been reports, additional visual reports of course, of the flashing light seen from the Yorktown. And now illuminating the area is a helicopter with a big floodlight. So the entire area should be visible from the Yorktown. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston. From the Yorktown, we have learned they're proceeding toward the spacecraft. They're now 4,500 yards away, 4,500 yards away. And that's our situation at 147 hours, 21 minutes.

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston at 147 hours, 25 minutes. Apparently Frank Borman is making small talk with the crew of that helicopter out there. It was just relayed to us that he had, in chatting with the pilot, he had asked him if anyone had seen the spacecraft on main chute. And of course, there were several reports and this has become the subject of a continuing chat, the pilot of that helicopter is Commander Donald S. Jones. And, that's all the new information we have right now. At 147 hours, 26 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston here; and Ken Mattingly, our Capsule Communicator here, has just tried to call through an ARIA aircraft. While we try to establish the communication on that shot, we've been advised that the ship is now 3,800 yards away, and it's off the port side of the ship. The Yorktown has also advised us that in about in 14 minutes, they expect to deploy their first swimmers, about 14 minutes from now. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a08_1470500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a08_1470500-pao.text: And this is Apollo Control, Houston. Ken Mattingly's call just worked and we were kind of frightened at the volume and at the level the answer came back. Borman responded enthusiastically, 'Hello, there, Houston, how are you doing?. Here's the tape.
